# Feature Ledger — every finding from 70 App Store review reports

**What this is.** One consolidated record of everything the review analysis found, built so that
any statement here resolves back to a report section and to individual review IDs. It reports the
evidence; it does not choose the product. The decisions are made on top of it, in
`PRD for App Store.md`.

**Scope.** 70 per-app reports in `App Store Reports/`, plus 2 research documents in
`Research Reports/`. Every review in every corpus was read individually in its original language —
no sampling, no keyword filtering. Apps whose corpora were too small to support claims were never
analysed, so the 70 reports here are the ones with enough evidence to carry findings.

**How it was built.** Each report was read section by section and turned into cards — one card per
distinct thing the report says, keeping the report's own words, numbers and review IDs
(7,590 cards). Cards were then attached to canonical points (281 live points,
17 merged away and kept for history). Cards are never rewritten or deleted, so
merging cannot lose a detail: 1,035 cards attached to no point at all and are reproduced in full
in Part 9.

| | |
|---|---|
| App reports | 70 |
| Research documents | 2 |
| Cards | 7,590 |
| Canonical points (live) | 281 |
| Points merged away (history kept) | 17 |
| Cards attached to a point | 6,555 |
| Cards in the nuance register (Part 9) | 1,035 |

---

## How to read this

**Apps are counted, not reviews.** Corpora differ in size by more than 100×, so two large apps must
not outvote forty small ones. Review totals appear as supporting magnitude, never as the ranking unit.

**Confidence** is computed from the ledger, not asserted:

| Level | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Certain** | ≥ 8 apps, same direction, and ≥ 2 reports label it high-priority |
| **Strong** | 4–7 apps, same direction |
| **Moderate** | 2–3 apps, **or** 1 app with exceptional magnitude (mean ≤ 1.7★ or ≥ 4.8★, lift ≥ ×4, or ≥ 50 reviews behind it) |
| **Single-source** | 1 app, ordinary magnitude — kept, and labelled research before deciding |
| **Contested** | apps genuinely disagree on free vs paid for the same capability — both sides listed with their conditions |

A point holding both `do` and `dont` cards is not a disagreement — those are the two faces of one
rule. *Contested* is reserved for the free-versus-paid axis, which is the one that changes what gets built.

**Positive and negative evidence** are counted separately, in apps. A point can be high on both
(the habit cap is praised in 40 apps and complained about in 45) — that is a signal about
the decision being contested, not a contradiction in the data.

**Every number carries its denominator.** Where a percentage appears it is the report's own, against
that report's corpus. Country claims need 50 reviews in that storefront to stand alone; below that the
report labels the evidence as limited and so does this ledger.

## Part 1 — What wins, ranked

Points ranked by the number of apps whose reviews show a **positive** reaction — praise, purchase
or explicit loyalty — attached to that point. This is the "get this right and people say so" list.
`+apps` is the count of apps with positive evidence; `−apps` is the count with negative evidence on
the same point, shown because the two together are what makes a point worth attention: a point high
on both is a live decision, a point high only on `+` is a safe bet.

125 points carry positive evidence from 3 or more apps.

<a id="part-3"></a>
## Part 3 — What drives purchases, ranked

Ranked by apps in which a reviewer's own words tie the point to a purchase — a card marked
`purchase-driver`, meaning the review says why they paid, or what they would have paid for, or what
stopped them paying. 289 cards across the corpus carry that marking. This is the closest thing
in review data to a revenue signal, and it is a different ranking from Part 1: the things people
praise and the things people pay for only partly overlap.

119 points have at least one app where a reviewer tied the point to paying.

## Part 4 — Hero features: what one app won on

Things that exist in only one or a few apps and carry outsized weight there — the feature a single
app's purchases hang on, or a finding with exceptional magnitude behind a single corpus. These do not
rank in Parts 1–3, because those rank by app count and these appear in one or two apps by definition.
They are listed separately so a narrow-but-decisive finding is not buried under a broad one.

**A. Purchase drivers marked app-specific.** The report judged the mechanism tied to that app's own
situation rather than portable — which is exactly why each one needs reading before it is copied.

**B. Narrow points with exceptional magnitude.** Canonical points standing on 1–3 apps that the
confidence rubric still rates *Moderate* because the magnitude behind them is extreme — a mean at or
below 1.7★, at or above 4.8★, a lift of ×4 or more, or 50+ reviews behind a single finding.

70 points.

| 2 | 7 | [C195](#c195) Premium pricing on a trust-based personal brand spends the brand | 16, 24 | 2 apps |
| 2 | 5 | [C232](#c232) Payment retries are bounded — daily dunning against a declined card reads as fraud to the customer and their bank | 24, 59 | 2 apps |
| 2 | 14 | [C250](#c250) Marketing e-mail needs consent and a working one-tap unsubscribe — never e-mail dormant or deleted accounts | 33, 46 | 2 apps |
| 2 | 8 | [C265](#c265) Tracker types beyond yes/no — numeric target, rolling average and project milestones — as the reason people switch from binary habit apps | 48, 76 | 2 apps |
| 2 | 8 | [C266](#c266) A generated programme escalates on observed completion, never on a fixed calendar — and never past what a health limit the user declared allows | 49, 64 | 2 apps |
| 2 | 4 | [C272](#c272) Built-in timers survive backgrounding, a call and screen lock, and always alert at the end — store the start time, compute elapsed | 53, 65 | 2 apps |
| 2 | 8 | [C273](#c273) The reward mechanic must never silently stall — a plant, pet or garden that stops growing reads as the app taking the reward away | 54, 90 | 2 apps |
| 2 | 4 | [C295](#c295) Backup and sync must run on infrastructure reachable in every storefront the app is sold in — a blocked provider makes the app's data unsafe in that market | 76, 85 | 2 apps |
| 2 | 10 | [C298](#c298) A public roadmap converts — and becomes a promise users hold you to | 79, 89 | 2 apps |
| 2 | 8 | [C308](#c308) Logging a lapse must not be the same action as destroying the count — a quit-tracker needs a way to record a slip, and non-judgemental wording around it | 90, Quit Habit Decision | 2 apps |
| 3 | 10 | [C079](#c079) Personal photos as habit icons | 2, 3, 86 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 3 | [C098](#c098) Time-unit flexibility for counters (hours → years) | 3, 48, 76 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 4 | [C100](#c100) Money-saved counter | 3, 90, Quit Habit Decision | 3 apps |
| 3 | 5 | [C102](#c102) Inverse / 'good habit' mode for a counter | 3, 86, 90 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 8 | [C136](#c136) When an item can be tracked more than one way, make the user choose the mode at creation | 6, 48, 49 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 12 | [C160](#c160) Honour what onboarding asks — a declared limitation must change the suggestions | 10, 24, 49 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 7 | [C166](#c166) Keep the therapeutic core in front of the game layer | 10, 13, 64 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 7 | [C169](#c169) Completion verification / anti-cheat | 10, 71, 85 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 6 | [C174](#c174) Multiple profiles (me, kids, pet, work) | 1, 23, 85 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 8 | [C187](#c187) No paid acquisition into an auto-converting trial in frictionless-payment markets | 13, 67, 68 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 6 | [C205](#c205) Aggregated, searchable journal / diary across days | 18, 53, 76 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 15 | [C211](#c211) No second, separately-cancelled add-on subscription | 19, 24, 88 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 9 | [C247](#c247) Never make a sibling-app bundle the only way to buy this app's own premium | 31, 36, 82 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 17 | [C263](#c263) An AI encouragement reply on each check-in as the premium hook — the first paid feature reviewers praise unprompted; its state must be visible | 47, 49, 83 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 17 | [C268](#c268) Journal / notes prompts are optional — a toggle to stop the post-completion journal prompt, and a text editor that never corrupts input | 50, 52, 82 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 9 | [C281](#c281) Brief every creator and acquisition channel to state the price — an audience told 'it's free' converts marketing spend into permanent 1★ | 64, 82, 88 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 4 | [C283](#c283) Never sell by telling the user they are deficient — an onboarding score that invents a shortfall reads as manipulation | 64, 82, 88 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 10 | [C287](#c287) Never answer a cancellation request with a retention offer — cancel first, confirm, stop billing; an offer may follow, never replace, the cancellation | 68, 82, 88 | 3 apps |
| 3 | 8 | [C293](#c293) Raising a free habit cap by a couple of slots does not buy back sentiment — the objection re-forms at the new number; change what the cap gates or when it is hit, and instrument it | 75, 86, Feature Gating vs Quantity | 3 apps |
| 3 | 8 | [C297](#c297) A free cap's acceptability is set by the bundle around it — the same number reads as generous or as a wall depending on what else is free; moving a loved feature behind the wall changes sentiment as much as changing the number | 79, 86, 89 | 3 apps |

**C. Everything rare that never became a point** is in [Part 9](#part-9) — the complete nuance
register, every card that attached to no canonical point, reproduced in full.

<a id="part-5"></a>
## Part 5 — Product rules and insights

Rules the evidence says must not be broken, and the *why* findings that explain the rest of the
ledger. These are not features — they are the constraints every feature decision sits inside.

42 points, strongest evidence first.

| apps | cards | Confidence | Point |
|---|---|---|---|
| 63 | 272 | Certain | [C002](#c002) Ratings follow the offer, not the feature set |
| 55 | 211 | Certain | [C006](#c006) Stay minimal — every addition is opt-in or off by default |
| 47 | 142 | Certain | [C218](#c218) Store listing and paywall copy stay true — disclose limits, and never advertise a feature you removed, lack, or don't integrate |
| 37 | 237 | Certain | [C001](#c001) Never move a free feature behind the paywall |
| 23 | 111 | Certain | [C186](#c186) Never revoke what earlier buyers paid for when the model changes |
| 22 | 58 | Certain | [C214](#c214) A bare checklist or task-slot paywall cannot carry a premium price — it is compared to Reminders, Notes, alarms and paper, free on every phone, and loses |
| 21 | 66 | Certain | [C157](#c157) Every guilt mechanic must be optional — streaks, repair prompts, countdowns |
| 19 | 59 | Certain | [C127](#c127) Never show ads or upsells to anyone holding an active or historical entitlement — including cross-promotion of sibling apps |
| 18 | 50 | Certain | [C236](#c236) A free-tier limit must announce itself before the user invests — at install, at setup and at the wall — never silently stop a visible progress signal |
| 15 | 42 | Certain | [C182](#c182) A pre-use hard paywall makes every purchase non-evidence-based and non-durable |
| 14 | 38 | Certain | [C240](#c240) Never interrupt the completion moment — no ad, upsell or rating prompt on the check-off tap |
| 13 | 45 | Certain | [C078](#c078) Ship the paid feature working before you sell it — the purchase trigger must never be the broken feature |
| 12 | 27 | Certain | [C264](#c264) Log-entry friction is sacred — never add a tap to the logging path; a logging redesign is the highest-risk change in the product |
| 11 | 22 | Certain | [C176](#c176) Never let fear of losing history be the reason people pay |
| 11 | 29 | Certain | [C191](#c191) Never shrink a tier someone already holds — a paid tier's limits, or free capacity a user has already filled |
| 10 | 21 | Certain | [C196](#c196) A subscription is a promise of continued delivery — back it with a visible cadence |
| 10 | 41 | Certain | [C203](#c203) Onboarding lets the user author their own routine first — suggested plans, surveys and pledges are optional |
| 9 | 61 | Certain | [C210](#c210) Bill App Store users through the App Store — never route them to an off-store subscription the app cannot show or cancel |
| 8 | 22 | Certain | [C262](#c262) Never gate a recovery action — back-dating a missed day, undoing a wrong entry and restoring history stay free forever |
| 8 | 20 | Certain | [C271](#c271) One membership at one price across every platform the app ships on — never sell the same entitlement twice or price it differently by store |
| 56 | 315 | Strong | [C003](#c003) Lead with a one-time lifetime purchase — and keep it visibly on the shelf if a subscription is ever added beside it |
| 31 | 85 | Strong | [C004](#c004) Price low and fair, anchored against subscription competitors |
| 17 | 60 | Strong | [C222](#c222) A hard habit cap is a defensible design position only with an opt-in pressure valve — the default never changes |
| 5 | 7 | Strong | [C204](#c204) Never destroy user work at the paywall |
| 5 | 15 | Strong | [C213](#c213) If you position on ADHD or executive-function help, cancellation must be the easiest flow in the product |
| 5 | 25 | Strong | [C251](#c251) If cross-platform is what people buy, ship every platform in parity — same release, same entitlement, or a visible 'coming' state |
| 4 | 16 | Strong | [C200](#c200) Never meter the completion action — a free cap may limit habits, never check-offs |
| 4 | 13 | Strong | [C296](#c296) The free tier must let the differentiator be experienced — a cap that hides the product's own thesis converts on nothing the user has felt |
| 40 | 171 | Contested | [C147](#c147) Let people use the product before they pay |
| 39 | 148 | Contested | [C133](#c133) Gate on capability, not on quantity |
| 37 | 78 | Contested | [C246](#c246) No ads in a personal habit tracker — 'no ads' is among the highest-rated topics and ads on the reward loop are the largest 1★ driver |
| 22 | 86 | Contested | [C155](#c155) Never remove a feature people bought the app for — add alongside, do not replace |
| 19 | 40 | Contested | [C185](#c185) Aesthetic and a polished onboarding convert; they do not retain |
| 3 | 7 | Moderate | [C166](#c166) Keep the therapeutic core in front of the game layer |
| 3 | 8 | Moderate | [C293](#c293) Raising a free habit cap by a couple of slots does not buy back sentiment — the objection re-forms at the new number; change what the cap gates or when it is hit, and instrument it |
| 3 | 8 | Moderate | [C297](#c297) A free cap's acceptability is set by the bundle around it — the same number reads as generous or as a wall depending on what else is free; moving a loved feature behind the wall changes sentiment as much as changing the number |
| 2 | 5 | Moderate | [C161](#c161) Values and identity screens are optional in both directions |
| 1 | 11 | Moderate | [C241](#c241) Sell entitlements as non-consumables — a consumable currency cannot be restored and has no 'paid member' state to honour |
| 1 | 10 | Moderate | [C299](#c299) Never attach an app subscription to another product's checkout by default — the subscription is its own opt-in line with its own amount, period, renewal date and final-total confirmation, and a 'book only' choice must never produce a recurring charge |
| 1 | 4 | Moderate | [C302](#c302) A premium currency must have a slow, honest earned path — a currency free players cannot earn turns free-core goodwill into 'pay-to-win' and rewards lying |
| 1 | 8 | Moderate | [C304](#c304) A discounted offer shown during or after a purchase must replace and refund the first purchase, visibly — never stack a timed second offer on a completed one |
| 1 | 2 | Moderate | [C310](#c310) A low request count for a feature the market leader already ships measures satisfaction with that implementation, not demand for the feature |

<a id="c002"></a>
### C002 — Ratings follow the offer, not the feature set

**Certain** · 63 apps · 272 cards · positive in 13 apps · negative in 52 apps

*Why Certain:* 63 apps, same direction (act on it, 90%), 48 reports label it high-priority

Trust (pricing, billing, support, delivering what was paid for) moves ratings more than features do. Report 16: the public 4.81 sat 1.21 stars above the written 3.60 — the largest gap in the set — with only 5.6% of raters writing, two-to-one about money. Report 18: the KR listing showed 4.8★ from ~25,000 ratings against a written mean of 3.824 (gap 0.98); praise for the product and condemnation of the paywall were frequently the same reviews, and more than a third of 1★ reviews (122/332) were about money rather than features. Report 20: the trust family (revoked purchase, restore failure, cancel/refund, billing mismatch, false advertising, silent support) was 810 reviews at mean 1.39 against every feature-gap theme combined at 513 reviews at mean 3.57 — trust complaints outnumbered feature complaints 1.58× and carried 2.2 stars less; the five lowest-mean themes were all integrity failures needing no new product surface. Report 23 (a one-time paid app with no offer change in eleven years): the rating decline 4.56 → 4.08 → 3.83 tracks reliability — sync 7.1×, data loss 14×, widget bugs 52× — while price objection stayed flat; when the offer is stable, ratings follow reliability. Report 24: the cleanest statement of the rule in the set — 43,469 reviews where those that mention money average 2.006 and those that do not average 4.356 (a 2.35-star gap); the 1★ and 5★ populations are talking about different things (billing vs product); the annual mean fell 2.09 stars below its 2021 peak while product-praise themes barely moved, and an earlier 2018–19 billing crisis was fixed in one month and the mean snapped back for four years. Report 25: a bimodal corpus (55% 5★, 23% 1★) where the 1★ band is 56% money and 11% the app not starting, and the 5★ band is converted power users plus prompt-driven one-liners — two populations reviewing two products. Report 26: engineering fixes moved the corpus mean 4.34 → 4.68 while payer satisfaction stayed flat at ~3.5 for five years — the paid experience is set by entitlement and trial mechanics, not by product quality. Report 27 (the free limiting case): with no offer at all, the app has no structural sources of 1★ — every 1★ ever is a reliability failure in one five-week window, and the 4★ band is a fully specified backlog from people who like the app (17 of 18 would plausibly become 5★ on one shipped item); 5★ here means 'I am grateful', not 'I have no needs'. Report 28: the offer here is an ad load — its half-year complaint rate (3.5% → 39.6% → 16.7%) and the corpus mean (4.729 → 3.810 → 4.048) move together; 2021 had zero 1★ and the launch honeymoon never returned. Report 29: the 1★ band changed composition completely — all 11 one-stars in 2024–25 were functional; 3 of 5 in 2026 were the new monetisation prompt; 'the app fixed its way out of one 1★ driver and introduced another'. Report 30: 16 of 19 one-star reviews (84%) are monetisation or billing and only 3 describe a defect — 'the app is rated down for its business model; engineering work will not move this rating, packaging will'; the organic 1★ rate rose 12.5% → 44.4% as complaints migrated from 'it's broken' (crashes gone after Jul 2025) to 'it's not worth paying for'. Report 31: every one of the fifteen worst-rated themes is money-handling, support or the app failing to run — no feature gap appears; the free cap (2.01) is far milder than purchase integrity (1.14–1.39): people tolerate a gate, they do not tolerate paying for a gate that doesn't open; the product concept is not what failed — simplicity, colour, sounds and streaks are quoted in the 1★ band as reasons the app is worth using. Report 33: the eight worst-rated themes are about leaving, being contacted, being billed or being ignored (account deletion 1.23, privacy 1.35, marketing e-mail 1.41, cannot cancel 1.62, support failure 1.70) and none is a missing feature; the free cap (2.31) and price objection (2.64) are milder — people tolerate a gate, not being trapped, spammed or charged for nothing; the praised qualities (simplicity, design, cross-platform, lifetime) are what the 1–2★ reviews say was lost. Report 34: a 4.58★ app whose 1★ band is the paywall almost alone — 28 of 37 1★ (75.7%) are monetisation friction and only 3 are reliability; 'reviewers love what the app is and push back on what it withholds'; era means drifted 4.71 → 4.40 as friction rose 8.4% → 16.4% / 14.3% with no reliability rise. Report 36: E5's rating collapse (3.722, 25.0% 1–2★) coincides with monetisation friction more than doubling (16.9% → 37.0%) while usability complaints halved (12.0% → 6.5%) and design praise fell 32.5% → 13.9% — 'the product did not get worse; the offer did'. Report 41: a 4.591★ corpus where monetisation friction (46, mean 2.80) produces 47.7% of all 1–2★ and every reliability defect together (50, mean 3.46) only 29.5%; nine of ten paywall 2★ reviewers praise the product in the same sentence — 'the rating is set at the paywall, not in the app'. Report 42: a 3.136★ written corpus (store aggregate 4.6) where monetisation friction (87, 42.23%, mean 1.85) produces 73.5% of all 1–2★ and every reliability defect together (31, mean 2.45) only 20.5% — 'fixing every bug in this app would recover roughly a fifth of its bad reviews; fixing the paywall would address three-quarters'; the written mean fell monotonically 3.96 → 2.69 as the paywall tightened and quality fell. Report 43: a ten-year corpus where the two negatives crossed over — monetisation friction 23.1% of 2020 reviews → 0.0% of 2024 and 2026, reliability 0.0% (2016) → 23.9% (2021) → 26.1% (2026); 'the product traded one problem for another; the monetisation fix was real and complete, the engineering debt that replaced it is not being paid down'; the mean moved 4.34 → 3.90 → 3.88 by era. Report 46: a 4.332★ written corpus (4.7 aggregate) where monetisation friction (373, 17.13%, mean 2.80) carries 66.4% of all 1–2★ in every era while praise almost never coexists with a low rating (15 of 250) — 'when this product loses a reviewer, it is not because they disliked the grid; it is because they were stopped by the paywall, disagreed with the price, or lost data'. Report 47: a 3.818★ corpus whose low ratings are a sequence of distinct causes — crashes (2019–21), monetisation (2024), data loss (2026) — not a slow decline; without the eight-month shock window the mean is 3.99 (n = 526); stated churn 27 (mean 1.48), 20 of them May–Dec 2024 — before 2024 churn was a reaction to one defect, in 2024 to the business model. Report 48: 72.38% of 4,402 reviews praise the product (mean 4.84) and 14.04% attack how it is sold (2.53) — those 618 supply 51.0% of all 1–2★; the 4★ band withholds the fifth star mostly over price (8.4%) and the cap (6.2%); five monetisation regimes over 11 years each produced their own complaint family; 'Nothing in this corpus suggests users dislike Strides. A large, repeated minority dislikes the deal.' Report 49: the widest written-vs-store gap in the ledger — 2.77★ from 1,232 writers vs 4.7★ from ~12,000 ratings; monetisation friction (538, 43.67%, 1.49) supplies 74.6% of all 1–2★ while only 35 reviews carry both praise and friction — 'two largely separate populations, one reviewing the funnel and one reviewing the product'; on the 901 reviews from people who used it the mean is 3.34★; the product improved sharply in 2025 yet the 1–2★ share held at ~50% because 'every improvement in this corpus happened behind the paywall'. Report 50: a 4.263★ corpus (69.3% 5★) where monetisation friction (26, 2.42) supplies 48% of the 25 1–2★ while more reviewers praise the pricing than complain (31 at 4.87 vs 26) — 'this product's pricing reputation was, until 2026, a net asset' — and 40 feature-gap reviewers average 4.38 and supply only 2 bad reviews: 'do not treat the feature backlog as a rating-recovery lever'. Report 52: a 4.25★ written corpus (4.78 public, 562,951 ratings) whose reviews turn negative almost entirely over how it makes money — monetisation friction 2,496 (12.10%, 2.98) and ads 885 (2.46) — while aesthetic praise is 3,537 (4.80) and requests come from satisfied users (4,160 at 4.38). Report 53: a 4.6-public app whose written mean fell from 3.90 (2017–19) to 2.55–2.71 (2023–26) as monetisation friction rose 14.8% → 40.1% → 45.0% of reviews; billing & trust failures (133) average 1.81. Report 55: praised for a decade as a simple, flexible tracker while the written mean fell 4.71 (2015–16) → 3.25 (2020) on crash waves, a paid sync that failed, a 2018 subscription switch and a 2020 pop-up — the complaints are not about the core. Report 56: a 4.91★ corpus with zero 1★ and zero 2★ in 199 days is selection bias, not proof of health — defect reporters average 4.50, two 5★ reviews report functional defects, and the users driven away wrote nothing. Report 57: the three lowest-rated families are all monetisation mechanics — churn 1.593, ads 2.234, paid-user trouble 2.528 — while UX praise sits at 4.753; outside Korea people complain about what the app costs, inside Korea about what it broke. Report 58: 97.80% five-star with zero 1★/2★ in 87 days — explained by removing the paywall grievance, an app too young to hit renewal, data loss or a year boundary, and founder-audience selection; 'Do not treat 4.956 as a quality measurement'. Report 64 (Critique AI): 69.93% of 419 reviews are about money (mean 1.81) while the 126 that are not average 4.41; the 1★ band is 66.7% blocked at the paywall and only 5.6% from inside — 'an acquisition problem, not a quality problem'. Report 65 (Rabit): era means 4.49 → 4.19 → 2.98 → 2.98 track monetization changes, not features; GEN_PRAISE (unqualified affection) 16.2% → 16.5% → 8.7% → 1.6%. Report 67 (Habio): era means 3.03 (free) → 1.73 (paywall) → 1.17 (web funnel) → 2.98 (seeded wave; non-seeded 1.11) → 1.59 — the positive share is the number that moves, and it depends almost entirely on the flagged reviews; billing harm stays high-priority under every exclusion. Report 68 (Ultiself): era means 3.34 → 2.42 (launch failure, tier traps) → 2.99 (web billing) → 2.23 (billing collapse) → 4.03 (five-star wave) → 3.34 (named agents) — the dips track billing mechanics and the peak tracks a review campaign. Report 75 (Habit Streak): 36 of 41 (87.80%) praise the product, including 9 of 12 money complainers and 4 of 5 1★; means 4.50 → 4.28 → 3.53 across free → 3-cap → 5-cap eras while praise themes persist unchanged — 'the rating damage in this corpus is not being caused by the product'. Report 76 (Way of Life): mean rose every era 4.51 → 4.70 while 1–2★ also rose 2.2% → 5.2% — the subscription era is carried by veterans (TENURE_LONG 20.6%) and developer praise, with the offer objection (MON_SUBSCRIPTION 4.4% of E6) underneath; 4★ reviews are 'the same praise with one missing thing' (frequency 96, price 100, free limit 81, sync 62 of 1,281). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): 5 of 6 one-star reviews are monetization and nothing else; zero 1★ report a crash or data problem; the product thesis drew zero negative reactions while the free/paid boundary drew every one-star — 'the product thesis is validated and the reliability is fine; everything that costs this app ratings happens at the free/paid boundary'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): mean 4.89 → 4.19 → 4.02 across three eras while craft praise held at 58–76% and COMP_BEST is awarded in the final review — the fall is entirely money (widget gated, subscription added, price ×2.3), broken purchases, a review prompt and a post-overhaul regression: 'Only 2 of 11 one-star reviews are about what the app charges; 6 of 11 are a promise not kept'. Report 82 (Lasting Change): the extreme case — the offer is the whole story: U:money_harm 115 (65.71%, 1.13★) vs app-quality complaints 46 (26.29%) and only 14 (8.00%) that criticise the app with no money problem; 83 reviews (47.43%) report money harm and never evaluate the product; APP_UNUSED 14 never opened the app they were billed for; ten reported outcomes against 115 reports of money harm. Report 83 (Roubit): E1 4.69★ → E4 3.52★ with praise 88.2% → 53.0% and defects 14.7% → 73.5% — the fall is reliability, not the offer: paywall friction is lower in E4 (6.0%) than E3 (14.8%) and none of PRICE_TOO_HIGH / WANT_ONE_TIME / PAYWALL_LETTERS appears in E4. Report 85 (Habitica): the offer is free and the ratings still fell — E2 3.52★ and E4 3.37★ are reliability and governance eras; 'Great idea, broken app' is the most typical low-star shape (PR_CONCEPT 285 at 3.40★, 82 at 1–2★); the rating recovers to 4.04★ in 2026 as crashes fall to 4 a year while gem-gating and request shares rise. Report 86 (Today): the offer changed twice (cap 1 → 3 → 1; one-time → subscription + $299.99) and reliability collapsed; the era means 4.16 → 3.07 track defects (12.36% → 50.85%), not the offer — 'In 2016 people left over the paywall. From 2018 they leave over reliability. That shift is the whole story of this product compressed into one table.' Report 88 (GetHabit): the extreme case — 290 of 355 one-star reviews (81.69%) describe paying before seeing the app or money taken; the product is barely evaluated (request_any 3.47%: 'requests are few because most reviewers never reached the product'); praise_any 18.37% and PRAISE_CONCEPT 15 at 1.53★ — 'the idea is liked more than the app'. Report 89 (Check Calendar): the 146 reviews without a paywall code average 4.438★ against 1.82★ for the 107 with one; the bands 'differ in kind' — paywall share 5% of five-star → 90% of one-star, specific praise 60% → 3%.

<a id="c006"></a>
### C006 — Stay minimal — every addition is opt-in or off by default

**Certain** · 55 apps · 211 cards · positive in 51 apps · negative in 20 apps · tied to a purchase in 6 apps

*Why Certain:* 55 apps, same direction (act on it, 80%), 46 reports label it high-priority

Simple/clean is table stakes and the most praised trait; 'no ads' is the best-rated topic; every feature request comes with 'don't make it complicated'. Report 20: minimalism was the most-praised attribute by a wide margin (1,111 reviews, 27.45%; 42.8% of the pre-conversion era, mean 4.25), framed against 5–20 cluttered or gamified competitors; 'no ads' ran at mean 4.86; 131 one-star reviews still praised the simplicity in the same breath as condemning the company. Report 23: simplicity is the moat — 1,780 reviews (24.48%, mean 4.58) praise it, and it measurably degrades as features are added: simplicity praise fell 32.30% → 20.80% → 18.36% of each era while UI-confusion complaints rose 0.69% → 4.93% → 5.33%; reviewers date the loss to the July 2017 expansion ('like they dipped a pickle in chocolate'). Every addition to a minimal product must be opt-in or off by default. Report 25 (both sides): 126 praise simplicity and 27 call it confusing; 65 praise configurability and others say 'so many options and no guidance that you get lost in configuration' — complexity is both the top praise and a top complaint; any simplification must be opt-in. Report 26: an aesthetics-and-calm product whose four largest themes are design (27.83%, mean 4.64), music/ambience (14.57%), simplicity (10.71%) and the garden metaphor (5.97%), stable across five years — 'A lot of apps in this area are too busy… This app is like a warm hug'; ADHD users say every other routine app 'has been deleted within a day because it's too complicated'; keep new configuration behind an advanced toggle. Report 27: simplicity is the largest theme (52, 37.68%, mean 4.90; 'cuts straight to the point, no fluff'; 'No other shinannigans'), 12 praise the absence of ads (8.70%), and the report's 'what not to do' list is: no gamification, no ads (even one interstitial), no required account, no feature removals without an opt-out, no over-building — 'does everything you need it to do with very little drama' is the product spec; one thing to watch: as refugees from feature-rich paid apps arrive, 'pleasantly minimal' starts shading into 'missing things'. Report 28 (the other side): a gamified pet-and-rooms tracker whose ad load — not its game — is 52% of the worst outcome the store measures; 'do not simplify away the gamification' is the report's first 'what not to change'. Report 29: simplicity (119, 32.51%) is framed as the absence of quizzes, upsells and bloat ('doesn't bombard you with stupid questions and a billion pop ups') and outnumbers 'too basic' 40:1 — 'the clearest do-not-fix signal'; simplicity and zero cost are the same story: 'this app is not trying to extract something from me'. Report 30: minimalism is the only attribute volunteered unprompted (23, 13.86%, mean 5.00; organic 14 — 'minimalist, no unnecessary junk'; 'Good app, minimalistic, effective'), and 'too basic' comes only from people objecting to price — add habit slots, not surface area. Report 31: simple, uncluttered, fast to log is the top praise in every era (458 rated 4–5★; 36.7% of 5★; 'The user discovers value rather than have thousands of distractions flung at him'), and also the top argument against the subscription ('a simple app shouldn't cost…', 104 simplicity mentions are 1★). Report 33: simplicity praise fell 15.9% (E1) → 6.0–7.3% as goals, timer, Health, mood, challenges, friends and AI accumulated, while 'confusing / hard to use' tripled to 5.8% of E5 ('None of the over-designed … gamification' was once the praise); the report recommends 'simple mode' defaults that hide friends, challenges and journal until enabled. Report 34: simplicity praised by 275 (37.01%, zero 1★) — 'no busy visuals, no hokey games'; 'Forget cutesy interfaces, overuse of emojis'; 'too many bells and whistles and I get decision fatigue' — named as the reason people left rivals. Report 36: simplicity 80 (14.81%, zero 1★) — 'Other habit trackers have too much other gunk like blogs or media'; a style-rejecting minority (6, mean 1.17) finds the 3D and piano soundtrack 'viel zu verspielt'. Report 41: 'add nothing' is stated every year 2021–2026 and more emphatically than any feature request — 'Please don't try to be an all in one app!'; 'No plant that grows along, no timer you never use, just habit tracking'; 'no feeling that managing the habit tracker becomes a habit in itself'. Report 42: simplicity ('nothing extra', 'no fluff', 'not over-engineered') is the one stable praise across seven years and six languages (22, mean 4.68) — the complaints are about access, reliability and two missing primitives, not about the app being too simple. Report 43: simplicity 123 (19.28%, mean 4.86), the top theme every year for ten years and in ten languages — 'you don't have to read a bunch of flowery, condescending you can do it! messages'; 'not all illustrated with pink & blue kittens and ribbons… nor is it incessantly asking me to note my feelings' — with the distinction that daily use is simple while setup is configurable ('after a couple days you will appreciate the robust settings over the bare minimum other apps give'). Report 46: simplicity 425 (19.51%, mean 4.87), the top theme and rising every era (16.40% → 21.59%) — 'I don't want to build a new habit of wasting time while tracking habits'; 'I'm really sick of apps with a million features and AI just to convolute things' (Apr 2026); 'A lot of great apps start this way, then they start adding weird features that nobody wants… pls dont do that' — and the same simplicity is the pricing liability ('Simple and overpriced'); rule 16: do not add complexity to justify the price. Report 47: simplicity 126 (21.39%, mean 4.61), the largest theme in every era including the shock; a 5★ who wanted weekly habits concluded '多機能を追加すると、今のシンプルさは壊れてしまう' ('adding features would break the simplicity'); '機能をつけまくった結果UXがボロボロです' ('they bolted on so many features that the UX is in tatters', 1★ 2024, quit) — the report's rule: do not enlarge the feature surface. Report 48: simplicity 817 (18.56%, 4.84) at 16–22% in every era for eleven years, coexisting with four tracker types — 'the most robust habit tracker without being bloated'; reviewers mean both fast to log and uncluttered to look at. Report 50: simplicity (20, 4.90) and flexibility (14, 5.00) praised simultaneously — 'the moat is that the app is both deep and uncluttered. Every roadmap decision should be tested against whether it preserves that'; 'Nothing comes close to the ease in navigation, creativity, options, and customizability'. Report 52: 'product manager, please don't add features blindly — restraint, restraint' (Aug 2026); to-dos, focus timer and AI titles are accepted but ranked below check-in speed; a crowded home screen (DES_DENSE 427, 1.4–3.9% every year) is the persistent fear. Report 53: simplicity is the largest substantive theme (DES_CLEAN 181, 10.38%, 4.66 — 'FINALLY a habit app thats not overpriced or over complicated!', 24 votes); a 21-vote cn reviewer asks the developer not to add a calendar. Report 54: simplicity 60 (16.26%, 4.50) is 'the constraint on every feature request' — 'Other apps feel overwhelming… cluttered with lists, graphs, and other features that can be anxiety producing' — anything shipped must not be visible to the 60. Report 55: DES_CLEAN 475 (23.47%, 4.89) is the largest theme in every era and every eligible storefront. Report 56: simplicity 39 of 67 (58.21%, 4.92), never below half in any period — 'knows what it wants to do and does exactly that and nothing more'; 'I lose interest in things if they're too complicated'; every request is a request to add something, so non-daily frequency must be one field defaulting to daily; do not add social, sharing or AI (zero requested). Report 57: UX praise 198 (25.42%, 4.753) in the same words for seven years (깔끔, 심플, 직관적) — 'Please don't add complexity — keep this leanness'; 'Other apps tried to do way too much'; §8.5: read the 267 requests as settings, not surface. Report 58: UX praise 58 of 91 (63.74%) defined by restraint — 'not overcrowded and overwhelming'; 'no visual noise'; 'doesn't have all the complicated tracking mechanics other apps have'; simplicity and aesthetics are separable, so cosmetic depth can ship without structural complexity; categories only as an opt-in invisible until used. Report 59 (Tappsk): PR_SIMPLE 1,704 (11.23%) — 'Ничего лишнего. Удобно' (nothing superfluous); 'the unneeded, obstructive options of the rivals are absent'; PR_KEEP_SIMPLE 49 explicitly ask the developer not to change it; the cost is NEG_LIMITED 115 (0.76%, 3.39★) who find it too basic, against NEG_BLOAT 5 — the trade is worth it at 15,176 reviews. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 11 of 45 (24.44%, mean 4.45) praise simplicity in six languages ('Sade ve kullanışlı'; 'Solo check y a seguir. Como debe ser'), including the user uninstalling over the cap ('Really clean, minimal UI… no-nonsense layout') — the moat is not in dispute even among 1★ reviewers; nothing asks for a busier main screen, the 4★ band asks for depth without complexity ('It's minimalistic I get it, but…'); design implication: every roadmap item additive-on-demand, not surfaced by default. Report 69 (TheFor): design praise 39 (48.75%, mean 4.74), 25 of them for what the app lacks — 'No bloatware, no hassle'; 'No extra junk!'; 'ничего лишнего, только то, что нужно' — 'This is a defended position, not a compliment'; P1: every new capability behind a setting or inside an existing screen — 'nothing on this list should add a tab'. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): 'The product works by subtraction: one small goal, one tap, thirty days' — PR_SIMPLE 448 (19.56%) in every era; 'At first I thought it was hard to use, with too many restrictions, but I realised they are firmly based on the maker's philosophy of how to keep going'. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): 「シンプルで使いやすい」 as a review title five times; UX_SIMPLE 36 with no 1★; competitive wins are all against apps described as 'overly complicated'. Report 75 (Habit Streak): simplicity 11 (26.83%, 4.64) stated comparatively — 'What sets apart this habit tracker app from the rest is its simplicity'; 'simple y sin ruido'; 'J'ai testé plein d'apps… (atoms, etc…) et celle ci remplit mieux mes attentes que toutes les autres'; fit 9 (21.95%, 4.89: 'So eine App hat gefehlt!'); a social request is 'lowest confidence… it cuts against the simplicity that 11 reviewers praise'. Report 76 (Way of Life, 7,764 reviews / 16 years): simplicity is the product — U_SIMPLICITY 1682 (21.66%), PR_SIMPLE 17.0–22.5% in every era; PR_KEEP_SIMPLE 64 ('Please do not change a single thing'), 61 of them in E5–E6 where TENURE_LONG is 20.6% of reviews — the request to freeze the product grows with tenure; Germany asks it 4.62× the global rate; 'Product Managers should study this app'; boomerang users come back to it after heavier apps (CHURN_RETURN 60 > U_CHURN 55); the cost is NEG_SIMPLE 43 (2.98★) who leave for a tally sheet. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): PRAISE_SIMPLICITY 14 (19.72%, 4.57★) and UX_TOO_MINIMAL 4 (5.63%, 2.25★: 'Maybe too simple'; 'This app lacks the punch'; 'beyond minimal, it feels bare') — 'minimalism is simultaneously the third-largest praise and the joint-largest non-monetary complaint'; two of the four also praise the design in the same review; the emptiness complaint never resolved across 603 days. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): PRAISE_SIMPLICITY 60 (34.88%, mean 4.98★ — the highest of any theme over 20) described by what is NOT there ('no frills, no 20 taps to log something'; 'No bloat. Just one page for all essentials'; 'no extra gamification, no ads, no BS'; 'Die App erfüllt genau ihren Zweck und nicht mehr'); U:anti_bloat 66 (38.37%, 4.98★); §8.5 do not add gamification, streak pressure, social feeds or AI — 'the product's position IS restraint'; do not rewrite the UI (68.02% craft praise). Report 82 (Lasting Change): the counter-case of a data-hungry tracker — daily long-form self-assessment ('a full blown psych ward evaluation every single day') drives APP_COMPLEX 10 and OUT_ABANDONED 5 within days; the two threads in the only pure product feedback both argue for fewer inputs. Report 84 (HabitGrid): 'simple' and 'complete' are praised together, not traded off — U:simplicity 40 (46.51%): 'Everything you need, and nothing more… no fancy or overly complicated features'; 'A laconic, simple tracker, and yet it has everything you need'; 'more simplistic, but it still has needed features, like reminders'; two US reviewers name feature bloat elsewhere as why they chose it ('too many features for my liking'); §8.8 do not add features for their own sake; the grid is named less often than simplicity (16 vs 40). Report 86 (Today): simplicity is defined negatively — 'No frills, no fuss—no need to sit through way-too-long animations and stories and celebrations every time you do something' (4★); 'a check-in app doesn't need lots of frills; this is just right' (cn); 'It doesn't give you confetti or a cookie but it helps form that path in your brain'; 'Perfect app. Don't ruin it with clutter!'; PR_SIMPLE 361 (20.22%, 4.68★); in China simplicity is valued above beauty (25.21% vs 21.25%, 简约不简单). Report 89 (Check Calendar): 'among apps with lots of unnecessary features, this one is very simple and easy to use' (jp); 'simple and not cluttered with too many options'; §8.9 no more features for their own sake — simplicity is the praise (U:simplicity 81, 32.02%). Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): minimalism is not a style here but an accessibility requirement — 'the interface doesn't trigger — important for people with addictions, where an extra detail can set you off'; PRAISE_SIMPLE_EASY 132 (21.50%, 4.91★), PRAISE_DESIGN 39, 'counter, reset and a comment to analyse a slip. Nothing else is needed'; the counter-pressure is FEATURE_THIN 12 ('just a timer: start, stop').

<a id="c218"></a>
### C218 — Store listing and paywall copy stay true — disclose limits, and never advertise a feature you removed, lack, or don't integrate

**Certain** · 47 apps · 142 cards · positive in 3 apps · negative in 38 apps

*Why Certain:* 47 apps, same direction (act on it, 90%), 16 reports label it high-priority

Report 20: the listing said 'Unlimited amount of habits. You don't need to pay a penny' for at least two years after the free tier was capped at 3; 24 reviews (mean 1.21 — the lowest of any theme) called it false advertising by name. Zero engineering cost, unmade for over two years. Report 18's screenshots advertised a timer a buyer could not find. Report 6 / 19: a buyer who paid for a feature that isn't there cancels and says 'there are free ones' — it turns a feature request into a refund cause. Report 2: sibling apps implied an integration that did not exist; the purchases it drove ended in 1★. Report 25: the App Store listing showed Apple Watch support that could not be installed. Report 26: the German store listing carried a typo — 'Eden-Gewohnheitstrinker' (habit drinker) for 'Gewohnheitstracker'. Report 28: a listing that says 'habit tracker' for a product that is a pet game produces 'it's not what it says it is' 2★ reviews. Report 29: a privacy label saying 'analytics and diagnostics' while the app asks to route third-party traffic through the user's IP — the store disclosure must cover what the app actually does. Report 30: the listing still says 'Track up to 2 habits' after the cap became 3, the advertised streak/interactive widget is not the shipped widget, and one reviewer says the IAP was not visible at the decision point — correct the listing to remove expectation-mismatch 1★. Report 23: reviewers said the task cap was not disclosed in the description and asked for refunds on that basis; the 68 'it's just a checklist' 1★ reviews are an expectation failure the listing could pre-empt. Report 30: the listing still said 2 free habits after the cap became 3. Report 31: 57 say the price was hidden or the listing implied 'free' ('needs an in-app purchases mark'; 'online ads … said it was under $10 one time'); 50 describe an intro price renewing much higher only 'in the small print' (9.99€ → 100.99€; £5.99 → £51.99, 'just hoping someone doesn't cancel'). Report 33: 'you finally mention that habits are limited … after they've created it'; 34 price-hidden / misleading 'free' reviews. Report 34: users who searched for free apps met a 2-habit wall — 'only to find out AFTER downloading the app that there is a fee'; 'I just wish it was said earlier (for example, here)'. Report 36: a store screenshot showing a habit named 'Run 15 minutes' made a buyer expect a built-in timer (2★). Report 41: Spanish and Portuguese are on the listing while reviewers in ES / CL / BR report them missing (2024–2026). Report 42: the listing names 36 languages including Hebrew and Ukrainian which the app does not deliver — 'They present it as if it's in Hebrew. In practice there's no option for a Hebrew interface' (IL, 1★); 'Preview on AppStore was on Ukrainian, I don't like that it's on russian' (three of Ukraine's eight reviews) — a factual misstatement, not a backlog item; a 'goal for the day' advertised and absent. Report 43: 'Not a free app. The whole app is an in app purchase'; 'Bait and switch. After 3 they make you pay' — 14 of 16 such reviews US, none after Oct 2021. Report 46: 'Every picture shows a bunch of colorful habit trackers, not a one shows what the free version looks like' — a screenshot of the actual 3-habit free view is the fix. Report 47: the Japanese listing (12 Sep 2026) says the free version offers 'unlimited task registration' while reviewers from Dec 2024 to Mar 2026 report a free cap of 6 ('6 habitudes gratuites'); two say the paid nature was not disclosed — state the cap and trial length on the listing and at the paywall. Report 48: the listing states 3 free trackers while reviewers report 10 / 8 / 7 / 6 / 5 / 4 / 3 / 2 / 1 across eras; 48 hit an undisclosed wall after setup (1.65★) — disclose the limit on the listing and at first run. Report 49: 'Free with In-App Purchases' and an ad saying 'get your free life reset plan today' front a product with no free use — advertised as free 37 (1.08), tripling after the trial launched. Report 50: search summaries of the listing state a 5-habit free cap, 1 reminder per habit and 3 journal notes per day while five 2026 reviewers in four storefronts get 3 habits and nobody mentions the other caps — 'Either way this is a disclosure problem'. Report 53: the listing claimed Family Sharing that in-app purchases don't support (M5: remove it). Report 54: three reviewer-reported listing-versus-product disagreements — 'Advanced Statistics' that is a calendar, a €2.50 subscription on the listing the app did not sell (a reader who 'would book that immediately'), and a listing that said 5 free habits when the app gave 3. Report 56: a store preview shows a widget-transparency setting the user cannot find in the app. Report 57: 'I bought Premium and nothing differs from before — I can't use the features shown in the screenshots'; Family Sharing advertised but not delivered. Report 59 (Tappsk): MON_DISCLOSURE 80 (1.95★) and MON_PAYWALL_SURPRISE 64 (1.70★) — 'Пишите сразу, что ПО платное, а не встроенные покупки' (say up front that the software is paid, not 'in-app purchases'); 50 + 44 of the 674 1★; the listing does not state the caps and the report's experiment is to state them. Report 60 (Mindway): M_MISLEADING_ADVERT 5 (all 1★: 'Click bait'; 'Not set up as advertised'; 'is it free? No. So Change to paid.'; 'it said it was free') and both ad-sourced reviewers at 1★ — F4: state the subscription price and the free-tier limit in the App Store listing and in the first ad frame, which 'removes the click bait / it said it was free class of review entirely'. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): a Health integration a reviewer believed was advertised does not work — 'either make it work, or remove the claim'. Report 67 (Habio): the listing claims App Store billing, 'optional subscription', 'designed in collaboration with mental health professionals' and sharing with friends, while reviewers describe off-store billing, a hard paywall ('Optional subscription was a lie') and no sharing; an old pinned 'it has a free version' review misled later installers. Report 69 (TheFor): the subtitle leads with 'Journal' while the listing body never mentions journaling and one reviewer uses it — P4: make it visible or stop leading with it; 'Unlimited Habit Creation' is a listing promise the corpus confirms is kept. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): a listing that lists every feature and never the time limit — 'This is the gap the corpus is complaining about, and it is verifiable from outside the corpus'; the listing also claims cross-device and cross-OS restore while 7 say sync does not work and 2 paying users could not move the purchase. Report 75 (Habit Streak): the description says 'Subscription options are: 1 month and 1 year with 7 days of free trial' while the IAP table sells a 'Premium Lifetime $79.99' — 'One of the two is wrong'; the cap the corpus complains about most appears on neither surface. Report 76 (Way of Life): the listing still marks 'backup to cloud' as premium while 4.3.0 release notes say it is free for all; declared languages omit Kazakh and Galician that reviewers asked for; the listing cites Tim Ferriss / Kevin Rose and reviewers name the same source — the listing's press citations are corroborated by the corpus. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the description states the concept well ('The first habit tracker without streaks') but never states the one-habit limit, names no price / tier / trial / one-time option, and omits widgets, Apple Health, the calendar, badges, the Habit Forest and iCloud — six capabilities reviewers discuss, two of which (widgets, Health) generated complaints from users who did not know what tier they were in; §8.1.4 name the features. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the description runs five headed sections and contains no monetization paragraph whatsoever — no free-tier limit, no Plus, no subscription, no price; §8.1.2 four sentences would close it: what the free tier includes, that the board limit is three, what Plus adds, and that both a subscription and a one-time option exist — 'the cheapest high-value change in the report'. Report 82 (Lasting Change): the listing states four checkable falsehoods — a payment rail it does not use ('charged to your App Store account' while hasInAppPurchases is false), a cancel path that does not exist ('manage or cancel anytime in account settings' vs 27 CANCEL_NO_PATH), a pricing heading with no prices, and a support address at a non-existent domain; it never mentions the book that 43 reviewers actually bought; §8.1 repair the listing is 'the cheapest item… with the most direct evidence'. Report 84 (HabitGrid): the listing understates the product — Languages: English only while 1.0.9 'Added languages', 62.79% of reviews are non-English and a Vietnamese UI is in use; 'No servers. No cloud.' contradicts the analytics label; the website's opt-in cloud backup is absent from the listing; §8.1 four text fixes, none a product change. Report 86 (Today): the listing says 'Quit bad habits and stay on track' and the feature does not exist — REQ_BREAKBAD 15 (2016 → 2026), USE_QUIT 16 trying anyway; 'the description talks about losing bad habits: we need an explanation. In what way does this app concern itself with our bad habits?' (fr 4★); §8.7 'advertising a capability, collecting users who need it, and having them discover the gap after purchase' is not defensible — build a 'maximum N per period' type (Done and HabitBull named as having it) or remove the promise. Report 88 (GetHabit): the listing said 'free' while the app could not be used without paying (PAY_FREE_LABEL_MISLEADING 33, 1.06★); the description today still says 'Our app is free to use' and lists $4.99 / $9.99 / $19.99 while the IAP list shows $7.99–$39.99; two reviewers said in-app prices were double the listing's; QUALITY_SPELLING 12 ('Makr a list of short term goals'). Report 89 (Check Calendar): the description lists widgets, notifications, backup 'even across different devices' and 'No login required' and says nothing about a trial, Premium or a price — in the 2026 capture and the archived 2024 and 2025 captures — while the app stops after 4–30 days; the developer apologised twice for the confusion and the listing text did not change. Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): the listing says Free with in-app purchases and 'works offline'; a Turkish reviewer read it as 'tamamen ücretsiz' (completely free), was charged and asked for a refund (2023); the store language field says English only while the description claims 70+ languages; and 'works offline' sat beside an ad banner that crashed the app whenever the network was on. Research: Feature Gating vs Quantity.md — quantity gating in adjacent apps is widespread and often silent: TickTick gives unlimited tasks and boards but limits the habit module, Trello allows unlimited cards but 10 boards, Todoist advertises 'unlimited tasks' against an undisclosed 300-task-per-project limit found only through user reports.

<a id="c001"></a>
### C001 — Never move a free feature behind the paywall

**Certain** · 37 apps · 237 cards · positive in 15 apps · negative in 30 apps · tied to a purchase in 6 apps

*Why Certain:* 37 apps, same direction (act on it, 87%), 23 reports label it high-priority

Every paywall regression produced a lasting rating drop; pick the free tier once and hold it. Report 8: a competitor adding a paywall sent its users to a free rival, and free users explicitly warn against gating what is free. Report 10: soundscapes, longer timers, the event micropet and the anxiety breathing exercise all moved from free to paid; paywall-creep is the largest monetization theme (715). Report 11: an app whose third-largest praise theme was 'it's free' ('all functions are free', Dec 2025) retrofitted a paywall by Apr 2026 with no disclosure; five years without a sub-4★ review ended in three 1–2★ reviews in nine days. Report 18: five years of moving existing capability behind Pro — highlighter (May 2023), to-do list (Nov 2023), trackers and statistics (2024–25), free routines 15→8 and short memos →5/week (Dec 2023–Jan 2024), earned friend-invite routines revoked — each produced a rating trough, and dozens of reviewers in three languages stated the rule themselves: 'take back what you gave and people resent it… it may work short-term but long-term I doubt it.' Report 27 (an entirely free app): 'free with no in-app purchases' is the largest theme (47, 34.06%, mean 4.89) and the stated reason users arrived — 13 fled competitors' paywalls, 4 plead 'keep it free', 3 praise unlimited habits, and one is watching ('No ads (yet, but I don't think there are any)'); the report ranks a retroactive gate on existing functionality as the highest-risk action available, and says any future paid capability must attach only to something that does not exist today. Report 29 (free limiting case, second corpus): 'it is actually free' is 46.99% of reviews (mean 4.83 vs 4.31), consistent at 42–69% across every top-five market and every income band; 'no subscription' is the highest-rated sub-theme in the report (44, mean 4.98); four 5★ reviewers publicly condition their loyalty on staying free ('as long as this continues I'm gonna use this app every day'; 'never change'); the report ranks never capping habit count and never adding a subscription among what not to change. Report 31: over ten years one listing moved a £2.99 one-time Pro (2016) → $19.99/yr (31 Aug 2020) → $39.99/yr → bundle-only $59.99–$99.99/yr → a $19.99 'lifetime' against $399–CA$499.99 anchors → ~$60/yr annual only; Touch ID was moved behind the paywall in 2019; the effective entry price rose ~15× in recurring terms and mean rating fell 3.94 → 2.75 in the step that coincided with the subscription switch and ownership change (−1.19). Report 33: the gate tightened in steps — one-time Premium replaced by subscription (17 Jan 2019; price objection 9.4% of 2019, subscription objection 29 in 2019; a buyer two days earlier got one year), notes (with 300 days of history), skip, multiple reminders, dark mode and history beyond 30 days moved to Premium (Apr 2019), a 15-per-week check-in cap (Oct 2020), and the free tier cut to 2 habits (2025–26, cap 9.3% of 2026, 'slowly chipping away at the most basic features') — the spikes in 1★ follow each take-back rather than the cap; 18 reviewers defend the cap and 48 call the free tier sufficient. Report 34: in E5 the objection moved from the habit count to everyday features behind the wall — 'other gated feature' rose to 3.2% of E5 while cap complaints fell 9.7% → 7.1%; widgets, notes, colours and backup behind the paywall average 1.55★ (72.7% 1★), worse than the cap itself (2.44). Report 36: the same retraction was run twice — widgets moved behind the paywall ~4 Oct 2023 (three 1★ from us / eg / in inside 36 hours: 'Tap to Unlock … I am deleting the widget and the app'; 2023 H2 mean 3.56) and unlimited free habits capped at 2 (Dec 2025) then 1 (Mar 2026) — CAP 30 (mean 2.30, 26.9% of E5), REGRESS 19 (mean 1.95, zero 5★): 'Never expect rewards for loyalty … 3 years and all my history is on there'; 'Bait and switch'. 2026 mean 3.636 with 27.3% 1–2★ vs 2024 4.312 / 9.9%, while usability complaints were at their lowest; the report's policy: if a tier must change, change it for new users only. Report 41 (counter-case: a gate that never moved): the 3-habit cap has stayed at 3 since 2020 and is still the only negative worse now than at launch (0.0% → 6.4% in 2025 → 4.2%) as category norms, features and price moved around it. Report 42: three long-tenured users describe free features becoming paid on update — 'I've used the app a long time, until today's subscription screen appeared… forcing subscription, disabling buttons… I and those around me will stop using it and stop recommending it' (TR, 1★); 'An app I used to love… but everything has become paid'; 'after the update, only useful in the paid version' — and the paywall complaint rose 7.7% (2020) → 35.4% (2024) → 57.1% (2026). Report 43 (the positive case): the free tier was loosened around 2021–22 and the cap complaint went 14.1% (2021) → 0.0% (2024, 2026) while 'deceptive free' stopped entirely after Oct 2021 — the reference case for what lifting a gate does. Report 46: dark mode was paywalled in 2020 and again in June 2024 ('New update moved dark mode behind a paywall. Immediate deletion'); the report's rule 19 — do not gate further existing capabilities, each episode produced immediate 1–2★. Report 47: the case study — in May 2024 a free, unlimited tracker with banners added a video ad per check-in, put back-dating behind a video and capped new habits; the following eight months (63 reviews) averaged 2.38 with 61.9% at 1–2★ against 14.9–17.8% in every other era, four themes exist only after the update (ad overload 24 at mean 1.46, 改悪 / free became paid 23 at 1.39, backfill gated 9, habit cap 7), 20 reviewers said they were leaving and 11 of the corpus's 23 self-described two-year-plus users wrote in that window ('改悪前は☆4-5くらいの日常使いでしたが、改悪後は☆1です'; '4年くらい使ってましたが、製作者の方が金儲け主義に走り'; 'ERA DE GRAÇA AGORA É PAGO'). Rolling the videos back to banners by December 2024 ended the complaint completely (0 ad complaints in 146 reviews Jan 2025 – Aug 2026; mean back to 4.02). Report 48: the Strides story is the cap variant — a free tier of ~10 trackers (Oct 2015) tightened to 7 (mid-2018) and 3 (2020 on): 'free cap too low' rose 0.00% → 0.32% → 1.59% → 7.00% → 9.87% of E5 and 12.1% of the last 24 months, the only negative theme still growing, while 'free is enough' fell 7.82% → 4.81% — 'as the free tier shrank, satisfaction with it fell and complaints about it rose, roughly in proportion'; 17 reviews record a feature removed from free (mean 2.82). Report 49: no free tier at any point in 29 months — the free product is the questionnaire, the 'analysis' and the paywall; hard paywall is the largest theme (256, 20.78%, mean 1.31) and a 331-review 'never used it' cohort (26.87%, 1.23) reviews only the funnel. Report 50: the free cap was cut 5 → 3 between 26 Jan and 17 May 2026 (nine reviewers state 5 at mean 3.78, five state 3 at 2.20, zero overlap); monetisation friction rose 3.1% → 35.3% of reviews across six half-years and August 2026 (9 reviews, 2.89) is the worst month; a Turkish-storefront reviewer had unlimited habits 'only for the first few days' then was told to 'buy a subscription or keep only three habits' and locked out of her own statistics. Report 52: year statistics moved from free to VIP at year-end December 2025 (PAY_WALL 12 and PAY_REGRESS in one month, 15 reviews since Nov 2025); the monetisation history is 'a sequence of re-scopings of what was already owned' (one-time → tiers → subscription 2020; free themes → paid → free; free year stats → VIP; ad-free for all → ¥8) and each re-scoping produced its own complaint wave; the money-grab theme (183, mean 1.36, 86.3% 1★) is triggered 'almost always [by] a re-scoping or an unexpected charge, rarely the price level itself'. Report 53: once over the 3-habit free limit, editing an existing habit's settings hits the paywall. Report 54: reviewers report the free cap moving 5 (early 2020) → 3 (late 2020) and one existing user's 'three habits got cut down to two' (CN, 2★). Report 55: 'The makers take the free user seriously too' (2018) described the product the July 2020 every-launch pop-up replaced. Report 56: in a fully free app, 9 of 67 name a competitor's paywall as the reason they left it and 35 (52.24%) restate the free promise — 'paywalling existing free capability attacks the documented acquisition path'; the appeal is flat between high-spend and other markets (47.1% vs 43.8%), so it cannot be paywalled in rich storefronts either. Report 57: the free tier was tightened silently and repeatedly — 'At first unlimited habits were free but now only three are for free?'; multiple daily check-ins became Premium ('did daily check-in suddenly become a paid feature? There was no announcement'); a daily-goal interval removed for a years-long user; free data retention cut to 30 days — monetization_model_change_complaint 10 (mean 1.700, the lowest with n ≥ 5), 8× over-indexed in 2★ reviews from the oldest users; monetisation friction rose 5.18% → 10.56% → 23.47% of reviews across eras as the mean fell 4.38 (2022) → 3.30 (2026). Report 58: a fully free, uncapped launch app whose largest theme family is praise for not charging (52 of 91, 57.14%) — the report's reading is that a future habit cap is 'the single worst monetization lever available' because 15 reviewers name a cap or paywall as what they fled. Report 59 (Tappsk): free habits were removed for some users in the 2021-01 cut and the 20-task cap was later lifted again — reviewers name 2, 3, 5, 10, 20 and 50 as the free cap in different months, and the report could not establish the cap at any date; a moving boundary is itself a grievance (MON_DISCLOSURE 80). Report 65 (Rabit): premium launched in Nov 2020 by taking a capability that already existed (marking the previous day); in 2023 the to-do list and backup moved behind the paywall; PAY_REGRESS 21 (4.22%, mean 1.48): 'Antes o Rabit não tinha anúncios, e dava para colocar vários hábitos… Eu adorava esse app'. Report 69 (TheFor): stats, day history and back-fill reportedly moved behind a subscription in late 2024 — 'You prided yourself on offering a great app with absolutely no payment or prices for subscription for stats … Now you're just like everything else' (a multi-year user, 2★); not corroborated by later reviews, whose free-tier praise rose to 40.0%. Report 76 (Way of Life): MON_FREE_CUT 2 ('free version reduced', 2011 and 2016) — rare here; the free tier held at three items for 16 years. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the home-screen widget — praised in 27 reviews at a perfect 5.00★ — was free until ~mid-2025 ('free for widgets and 3 habits without limitations'; 'Widget without premium(powerpack)') and then gated: 'Useless if you dont pay, can[t] even put a single widget!!' (1★); paywall-shape complaints 0 of 110 before, 6 after; §8.8 #3 put the widget back in the free tier or replace it with an equally visible free surface. Report 84 (HabitGrid): the pre-emptive form of the rule — a free app whose terms reserve the right to 'charge for their services at any time'; two reviewers make continued use conditional on it staying free ('I really hope it stays free, otherwise I will have to find a different habit tracker'; 'I hope it won't become a subscription, or at least that there will be an option to buy it once!'); §8.4 'charge for new capability, never for the free core' — do not cap habits, move widgets or statistics behind payment, or add ads; test an optional one-time purchase or tip for unshipped extras (watch, cloud backup, advanced frequency), announced in advance; 'the baseline is zero'. Report 89 (Check Calendar): dark mode moved behind payment in 2022 ('previous free features into paid ones', 1★), then in 2024 the whole core tick moved behind a trial — PAY_FEATURE_REVERSAL 7.

<a id="c186"></a>
### C186 — Never revoke what earlier buyers paid for when the model changes

**Certain** · 23 apps · 111 cards · positive in 3 apps · negative in 22 apps · tied to a purchase in 2 apps

*Why Certain:* 23 apps, same direction (act on it, 88%), 9 reports label it high-priority

Report 13: in Aug 2017 a $3.99 one-time purchase became a subscription, unannounced in the release notes, and prior buyers were downgraded to free ('my purchase was worthless'); the mean fell 1.79 stars in nine months and no month since has been above 4.0. Subscriptions later silently expired after updates. Grandfather, always. Report 17: an abandoned one-time-purchase app relaunched as a subscription with no grandfathering, no discount and the old app left broken split one loyal base into delighted returners (4.46) and betrayed buyers (1.17); the reviewer listed the three remedies himself — grandfather, discount, or leave the old app working — none was done. Report 20: the cleanest natural experiment in the set — on 27 Jan 2021 a pay-what-you-want one-time purchase became a $39.99/year subscription, every prior buyer's entitlement was revoked and the free tier capped at 3; daily review volume went 2 → 61 → 135 at means of 1.15–1.36, 615 reviews (15.19%) describe losing a purchase, and the mean never recovered in five years (4.56 before, 1.62 after). The Feb 2021 patch was three weeks late, offered one free year instead of permanent restoration, was never announced and did not hold — revocation reports recur to Jan 2026. 'I bought your app precisely because it wasn't a subscription.' Report 23 (receiving side): an entire cohort arrived at a one-time-purchase competitor after another app revoked already-purchased premium features. Report 26: the late-2022 move from a $5–7 / €6.99 one-time unlock to $25 lifetime / $19.99 yr / $4.99 mo withdrew the unlock earlier buyers had paid for — 'the premium version I bought was taken away from me… I consider that a breach of contract' (7 in Sept–Oct 2022, recurring in 2024–25); losing what they bought is the top paid-user complaint (16.7% of explicit payers). Report 31: 189 legacy one-time / lifetime buyers (mean 1.38) found their purchase shown as 'Done Basic' after an update, reinstall or new phone, beginning at the Dec 2020 ownership change and spiking Apr 2023 — support 'told me they wouldn't honour my previous purchase', offered a free trial, or removed 'grandfathered access'; one wrote the top 'Done app review' article and then a 1★; validate receipts for every historical SKU and grandfather them automatically — worth more than any feature. Report 33: a lifetime purchase is a bet on continuity — hostile lifetime reviews are about removals, not price ('I paid for the lifetime subscription because the old app was exactly what I wanted. It never occurred to me that they would update it and actually remove things … I wish I had got the monthly subscription so I could cancel'); the 2019 switch converted a £9.99 buyer from two days earlier to one year; a lifetime model obliges the developer to migrate, not delete. Report 34: lifetime holders' only negatives are continuity — the one-time option gone after an update (Nov 2025) and a lifetime licence that 'wont be working anymore' (Jun 2026, 'False claim', 2★); 'a lifetime model obliges the developer to honour and migrate, not withdraw'. Report 42: retroactive paywalling of an installed base — 'forcing subscription, disabling buttons'; 'everything has become paid'. Report 43: a Chinese payer had to re-buy after a system reinstall (1★); 'How do I restore purchase' (1★). Report 46 (fear of it): 'Among apps that charge ¥30 for lifetime, this one wants ¥328 — I really don't dare buy it, in case it disappears'; five Chinese reviews hesitate for fear the app will 跑路. Report 48: the corpus's defining event — a paid app converted on 19 Jan 2015 to a $4.99/month subscription with a mandatory account; nine months at 2.21★ with 68.2% 1–2★ (February 1.66★, 83.9%), 92 'broken bargain' reviews (paid-then-subscription 60, forced account 25, grandfather promise broken 14 — 'Rent what you've paid for'); reversed in October 2015 (free unlimited tier) and the mean jumped to 4.62 — 'The recovery is as clear as the crash'; the theme is extinct after 2016 but still 10.7% of all one-stars. Report 52: in 2020 buyers were told their lifetime purchase is now annual; PAY_REGRESS 75 at 2.15; M1: grandfather every past entitlement explicitly ('you bought X in 2019; you keep X') — 'Honouring old purchases costs almost nothing and is the single strongest trust signal in these reviews'. Report 53: one-time buyers were pushed into a subscription — 'the VIP I bought outright has turned into a subscription? Charging twice is unreasonable' (cn, 2023); 'I had previously PAID to have full access… now they're forcing a yearly subscription' (ca, 2025); 10 in Feb–May 2026 under a new 'AppLife' plan ('all of a sudden I can't use the additional habits I created… without purchasing a $14.99 upgrade'); PAY_REGRESS 16, mean 1.50, payer lift 5.53. Report 55: 'I specifically paid for the app because it was a one-off rather than subscription, so I actually feel I should now get my money back'; 'they offered life time… the people who bought the lifetime pass are no more able to use it' (PAY_REGRESS 9, 1.33, lift 12.27). Report 57: 'I paid for the premium and now it asks for subscription??! DO NOT BUY IT' (HK, 1★, Jul 2026) — §8.2: an explicit, published grandfathering policy; 'One public DO NOT BUY IT on the storefront costs more than the subscription it was protesting'. Report 59 (Tappsk): lifetime buyers are the ones asked to pay again — BUG_PURCHASE 45 and MON_PAID_TWICE 28 of the 430 lifetime reviews; 57 lifetime reviews are 1–2★; the 2021-01 update is the largest cluster and the rest spread to 2026: 'Покупала версию «Навсегда», спустя год написали, что пора опять оплатить «навсегда» ещё раз' (bought Forever; a year later told it was time to pay forever again); 'Купила навсегда, а получается не навсегда'. Report 76 (Way of Life): the 2023 subscription switch — lifetime buyers from 2015 told they no longer have premium (1★, de/kz/cn), restore failures up to 1.55% of E6, 15 of 181 corpus 1★; grandfathering existed ('grandfathered into the new system', 5★) but was unreliable; §8.1 restore for any old App Store receipt on any device without a subscription prompt. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): 'Lifetime purchase doesn't work. Restore purchases doesn't work. Developer doesn't respond' (1★, 2026-01-01) — consistent with a migration failure when subscription SKUs arrived, though one review is not a mechanism; whether one-time buyers were grandfathered is an open research question (§8.7). Report 86 (Today): 'I bought the one-time version from before the subscription started' — now unable to manage habits at all (jp 1★, 2026); a one-time buyer's covers removed when photos went premium (MON_REGRESS 3). Report 89 (Check Calendar): a freemium tier (two calendars free, ads, dark mode paid) replaced by a trial wall in January 2024 caught users who had chosen the app on the earlier terms — PAY_FEATURE_REVERSAL 7 (2.77%), 'previous free features into paid ones'; the two-calendar-limit complaint disappears after 2024-01-20, 'consistent with the free tier being replaced by the trial'.
