<a id="c214"></a>
### C214 — A bare checklist or task-slot paywall cannot carry a premium price — it is compared to Reminders, Notes, alarms and paper, free on every phone, and loses

**Certain** · 22 apps · 58 cards · positive in 5 apps · negative in 19 apps · tied to a purchase in 4 apps

*Why Certain:* 22 apps, same direction (act on it, 76%), 12 reports label it high-priority

Report 19: 13 of 105 (12.38%) said the phone's alarm, Notes, calendar, paper or Excel did the same job for free ('If you can set an alarm on your phone you don't need this app'); at $45–$99 that ceiling read as theft rather than expense and produced 96 one-star reviews. A product charging above a few dollars must deliver what a checklist structurally cannot — real personalisation, coaching content, human accountability, or data the user could not assemble. Report 23: 68 one-star reviews (0.94%) make the coherent case 'this is a checklist, iOS Reminders does it free, and it cost me money' — a positioning failure: the listing sold a to-do list rather than streak psychology plus HealthKit automation; Apple Reminders is the low-end competitor (9 mentions, mean 3.67). Report 25: among people who hit the paywall the comparison set is Apple Reminders, Health, Notes and a paper notebook (nine reviews explicitly) — a free tier must beat Reminders, not beat Streaks; ~7 reviewers would rather the app were honestly paid up front than 'fake-free'. Report 27 (the other side): a free, minimal, account-less tracker wins the category comparison outright — 13 reviewers explicitly rejected rivals over price ('Don't get streaks for $6. 👎 Get this!'; 'way better than those paid apps'), and switched-from-competitor rose 0% → 16.7% across eras without the app changing; as the category monetises harder, the free position sharpens by market drift. Report 29: 52 comparison shoppers (14.21%) arrived after rejecting paywalled trackers ('downloaded 20 habit tracking apps and none was satisfactory'; 'premium this, subscription that… here it's just free, like properly FREE') — the app 'wins a bake-off it never enters', so competitors' pricing drives its installs. Report 30: every reviewer calling the app 'too basic' also objects to paying — 'a value complaint wearing a feature costume'; do not add features in response. Report 31: 'How is this app worth $499.99?'; '$90/pY for what?' — simplicity is quoted both as the reason to use the app and the reason a subscription is unjustified. Report 60 (Mindway): the same verdict from buyers — 10 (4.63%, mean 1.50), five of them confirmed payers, say the paid product is 'nothing more than preloaded to-do lists'; 'just a suggestion list'; 'basically just a load of lists and reminders'; 'I cannot believe I spent $40 to use this app for one day' — and six non-buyers price it against Reminders, Notes, Calendar and paper ([[C277]]). (Consolidation after report 60: C277 was created by the report 60 merge and folded in here the same pass — the report's D2 'sell the outcome, not the task slots' is the constructive half of this rule.) [Merged from C277: Report 60 (Mindway, 216 reviews): price objections are relative, not absolute — 13 reviewers (6.02%, mean 1.69, no 4★ or 5★ among them) reject the price by comparing it to a substitute they already own, and 6 (2.78%) name it: Apple Reminders, Notes, Calendar, a paper planner — '8€/WOCHE für einen Tagesplaner, den man sich auch selbst im Kalender bauen kann. Frech.' (€8 a week for a day planner you could build in your calendar. Cheeky.); 'einfach zu teuer dafür dass ich das auch gratis in meinen Notizen machen kann'; 'paper planner is cheaper than this LOL'; 'Just use your remind app it's the same thing'. The report's reading: 'the competitive set Mindway is being priced against is not other habit apps — it is the free tools already on the phone', and a count-based paywall ('you have used your 2 free tasks') invites exactly that comparison because task slots are what those tools give away, whereas guided routines, progress history and a self-care library are not comparable to Reminders — 'the corpus shows Mindway losing a fight it chose' (D2: sell the outcome, not the task slots). Related: [[C214]] (a bare checklist cannot carry a premium price), [[C133]] (gate on capability, not quantity), [[C004]] (price against subscription competitors).] Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 'Asked for a payment in simple app like this' (MN, 1★) — an objection to paying for simplicity, the flip side of the app's own positioning; one of only two flat price objections in 45 reviews. Report 64 (Critique AI): 'I don't think any one is gonna pay 40$ just to check off a list'; 'I lost 40 dollars on something I could've just done on the notes app'. Report 68 (Ultiself): NEG_SIMPLE 97 (2.15%, mean 1.40) 'just a manual checklist' — thin union 137 (3.04%), 32 of them also objecting to price; lift 4.15× among purchasers. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): 'Excel would do this' — PAY_FEATURES_THIN 4 (1.75), three of four written while angry about the trial. Report 76 (Way of Life): 'Ich kann das gleiche auch mit einer einfachen Strichliste machen' (I can do the same with a simple tally sheet, 2★; NEG_SIMPLE 43 at 2.98★, NEG_POINTLESS 15 at 2.53★) — the tally-sheet comparison is the ceiling on a $4.99 unlock for a minority. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): 'nothing special.. just wastage of funds' (pk 1★, spend implied) — the too-minimal reading at the paywall. Report 82 (Lasting Change): APP_SHALLOW 13 and APP_NO_VALUE_FOR_PRICE 14 at ~$30.99/month — the recurring comparison is paper: 'Nothing you couldn't do yourself with a piece of paper and pen'; 'You can use a paper checklist for the same results'; 'the to-do lists I make on my notes are better than this app'; 'the app itself is well designed, but it's basically a glorified tracker and not at all worth the monthly cost' (2★). Report 84 (HabitGrid): the counter-case from the free side — 'Why anyone would be pay a monthly sub for an app like habitkit, which offers no benefit over this app, I haven't a clue' (5★); a developer 'sat down to write a similar app because the alternatives have paid subscriptions… I downloaded it and immediately closed Xcode' — a free, uncapped, ad-free grid tracker is the reference point the category's subscriptions are now compared against. Report 88 (GetHabit): U:value_content 105 (21.43%, 1.33★) — 'There are like 5 challenges and they are laughable'; 'the cleaning list is like Day 1 do the dishes, day 2 make the bed'; 'just 5 articles'; COMP_FREE_ALTERNATIVE 33 name the phone's own reminders and notes; at $7.99 a week the comparison to paper is fatal. Report 89 (Check Calendar): PAY_NOT_WORTH 28 (11.07%, 1.71★) — the argument is almost always that ticking a calendar should not cost money, not that $4.99 is a lot: 'Why would using a calendar cost money? You can do this for free on your iPhone'; 'Not paying any amount of money to put check marks on a calendar'; 'who pays for a calendar?' (jp); 'too simple to pay 90 pesos' (mx); only one reviewer in 253 names a lower number they would pay; COMP_FREE_ALTERNATIVE 9 (1.11★) name a physical calendar, the phone's calendar, Google Calendar, a paper diary — and, in July 2026, an AI assistant ('Uninstalled this and created my own in 10 mins with Claude'); 'the simplicity that earns the praise is also the paywall's biggest obstacle'; §8.9 country-specific pricing will not help because 'price objections are about paying at all, not the amount'. Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): FEATURE_THIN 12 (1.95%, mean 3.33★) — 'just a timer: start, stop'; 'no more complex than a timer' — the same comparison-to-a-free-primitive objection, here aimed at a free app, which is why it costs three stars instead of a refund.

<a id="c157"></a>
### C157 — Every guilt mechanic must be optional — streaks, repair prompts, countdowns

**Certain** · 21 apps · 66 cards · positive in 11 apps · negative in 9 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Certain:* 21 apps, same direction (act on it, 79%), 6 reports label it high-priority

Report 10: the app was praised specifically for not guilting users (476 reviews, mean 4.87); after streaks shipped mid-2024, 96 reviews say it now punishes the missed day the audience was promised it wouldn't, and repairing a streak costs currency. A single 'gentle mode' toggle is the corpus's own proposal. Report 18: an automatic streak 'shield' made the streak number feel fake ('I get complacent since the number won't disappear'), while an ADHD reviewer said a broken streak is the feature that makes them quit and asked to hide the UI; another sat in red all day because the routine could only be finished at night. Conclusion: streak, shield, light and cheer messages are per-user toggles, default shield off. Report 23: loss-framed reminder copy is a guilt mechanic users in four languages ask to switch off or reframe. Report 26: a 'no wither' / Zen mode (the garden does not decay) exists as a premium option; gentleness and no streaks are praised at mean 4.76 and the mental-health segment (32, mean 4.66 — 'this app helped me fix my severe depression') is the clearest argument against any harsher rule. Report 28: rabbit health/energy decay with guilt notifications ('YOUR BUNNY'S LOSING HEALTH COME AND DO HABITS TO FIX IT!') and a challenge-mode full reset penalise exactly the cautious beginner ('I have few habits because I'm starting a healthier lifestyle slowly'); a defender values the stakes — make decay a setting, separate it visibly from the data model. Report 33: an 'Are you sure the day is over?' confirmation on fail/skip with no off switch. Report 36: 7 ask for streaks / reps / loss-on-break (incl. a 45-vote review) while 11 praise the absence of streak shame — make streaks optional, with a 'don't skip twice' rule proposed. Report 41: 'the percentage focus and backseating of streaks made this a thing i actually use' — one streak-prominence request is treated as a minority against the differentiator. Report 46: the skip mark is why perfectionists stay — 'you don't want to break a streak, so you keep going' with 'no punishment other than a break in the color gradient'; rule 17: do not remove or harden the forgiving skip. Report 47: the streak resets to zero on a miss and is praised by 3 as motivating, while the grid's kept colour is the non-punitive part reviewers love; a missed-day marker (4 requests, 3 KR) should be optional. Report 49: an optional hard mode that resets to day 1 with penalty tasks on a miss is loved by a small, intense, entirely satisfied group (13, 4.77) — opt-in severity works; guilt-inducing tone as a default is criticised (13). Report 54: 12 (3.25%, 4.75) praise the deliberate absence of streaks — 'most likely because it does not track streaks (which my black and white brain reads as failure if I am not perfect)… These are skills. Skills can be learned. I am not broken'; 'I have adhd and using streaks has always resulted in beating myself up'; one downloaded because a review said there were no streaks; D6: claim it; §8.5: do not add streaks with penalties. Report 59 (Tappsk): a daily productivity score with a trend arrow demotivates a minority — NEG_SCORE 23 vs PR_SCORE 84: 'ОЧЕНЬ ДЕМОТИВИРУЕТ эта стрелочка которая показывает насколько я продуктивна' (this arrow showing how productive I am is VERY demotivating, 4★). Report 65 (Rabit): a missed habit kills the plant — 'Missing one scheduled habit completely kills a plant?!! … I don't mind a penalty but this is dark souls level'; 'are we supposed to lie?' — users accept the penalty when deserved and reject it when not, so plant death is 'the single riskiest design decision in the product'. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): the reset divides users — PR_RESET_TENSION 40 value the discipline; a March 2018 update removed the automatic reset (6 welcomed it, 13 asked for it back as late as 2024: 'For some people motivation drops sharply without the reset'); the answer is an option in both directions, not one rule. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the counter-case — an app whose entire thesis is no streak pressure drew zero negative reactions to that thesis across 71 reviews, 28 storefronts and six languages; CONCEPT_FORGIVING 11 (4.82★): 'if you miss a day it isn't all for nothing; it reflects a healthy relationship with habits'. Report 83 (Roubit): a 1★ from someone for whom the app 'feels too much like a game to use'; the game layer is default-on and not hideable. Report 85 (Habitica): the health penalty for missed Dailies is the pressure some need (PR_PENALTY 34) and drives others out — NEG_PUNISH 23, BUG_DEATH 12, REQ_PAUSE 7: 'I don't want to be punished again for my health problems' (3★); 'I crashed out from the penalties when having a tough time and ended up uninstalling it for almost 3 years' (4★, returned); §8.9 make resting in the inn discoverable and time-limited and test milder death penalties (keep levels) — 'fewer punishment-triggered quits without losing the pressure PR_PENALTY reviewers value'.

<a id="c127"></a>
### C127 — Never show ads or upsells to anyone holding an active or historical entitlement — including cross-promotion of sibling apps

**Certain** · 19 apps · 59 cards · positive in 2 apps · negative in 16 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Certain:* 19 apps, same direction (act on it, 94%), 8 reports label it high-priority

Including reward-gated features like streak savers; a 30-second unskippable ad to a payer is the most reliable way to turn an advocate into a 1★. Report 10: a sponsored movie tie-in as the monthly event drew 'I am paying to be advertised to' from multi-year subscribers (mean 3.09, 8× over-represented among payers) after 857 reviews had praised the app for being ad-free. Report 18: 'A pro member should be a pro member regardless of whether they are paying monthly or yearly' — monthly subscribers nagged daily to go annual, and a 'buy the next term' screen that blocked the app entirely. Report 24: in-app advertising of the developer's own sister apps inside paid accounts — 308 reviews, mean 1.932, only 14.6% 4–5★, the lowest satisfied-share of any UX theme ('I'm on the purchased version… I don't want to see adds'); rose 0.11% → 2.03% across eras. Report 28: 'I paid 10$ to remove ads but I still get ads'; a 5★ 'purchased the full version and I am still getting ads' — and even after buying no-ads there is still a prompt to double carrots by watching an ad after every level. Report 31: the promotional banner hid a habit even for paid users (Dec 2020). Report 50: no ads at any tier (5 confirm). [Merged from C248: Report 31: 314 reviews (6.05%, mean 1.57) were upsold after paying — 197 of 625 explicit payers (31.5%) — rising 0.3% (E1) → 12.1% (E4): 'It's not encouraging customer loyalty!!'; mood-disorder tracking interrupted by the offer; a banner in Dec 2020 hid the bottom habit even for paid users. The report's first upsell rule: suppress every offer for any past or present entitlement, and test every-launch vs weekly vs never-for-past-payers on conversion, D30 retention and 1★ rate. Report 33: cross-promotion ads for the developer's other apps (Nirow, Poly) shown to lifetime payers — 'False advertisement – Still get ads with lifetime premium'; a premium user shown notices: 'No. deal with it'; 'I wish the upgrade button would disappear when you buy premium' — 14 + 12 reviews.] Report 52: 40 paying reviewers (including legacy lifetime and ¥8 ad-free buyers) still saw ads — 'I bought lifetime membership before… an ugly ad pops up at every check-in'; F2: verify the entitlement before rendering the first ad. Report 59 (Tappsk): 'never show the lifetime buyer a subscription paywall' is an immediate fix — an app that sells lifetime, annual and monthly SKUs plus a 7-day trial side by side let a subscription charge reach lifetime owners ('купил полную версию на всегда за 1500 тыс, сегодня списалось 999 рублей за подписку' — bought forever for 1,500; today 999 ₽ taken for a subscription); lifetime buyers carry the highest problem lifts among purchasers (MON_PAID_TWICE 8.89×, BUG_PURCHASE 8.43×, SUP_NONE 6.09×) even though the one-time option is praised 93 times against 23 subscription objections. Report 64 (Critique AI): a subscriber reports seeing ads while paying £40/yr (4★) — 'the worst of both models'; F6, verify before acting. Report 65 (Rabit): 'I have ads on a paid subscription- I want a refund'; 'despite buying a premium subscription, I'm still being asked every time I'm in the app to upgrade to premium'. Report 68 (Ultiself): 'I bought a lifetime premium account but I don't get everything'; 'To do that, you have to pay yet another $40'; 'After subscribing, lets you PAY AGAIN' — MON_TIER_TRAP 24 (peak 4.6% in 2023), MON_UPSELL 80 predating the billing wave. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): the add-on kept being advertised after it was bought (NEG_UPSELL_NAG 5, mean 1.40); 'I can't tell the difference between the comments before and after paying'. Report 76 (Way of Life): ads briefly appeared for paying users after the 2015-11 update ('Ads when already paid', 2★) and a 2020-01 bundle promotion shown to paying users drew 5 complaints ('Ads now constantly appear in paid version', 4★) — the last ad complaints in the corpus are from payers. <a id="c236"></a>
### C236 — A free-tier limit must announce itself before the user invests — at install, at setup and at the wall — never silently stop a visible progress signal

**Certain** · 18 apps · 50 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 15 apps

*Why Certain:* 18 apps, same direction (act on it, 88%), 7 reports label it high-priority

Report 26: the free tier lets the garden grow to ~17% and then silently stops; 50 verified reviews (1.30%, mean 2.96) report the flower 'not growing', 17 of them naming the same 17% across April 2022 → December 2025, filed as 'Glitches 🙄', 'Bug', 'Fake Flowers' — several learned only from support that it was intentional. Users conclude the app is broken and say so publicly. A one-line in-app explanation at the moment the ceiling is hit converts a 1–3★ 'it's broken' review into a legible upgrade prompt — the cheapest high-value fix in the corpus. Report 33: the habit limit was announced only after users created habits. Report 46: the free tier cannot fill the product's own 4-row widget ('it leaves the 4th row blank… it bothers me so much'; 'makes many widgets appear broken as they tend to have a multiple of 4 rows'). Report 48: the cap 'announces itself' only after setup — 48 reviews at 1.65★ met the wall after investing effort. Report 50: own statistics locked after hitting the reduced cap (TR). Report 71 (MyStreaks): both 1★ reviewers met the cap after investing setup effort — 'i was going to make my 3rd streak and i was met with an unavoidable monthly subscription'; 'I was really excited about this app… But a paywall for more than 2 streaks?' — §8.1 #3: disclose the cap at onboarding, 'honesty about the limit before the third streak, not a change to the limit'. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): §8.1 #2 show the trial state in-app from first launch — a persistent 'N days left in your free trial' — so day 8 is never a surprise; the lockout is a hard stop, not a degraded tier (one reviewer alone reports rows being cut back first). Report 75 (Habit Streak): the App Store description never states a habit-count limit, names only subscriptions, and omits the $79.99 lifetime — two reviewers say they were not warned ('il aurait pu prévenir que c'était payant'; 'man muss Geld ausgeben um die App zu benutzen, wenn nicht klärt mich bitte auf den die App wirkt perfekt' — a 2★ from a confused user calling the app perfect); §8.1 #1 'Track up to 5 habits free, forever' in the description and first onboarding screen — 'Zero engineering cost', addressing 8 of 11 low ratings; E3 disclose and measure the 1★ rate — 'the current listing makes the honest version of it impossible to test at all'. (Consolidation after report 75: title widened from 'A free-tier limit must announce itself — never silently stop a visible progress signal' to name when the announcement has to happen; the report 40-era evidence stays in the statement.) Report 76 (Way of Life): MON_DISCLOSURE 33 (0.43%, mean 2.06★) — 'not particularly clear in the iTunes store that the free app allows for only three categories' (2★); 7.73% of 1★ and 6.73% of 2★ carry it. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the free tier is one habit and the App Store description states no habit-count limit anywhere ('helps you build your new habit' — singular); three reviewers on three storefronts across ten months independently state the number (mean 2.33★), two say in as many words the boundary surprised them (MON_UNEXPECTED 2, mean 1.50★: 'What's the point of making a free app if it's unfunctional unless you buy a premium plan'; 'Ich hatte erwartet, dass mehrere Gewohnheiten frei sind'); 'A one-habit free tier is a defensible business decision. Not disclosing it is a separate, cheaper-to-fix problem, and it is the one the corpus actually punishes'; §8.1.1 one sentence in the description is 'the highest ratio of impact to effort available here' — it removes the surprise, which is what the 1★ and 2★ text objects to. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the 3-board cap and the paid widget are undisclosed in a description with no money text; §8.6 E2 disclosure A/B measuring the 1★ rate, not installs. Report 82 (Lasting Change): BILL_UNDISCLOSED 26 (14.86%) — disclosed only in the T&Cs: 'Why can't you write it loud and clear in the sales order and not hide it in the T&C fine print if you are transparent'; 'hidden in the small print rather than being clearly and prominently disclosed'; BILL_FREE_CLAIMED 7 — presented as free or a trial ('Said the app came free… I am getting charged 30.99 a month'; '$30.99 / month after the trial period, which i didnt see mentioned anywhere'); REQ_DISCLOSURE 4, all from people harmed. Report 83 (Roubit): the letter allowance is undisclosed and moves — 'you have to pay for the AI letter, but the app didn't warn you and it just stops' (2★); 'I'm not sure though' about the rule; §8.6 state the allowance before the user writes. Report 89 (Check Calendar): the wall arrives after the reviewer has invested — install, log for days, then lose the ability to tick a box ('Works great the first weeK. After the free trial ends, even the basic function of checking off 1 day is behind a paywall'; 'it says you have to pay 6 dollars after I already did a lot of stuff with the app'); the durations reviewers name disagree (7 days, 4 days, two weeks, a month), which is itself evidence that nothing in the product announced the period; 'it is a disclosure and lock-out problem more than a price problem' — U:trust_breach 42 (16.60%) outnumbers U:value_objection 33 (13.04%), and 30 of the 107 paywall reviews also praise the app. Research: Feature Gating vs Quantity.md — undisclosed caps are the norm in adjacent productivity apps and are discovered as a surprise: Todoist advertises 'unlimited tasks' while limiting each project to 300, 'a restriction discovered only in user reports'; capping the core count in a habit app 'often feels like a hidden trial', and freemium design guides are cited for the test — users should never feel 'cheated if we moved it behind the paywall'.

<a id="c182"></a>
### C182 — A pre-use hard paywall makes every purchase non-evidence-based and non-durable

**Certain** · 15 apps · 42 cards · positive in 5 apps · negative in 12 apps · tied to a purchase in 5 apps

*Why Certain:* 15 apps, same direction (act on it, 83%), 12 reports label it high-priority

Report 12: no reviewer in 404 said they paid because of a feature they had seen working; purchases were made to evaluate, under an exit discount, or on the strength of the intro — and 0 of 80 self-identified payers rated 5★. What the gate protects must be able to survive inspection: 13 buyers said it was a worse version of Apple Calendar. Report 25: an onboarding questionnaire followed by an immediate paywall — 'I did the whole survey and at the end I had to pay'; 'first 10 minutes of test… then it turns out you need a subscription' — every such reviewer left 1–2★ (mean 1.17). Report 49: a hard paywall before any use — 43.67% of the corpus attacks how it is sold; buyers convert on a 2am impulse, the Solo Leveling frame or a low point, and payers then average 1.92. Report 60 (Mindway): the pre-value paywall follows a mandatory onboarding questionnaire — 'it was really strange like answering a questionnaire. Then it asked for money right away' (1★); 'Stop playing games and get to plan'; 19 blocked plus 3 interrupted (8.80% + 1.39%) are the largest upgrade barrier. Report 64 (Critique AI): only three first-person purchase accounts in 419 — a $2/month exit discount, 75% off annual, and creator trust; 'No reviewer in this corpus says they paid because of a specific feature' — 'sold on price anchoring and creator trust, not on value demonstration'; 13 self-stated payers average 1.85, 12 of 13 report a defect or shortfall, 1 of 13 unreservedly satisfied. Report 67 (Habio): the purchase path is ad → quiz → small paid trial ('€5.49 seemed like a reasonable amount to see if the app could fulfil on the promises') → immediate add-on → auto-renewal; 995 reviewers say money left their account (mean 1.05) and only 35 describe a deliberate purchase (mean 1.23); very few buy because of the product. Report 68 (Ultiself): purchases are triggered by an ad and a cheap intro plan ('I signed up for this app via an instagram ad and paid £7 for one course'; MKT_AD lift 6.26× among purchasers) and by a problem the ad sold (add-ons 10.14×), rarely by the free tracker. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): stated purchase triggers are trust from another app in the family, buying on sight from the design, a sale price, and wanting to support — never hitting the cap; 'Nobody who bought it thinks it was expensive'. Report 82 (Lasting Change): a subscription-gated app whose purchase happens on a website before the app is ever opened — 'Not one review in 175 describes choosing to subscribe to this app because of something the app does'; 14 reviewers never used, activated or downloaded it. Report 88 (GetHabit): the hardest pre-use wall in the series — U:pre_use_wall 132 (26.94%, 1.17★): PAY_HARD_WALL 96 ('It asks for your name, then tries to sell you a subscription'; 'you can't get past the subscription page without making a selection. There is no free version'), PAY_NO_FREE_TRIAL 58, PAY_FREE_LABEL_MISLEADING 33 ('listing it as Free in the store seems bad faith'); 97 of the 132 did not pay — lost installs; those who paid to see it found little (CONTENT_THIN 54; 'the concept is amazing but of course you have to buy everything for it to work'); of 182 buyers one is satisfied; 'the barrier is the order of events, not the price alone'. Research: Feature Gating vs Quantity.md — the retention arithmetic behind this: only 1-4% of free users convert in B2C, and surviving the first week multiplies conversion 5-8x, so a paywall placed before habit formation (~66 days) removes the cohort that would have paid. 'Only after they've built some usage habit do they become sensitive to missing extras.'

<a id="c240"></a>
### C240 — Never interrupt the completion moment — no ad, upsell or rating prompt on the check-off tap

**Certain** · 14 apps · 38 cards · positive in 3 apps · negative in 10 apps

*Why Certain:* 14 apps, same direction (act on it, 97%), 6 reports label it high-priority

Report 28: a forced full-screen interstitial fired on every habit check-off is the single largest fact in an 821-review corpus — 164 complaints (19.98%, mean 2.73 vs 4.35 for every other review; 52.4% of all 1★), 33 naming the per-tap mechanic as a punishment ('it feels like a punishment for doing what you were meant to do'; 'replacing the feel-good with this uncanny worry'), 30 calling the app unusable, 19 five-star reviewers still complaining, and the users most helped by the reward loop (ADHD) the most damaged by breaking it. Users are not asking for zero ads; they propose batching ('let me tick them all off and then show me an ad') or a cap per session. Report 24: checking off one habit takes 3–5 screens of celebration; report 25: upsell sheets on every action; a 2026 rating prompt fired on check-off produced a 1★ purely about the prompt. Report 29: the rating prompt fires on the first habit check-off. Report 42: a mandatory 'congratulations' trophy modal on every check-off blocks the Continue button and freezes the app for heavy users ('It takes me at least 5 minutes to mark two tasks as done'; 'pops up far too often'; messages 'not coherent') — 4 reviews; a settings toggle is the cheapest fix in the report. Report 43: the Oct 2025 redesign put a journal prompt on every skip — 'Bad design to have to do skip every time' (long-time payer, 1★). Report 46: a rating prompt 'every other time I marked a habit as complete'; a Dec 2022 completion animation on every log ('so annoying'). Report 47: the clearest evidence in the ledger — a video ad on each check-in (May–Dec 2024) produced 24 reviews at mean 1.46 and 20 exits in eight months, banners before and after were tolerated, and the 2025 upsell page after each completed task (4, mean 1.25) and the rating prompt shown to payers repeat the same mistake; the report's rule: nothing between 'tap' and 'done' — monetise elsewhere. Report 48: a post-log upgrade prompt (Jul 2024) is 'the only monetization mechanic in the corpus that users say actively reduced their intent to pay' (6 in three months); the 2021 logging redesign added taps to the same moment and was rolled back. Report 52: an ad after every check-in (2025) and a status sheet added to the check-in tap (2021) are both named as the moment the app broke. Report 60 (Mindway): the upsell interrupts the planning task itself — three reviewers (1.39%, mean 1.33) describe pop-ups 'every 5 seconds' while building a routine ([[C093]]). Report 65 (Rabit): an interstitial on habit completion from 23 Dec 2022 — 'Cada que completo un hábito me aparece un anuncio!!!'; 'vengo a desinstalarla después de ver unos 40 anuncios'; 'They don't even let you finish what you were doing' — ADS_BAD 15 (3.01%, mean 2.33), 12 of 46 reviews in the launch window (26.1%); 'An app whose entire behavioural model is complete the habit → see your plant grow → feel rewarded inserted an interstitial exactly at the reward moment'; the close button rendered under the iPhone 13 status bar and forced a restart; F5. Report 76 (Way of Life): 'app solicited a review 3 days in, after I paid for the premium version' (4★); §8.7 never prompt right after a purchase. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the review prompt fired 'after every check in' — the completion moment — and a previously-5★ paying user dropped to 1★ until it stops. Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): ADS_TOO_MANY 18 (2.93%, mean 2.72★) describe an unskippable ad after every action in an app whose action is logging abstinence — '15 mandatory seconds of ads every time you use the app' (co); 'a long ad after every action. Deleting'; 'to close it you have to exit completely'.

<a id="c078"></a>
### C078 — Ship the paid feature working before you sell it — the purchase trigger must never be the broken feature

**Certain** · 13 apps · 45 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 13 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Certain:* 13 apps, same direction (act on it, 95%), 7 reports label it high-priority

Paid features carry a higher reliability bar; selling broken sync/calendar/stats put payers a full star below free users. Report 20: the widget was by a wide margin the most-named purchase trigger and the feature that most often didn't work — 182 reviews (mean 1.94), 113 from confirmed payers, broken for five years with an in-app FAQ offering 'restart your phone'; even when present it was a Today-view widget while screenshots implied Home Screen. Ship it properly or remove it from the paywall copy and refund on request. Report 23: the Apple Watch is a purchase driver, not a feature — ≥15 reviews name it as the reason to buy and the explicit-bug subset runs at mean 2.57; if you ship a Watch app its reliability budget is your main reliability budget. Report 41: four of ten post-purchase failures bought for one named capability that then failed (backfill, widget ×2, Health sync) — any single-feature failure is a total failure of the purchase. Report 43: 'purchase not delivered' is the most damaging pattern for a one-time product — 4 buyers got nothing ('I paid to upgrade to get the edit function, but no changes happened… Something broken in the backend??'; 'Purchase premium but still getting free trial capabilities'; 'just took my money'), one could not buy, one could not restore. Report 48: the Jan 2015 subscription launch shipped with a broken release — 81 crash-on-launch, 25 data-loss and 20 duplicate-tracker reviews in the same window — and reviewers linked the two: 'they were asked to start paying for an app that had just stopped working'; the 19 Jan – 30 Sep 2015 window averaged 2.06★ with 73.2% 1–2★. Report 53: statistics — a main reason to pay — crashed for paying users from Sep 2024 (STAT_CRASH 28 of 33 since then, 21.7% of all E4 reviews; payer lift 2.95; the 7-day trend view named by 14); a reviewer reset two years of data trying to fix it; F3 'the feature people pay for'. Report 54: the paid tier's named benefit 'Advanced Statistics' is a calendar — 12 value-gap reviews (2.58), 10 payers (22.7% of payers), three quoting the phrase back ('I bought this app bcs it stated advanced statistics for paid version. But I can not call these statistics even basic'); both payers who bought specifically for statistics were disappointed; F4: build it or delete the claim. Report 55: sync and export — the server-dependent parts of the premium bundle — are the two paid features reviewers most often report broken, while 'more habits' costs nothing to deliver. Report 76 (Way of Life): 11 reviews on cn in one week of 2015-01 report the app crashing immediately after buying premium ('钱扣了就开始闪退，无限闪退' — the money was taken and it started crashing, endlessly, 1★).

<a id="c264"></a>
### C264 — Log-entry friction is sacred — never add a tap to the logging path; a logging redesign is the highest-risk change in the product

**Certain** · 12 apps · 27 cards · positive in 7 apps · negative in 6 apps

*Why Certain:* 12 apps, same direction (act on it, 85%), 7 reports label it high-priority

Report 48: a mid-2021 redesign of history logging that multiplied the taps to back-fill days drew ten reviews in three months (May–Aug 2021 window n = 78, mean 3.86★, 28.2% 1–2★ — 'Latest update forces you to double click for every single activity'; 'turning a 10 second daily update to about 60'), disproportionately from long-term users (7) and payers (6); the developer restored the one-click behaviour and the reinstatement was welcomed by name, after which too-many-taps fell to 0.24% — 'log-entry friction is uniquely expensive for this product' because simplicity of logging (817 reviews, 18.56%, mean 4.84 — 'open the app, click a check mark, exit') is its most load-bearing quality. Report 47 (DotHabit): a long-press → record screen → done flow counted as too many taps by 14 (mean 2.86) with one-tap logging requested since 2019. Related: [[C240]] (nothing between tap and done), [[C159]], [[C229]] (a deliberate gesture must complete the log, not open a form). Report 52: 'a check-in used to be one tap… now it's at least two' (Jun 2021 status sheet, 29 reviews in a month); every added step on the check-in was reviewed negatively within days; R2: protect one-tap check-in and one-tap undo. Report 53: swipe-to-complete and the completion sound are liked; editing habits 'are a nightmare - you have to tap in multiple times'; compared unfavourably with Productive's one-swipe check (DES_UX_NEG 38). Report 59 (Tappsk): entry speed is a named reason for choosing the app — 'позволяет тебе записать задачу быстрее чем ты ее забудешь' (write the task down faster than you forget it); 'Задачи добавляются за пол секунды' (added in half a second); voice entry by holding the add button praised by 52. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 'just check and carry on. As it should be' — one-tap check-off is the praised loop; when the June build broke tapping, the app was unusable. Report 71 (MyStreaks): the core loop reviewers praise is the tap count — 'it's a simple tap to say that you've done it, but it's so satisfying!'; '3 clicks is all it takes to update a daily streak'; 'I get a little thrill every time I check off my streaks'. Report 75 (Habit Streak): 'Porque deshabilitado la opción de pulsar para check el hábito' (5★, tap-to-check unavailable) and a request for an auto-check-with-undo mode — both about reducing the friction of the daily tick. Report 76 (Way of Life): 'I track 30+ items in under 2 minutes' (5★); PR_FAST 197; NEG_TWO_TAPS 4 — logging cost in seconds is why it survives 13 years of daily use ('almost 9 years since my last review and 13 since the first'). Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): 'no frills, no 20 taps to log something' — logging friction as the stated reason for choosing it; UX_BULK_ENTRY 1 ('If I want to add 10 check-ins to a previous day it's very painful!', a 5★ whose whole body is the complaint); DEF_CHECKIN_SPAM 1 asks that a second tap undo a check-in. Report 86 (Today): 'Instead of a single tap to log a habit for the day, you're forced to go through multiple steps now!' (1★) — the Nov 2018 redesign that added taps to check-in was rolled back and the 1★ became a 5★; UX_FRICTION 41 (too many taps); the visual model's latency ([[C303]]) is the other tax on the tap. Report 88 (GetHabit): DEF_CANT_TRACK 7 — 'unable to mark my habits done'; 'it wants more money for every little thing' on each tap. Report 89 (Check Calendar): the whole proposition is one tap — 'typical apps often need at least 2 taps to record… in this app, tapping the date on the calendar completes the record… it became stress-free' (jp, 5★); PRAISE_ONE_TAP 7, U:calendar_core 25 (9.88%, 4.72★), U:simplicity 81 (32.02%, 4.42★) framed against other apps' clutter ('It's perfect because it's simple. All the other apps have a bunch of functions and distractions'); the developer's reply: 'we designed it so you reach your goal in as few actions as possible'; FRICTION_CHECK_INPUT 3 are the only logging-path complaints (a mis-tap confirmation that appears too often; a future date checked by accident; a check that cannot be erased).

<a id="c176"></a>
### C176 — Never let fear of losing history be the reason people pay

**Certain** · 11 apps · 22 cards · positive in 2 apps · negative in 10 apps · tied to a purchase in 2 apps

*Why Certain:* 11 apps, same direction (act on it, 81%), 3 reports label it high-priority

Report 11: the only stated purchase motive was 'I had 3 years worth of history I didn't want to lose' on an app with no export or backup; when the entitlement then failed, the loyal long-tenure user became the 1★ 'scam' review. Sell durability (backup, export, long-history analytics) as a gain, never gate access to what the user already built. Report 33: a weekly check-in cap locked free users out of long streaks ('After 500 days I was pay-walled'). Report 34: 'forced to keep paying … if you don't want to lose all your history' — export disabled and a paid backup before delete, both 1★. Report 36: 'the most dangerous customer' is the multi-year free user who changed device or ran out of habits in 2026 — data in the app, no export and no sync, 'cannot leave cleanly and cannot continue without paying' (LOCKIN). Report 57: free-tier history cut to 30 days while backup is Premium — 'in the end I learned for the first time that without paid Premium, backup and recovery are impossible'. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): 'Going paid is unavoidable, but suddenly not being able to see my past history either — isn't that unkind?' — locking history converts a pricing decision into hostage-taking in the users' own words; 'the difference between I decided not to pay and they took my medication log'. Report 76 (Way of Life): 'I lost all my habits when I got a new phone even though I paid for the app' (5★) — cloud backup sold as premium for most of the app's life, then made free in 4.3.0. Report 86 (Today): backup and restore is the paid feature and 12 of the 55 data-loss reviewers had paid — 'selling backup and then losing data is the corpus's sharpest breach of trust': 'the third time I've opened the app to find months worth of data has been randomly corrupted/lost… despite having paid extra to back it up' (1★); 'I lost my 3 years data due to an issue in restore backup' (it 1★); 'the crucial backup was overwritten and even the restore data was wiped' (jp, titled 'Farewell, Today'); nobody in the corpus reports buying for backup — 'the paid features that convert are the ones users can see'. Report 89 (Check Calendar): PURCHASE_LOCKIN 2 — 'didn't want to pay, but had already entered records, so bought' (jp); two others bought specifically so their records would be safe ('so they store my data and i don't loose it'; 'para ter o backup automático') and both then lost their data on a new phone — 'two of the stated reasons to buy — keeping data safe and not losing records already entered — are the same things that failed for other buyers and that the trial wall threatens for non-buyers'.

<a id="c191"></a>
### C191 — Never shrink a tier someone already holds — a paid tier's limits, or free capacity a user has already filled

**Certain** · 11 apps · 29 cards · positive in 2 apps · negative in 10 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Certain:* 11 apps, same direction (act on it, 74%), 6 reports label it high-priority

Report 16: Pro was capped at 3 habits, then 6, for 29 months; a cap on the paid tier has no monetisation function (there is no higher tier to drive to) and two of three buyers who paid specifically to escape the free cap hit the next one and rated 3★ — 'A paid user pays $40/year just to create only 6 habits simultaneously?' Report 48: 23 users who built history on 10 or 7 free trackers found the cap shrunk under them (mean 2.22) — retroactive reduction lands on the longest-tenured users; fix #2: never reduce existing users' free capacity. Report 50: grandfather existing free users at 5 — the two cap-cut reviews describe loss, not a low starting cap; experiment: grandfather-vs-migrate. (Consolidation after report 50: the title was widened from 'Never cap the tier someone has already paid for' because the Report 48 and Report 50 evidence is free users losing capacity they had already filled — grandfathering is the fix in both.) Report 59 (Tappsk): the 2021-01 cut shrank free capacity users had already filled — habits removed from the free tier for existing users and a 20-task cap on lists people were using; 2021-01 was the busiest month of the corpus (372 reviews) and 2021-03 the lowest-rated (4.19★). Report 65 (Rabit): capping the free tier after years of generous use drove the E1/E2 cohort out — a user since 2020 uninstalled in 2023 ('antes era mejor'), another had recommended it to about 30 people ('ate eles se importarem mais em ganhar dinheiro que ajudar os outros'); COMP_WORSE 11 (mean 2.09), all Dec 2022 or later — 'The competitive position was not lost to a competitor's feature. It was given away'. Report 71 (MyStreaks): the reported free allowance shrank from 2 to 1 streak between Feb and Nov 2024 while the release notes show 'improved subscriptions' and 'Fix subscription bug'; a 4★ on the 1-streak tier pre-announces churn: 'I like this app but if I find a better one I'll definitely switch'. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): cutting the free allowance from 3 to 1 over Christmas 2024 produced 13 of the app's 20 lifetime 1–2★ reviews in six weeks, then was quietly reverted; two reviewers independently concluded 'it should just be a paid app'. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): users of a year or more hit the sudden paywall — one bought at once and asked the app not be shut down; others 'had been thinking I might as well pay' and lost the desire to — 'Amazing how much one attitude from the developer changes how you feel' (4/6 helpful). Report 83 (Roubit): the free cap has been moved repeatedly — a 150-record cap in 2021 ('it's like don't use it unless you pay'), 8 routines for most of the window, 9 in 2023-02, 4 in 2025-02 — each move a separate grievance (FREE_LIMIT_ROUTINES 12, a 1★ 'I'll just use another app'). Report 86 (Today): the free tier was narrowed back from three (or five) habits to one in ~2022 and 'the complaint came back with it' — 'I understood the free version allowed up to 3' (pe 1★); premium photo covers were also moved behind payment 'and completely took everything i had on my profile off to do so' (MON_REGRESS 3). (Consolidation after report 90: see [[C296]] — this rule is about taking capacity away; C296 is about what the free slice has to contain before anyone pays.)

<a id="c196"></a>
### C196 — A subscription is a promise of continued delivery — back it with a visible cadence

**Certain** · 10 apps · 21 cards · positive in 2 apps · negative in 6 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Certain:* 10 apps, same direction (act on it, 84%), 2 reports label it high-priority

Report 17: an app relaunched on a subscription went 3.5 years without a release while still charging; four of its last six reviews were about abandonment and the one paying 3★ stated the deal plainly — 'If we can get iPad and watch apps along with more regular debugging, I will keep paying. Otherwise, I am switching to Blocos.' Subscribers believe they are funding development; when it stops, the subscription has no story, and a 'lifetime' tier sold against a dormant build compounds the grievance. Report 20: an annual subscription was charged for seven years against a product that shipped nothing new; the 4★ band told the developer exactly what would make it a 5 and almost none of it was built. Report 24: repetitive coaching content (103, mean 2.660) in a content subscription. Report 31: 'a subscription for a checklist is unjustifiable' — the subscription came with removals, lag and no visible new delivery. Report 41: a German reviewer chose the subscription over lifetime deliberately — 'I want the app to still work in 3 years'. Report 55: 'It's not like a yoga or meditation app, which is constantly adding new videos/content, so why a yearly fee?!?' — an annual fee reads as a promise of ongoing development, and reviewers measured the app by its update log; M3: price the subscription only on features that work. Report 57: 2★ reviews concentrate the oldest users hit by silent tier changes (long_tenure_user 10.3% vs 2.95%). Report 59 (Tappsk): stagnation is the dominant criticism of the latest era — 'nothing changes' (NEG_DEV_PROMISE 1.1%) alongside subscriptions still being sold. Report 60 (Mindway): benefit claims (habit outcome, motivation, wellbeing) peak in the burst period and vanish to zero in the 14-review tail while paywall complaints rise to 28.57% — 'the corpus's least comfortable pattern' for a subscription product. Report 76 (Way of Life): E6 subscription-era reviewers praise 'steady updates' (PR_UPDATE 5.1% of E6, PR_DEV 6.7%) — the visible cadence is what keeps veterans on side while the subscription objection runs underneath.

<a id="c203"></a>
### C203 — Onboarding lets the user author their own routine first — suggested plans, surveys and pledges are optional

**Certain** · 10 apps · 41 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 8 apps

*Why Certain:* 10 apps, same direction (act on it, 81%), 2 reports label it high-priority

Report 18: the lowest-rated theme (34 reviews, mean 2.03★) was an onboarding that ran a long survey, built the routine for the user, assumed a 9-to-5 weekday life, demanded a signed pledge and then showed the paywall — 'I wanted to create my own routine not have you suggest one for me. Hence the name of your app. MY routine not your routine'; 'an app that wants to turn you into a very ordinary machine'. Shift workers, night workers and parents were excluded before they reached the product. Report 24: the forced first habit ('drink water', gated three days, then breakfast) is the concrete example inside every larger personalisation complaint; the fix is an 'I already do this' branch, keeping the default. Report 25: an onboarding questionnaire suggests starter habits (free) — and from Nov 2025 those starter habits could not be edited without paying. Report 26: onboarding offers preset-only habits and custom habits could not be created (8 verified, mean 2.50). Report 49: cannot add own tasks 80 and cannot edit the generated programme 70 are the top themes of the 3★ and 4★ bands (9.43% / 15.09% among payers) — 'the design is excellent, the idea is right, and I cannot make it fit my life'; custom tasks shipped mid-2025 cut 'cannot add' 10.2% → 1.0%; still needed: week-by-week edits, swapping running, entering existing fitness. Report 60 (Mindway): a mandatory onboarding questionnaire followed immediately by the paywall ('answering a questionnaire. Then it asked for money right away'; 'Stop playing games and get to plan') and preset packs the user must delete rather than a routine they author; one reviewer asks for '3 complete day schedules' to pick from so 'adding and subtracting would not be so overwhelming'. Report 67 (Habio): preset routines only — 'What if I want the routine to include a workout but not meditation?'; REQ_CUSTOM_ROUTINE 18 and NEG_NO_CUSTOM_HABIT 9, 'the most consistent product request from people who got past the paywall'; forced intentions / rewards / reflections steps (7). Report 82 (Lasting Change): 'The ads made it seem like you could track whatever habits you wanted, but you in fact can not add your own habits to the daily activities' (APP_NOT_AS_ADVERTISED 3; REQ_OWN_HABITS 1) — while four other reviewers praise custom trackers, so the capability is either gated or undiscoverable.

<a id="c210"></a>
### C210 — Bill App Store users through the App Store — never route them to an off-store subscription the app cannot show or cancel

**Certain** · 9 apps · 61 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 9 apps

*Why Certain:* 9 apps, same direction (act on it, 93%), 7 reports label it high-priority

Report 19: the app was the front door to a web-billed subscription that did not appear in Apple's subscription list, carried non-refundable website terms, and could be cancelled only by email; 18 of 105 reviewers (17.14%) described the consequence, 19 were charged after cancelling, 19 were charged with no subscription they recognised, and 60 distinct reviews flowed from a customer who could not see or stop their own plan. If a web funnel must exist, the app shows the active plan, price, next charge date and a working cancel button. Report 24 (43,469 reviews): the largest theme in the corpus — 5,791 core billing disputes (13.32%, mean 1.110, 94.2% 1★; 52.4% of all 1★; 38% of 2024–26) — follows mechanically from selling the subscription through a web checkout (Chargebee; 'Fabulous SAS' on statements): it is invisible in Apple Subscriptions, cancelling in the App Store does nothing, Apple cannot refund it, and the user is routed to a 250-character web form with no phone; 212 escalated to their bank, the BBB, the FTC or a lawyer. The failure is dated — quarterly rate 5.4% (2023Q1) → 12.0% (Q4) → 33.1% (2024Q4) → ~50% from 2025Q2 — and an earlier 2018–19 episode was fixed in one month (Dec 2019: 12.7% → 2.6%, mean 2.884 → 4.206), so it is recoverable. Reviews that mention money average 2.006; those that do not, 4.356. Report 33: web purchases through Paddle did not unlock the iPhone (18 days; 6+ weeks) and had no in-app cancel; refunds were routed to Apple and then refused ('denied a refund due to the company's arrangement with Apple'). Report 59 (Tappsk): the one case where off-store billing was forced (App Store payments blocked for Russian users from 2022-03) shows the cost: the direct-card route is praised by those who wanted to pay (54 of 74 payment-route reviews are 5★) but produces charges after deletion and a subscription the phone cannot show or cancel ('После отмены подписки приложение каждый раз пытается списать с карты средства' — after cancelling, the app keeps trying to charge the card) — if an off-store route is unavoidable, it needs in-app cancellation and bounded retries ([[C232]]). Report 67 (Habio): a web quiz funnel from Instagram / Facebook ads sold subscriptions billed off-store — MON_OFFSTORE 137 (6.68%) 'not displayed in the AppStore and the receipt comes directly from Habio'; 'even after you delete the app you will still be charged $50 every 180 days unless you redownload the app and cancel through there'; MON_WEB_FUNNEL 30 paid on the website before installing; the listing still says payment is 'charged to iTunes Account' and cancellable in Account Settings; web purchases were not linked to app accounts so buyers could not restore ('couldn't find any purchase history'); U_CANCEL_TRAP 597 (29.11%, mean 1.03); off-store complaints 13.81% of the 2023-07 → 2024-02 era. Report 68 (Ultiself): the same chain across 87 storefronts — purchase on a website or in-funnel Apple Pay / PayPal / card → not in Apple's subscription list → the in-app 'Manage subscription' button opens Apple's list anyway (BUG_MANAGE_SUB 60, from 2025-03-14: 'button directs to the App Store, but the actual subscription is handled outside via their website, to which access is blocked') → email-only cancellation → retention offers or silence → the charge recurs; MON_WEB_BILLING 303 (6.72%), 26.3% of Belarus reviews (two of its reviews are the most-voted complaints: 'DOES NOT show their active subscription'); U_BILLING_COMPLAINT 1,434 (31.79%, mean 1.12) in 88.2% of 1–2★; the listing says only 'charged to your iTunes account… Monthly and Yearly'; §8.1: route Manage subscription to wherever the subscription is billed and add in-app cancellation for web subscriptions. Report 76 (Way of Life): 'This is not a Free app with in-app purchases. This is a $7 app' (1★) — the free listing with a 3-item cap is read as a mislabelled paid app by some. Report 82 (Lasting Change): the subscription is sold on the developer's website and charged to card / PayPal / bank — the listing's own metadata reads hasInAppPurchases: false while its description says 'Payment is charged to your App Store account'; a reviewer quotes the seller's terms: 'subscriptions will not appear on apple or google if purchased through the website'; consequences — it cannot be cancelled in iOS Settings (CANCEL_NO_PATH 27, 15.43%), Apple cannot refund it (36 refusals, zero Apple refunds), 17 discovered the charge from a bank statement, 7 blocked their card or closed the account, 16 escalated to a chargeback, FTC, FCC, BBB or trading standards; 'Apple thankfully denied all three of their attempts'. Report 88 (GetHabit): from June 2021 purchases and trials moved to a website reached from Instagram or Facebook ads, billed by card or PayPal outside the App Store (BILL_WEB_CHECKOUT 19, first 2021-06-03) — in that era unwanted charges 47.7%, charged without choosing 39.8%, could not cancel 25.0%; 'checked Apple's subscriptions to be safe — it wasn't there; still a 30 € PayPal debit' (de); 'the only way to cancel your subscription is through mail' (fr); 8 of 19 web buyers could not get the purchase into the app ('cannot use the premium offer, it's asking me to pay again'); §8.3 if web checkout is used, link it to an account that unlocks the app, bill under the app's own name, put a self-serve cancel link in every receipt.

<a id="c262"></a>
### C262 — Never gate a recovery action — back-dating a missed day, undoing a wrong entry and restoring history stay free forever

**Certain** · 8 apps · 22 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 6 apps

*Why Certain:* 8 apps, same direction (act on it, 80%), 3 reports label it high-priority

Report 47: back-dating is a trust feature (it makes the streak honest) and charging for it reads as charging to undo the app's own penalty — the backfill-demand union is 52 reviews (8.83%: check off a past day 22, a start date before creation 21, the 2024 gate 9), named in the very first review in the corpus (Feb 2019); it shipped 29 March 2020 (the most-voted review, 23 votes: '日付を遡ってチェックインできるようになってました！！！') and the request fell from 7.1% of 2019–21 reviews to 0.7%; then in April–June 2024 it was put behind a video ad and produced 9 reviews at mean 1.67 ('¥200 a month to log past days is too much') alongside the 2024 exits. The rule the report draws: every purchase trigger reviewers name is additive (AI coach, photos, stats, sync) and none asks to pay to restore something that used to be free — recovery actions are the one surface where a gate is read as extortion. Related: [[C010]] (backfill is a free feature), [[C176]], [[C204]]. Report 52: 32 reviews say restoring their own data after a crash-reinstall required buying membership — 'after reinstalling I bought lifetime membership to restore my data, and restoring crashed the app'; F3: never gate restoring a user's own backup. Report 57: backup and restore gated behind Premium while 12 users lost data — §8.2: 'Gating recovery behind a purchase converts a bug into a grievance'; at minimum an automatic local export or a one-time free restore after detected loss. Report 65 (Rabit): premium took previous-day marking in Nov 2020, and when the app falsely marked completed days as missed a reviewer concluded it was deliberate — 'the app marks completed days as missed so you will buy the subscription that lets you edit past days… Tática desleal' — the perception is a monetization cost even where the cause is a bug. Report 69 (TheFor): back-fill of forgotten days praised in 2023 ('you can edit habits from past dates!!') and reported gated in 2024 by a user who then left. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): 'Nice but to greedy — You don t let me modifie my habits whitout paying, serios!' (2★) — the only attestation that editing an existing board is gated, 'a sharper paywall than the 3-board cap alone'. Report 83 (Roubit): checking off yesterday's routine requires watching an ad (ADS_FOR_PAST_CHECK 4, since 2022: 'making me watch an ad for each record just to check off the previous day is very inconvenient'); when the ad would not load for a month, past tasks could not be completed and the user uninstalled (jp 3★); §8.4 'let yesterday's routine be completed without an ad; if an ad cannot load, complete anyway. Keep rewards, not records, ad-gated.'

<a id="c271"></a>
### C271 — One membership at one price across every platform the app ships on — never sell the same entitlement twice or price it differently by store

**Certain** · 8 apps · 20 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 6 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Certain:* 8 apps, same direction (act on it, 94%), 4 reports label it high-priority

Report 52 (ShineDay / 小日常): the membership is sold separately on Android and iOS, at different prices and with different logins (QQ on Android, WeChat on iOS) — 49 reviews combine an Android mention with a tier or restore failure (mean 2.80); 'only after buying did I find Android membership must be bought separately'; 'iOS lifetime 88, Android 48? Where's the justice' (Feb 2026); the iOS free quota was also tighter than Android's ('on Android I could add a dozen, why treat us differently?'). PAY_TIERS carries the highest payer lift in the corpus (×5.11). Report's M5: price parity or a single cross-platform membership (platform-fee constraints noted). Related: [[C251]] (platform parity), [[C033]] (restore), [[C035]] (account). Report 54: a buyer on Google Play had to pay again on the App Store (ES, 2023). Report 59 (Tappsk): the Mac app shipped 2020-06 and was sold separately from iPhone Premium — MON_PER_DEVICE 59 ('is it paid for those who already have premium?'), its peak 0.8% of that era; later reviewers describe Mac sync as part of Premium. Report 65 (Rabit): an Android build exists but does not bridge — 'a opção de restaurar só acontece de celular androide para androide'; an Android→iPhone payer could not restore and got no reply; another could not find the sign-in button on iPhone. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): a one-time purchase that will not move between iOS devices or from Android to iOS while the listing promises cross-device and cross-OS backup. Report 76 (Way of Life): MON_PAID_TWICE 3 — 'you have to pay for each iPhone or iPad you use' (1★); MON_FAMILY_SHARING 3. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): 'Pagué por la versión premium pero no puedo usarla en mis dos celulares' (1★, titled 'Estafa') — a paid entitlement unusable on the buyer's second device; a Family SKU exists yet no review mentions Family Sharing. Report 89 (Check Calendar): PLATFORM_PRICE_GAP 2, both January 2026 — 'Why is the iPhone app paid? And only gives you a week-long trial, while it's free on Android?'; a Uruguayan reviewer paid on iPhone after using it free on Android and still gave five stars — the gap is a complaint on one platform and a purchase on the other.

<a id="c003"></a>
### C003 — Lead with a one-time lifetime purchase — and keep it visibly on the shelf if a subscription is ever added beside it

**Strong** · 56 apps · 315 cards · positive in 34 apps · negative in 37 apps · tied to a purchase in 33 apps

*Why Strong:* 56 apps, directions mixed (act 118, paid 108, open 42)

People buy because it is not a subscription; lifetime is the strongest pricing signal. Report 13: 239 reviews across every year 2017–2026, including 5★ ones ('It would be better to charge only once. It would attract more users, trust me'), asked for the one-time purchase back after it was withdrawn. Report 14: a $1.99–$3 one-time unlock produced zero refund, unexpected-charge or restore complaints in 70 reviews — a materially cleaner record than the subscription apps in the set. Report 16: the price fell ~67% ($119.99 → $40/yr) and the objection rate did not move (31% → 30%); 37 reviews asked for a one-time SKU and Streaks was named eight times, every time for its one-time price — 'I will not rent a checklist'. Report 17 (contested): a $64.99 lifetime beside a $19.99 annual — 3.25 years of payback demanded up front from a developer with an abandonment history — drew 'three times the price of a premium word processor'; the lifetime option must be credible, not just present. Report 18: 34 lifetime buyers averaged 4.12★ against 3.53 for all payers; nine reviewers rejected the subscription outright and asked for a one-time purchase; the report's recommendation is to keep the lifetime tier and protect its entitlement absolutely. Report 20: 35 reviews praised a pay-what-you-want one-time model at mean 4.83 ('£4.99 to say thank you, £6.98 for liking the app and £14.99 for loving it'); after the subscription switch 26 reviewers walked to Streaks explicitly because it is a one-time purchase ('even though I like this app better'); stated willingness clustered at $5–15 one-time, and the report's recommendation is a $15–25 lifetime unlock with legacy buyers grandfathered free. Report 23: a paid-up-front one-time tracker where 'no subscription' praise (398, 5.47%, mean 4.43) rose 3.61% → 5.55% → 8.00% across eras as the category subscription-ised — the one competitive position that strengthened; 'worth it' outnumbered 'not worth it' 3.2:1, and an entire cohort arrived after a competitor revoked already-purchased premium features. Report 25: the lifetime option is a stated purchase driver (44 mentions, 3.36%, mean 3.95; 8 name it as the deciding factor — 'you dont have to do subscription stuff thank you'); subscription fatigue is explicit in German ('One-time payment €50 or subscription. No, on principle'), French and US reviews; one Brazilian buyer could not find the lifetime option and thought only monthly existed. Report 26: one-time pricing is a repeatedly praised differentiator in a calm-aesthetic tracker — 57 (mean 4.18) defend the price, most because it is not a subscription, and 11 name it as the purchase trigger; the lifetime option survived the 2022 restructure ($25) but rose to €40 by 2026. Report 27 (the limiting case): a tracker with no price at all — 47 reviews (34.06%) name 'free / no IAP / no subscription' in a register of relief and disbelief ('How is this free?'; 'In a world where literally every service is locked behind a pay wall, this is like a breath of fresh air'); the free position is the acquisition channel, and the only monetisation the corpus endorses is a voluntary tip jar. Report 29: the one explicit payment offer in a free app is 'please add widget support happy to pay for a lifetime subscription' — lifetime, attached to a new capability; the report's proposed test is a one-time Pro unlock for widget + dark mode + flexible frequency that touches nothing existing users have. Report 31: 27 E1 reviewers (mean 4.78) chose Done because it wasn't a subscription ('happily paid the one-time fee because many other programs are switching to a subscription'), 13 later reviews leave for Streaks because it still is one-time, and one-time pricing praise went 2.9% (E1) → 0 in every later era; the report recommends offering a genuine one-time lifetime price alongside monthly and annual and testing all three on conversion and 1★ rate. Report 33: a lifetime option restored in Apr 2019 alongside monthly and annual is the most-cited purchase trigger (112 payers, mean 3.62; 'Habitify allows you to unlock all premium features with a 1 time in-app purchase of $10'; 'you'll pay double in a year for some other similar apps'); E2, when lifetime coexisted with a stable app, is the payer high (mean 3.77) and price praise never fell (1.9% → 3.2%) — rivals that only rent are named as the reason people chose Habitify; the report says keep it and publish what lifetime includes. Report 34: a $5–9 one-off (2018–19) gave the highest payer share of any era (18.9% of E1 reviews vs 3.9–8.4% later); lifetime (~$40) beside ~$20/yr and ~$9/mo is praised by 15 (mean 4.87) — 'I hate subscriptions so I paid for lifetime … as an investment'; 'you only pay once which is refreshing in the current year' — and is a US differentiator (3.02% vs 1.46%). Report 36: subscription-only for 4.7 years — SUB- 35 (6.48%, mean 2.60, ~6% every era) and ONETIME 24 (4.44%, mean 3.42, only one 1★), volunteering £5, $20–30, €5–7.99, ¥50 and ~$100 ('I would be more than happy to pay for it outright, but that is not an option. So, I'm not gonna be paying anything at all'); a ¥398 one-time price appeared in China in Aug 2026. Report 41: Lifetime Premium ($22.99 beside $4.99/mo and $12.99/yr) is the most-cited commercial feature — 81 reviews (9.94%, mean 4.70, 67 at 5★) and the top purchase trigger: 'Thank you very much for providing a single purchase option. It is much appreciated in the sea of subscriptions'; 'the option to pay once makes this a no-brainer'; zero US subscription objections with lifetime mentioned by 14.4% of US reviewers; a lost sale when it was not visible at the moment of friction ('It's been deleted and I've bought an app that just has one payment'). Report 42 (absence): no lifetime tier — seven concurrent subscription SKUs at $4.99–$59.99; the only explicit lifetime request is 'Нет перманентной, только подписка на год'. Report 43: a single one-time unlock ($2.99 → $4.99) with no subscription in 638 reviews over ten years — monetisation praise (89, 13.95%, mean 4.70) outnumbers all monetisation friction (87) and is rated 2.25 stars higher, the only corpus in the series with that shape; the one-time model is the dominant purchase trigger ('If it was going to be a subscription app I was not going to bother'; 'one wanted 13 dollars a year, while another wanted 7 dollars upfront. I only paid a small $4'); a payer volunteered to pay annually to fund maintenance — the report's shape for recurring revenue is an optional supporter tier, not a gate. Report 46: the one-time ask (53, 6.99% of 2018–20 reviews) was answered with a $99.99 lifetime in May 2021 and fell to 0.68%, while 'lifetime price too high' rose from nothing to 27 (2.02% of the second half); reviewers converge on $30–70 ('I have never seen someone charge more than $30 for it… happy to pay $30'; 'Would probably buy it lifetime if it was 30 or less'; 'asking for almost $100 for lifetime is GREEDY'; '69.99 and I probably would have paid'; '¥30 elsewhere, ¥328 here — I don't dare buy it in case it disappears'); 16 bought lifetime (mean 4.56: 'now there is a lifetime option, so I bought it straight away'); non-English storefronts ask to own it outright 2.1× more, China 4.5× — the report's E1 is a $49 / $69 lifetime test. Report 47: one-time purchase wanted 4 (2022–25: 'opção de comprar vitalícia, sem ser por assinatura'; '買い切り版が出たら検討しますが、とりあえず乗り換えます'), ad-removal-for-a-one-time-fee asked 2019–23 ('一度払い切りで広告を消すことができたら嬉しい'), and a 2026 lifetime price called 'so expensive it's funny' against ¥600 → ¥14,800 listing items; the report's E1 is an ad-free lifetime in Japan priced against the annual plan. Report 48: 58 want a one-time purchase (several naming $10–$20), 48 reject subscriptions in principle, and 28 accept the model but call a $79.99–$149.99 lifetime 'disproportionate for a tracker' (mean 2.46; China frames it as a quarter of a second-hand iPhone); 23 payers name a lifetime purchase (mean 4.52); reviewers who leave for Habitify cite 'one time $10 and comparable features'. Report 49: prefers a one-time purchase 23 (1.87%); a 66-day programme sold as a 12-month subscription is itself an objection (15). Report 50: a lifetime tier existed ('Love that there is a lifetime membership so I don't have to pay monthly', Aug 2025) but later reviewers ask for one as if absent — 'I would like purchase a lifetime access subscription for this' (4★, Nov 2025) — withdrawn or undiscoverable; the report's S2: make it discoverable; subscription-model objectors 4 (mean 2.00). Report 52: a lifetime option drives the strongest payer segment (PAY_LIFETIME lift ×7.39, 199 lifetime buyers at 4.36; 'one time purchase instead of a subscription'); lifetime was withdrawn for subscriptions in 2020 and re-offered at ¥88; honoured lifetime memberships produce the highest-mean theme above 100 reviews (DEV_TRUST 213, 4.93 — 'it said: you are a lifetime member. I nearly cried'). Report 53: 'because unlike many apps you don't need a subscription, you just pay once' (de, 19 votes); PAY_ONETIME lift 3.40 among payers and none after Jul 2023 once only an annual plan was offered; report's M2 — offer lifetime again beside the annual plan. Report 54: a one-time lifetime Pro with 14 advocates at mean 4.93 and zero detractors of the model — 'I love the honesty of a pricier lifetime membership versus the subscription model that so many extortionists are using now'; 'subscriptions totally stress me out' (DE); D2: do not move to a subscription. Report 55: 'Premium worth it' was said while premium was one-time (22 of 27 PAY_WORTH predate June 2018) and vanished after; reviewers repeatedly name $5–$10 one-time as what they would pay ('Would I pay a one-time fee of $5, absolutely, but a yearly fee, nope!'); M1: a lifetime option beside the subscription. Report 57: a one-time lifetime Premium (₩9,900 → ₩29,000; ¥1,600 → ¥4,500; $13 → $30–35) was the purchase reason for 8 (4.875, 6 non-Korean, 4 US — 'Better than the apps that charge hundreds of dollars a year'; 'charging monthly for a simple calendar or diary seems abusive'), then a subscription appeared in 2025–26 and a lifetime buyer was asked to subscribe ('DO NOT BUY IT'). Report 59 (Tappsk): the lifetime unlock is the monetization asset of a 15,176-review app — 396 of 1,090 stated purchases name it (36.3% of purchasers, 12.82× lift), MON_ONETIME_PRAISE 93 against MON_SUBSCRIPTION objections 23 ('the reverse of most habit apps'), MON_VALUE 465 at 4.93★ ('спасибо разработчикам за отсутсвие подписки'; '5€ de por vida que es lo que te cobran las demás al mes' — €5 for life, what the others charge per month); Germany praises the one-time option at 2.95×; the seasonal discount is what sells it (MON_DISCOUNT 129 of purchasers, 8.02× — 'дождался скидку и купил премиум навсегда'; an offer popped up 'с хорошей скидкой, не задумываясь взял') and the free cap barely does (13 purchasers cite it); buying to support the developer is a stated trigger (MON_DONATE_WISH 18). Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): a one-time option was requested in Apr 2025 and a lifetime purchase reported in Jun 2026 — probably added in between; 'if it exists and is still being asked for, that is discoverability, not roadmap' (M4: surface the lifetime SKU more prominently). Report 64 (Critique AI): 'you might as well just sell your app instead of using subscriptions' — PAY_TIERS 21 (5.01%, mean 1.48) ask for tiers, one-off, monthly split or a teen tier; no lifetime SKU is visible. Report 65 (Rabit): a $40 lifetime tier existed by 2024 and was praised ('I love how affordable it is to get Rabit Plus for $40, which last forever!') while 2023 reviewers still asked for a one-time purchase as though it did not — 'Uma pena a versão paga ser assinatura mensal… se fosse compra única com certeza adquiria' — M2: 'Discoverability, not creation'; two lifetime purchases were blocked by missing notifications. Report 67 (Habio): a $49.99 lifetime unlock is listed but no reviewer says they bought it; 'consideren una que sea de un único pago o Lifetime, anima más a los usuarios'. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): the add-on moved from a one-off ¥960–980 (2017–2021) to monthly (first described 2022-05-15) — 'it seems it used to be a one-off purchase and has changed to monthly, which is a shame'; 'a one-time purchase option would be nice too'; explicit purchases fell from 3.7% to 1.6% of reviews across that change (directional). Report 72 (Habit Hearts): the listing sells Monthly $3.99 and Yearly $14.99 beside Lifetime, but buyers describe and repeat the one-time unlock — 'Not subscription based. But once keep forever.'; 'бонусом подписка за 899₽ навсегда'; 'Pour 9,99€ à vie, franchement j'aime beaucoup' (PAY_ONETIME 7, 4.71) — and nobody describes a renewal or cancellation. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): the paid tier is a single buy-once SKU ($4.99 / ¥780 today; reported ¥600 → ¥800 → ¥1,000) and the 20 self-stated buyers average 4.15 and name the one-time model — PAY_ONETIME_PRAISE 14 (4.71): 'I hate apps that require a subscription… Best 3.99 I've ever spent'; 「Så skönt att det går att köpa appen för en engångssumma!!!」; 1 of 151 objects to the amount against 23 objecting to how it was revealed; no refund, cancellation or regret exists — 'Keep the one-time price; stop hiding it'. Report 76 (Way of Life): a $4.99 one-time unlock sustained a 4.62★ corpus for 13 years — MON_VALUE 342 (4.40%, mean 4.90★): 'it is a one time charge and it unlocks the full capabilities of the app'; 84.2% of 349 self-reported purchasers rate 4–5★; after the 2023 switch reviewers still ask for it: 'happy to pay up to £50 even for lifetime access' (3★), 'I'm not paying a yearly subscription'; §8.6 experiment: a published lifetime price alongside the subscription, measuring purchase mix and 1★ share among new users. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): a lifetime SKU is the only monetization attribute anyone in the corpus praises by name ('The one time purchase rather than a subscription model is also a lovely thing', 5★, who intends to buy 'the moment I can afford it'); a 2★ whose entire text is 'there is no possibility to get a lifetime version of subscription'; MON_SUB_FATIGUE 2 at 1.50★ ('This subscription fanaticism is getting out of hand'); §8.1.3 'if a lifetime SKU exists, say so'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): MON_ONETIME_PRAISE 12 (6.98%, 4.67★), 9 in year one — 'the premium subscription is a one time 10 dollar payment is incredible'; 'in comparison to other habit trackers that are subscription based'; 'best of all — it's a one time purchase!!'; 7 of 12 frame it as the reason to choose this app over rivals; the listing then added Plus Monthly $2.99 / Yearly $9.99 beside a $24.99 lifetime and the corpus records the arrival ('Nutteloos zonder subscriptie'; 'after a while it turns out I have to pay a monthly subscription'); §8.6 E5 lifetime-forward paywall: show Lifetime first and measure whether the 'no subscription' audience converts higher. Report 83 (Roubit): WANT_ONE_TIME_PURCHASE 6 (1.20%: 'a subscription feels like slavery', kr; 'どうしても買い切りが欲しい', jp); Korean users anchor a routine-app subscription against a one-time game — 'Animal Crossing is ₩50,000 for life; a routine app is ₩55,000 a year… the first app where I'm upset that I can't bring myself to pay' (5★); §8.5 test a lifetime or long-term plan and a student price against the yearly ₩55,000. (Consolidation after report 83: title widened from 'Lead with a one-time lifetime purchase' to cover what happens to the lifetime SKU once a subscription is introduced; the original evidence stays in the statement.) Report 84 (HabitGrid): the only payment model any reviewer proposes for a free app is a one-time purchase ('or at least that there will be an option to buy it once!'); zero volunteer a subscription; two reject subscription pricing for the category. Report 85 (Habitica): 'I'd gladly pay $10-$15 for the full program but nickel and diming users is off-putting' — a one-off wanted instead of subscription + consumable gems. Report 86 (Today): a one-time ~$4.99 unlock (2016–~2021) was praised as the reason to choose the app — PR_ONETIME 23 (4.61★), U:pro_pricing 124 (6.95%, 4.75★): 'Paying once (4.99) for all these features is the prime reason I use this app as a Habit Tracker compared to others'; 'some apps out there have a yearly subscription circa £30… this one is a steal at £5'; MON_DEFEND 44 argue against other reviewers' price complaints; the model was then replaced (~2022) by $3.99/month, $9.99/year and a $299.99 'All premium features' tier — MON_SUBSCRIPTION 8, all post-2022, none positive. Report 89 (Check Calendar): a single 'Premium (Pay Once)' SKU at $4.99 / ¥780 — PAY_ONCE_PRAISE 10 (4.60★: 'really great that payment is one-time'; 'an ad-free version for a few bucks without subscription!'), PRICE_FAIR 14 ('it's one-time $4, people! A cup of coffee!'; 'by far the cheapest'); buyers name the one-time model as the reason ('it's a one-time purchase, so I bought the paid version'; 'buying outright felt better'); 15 of the 20 price-positive reviews are five-star — 'the one-time price is part of what earns the top rating'; §8.9 do not add a subscription — believers already rate it 2.20★ ([[C305]]). Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): ad removal is sold only as a monthly ($0.99 / 99 ₽) or yearly ($9.99 / 699 ₽) subscription, and the objection is the format — 'sad you can't switch ads off for life' (kz); 'you should add a lifetime purchase; I want to buy' (vn, 5★); §8.6 add a one-time 'remove ads forever' purchase beside the plans and measure the purchase rate and one-star 'paid app' reviews in Russia. (Consolidation after report 90: see [[C305]] — a one-time price only earns its goodwill if it is labelled as one; report 89's five subscription-believers rate the same one-time app 2.20★ against 4.60★ for readers who understood it.)
