<a id="c004"></a>
### C004 — Price low and fair, anchored against subscription competitors

**Strong** · 31 apps · 85 cards · positive in 22 apps · negative in 13 apps · tied to a purchase in 15 apps

*Why Strong:* 31 apps, directions mixed (paid 26, act 19, open 16)

'Cheaper than a coffee' framing produces near-perfect ratings; know the price anchors users cite. Report 23: the one-time price rose ~2.5× nominal over eleven years ($3.99 → $9.99) and the objection rate stayed flat (1.75% → 2.41% → 2.21%); objections are feature-per-dollar and paired with the cap or 'Reminders does this free', never the number itself. Report 25: the lifetime price roughly doubled ($24.99 → $49) between early 2024 and mid-2025 and price objection stayed flat (3.8% → 4.9% → 3.8%); 64 reviews (mean 4.31) call the price cheap or fair ('less than 30 euros for life'; 'Premium is 1000% worth it'). Report 26: lifetime moved $5–7 (2021) → $25 (late 2022) → €40 (2026) — roughly 5× — while price objection stayed the smallest of the four monetisation objections (29, 0.76%); the €40 point 'risks spending' goodwill. Report 28: a $6.98 skin, $9.99–$14.99 consumable packs; 'Study bunny costs like $15-20 so the price could go up for this one too… kind of uncool'. Report 31: 119 price-praise reviews (mean 3.82), 63 of them E1 (6.7% of the era): 'I'm only paying to support the developers'; 'a one-time charge is a lot less exploitative, and doesn't come with the same guilt'; 'Best $8.99 spent in a long time!' — price praise fell 6.7% → 0.7–1.7% after the subscription. Report 33: 99 price-praise reviews (mean 4.85, zero 1★) — 'permanent premium is only equal to other apps' annual fee'; 'I would have paid triple'; 'the best £30 I ever spent'. Report 34: price fair / worth it 34 (4.58%, mean 4.91; US 6.79% vs 3.35%) — 'I never buy apps. This is worth it … Take it from a penny pincher'; the price objection (25, mean 3.16) anchors against an indie game ($5–25) and Netflix. Report 36: $14.99/yr was anchored as 'less than a quarter of the price for competitor habit trackers' (4 of 34 payers); the price objection is about ratio to substance ('$15 for permission to buy a $10 skin. Scam!'), and by 2026 prices of $59–70 met 'the demographic which can drop 60$ on a reminder app'. Report 41: positioned as the value option by 6 reviews ('My favourite app was Strides but I refused to pay the almost £80 premium'; 'die schönste und günstigste') against 1 calling it expensive; 'It is worth the absolutely fair (!) price of only 25 euros for the lifetime version'. Report 43: price / value praised by 57 (8.93%, mean 4.89) — 'I've tried 3 other apps that ranged from $25 to $60 per year'; 'Others… will charge double the one time payment for this as a monthly subscription!'; 'accessible to super low income people like myself'; value praise rose 3.98% → 11.04% → 10.39% by era even as the price rose $2.99 → $4.99, because the alternatives moved to subscription. Report 46: a subscription priced against 'simple' invites 'simple things should be cheap' — '$4.99 a month is too much to ask for the ability to electronically check a box'; 'essentially a checkbox $30 (a year)'; benchmarked against Spotify, Lightroom, 200 GB iCloud + Office, 1Password, Notion; price objections 163 (7.48%, mean 2.84) spiking with each rise ($12 → $30/yr in 2020: 'Most of the worth it reviews reflect the original pricing'; $7.49 / $29.99 / $99.99 in 2023) and fading to 4 in 2026; payers justify the price by outcome ('$29/year for what this app is giving me in terms of mental health is an absolute steal'), non-payers by comparison. Report 47: price is rarely the objection but the shape is — 'このシンプルなアプリに月額320円は高い' ('¥320 a month is too much for an app this simple'); a Korean reviewer would pay about ₩9,000 once for stats, sync and iPad (2020); ¥200/month to log past days (Apr 2024) was refused. Report 48: price complaints fell from 21.43% of the 2015 conversion era to 4.69% of 2022–26 — 'pricing anger has migrated from "too expensive" to "I can't try it"'; Canada (9.47%), Australia (9.68%), Germany (10.92%) and China (10.96%) are the price-sensitive storefronts; 73 say it is worth it at 4.97★. Report 49: 'too expensive' (113, 1.65) is flat-to-rising while 'not worth it' (55) collapses 6.8% → 1.4% — 'reviewers increasingly accept that the product delivers, while continuing to object to what it costs'; 39 defend the price at 4.74 ('Yeah, You Have to Pay. Yeah, it's Worth it'); ten live price points from $12.99 to $59.99 under two product names. Report 50: payers judge the price low for the category ('relatively low compared to similar services'; 'Honestly would pay more for this'); price objectors 3 (a French student: '2,99€/month would be fair'); quoted $5 / €5.99 / ≈$2.99 monthly and $14.99–$20 yearly. Report 52: payers find the price fair (PAY_PRICE_OK 256 at 4.86, payer lift ×4.58; 'less than a Starbucks for a good mood every day', 54 votes) about as often as non-payers call it too high (254 at 3.28); outside mainland China price is praised, not resisted (US PAY_PRICE_OK 23 outnumbers every price complaint combined). Report 53: payers who talk about price mostly call it fair (PAY_PRICE_OK 47 at 4.79, payer lift 3.95; 'RAISE YOUR PRICES… I would genuinely pay more'), then the praise vanished (2 reviews from 2023) when an annual $39.99 plan replaced a ~$8–20 one-time unlock. Report 54: price fair 16 (4.69) against too high 16 (2.75), the objections clustered in lower-ARPU storefronts (CN, TW, PH, TR, CO: 9 of 16); US price sentiment net positive 21 to 1. Report 55: a $3.99–$4.99 one-time premium ('I got Premium, was worth $4') became ~$19.99/yr in June 2018 — 'about 400% increase in price'; 40 of 42 price complaints date from the switch. Report 57: price_too_high 20 — 14 non-Korean (8.05%) vs 6 Korean (0.99%); Japan 7 of 26 (26.92%) after ¥1,600 → ¥4,500 ('I was going to buy at around ¥300'); reviewers name ¥2,000 and 'under ₩20,000'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): a $10 one-time price was named as the reason to choose the app over subscription rivals; at €23 the same product loses a supporter-motivated buyer ('23 Euro sind doch recht viel für eine einzelne App mit einer Funktion') while ten others still call it fair — the objection is the multiple, not the level. Report 83 (Roubit): PRICE_TOO_HIGH 10 (2.00%), eight in Korea, anchored on the yearly price (₩39,000 in 2023, ₩55,000 from 2024) and against one-time games; PRICE_FAIR 2 ('honestly isn't that bad at 7.99'); 'about $60/yr' while an ad still plays on every task completion (4★).

<a id="c222"></a>
### C222 — A hard habit cap is a defensible design position only with an opt-in pressure valve — the default never changes

**Strong** · 17 apps · 60 cards · positive in 9 apps · negative in 10 apps · tied to a purchase in 2 apps

*Why Strong:* 17 apps, directions mixed (open 25, act 21, paid 1)

Report 23: a paid one-time tracker capped at 6 → 12 → 24 tasks drew the largest request in twelve years (620, 8.53%) in every market and every year; each raise cut the complaint rate roughly in half (8.76% → 5.06%; 11.90% → 6.16%) and bought about three years before it rebounded, and it never fell below ~6%. Against it 118 (1.62%) defend the cap as the reason the app works, and nobody in the 620 asks for the default to change — they ask for the ceiling to move. The cap is a durable position and a permanent 6–12% complaint tax; ship extra capacity off by default behind a setting that states the rationale. Report 24 (the same principle from the coaching side): the product's real moat is a refusal — it declines to let users add more habits; small-steps pacing is the highest-rated theme of any size in 43,469 reviews (1,817, mean 4.692, 2.0% 1★; 'I stacked everything I wanted to change and failed miserably; this time I followed the program'), and the same constraint produces the four complaint shapes ('I already do this' 124, 'it ignored my answers' 175, 'too slow' 168, 'doesn't fit my week' 31). The corpus asks for one branch — declare a habit already-held and start at habit two — not for the constraint to go. Report 25: 19 reviewers (mean 4.32) defend a 3-habit free cap on principle ('helps me to only keep track of what is the most important to me') while 138 object — and the objectors name the number they would accept, median 8–10. Report 26 (the reward side): the cap is 3→5→6 habits plus a growth ceiling; users who love the constraint-free gentleness still say five slots cannot hold a routine, and propose their own valve — one full garden free. Report 46: 66 reviewers (3.03%, mean 4.92) defend a 3-habit cap on habit-science grounds ('shouldn't be tracking more than three in the first place'; 'the limit is beneficial since it kept me from piling expectations onto myself') while the counter-offer is 4–7 — the defensible cap is disclosed and framed as focus. Report 47: a user proposes buying slots — 'タブ数だけ買わせてください' ('let me buy just the number of tabs I need', 4★, 2025); the report's E2 is a per-slot purchase for free users at the cap. Report 48: the pressure valve reviewers propose is a cheap, narrow tier that only unlocks trackers — pay once for capacity, subscribe for sync / reports (58 one-time requesters, $10–$20); 15 ask to raise the free cap. Report 49: 40 want a free tier, ads or donations instead of a hard paywall (several volunteering heavy advertising); an Indian reviewer proposes 3–5 free habits with premium above — a report experiment. Report 59 (Tappsk): the cap held at 2 habits for five years generates a steady 4.4–5.1% objection per era with no sign of decay; three is the number reviewers repeatedly propose as enough to evaluate. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): a fixed cap of 3, unchanged over 17 months, produces a steady trickle of cap reviews from otherwise satisfied users; the report's alternative to a raise is a time-limited 4th habit — a pressure valve rather than a moved wall. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): the purest defended cap — one goal at a time, free, by design (US listing: 'the app only allows you to set one goal at a time'); praised by 148 (6.46%, mean 4.87) and 28 (ONE_GOAL_CONVERT) say they resented it and came to agree ('At first I was saying let me add another goal!, but as I kept going I came to think this is how it should be'); the request for more (REQ_MULTI 44, mean 4.39) is growing (4.7% of 2025–26) and is narrower than 'many habits' — keep a completed habit while starting the next; reviewers volunteer the valve themselves: unlock a second goal only after a first 30-day cycle. Report 76 (Way of Life): the 3-item cap is defended by users as a focusing device (#7013, #4439, #6073) and §8.8 says keep it; the objection never went away (every era) but fell from 6.1% (E3) to 1.5% (E6). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): at one habit the cap is 'an aggressive but coherent strategy' whose cost side is precise (2.50★ from those who hit it) and whose conversion effect is unmeasured; the decision should be made 'on strategy grounds, not on review grounds'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the 3-board cap was tolerated ('Man kann aber auch gut ohne Leben'; 'without huge limitations') while widgets were free and rejected ('totaal niks') once they were not — the pressure valve here was the free widget, and removing it is what broke the cap. Research: Feature Gating vs Quantity.md — the calibration window a cap has to hit if one is used at all: 'if the cap is set too low, new users hit it before forming a habit and churn; if too high, they never hit it and never pay', with the stated target that a typical engaged user meets the cap after about 30 days. Set against ~66-day habit automaticity, that window is narrow, and the 3-5 caps shipped in this category fall far below it.

**Reports:** [23](<../App Store Reports/23. Streaks - The habit-forming to-do list (REPORT).md>), [24](<../App Store Reports/24. <a id="c204"></a>
### C204 — Never destroy user work at the paywall

**Strong** · 5 apps · 7 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 4 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Strong:* 5 apps, same direction (act on it, 100%)

Report 18: two users each spent an hour building routines, were asked to pay to save them, and lost the work anyway. Work the user has already done is never the hostage of a purchase sheet — save it, then ask. (The labelling half of the original point — 'reviewers cannot tell what they are buying' — lives on C110 and C218, to which the same cards are attached.) Report 53: reviewers over the free limit hit the paywall when editing an existing habit. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): months of check-ins and memos made unreadable at the paywall; setup effort framed as deliberate sunk cost (TRL_WASTED_SETUP 4, all 1★). Report 89 (Check Calendar): locked records are one of the seven upgrade barriers named and the one that removes the clean exit — 'Records locked, so no way to leave cleanly' (PAY_DATA_LOCKED 8); the same records are what converted two reluctant buyers (PURCHASE_LOCKIN: 'didn't want to pay, but had already entered records, so bought').

<a id="c213"></a>
### C213 — If you position on ADHD or executive-function help, cancellation must be the easiest flow in the product

**Strong** · 5 apps · 15 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 4 apps

*Why Strong:* 5 apps, same direction (act on it, 100%)

Report 19: 13 of 105 (12.38%) accused the product of targeting people with ADHD because they will forget to cancel — 'preying on ADHDers they know may not remember to cancel'; friction a neurotypical user calls annoying this audience calls predatory, because the marketing itself asserts they cannot complete multi-step tasks. The ADHD positioning and a retention funnel are incompatible; six reviewers escalated to banks, card networks and the FTC. Report 24: an app whose subtitle is 'ADHD Help' has ADHD users as its angriest segment (933, mean 2.747, 54.2% 1–2★) and 201 of them (mean 1.159) say the cancellation design exploits the condition — 'they know because of your poor executive function that you won't take the extra effort to find the cancel button'; the segment grew 30× across eras (0.20% → 6.01%) as the marketing worked, and the outcome got worse. Either build for the condition or stop claiming it. Report 25: the same segment that rates the product highest (ADHD, mean 4.44) writes the most cutting paywall criticism — pop-ups 'hyper désagréable et malvenu pour des TDAH'; 'profit off of your disability'. Report 60 (Mindway): an ADHD-positioned routine planner whose subscription four users could not cancel and whose paid trial billed within hours — the positioning makes the billing failures a betrayal of the audience it names. Report 67 (Habio): ads pitching ADHD help and a 'bionic reading' tool; USE_ADHD 97 (4.73%, mean 1.25 — below even the non-seeded 1.31), 35.05% refund denied, 23.71% describe dark patterns: 'en sachant pertinemment à quel point le TDAH est difficile à vivre au quotidien notamment vis à vis de la gestion financière'; 'they're using your own ADHD against you' (UK, where ADHD is 14.47% of reviews).

**Reports:** [19](<../App Store Reports/19. Wisey - Habit Builder - Form habits, change your life (REPORT).md>), [24](<../App Store Reports/24. <a id="c251"></a>
### C251 — If cross-platform is what people buy, ship every platform in parity — same release, same entitlement, or a visible 'coming' state

**Strong** · 5 apps · 25 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 4 apps

*Why Strong:* 5 apps, same direction (act on it, 90%)

Report 33: one account across iPhone, iPad, Watch, Mac, web, Android and Windows is a top purchase trigger (106 cross-platform praise reviews rated 4–5★; 'since I get Mac OS, iPad, and Apple Watch apps all for one subscription … I'm fine with it'; 'signed up for premium mainly because this has a web interface') and the top engineering complaint of 2020–23 — platform issues 354 (8.99%, mean 2.87), 18.7% of E3 and 19.9% of E4; the Mac app stalled for a year ('left for a year at a time'; support: 'the update version is only released on phone, not the MacOS yet'), Mac/web reached 12.2% of E4 and fell to 2.2% after the macOS 13.0.1 fix; entitlements did not follow the person across web (Paddle) → iPhone, guest → account or a new phone (~25 cases, some taking 6+ weeks). Cross-platform wins sales and loses stars unless every device ships on the same day with one entitlement. Report 49: no restore between iPhone and iPad (3). Report 54: a Google Play buyer must rebuy on the App Store (ES, 1★). Report 55: the Android version is described as more capable and reliable (reminders with sound control, one-tap sync, fewer crashes) — 'I recently switched my Android for an iPhone and unfortunately it doesn't work well' (USER_ANDROID 16, 2.81). Report 59 (Tappsk): the Mac app was left behind — 'Там какое то старое приложение, которое давно не обновляется' (some old app that has not been updated in ages); 'garder à jour la version Mac qui semble délaissé' (keep the Mac version up to date, it seems abandoned) — and is the reason several leave for Things ('пришлось отказаться в пользу things из-за отсутствия поддержки Mac'). Report 85 (Habitica): NEG_PARITY 141 (4.09%, in every era 1.9–7.2%) — challenges, guild management, the market, stats and inbox exist only on the web and the web is faster; NEG_IOS_BEHIND 21 — Korean and Ukrainian on Android but not iPhone, a Wear OS watch app but no watchOS ('安卓使用者是人，蘋果不是人喔' — Android users are people, Apple users aren't?); the corpus's last review (2026-09-06, 5★) recommends the website as the workaround; §8.10 'the web version as a stable fallback until the app matches it'.

**Reports:** [33](<../App Store Reports/33. Habitify - Habit Tracker - Daily Goals, Routine & Streaks (REPORT).md>), [54](<../App Store Reports/54. <a id="c200"></a>
### C200 — Never meter the completion action — a free cap may limit habits, never check-offs

**Strong** · 4 apps · 16 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 3 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Strong:* 4 apps, same direction (act on it, 87%)

Report 18: the free tier advertised 10 habits but ticking a habit consumed a 14-per-week memo quota (two check-offs a day), so tapping 'complete' produced a purchase sheet; 139 reviews (6.79%, mean 2.32★, 19.6% of all 1★) and five years of 'stops working on day 3/5/6/10'. A habit tracker that refuses to record a completion in the first week demonstrates that it does not work, to a user deciding whether it works — 'I was 90% ready to buy… I just lost all feeling for it and deleted it.' Report 25: from Nov 2025 editing an existing habit — including the ones onboarding created — was reported as paid; five 1–2★ reviews, zero before that date; 'never gate editing of habits the onboarding created'. Report 33: a free-tier cap of ~15 check-ins per week (Oct 2020 → 2024) drew 29 reviews at mean 2.00 — the worst-rated monetisation mechanism, 4.2% of E3 — and punished the most engaged free users ('three habits is reasonable. The problem … I can't check into those habits more than 15 times a week'; 'limiting the number of check ins per week ruins the whole point'). Report 89 (Check Calendar): after the trial 'even the basic function of checking off 1 day is behind a paywall' — the completion action itself is what the wall meters, and §8.5 proposes the inverse: basic ticking free, Premium sold on backup/sync, unlimited calendars, per-emoji reports and widgets.

<a id="c296"></a>
### C296 — The free tier must let the differentiator be experienced — a cap that hides the product's own thesis converts on nothing the user has felt

**Strong** · 4 apps · 13 cards · positive in 2 apps · negative in 3 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Strong:* 4 apps, directions mixed (act 7, open 4, free 1)

Report 77 (Habit Tracker: Streak-Free / Momentumly, 71 reviews): the product's thesis — forgiving, multi-habit momentum instead of streaks — is the best-supported finding in the corpus (19 of 71, 26.76%, mean 4.89★, zero below 4★), yet the free tier is one habit, so 'the product's own differentiator (forgiving multi-habit momentum) is not experienceable free'; 'a habit tracker with one habit is a demo'; the four who hit the cap rate it 2.50★ ('you can't really explore the app'), MON_PAYWALL_BLOCKS 7 (9.86%, 2.86★) is the largest negative code, and the three reviewers who did convert converted on comparative value against trackers they had already tried — 'an informed judgement they could only make after using it'; §8.4.1 the paywall does not lead with the concept although the listing and title do; §8.4.3 a trial or an unambiguous free window is the mechanism that lets the cap be tested without changing it. The report does not recommend raising the cap (no conversion data) — it establishes that at one habit the thing being sold cannot be felt. Related: [[C147]] (let people use the product before they pay), [[C182]] (a pre-use hard paywall makes every purchase non-evidence-based), [[C133]] (gate on capability not quantity), [[C007]] (generous fixed cap), [[C063]] (free trial before purchase). Report 86 (Today): 'one habit is not a trial, it is a screenshot. A one-habit cap in an app whose paid value is multi-habit dashboards prevents the prospect from ever seeing the thing they would be buying' — MON_TRIAL_REQ 33 (1.85%) made identically in 2016 ('Expand the free app to allow a proper trial and then ask for money') and 2024 ('one is not enough for a trial'); a confused user who deleted the app 'otherwise I'd have bought it'. Report 88 (GetHabit): five reviewers got past the wall only by waiting for an X to appear ('if you wait 5 or so seconds an X pops up'); the free tier showed a name field and nothing else. Report 89 (Check Calendar): §8.5 sell Premium on what buyers name — the one-time price (PAY_ONCE_PRAISE 10), keeping records safe, unlimited calendars, per-emoji reports and widgets (a stated purchase condition) — with basic ticking free; paid-extra willingness predates the wall (2021: reminders, icons, colours 'even as a paid option').

**Reports:** [77](<../App Store Reports/77. Habit Tracker - Streak-Free - Streaks & Habits (REPORT).md>), [86](<../App Store Reports/86. <a id="c147"></a>
### C147 — Let people use the product before they pay

**Contested** · 40 apps · 171 cards · positive in 19 apps · negative in 34 apps · tied to a purchase in 15 apps

*Why Contested:* 40 apps; free vs paid genuinely split — 10 apps' cards say build-free, 7 say build-paid

Users forgive a price; they do not forgive paying blind. Report 9's hard paywall before any experience produced 159 'let me look before you charge me' reviews at mean 1.79, and buyers who paid before seeing the product became the angriest cohort (mean 1.94). Report 12: a hard paywall with nothing evaluable produced a paywall corpus — 46.5% of 404 reviews complain about the gate, 172 reviewers left without ever seeing the product, and the theme never dropped below a third of reviews in any year. Report 17: seven reviewers rated an app they never saw ('Can't even look at the settings or examine how the app will handle cancelation'); confirmed payers averaged 3.63 against 1.14 for those blocked at the paywall — the strongest argument in a 38-review corpus for letting people in. Report 18: the reviews that converted best came from people who used the app free for a week or a month first; the reviews that generated refund demands came from people charged before they could evaluate. Report 19: only four non-payers appear in the corpus and all four refused for the same reason — no way to evaluate first; everyone else went through the paywall and then tried to reverse the transaction. Report 25: 'I could not evaluate the product' outweighs 'too expensive' — ~31 of 55 price objections are gate objections; every positive trial review describes having had enough product access to form a judgement; a survey-then-paywall sequence is the lowest-mean theme in the corpus (1.17) because it spends the highest-intent moment and then gates it. Report 26: an evaluation-window problem, not a pricing problem — 'You get about 5 days free to make one flower then you have to pay'; 'the flower stops growing once you reach 17%, which I finished in about 2 weeks'; a user writes the hypothesis: give one garden free 'and that would probably get me intrigued enough to get a subscription'; proposed tests: time-boxed full access, cap 8–10, or one garden to 100%. Report 30: 'nobody forms a habit portfolio of two — the cap converts evaluation into rejection'; the cap, not price, is the top upgrade barrier (15), and the substantive rating of everyone with something specific to say is 2.87. Report 31: 'Free is useless, paid is too expensive to try' — the evaluation argument is the plurality monetisation objection since 2016; 'Tried the 3 free habits and wanted more' was an E1 purchase trigger when the unlock was a $4–9 one-off. Report 33: 'Three habits, and three days, is simply too little'; the evaluation argument is the plurality of monetisation objections; 44 say 'would buy if…'. Report 34: 'two habits is too few to judge the app' is the plurality of 78 monetisation-friction reviews; a 2-habit tier converts believers and repels evaluators. Report 36: a 1-habit free tier 'you can't really test the app without paying'; roughly half of 121 friction reviews are willingness to pay the model cannot accept. Report 41: purchase decisions in hours on a 3-habit free tier ('I bought the lifetime after trying it for like 20 minutes'), while others say 'you can't get a proper demo out of this without having at least 8 or 10 habits'. Report 42: 'you can't get… a test to see whether it's actually worth paying'; a migrating HabitBull power user lost at the wall ('I couldn't move around or familiarize myself enough to justify paying to unlock integral features'); 'every tab I open to poke around is locked'; the 1★ band's 'never used the product' population (~20) needs a trial, the 'paid and regret it' population (13) needs the product to be worth it. Report 43: 'Why not give 2 weeks fully functional, then handicap it to 3?'; 'Would have more stars if I cd test out >3 goals — Prior to paying!' Report 46: 'By the time you discover that you can only track 3 habits with the free version, you've already spent 20 minutes or more setting it up' (16 votes); 'every tab I open to poke around is locked'-style evaluation failures; a 30-day full trial asked for. Report 48: 43 state an intention to pay that the current terms defeat (4.12) — 'I will pay for an app after I use it for a couple weeks and have grown to appreciate the app'; 38 payers describe long free use before paying. Report 50: three of four intent-to-pay reviewers use the free tier first, and two actual payers state the sequence (months free, then pro) — the path a cap cut interferes with. Report 53: 'I was asked to pay too soon, without really trying the app'; 'Let me try before upselling'. Report 54: the strongest conversion stories got enough free room to be convinced — two weeks, one week, a few minutes with the whole feature set visible — while the cap 'terminates evaluation rather than gating it'. Report 56: free-trial-then-charge patterns at competitors are explicitly rejected — 'No obnoxious free-trial trick. Actually free'; 'really free, no false promises'. Report 57: new users who hit the creation ad 'stop using the app before finding out if you like the functionality'. Report 59 (Tappsk): 40 purchasers bought within days because the app worked in the first days ('Поюзал один день и купил навсегда' — used it one day and bought forever; 'took premium the same day I downloaded it'). Report 60 (Mindway): 'the decision the corpus forces' — move the paywall behind first value: the value users report (structure 15, habit outcomes 12, wellbeing 9, mean 4.79) takes days to appear and the current design charges before any of it can happen (ad → questionnaire → 'asked for money right away'); the three reviewers who met the cost as optional averaged 4.33★, the thirteen who met it as a wall 1.69★ — 'how the cost is encountered, not the cost itself, determines the rating'; every one of the 13 confirmed payers wrote a negative review; E1: raise the free cap to a full day's routine (8–10 tasks) for a randomized cohort; E2: replace the count-based paywall with a time-based one — full app, 7 days, no card ('I wish it would of let me try it out first'). Report 64 (Critique AI): the purest case in the ledger — no free tier, 0 of 419 report free ongoing use; 166 (39.62%, mean 1.52) blocked at the paywall; 82.58% never got in (mean 2.35) against 3.87 for those who did (+1.52 stars); 95 (22.67%) propose a way in (free tier 66, trial 26, tiers 21, ads 12); strip out money and 126 reviews remain at 4.41; the 3★ band is 'I want to buy this and cannot' (PAY_PRICE 45.7%, PAY_SCAM zero) — 'If a free or cheaper tier ships, this band converts first'; M3: tracking + XP / leaderboard free, AI analysis, focus mode and coach paid; 'Nobody defends the price from outside the paywall — which is the whole argument for a free tier in one sentence'. Report 67 (Habio): the E2 objection was paying blind — 'I'd love an opportunity to try before I buy!'; MON_HARDWALL 47; the free era E1 averaged 3.03 with 53.42% praise against 1.73 once the wall arrived; §8.8: a real free tier or card-free trial, measuring chargebacks and refund requests rather than only conversion. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): no trial exists anywhere in the corpus and a one-habit free tier cannot demonstrate the product — 'перевірити додаток без покупки було не можливо' ('it was impossible to check the app without buying'); that reviewer bought blind, disliked it, was refused a refund and left 2★; E2: a time-limited full-feature trial measured on refund rate and D7 retention. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): the trial is survivable when disclosed and the product lands — five 5★ met it and converted or shrugged ('I was using it without realising you have to pay after a week — but it was so good I paid'); several bought immediately (「即購入」) — 'the buyers were never the ones who needed persuading over a week'. Report 75 (Habit Streak): the 'everything is paid' reactions (4, mean 2.50: 'Pretty useless unless you pay money'; deleted after ten minutes, titled 'Tư bản' — Capitalist) come from users who bounced within minutes although the free tier permits five habits — the cap 'is hit at setup, before value is felt'; hypothesis: 'the people most likely to pay are the ones who got value free first'; E2: enforce the cap at day 14 rather than at setup. Report 76 (Way of Life): 'only by buying will you know if you need it' (ua 2★); 'This is not a Free app with in-app purchases. This is a $7 app' (1★); REQ_TRIAL 4 at mean 1.75★; §8.9 Q4 asks whether the 3-item tier converts better or worse than a time-limited full trial. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): 'you can't really explore the app' (bg 4★) — 'a habit tracker with one habit is a demo'; the three who converted did so on comparative value after using it; zero of 71 mention a trial and the description offers none; §8.4.3 a trial or an unambiguous free window. Report 82 (Lasting Change): no free tier exists in the corpus (zero mentions of a free tier or habit limit); 'Continued access to all features requires a subscription'; APP_UNUSED 14 were billed for an app they never opened; the only deliberate buyer converted 'just in case' on fear of a later price, 'not on value', then preferred a paper bullet journal. Report 86 (Today): 'unable to evaluate it with only one card… this should be listed as a paid app not free' (1★, 2016); the paid value (multi-habit dashboards, cards) is invisible at a one-habit cap; §8.9 caveat: the 1★ at a one-habit cap come disproportionately from people who never used the app — removing the cap 'may raise the rating without raising revenue', so test with revenue as the metric. Report 88 (GetHabit): 'you have to pay to even access the app. Whatever, did that' — and 51.1% of buyers then hit a problem, 35.7% regret; PAY_CONDITIONAL_WILLING 8 name a real trial as their condition ('A successful 30 day trial and I probably would have paid the subscription'; 'If I had a 14 or even 7 day trial I would have actually given it ago'); §8.2 a usable free core (a few habits and one challenge) before any purchase screen. Report 89 (Check Calendar): PAY_CONDITIONAL_WILLING 6 — the conditions are disclosure (4), a widget (1) and paid extras rather than a paid base (1, from 2021: 'even as a paid option'); U:would_pay_signal 25 (9.88%); §8.4 experiment an ongoing free tier (one or two calendars, or ads) against the wall — before 2024 the app was freemium and paywall complaints were 11.1% of reviews, against 42.0–56.7% in each year since; 'the corpus cannot say which converts better; it says which one reviewers resent'. Research: Feature Gating vs Quantity.md — the quantified version of this rule: B2C freemium converts at 1-4%, users active past the first week are 5-8x more likely to convert, and a new habit takes about 66 days to become automatic, so a limit or trial landing at day 7-14 arrives before the value it is trying to charge for exists. A consumer PM app that removed its 3-project cap and gated storage and templates instead went from 0.8% to 2.6% conversion. The free-user 'bill of rights' named is unlimited logging, streaks and reminders.

<a id="c133"></a>
### C133 — Gate on capability, not on quantity

**Contested** · 39 apps · 148 cards · positive in 10 apps · negative in 27 apps · tied to a purchase in 7 apps

*Why Contested:* 39 apps; free vs paid genuinely split — 8 apps' cards say build-free, 12 say build-paid

A quantity cap set above the point of core value is noticed, tolerated and does not convert; move the wall to analytics, sync, Watch, widgets, icons, family sharing. See Research Reports/Feature Gating vs Quantity.md. Report 6 contests the 'icons' part: the listing sold Premium on themes and icons and zero of 44 reviewers mentioned them. Report 18: users who paid said the paid tier 'adds nothing, it only removes limits' — 'not so much an amazing paid service as being forced to pay because the basics were cut'; the corpus's own purchase-condition backlog (export, trend statistics, routine modes, timer with time tracking, Watch parity, themes, web/Mac) is entirely additive capability. Report 20: after the conversion the paid layer was colours, dark mode, extended notifications, manual backup and a non-functional widget above a 3-habit cap — the cap sat below the threshold of usefulness and the paid depth did not deliver. Report 24: the free tier gates coaching content (the product's value) at ~3–4 habits; the constraint that makes the product work is pacing, not a paywall. Report 25: gating expanded over time from a habit count to statistics, the calendar view, group creation and — from Nov 2025 — editing the starter habits the onboarding itself created ('You need to get the premium to edit habits, even the ones they start you out with'), which turns a reduced product into a demo; weak by rate (5, mean 1.20), high by consequence. Report 26: the gate sits on quantity (habit count) and on the visible reward (growth stops at 17%) rather than on capability; extra gardens, themes and 'no wither' mode are the paid layer that users accept. Report 28: capping semantics — how important a user is allowed to say something is (1 red / 2 orange priority slots) — reads as the app overruling the user: 'it feels disingenuous to put exercise as low priority just so that i can put washing my face as medium'; 'if I put hygiene as yellow it's just wrong'; if a cap must stay, rename the tiers as labels or let users choose colours; a to-do list that earns nothing while habits do is the same class of gate. Report 30: 'Quer cobrar? Coloque algumas versões na versão pro. Não faz sentido deixar cadastrar 2 habitos' — users themselves ask to monetise depth (widget, sync, themes, history, stats) rather than habit count; a 2★ says the price is fine ('ce n'est pas cher') and still rates 2★ for the cap — the cleanest evidence the cap, not the price, produces low ratings. Report 31: the cap stayed fixed while packaging changed; buyers valued unlimited habits, reminders, charts, groups and export. Report 36 contests the widgets part: reviewers accept paid skins but reject paid widgets and habit caps — skins-only gate mean 2.77 vs widgets 2.64 vs habit cap 2.30 ('Pay for the skins. I am fine with widget restrictions but 59$?'). Report 41: the report's experiment E1 is to move the gate off habit count onto history depth, statistics, widgets, sync or customisation, measuring conversion and the 1–2★ rate together. Report 42: the report proposes moving the wall to history depth, statistics depth or reminder count rather than habit count — statistics already being the top named purchase trigger. Report 43: the report's experiment E3 is to surface the unlimited-habits unlock at a moment of demonstrated value (e.g. a 14-day streak) rather than at a count limit — the historic cap failed because it blocked before value was shown. Report 46: the report's #9 is 3 → 4 free habits — the smallest change that fixes the widget defect and answers the counter-offer without touching the habit-science defence. Report 47: every purchase trigger reviewers name is additive — accumulated value ('プレミアに入ったくらい重宝してます'), study stats, motivation photos, the AI coach, a platform bundle — and none asks to pay to restore something that used to be free; the report's rule: grow premium only through additive value. Report 48: the cap is the dominant mechanical purchase trigger ('I'll probably upgrade to the paid version soon to get more trackers') but a 3-tracker cap on a multi-goal product blocks evaluation — 'You are not allowing a certain group of people try out your app'; multiple reviewers propose the split themselves: pay once for capacity, subscribe for sync / reports. Report 49: 'just a checklist' 38 (1.68) and 'do it yourself instead' 36 (1.36) — a bare checklist reproducible by ChatGPT cannot carry the price; the level-up loop, art and community can. Report 50: 'the entire monetization surface is one number' — no reviewer reports reminders, statistics, journaling, widgets, Health or the Watch app individually gated — 'That clean one-gate model is worth protecting — and §7.2 shows what happens when the one gate moves.' Report 59 (Tappsk): the quantity gate (2 habits, 2 recurring tasks, a few reminders) is the top objection at 697 reviews while the capability gates (iCloud sync, Mac) draw a fraction of that. Report 60 (Mindway): the purest count gate in the ledger — a free tier of roughly 1–3 tasks in a daily routine planner (M_PAYWALL_BLOCK 19, 8.80%, mean 1.63, 13 of 19 at 1★, in six languages: 'I wanted to add third task to do and I can't do it without paying'; 'you need to pay money to just write some freaking habits'; 'quería organizar mi día y no puedo ya que solo por hacer algo me pide pagar'); the cap sits below the app's own minimum viable use — 'a daily routine of two tasks is not a routine, so the free tier cannot demonstrate the thing the paid tier sells' — and it is the only major theme still growing in the 2026 tail (5.33% → 8.66% → 28.57% of period); D1: gate on depth — multiple routines, history, advanced recurrence, the guided content — rather than on count. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): the price is not the problem (three unprompted 'the price is fair' against two one-line objections) — 'packaging (what the free tier contains) and delivery (whether the purchase works) are'; repackage, do not reprice. Report 65 (Rabit): §2.4 — 'Rabit monetises the number of habits. Its behavioural engine — plants, streaks, reminders — is what people love, and it rewards consistency, not volume. So the paywall taxes the axis users do not value while leaving the axis they do value free-but-broken'; a reviewer asks for exactly the inverse ('manter uma versão free com outras funcionalidades pagas mas não bloquear o uso do aplicativo'); M1: raise the cap materially and paywall depth instead of count; the paid tier 'não há grandes diferenças quando paga'. Report 69 (TheFor): 'a product whose free tier is its moat has no obvious upgrade ladder that does not damage the moat' — M2: build Pro from additive capability the corpus asks for (sync free for one device / paid for multi-device, automatic backup, deep analytics, Face ID lock), never by removing free capability; a Pro buyer's only request (auto-backup) is not in Pro. Report 71 (MyStreaks): the clearest case of charging for the commodity — the paywall gates the number of streaks, 'the private, single-player counter' every free competitor gives away ('there are so many alternatives that don't make you pay when you've hit a max of 2 goals'), while the surfaces reviewers praise and competitors cannot copy — community (8, 4.88), sharing, accountability, outcomes (21, 4.95), the book and podcast (8, all 5★) — sit ungated or unclear; §8.4: 'charge for the part that is hard to copy… and stop charging for the part every free competitor already gives away'; §8.1 #1 re-cut the paywall to gate a feature, not the streak count. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): 'The free tier is an acquisition instrument, and it is currently priced as a monetization instrument' — 24 cap complaints and zero reviewers who say the cap made them buy; eight of nine price objections also carry the cap — 'The price is not the problem; the ratio of what is free to what is charged for is'. Report 75 (Habit Streak): 'not one person names a premium capability other than more habits' in 41 reviews — 'the paywall is being read as a quantity gate rather than a value gate'; E1: A/B unlimited habits with premium features gated against the current cap; §8.1 #4 show what Premium unlocks besides more habits — 'if there are not, the offer is a quantity gate and reads as one'. Report 76 (Way of Life): premium = unlimited items only; purchasers still ask for frequency (2.39×) and sync (2.72×) more than the corpus — the paid tier unlocks more of the same rather than the two capabilities people want; §8.5 sync is the paid feature reviewers say they would pay for. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): money-negative reviews object to structure 12 of 14 (85.7%) vs price level 2 of 14 (14.3%); 'the corpus says the price is broadly acceptable and the boundary is not' — a structure problem, not a pricing problem; MON_PAYWALL_BLOCKS 7 (9.86%, 2.86★: 'only a tiny bit of the app's uses are free'; 'most features require the pro subscription') vs MONP_VALUE 3 at 5.00★ ('the price is just right'); no reviewer names a specific feature as the thing they paid for. Report 82 (Lasting Change): consent objections outnumber price objections 56 to 4 (14:1) — PRICE_TOO_HIGH 4 (2.29%) vs U:consent_failure 56 (32.00%); §8.9 do not lower the price; the only clean pricing signal is a 4★ who likes the app and finds it 'too steep… especially for retirees or disabled people'. Report 84 (HabitGrid): 'the distinction the corpus supports is between charging for what users already have (which is what they chose the app for) and charging for things they have asked for and do not yet have' — watch app, cloud backup, frequency modes are the only asks and none exists yet. Report 88 (GetHabit): PAY_PRICE_TOO_HIGH 54 (11.02%, 1.52★) 'usually against how little the app contained, not against a competitor's price'; COMP_FREE_ALTERNATIVE 33 — the phone's reminders and notes, a journal, Pinterest, Google lists; 'the barrier is the order of events, not the price alone'. Report 89 (Check Calendar): before 2024 the free cap was two calendars (PAY_CALENDAR_LIMIT 3: a third required payment) — a quantity gate replaced in 2024 by a time gate on the core tick, which drew five times the complaint share (11.1% → 56.7%). Research: Feature Gating vs Quantity.md — the external corroboration for this point, and the one place in the ledger where industry literature is the evidence rather than review corpora (sources named only in aggregate: freemium strategy guides, habit-tracker analyses, habit-formation research). Its conclusion is this rule in other words — 'capabilities not quotas': 'don't cripple the core habit/task loop in free tiers', let free users track unlimited or many habits, and monetise capability — advanced analytics, custom themes, widgets, device sync/backup. The one quantified case is a consumer project-management app that limited free users to 3 projects and locked collaboration: consumer conversion 'crashed to 0.8%'; after removing the project cap and gating storage and templates instead, conversion rose to 2.6% — more than threefold, and notably gating the team-shaped features (collaboration, analytics) did not help in a consumer market while gating optional advanced capability did. The stated causal chain is retention, not pressure: B2C freemium converts at 1-4%, users still active past the first week are 5-8x more likely to convert, and habit-formation research puts automaticity at about 66 days — so 'if a habit app slams a limit or trial around day 7-14, users quit before they've truly engaged.' A paraphrased internal study found free users who complained about task/habit caps were less likely to ever pay: 'They were likely turning off the app instead of upgrading' — the cap produces exit, not purchase. Two caveats this ledger must keep attached: the document concedes that a usage-cap ('taster') model is the general B2C pattern and feature gates the B2B one — Dropbox's 2 GB is its example — so the habit-app conclusion is an exception argued from habit-formation time, not the industry default; and it accepts capability gates work partly because users expect to buy non-essential extras 'once they've already invested time', which makes the gate's timing as load-bearing as its object ([[C137]]). The market's actual gated set is named as Apple Watch support, widget access, detailed analytics and backup/sync ([[C022]], [[C107]], [[C011]], [[C013]]).

<a id="c246"></a>
### C246 — No ads in a personal habit tracker — 'no ads' is among the highest-rated topics and ads on the reward loop are the largest 1★ driver

**Contested** · 37 apps · 78 cards · positive in 27 apps · negative in 11 apps · tied to a purchase in 4 apps

*Why Contested:* 37 apps; free vs paid genuinely split — 5 apps' cards say build-free, 3 say build-paid

Report 1: 'no ads' is the highest-rated topic in the corpus (181 of 182 mentions positive, mean 4.91). Report 3: 206 reviews praise the absence of ads at mean 4.94 with zero 1–2★. Report 4: no advertising business; 67 praise it (mean 4.45). Report 20: no ads is a top-rated praise theme. Report 2: ads in the free version are a stated reason for 3 purchases. Separated from C006 because the ad decision now has its own counter-evidence and cost data — C082 (ads in the free tier, report 28: an interstitial on every check-off was 19.98% of reviews, 52.4% of 1★) and C240 (never interrupt the completion moment). Report 34: no ads; 'no ads / no nagging' praised by 6 (mean 4.83). Report 36: no ads — '0 ad clutter. 0 monthly charges'; NOADS 6 (mean 4.33). Report 41: no ads anywhere; six name the absence as a reason they chose the app vs one who would prefer ads to paying €1.99/month. Report 42: no ads and none asked for — the complaint is the upsell interstitial. Report 43: no ads ever; praised by 5 (mean 4.80). Report 46: zero ads; no ads praised by 10 (mean 4.90). Report 47: banners in a free tier are tolerated (11 mild complaints over five years, most offering to pay) but a per-action video is not — ad overload 24 at mean 1.46 and 0 ad complaints in 146 reviews after the rollback. Report 48: no ads in eleven years — 33 praise, 0 complaints; the report's first 'do not change'. Report 52: see [[C269]] — the 2025 in-flow ad wave drove 35.0% of six months' reviews at mean 3.70. Report 54: no ads — the 7 reviewers who praise the absence are all 5★. Report 56: 9 of 67 name ad-freeness; ads 'caused instant deletion' of competitors. Report 58: 8 of 91 praise no ads, and 'no ads' plus 'no bad free version' is the pitch against competitors. Report 59 (Tappsk): PR_NO_ADS 127 (0.84%, 4.91★) with no ad complaint coded across 15,176 reviews; 'no ads in the free tier' is on the report's keep list. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): zero ad complaints in 45 reviews; §8.5: do not build ads — 'a habit app whose appeal is calm minimalism has more to lose than to gain'. Report 65 (Rabit): ads introduced into a formerly ad-free app cost it its distinguishing praise; a reviewer names the perceived intent — 'se o objetivo é fazer pagar o premium ou desistir de usar o app'; M5: consider removing ads for free users entirely and monetising on depth. Report 69 (TheFor): 'Es genial y no tiene anuncios'; zero reviewers report an ad in 80 reviews; M5: do not add ads — they would attack the two largest positive themes at once. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): 「広告なし。（そのため、清々しいほど儲かりません）」 ('No ads. That is why we make refreshingly little money') — PR_FREE 149 (6.51%, 4.87) rising 1.4% → 11.2% of eras as reviewers contrast ad-supported and subscription-first apps (60 comparisons). Report 75 (Habit Streak): 'For a free app without adds, this is great' — the only ad mention is praise. Report 76 (Way of Life): ad removal as the paid unlock's side benefit was worth paying for (6.59× lift among purchasers) and the objection vanished once the free tier went ad-free in 2018. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): PRAISE_NO_ADS 5 (5.00★); zero ask for a cheaper ad-supported tier; §8.5 do not add ads. Report 83 (Roubit): ads moved into the core loop in 2026 — 'ads now play when opening the app and when writing the diary' (jp 1★); 'as long as ads don't appear, I'll keep using it' (2023); U:ads_any 16 (3.20%), 3 of 13 stated churns cite ads; release notes 2026-04-29 'watch ads and earn additional rewards', 2026-06-09 'Premium users can now receive rewards without waiting for ads'. Report 84 (HabitGrid): MODEL_NO_ADS 12 (13.95%) cite 'no ads' as a reason for their rating; 'because it has no ads and no paying' (vi); §8.4 adding ads would contradict a stated reason 12 reviewers give. Report 86 (Today): no advertising at any point in ten years; PR_NOADS 7. Report 88 (GetHabit): video ads in the free tier (ADS_IN_APP 21, 1.14★) on top of a hard paywall — the worst of both; the ads disappear from the corpus after April 2021. Report 89 (Check Calendar): ADS_COMPLAINT 5 (1.98%), all 2022-05 → 2024-10, two from buyers who still saw ads; two reviewers ask for ads instead of the wall (PAY_PREFER_ADS) — ads are the lesser resentment beside a silent trial. Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): a free counter praised for having no ads at launch (PRAISE_NO_FEW_ADS 19 from day one, 'great that there are no ads') became an ad-carrying app — first complaint 2024-06-12, U:ads_negative 20 (3.26%, mean 2.65★), 6 of the 20 deleted the app and 7 of the 20 carry a lost-user signal against 5 of the 536 reviews with no money code: 'reviews that criticise ads are the churn segment'; some tolerate it ('far too many ads in the free version, but it's pointless complaining'; 'the ads are fully justified'), and two ask for ads instead of payment.

<a id="c155"></a>
### C155 — Never remove a feature people bought the app for — add alongside, do not replace

**Contested** · 22 apps · 86 cards · positive in 5 apps · negative in 20 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Contested:* 22 apps; free vs paid genuinely split — 2 apps' cards say build-free, 3 say build-paid

Report 10: every major removal (Journeys → streak-based Self-Care Areas, automatic mood check-ins, exact-time goals, milestones, colour palettes) produced a dated backlash, explicit paid cancellations, and none were reversed; generic 'you removed a feature I used' grew 16× in four years. Report 18: the Sept 2024 split of the interleaved routine + to-do list into two tabs drew 32 protests at mean 4.25★ — the paying base — including subscribers who had bought a year because of the merged view days earlier; the weekly view and the Challenge feature were removed in the same release; nobody had asked for the split. Recommendation: restore it as a toggle, since a minority came to prefer the split. Report 23: the interactive widget lost at iOS 14 was partly an Apple platform change, but the five-year gap before restoration cost a top-three downgrade reason; a capability users bought for must be restored, not left behind. Report 24: the 'Make Me Fabulous' activity launcher was removed or hidden after a redesign and background music was removed — both named by long-tenure payers as renewal reasons. Report 25: an Apple Watch app reported 'suddenly removed' (Oct 2025) and Vision Pro support withdrawn — single reports, recorded not asserted. Report 27: the year-at-a-glance grid — the signature view the bundle ID is still named after (goalStreakCalendar) — was demoted behind a per-habit tap in 2025; its praise fell 16.7% → 0% and by late 2025 it appears only as a loss, even from a reviewer who still gave 5★ ('I loved it before the previous update'); the removed one-tap note export produced the corpus's only 2★ — 'one reviewer represents a workflow, not a preference'. Report 31: 'The app gets prettier. The actual functionality gets worse. Every time.' — removed monthly/yearly frequency (58), streak on the main list (52, partly restored then removed again), swipe between days (41); 'That is one of the biggest reasons I paid' (feature removed after paying, 21); a minority liked the redesigns. Report 33: removals came in release-shaped spikes — v2.0 charity points and data (2016), skip and Russian UI (2017), notes/skip to Premium (2019), Habitify X (2020), notes back-dating and editing (Dec 2024 – Jan 2025), compact/incremental/streak widgets (May 2025), passcode lock (2025) — regression 197 (5.00%, mean 2.51), 14.9% of E3; 2★ is the 'I used to love it' band (regression 15.1%, churn 12.2%); every removal needs a toggle or a migration. Report 34: CSV export, present for years, was disabled in 2026; the one-time purchase option vanished 'after updating the app'. Report 36: 'Antes: Excelente. Ahora: Pésima' — a 2★ after widgets went paid. Report 43: 'pause a habit' removed by the 2026 update. Report 46: an unrequested Dec 2022 completion animation cost a subscriber ('I'll not renew'). Report 48: the web app (2015 – ~2019) was discontinued and Windows users lost access — 17 still ask for it; widget interactivity was removed after shipping. Report 50: an update removed single-occurrence editing of recurring habits (see C073). Report 52: a ¥68 buyer asked for a refund after a Dec 2024 redesign removed to-do sorting. Report 76 (Way of Life): the 2023 removal of the old Today widget drew NEG_LOST_FEATURE 7 ('Any updates on when the widget will be fixed?', 3★); §8.8 lists what to keep — the three-state grid, good/bad inversion, skip, charts, the 3-habit free tier. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): a v2.1.0 'major internal overhaul' reset widgets and custom shortcuts and coincides with the corpus's only 'used to be great' review; the era that followed carries 8 of 9 defects. Report 83 (Roubit): the iPhone widget disappeared in a July 2025 update (a paying user, 3★); Dr. Eddy (AI counsellor) is praised 2023-08 → 2024-10 and then asked about as removed (FEATURE_REMOVED 6: 'is it gone or premium-only?'). Report 85 (Habitica): closing guilds and the tavern on 2023-08-08 — NEG_GUILD_SHUTDOWN 32 (2.25★, 2023 → 2026: 'The guilds were the soul of this app'; 'I was in a guild that basically acted as a sort of support group'), multi-year users at 23.3% of these reviews vs 3.86% overall, two of the thirteen most-voted reviews in the corpus, E4 the lowest-rated era (3.37★), community praise 4.4% → 1.0%; the US description still lists Guilds three years later; §8.7 replace what the guilds did with small opt-in moderated groups and a party-matching queue. Report 86 (Today): a widget that had become the primary interface for many (PR_WIDGET 28, 4.50★) was removed without a word and restored under pressure; the iOS-14 home-screen widget requested from 2020-09 to 2025-12 was never built — REQ_WIDGET 47 is 'the only request that grows as the corpus shrinks' (1.98% of E1 → 16.95% of E5).

<a id="c185"></a>
### C185 — Aesthetic and a polished onboarding convert; they do not retain

**Contested** · 19 apps · 40 cards · positive in 13 apps · negative in 6 apps · tied to a purchase in 5 apps

*Why Contested:* 19 apps; free vs paid genuinely split — 3 apps' cards say build-free, 2 say build-paid

Report 12: 17 reviewers praised the design and 11 of them rated 1–2★; nine 5★ reviews praised the narrated intro before using the product; 'The intro before you purchase seems to have more thought put into it than the actual app itself.' See also report 9's warm shell over a thin product. Report 26: Eden converts on beauty and on the absence of a subscription, fast, often before the user has evaluated the functionality — which explains both high purchase velocity and payers rating a full point below the corpus (3.56 vs 4.570): 'I bought this one a little too soon I think'. Report 49: the questionnaire and personalised 'analysis' convert the segment it fits, but fit, disciplined reviewers told they have '40% more bad habits than the average person your age' read the assessment as a sales device (13). Report 52: the look converts within days — 'Downloaded, five minutes later bought premium'; 'within 24 hrs of the trial I bought lifetime' — while cuteness praise fell 18.5% (2017) → 2.9% (2026) and calm / clean held. Report 60 (Mindway): design praise sits beside price rejection in the same sentences — 'Es ist eigentlich sehr schön gemacht und gestaltet aber einfach zu teuer'; 'It is a good app well designed but cost abit of money' — P_DESIGN has a mean of 3.00; one dissent finds the cute styling 'too bubbly… better off to be more neutral and simple', and the report says do not redesign on that one complaint. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): praise_ui_design 6 (13.33%, 4.17★) sits beside the cap-driven uninstall — 'Really clean, minimal UI and super easy to use' then 'so I ended up uninstalling'. Report 64 (Critique AI): the onboarding analysis works as a hook — a reviewer praises the personalised analysis then refuses to pay (PERSONALIZE 5, mean 4.40); a physique scan and a projected score are the free teaser before the wall. Report 72 (Habit Hearts, counter-evidence): here the aesthetic is stated as the retention mechanic — 'I am someone who needs things to be pleasing to keep doing it, and this gives me that'; 'When i usually use a routine app, i give up after a few uses as it feels like a chore. But this app … has a gorgeous layout'; OUT_MOTIV 48 (19.20%) framed as a consequence of the design; outcomes 106 (42.40%, 4.97) — the design retains when the product behind it works and the free tier lets people use it. Report 76 (Way of Life): PR_DESIGN 602 (7.75%, 4.78★) and NEG_DESIGN 70 (0.90%, 'dated or ugly', 2011 → 2023) — design praise is high but it is simplicity, not looks, that retains for 13 years. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): PRAISE_DESIGN 17 (23.94%) — 'cute' across four languages — carries a mean of 4.65★, below the concept theme's 4.89★, because two low-rated reviewers praise the design while complaining about something else: 'design praise is not a satisfaction proxy'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): PRAISE_DESIGN 71 (41.28%, 4.87★) and PRAISE_NATIVE_FEEL 11 ('looks and feels like an app made by Apple'; 'even Apple apps don't feel this good'; 'Love the adoption of Liquid Glass') — craft praise persisted at 58.5% even in the era where the mean fell to 4.02★: 'the decline is additive — the same praise, now with something attached to it'. Report 82 (Lasting Change): APP_UGLY 9 ('Very old and simple tracking app design'; 'Very weridly design app, very messy') alongside 'the app itself is well designed' — craft is contested and irrelevant next to consent. Report 83 (Roubit): PRAISE_CUTE 157 (31.40%, 4.50★) and PRAISE_DESIGN_UI 43 — cuteness converts on day one ('paid for premium immediately and don't regret it at all'; paid 'after one day') and is what remains when the app breaks (19 of 40 blank-screen reports at 4–5★). Report 84 (HabitGrid): 'aesthetic, beautiful, intuitive'; PRAISE_FLEXIBLE 6 (colours, icons, look — 'personalise to your taste'); design praise rides with simplicity rather than standing alone. Report 86 (Today): PR_DESIGN 460 (25.77%) appears in every star band — 10.6% of 1★ still praise the design: 'beauty does not protect the rating; it is what makes the failure worth writing about'; PR_BEST 204 at 4.78★, the highest mean of any large theme; a Good Design Award recipient calls it 'one of the most thoughtfully designed apps I have used' (2026); design praise held at 15.25% even in the abandonment era.

<a id="c293"></a>
### C293 — Raising a free habit cap by a couple of slots does not buy back sentiment — the objection re-forms at the new number; change what the cap gates or when it is hit, and instrument it

**Moderate** · 3 apps · 8 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 3 apps

*Why Moderate:* 3 apps

Report 75 (Habit Streak, 41 reviews): v1.56.0 (2025-10-21) raised the free tier from 3 to 5 habits with the release note 'You asked, we listened' — the corpus confirms the change (three reviewers report 3 before it, two report 5 after, never both) and measures no benefit: money-negative share flat 33.3% → 35.3%, cap objections flat 2 → 2, mean rating 4.28 → 3.53, 1–3★ share 16.7% → 41.2%, and the tone hardened from 3–4★ with volunteered praise ('which is unfortunate… other than that, I would recommend!') to two 1★ ('se stupide'; 'Pff franchement c est soulant'); at n=17/18 the differences are not statistically separable, but 'the objection survived the concession in identical form, at the new number… Anyone proposing to move it to 7 should know that the last move bought nothing measurable'; the best-argued complaint asks to gate features, not habit count ('faite le gratuit ça et mettez des trucs premium en plus'); §8.2 do not raise the cap again as a sentiment fix. Related: [[C007]] (generous fixed cap), [[C133]] (gate on capability not quantity), [[C222]] (hard cap with a pressure valve), [[C270]] (earned capacity). Report 86 (Today): the counter-evidence at small numbers — raising the cap from one to three did buy back sentiment (71 complaints in 2016 → 0 in 2017–2020, one angry 1★ converting to full price the same month) because one habit is 'a screenshot, not a trial'; the null result in report 75 was 3 → 5, past the point where the cap stopped being the objection. Research: Feature Gating vs Quantity.md — the quoted reviewer asks for exactly one extra slot ('extend the habit limit for free users from 3 to 4…(or better make it unlimited)') and is already considering switching apps, which is this point's mechanism in a single review: the small raise does not resolve the objection, it relocates it.

**Reports:** [75](<../App Store Reports/75. Habit Streak - Daily Tracker - Build Routines & Reach Goals (REPORT).md>), [86](<../App Store Reports/86. Today Habit tracker - For to-dos, routines & goals (REPORT).md>), [Feature Gating vs Quantity](<../Research Reports/Feature Gating vs Quantity.md>)

</details>

<a id="c297"></a>
### C297 — A free cap's acceptability is set by the bundle around it — the same number reads as generous or as a wall depending on what else is free; moving a loved feature behind the wall changes sentiment as much as changing the number

**Moderate** · 3 apps · 8 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 2 apps

*Why Moderate:* 3 apps

Report 79 (Ripples / Checker, 172 reviews): the free tier was three boards for the whole 770-day window and three reviewers on three storefronts state the number — in October 2024 and July 2025 as generosity ('for widgets and 3 habits without limitations'; 'three habits… without huge limitations', both 5★), in January 2026 as 'met 3 boards ben je totaal niks' (3★). What changed between those dates was not the cap but the home-screen widget — the single most-praised feature in the corpus (PRAISE_WIDGET 27, 15.70%, mean 5.00★, not one below 5) — moving behind the paywall in a 101-day window (2025-07-16 → 2025-10-25); paywall-shape complaints went from 0 of 110 reviews in the first era to ~10% of reviews after, the one explicit upgrade in the corpus was 'for more boards' (the cap was converting on its own), and a 4★ proposes the compromise himself: 'make 2 widgets available in free version, one the bigger one and one the minimalist one'. 'The cap is not the lever that broke; the bundle around it is.' §8.4.1: a widget is a daily impression of the product — removing it from the free tier removes the strongest retention and word-of-mouth surface in exchange for pressure on a cap that already worked. Related: [[C007]] (generous fixed cap), [[C222]] (hard cap with a pressure valve), [[C293]] (raising a cap does not buy back sentiment), [[C001]] (never move a free feature behind the paywall), [[C009]] (basic widgets are free). Report 86 (Today): the cap's own size is the bundle here — the same one-habit grievance at 1.97★ vs the three-habit grievance at 3.60★, and a four-year silence in between; a single review attests a 5-habit stage. Report 89 (Check Calendar): the same two-calendar cap read as acceptable freemium in 2022–2023 (paywall complaints 11.1% of E1 reviews, 'the premium features makes sense like more tabs, and more customization') and its replacement by a trial on the core tick read as a wall (42–57% in every year since).

**Reports:** [79](<../App Store Reports/79. Habit Tracker - Ripples - Routines, streaks, reminders (REPORT).md>), [86](<../App Store Reports/86. Today Habit tracker - For to-dos, routines & goals (REPORT).md>), [89](<../App Store Reports/89. Check Calendar - Habit Tracker - Check your habit calendar! (REPORT).md>)

<a id="c241"></a>
### C241 — Sell entitlements as non-consumables — a consumable currency cannot be restored and has no 'paid member' state to honour

**Moderate** · 1 apps · 11 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 1 apps

*Why Moderate:* 1 app, exceptional magnitude (mean 1.0★; mean 5.0★; n=10000)

Report 28: one consumable currency ('carrots') sells cosmetics, functional caps, ad removal and cloud sync; 10 of 24 identifiable payers (41.7%) report a purchase that did not deliver or could not be restored — 'I paid 10$ to remove ads but I still get ads'; 'cannot restore purchase on a new device'; 'I paid the 14.99… it's still saying I need to purchase'; and a $10 buyer is charged again when a new paid feature ships ('i'm already a paid member; why do i have to make another purchase?'). Reviewers cannot tell what they are buying ('I now realize just buying anything gives u cloud access') and ask for it unbundled ('just pay like two dollars to just get unlimited tasks'). An architecture problem presenting as a trust problem. Report 49: an under-18 / student free programme granted case by case is invisible to almost everyone.

<a id="c299"></a>
### C299 — Never attach an app subscription to another product's checkout by default — the subscription is its own opt-in line with its own amount, period, renewal date and final-total confirmation, and a 'book only' choice must never produce a recurring charge

**Moderate** · 1 apps · 10 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 1 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Moderate:* 1 app, exceptional magnitude (mean 1.05★; mean 1.0★; mean 1.11★)

Report 82 (Lasting Change, 175 reviews, mean 1.88★): the product people set out to buy is a personalised book from the developer's website; the app subscription arrives attached to that purchase — BILL_TIED_TO_BOOK 43 (24.57%, mean 1.05★), the largest non-rhetorical code ('I had only intended to purchase the Lasting Change book and ended up with a subscription to this app'; 'I purchased the book for $50.99 which was fine. Along with that purchase is an undisclosed subscription that is $30.99'; 'a $131 purchase has turned into an ongoing financial commitment of $55 per month'); U:consent_failure 56 (32.00%, 1.11★) and BILL_NO_CONSENT 36 with a perfect 1.00★ mean; one reviewer explicitly unselected the app at checkout, was billed anyway, re-ran the checkout to test the seller's claim and found no opt-in ('you are automatically subscribed to it with a purchase of the physical book'); a post-pay upsell page positioned a £74.69 lifetime price so it read as an upgrade delta with 'no explicit confirmation step showing the full amount'; the bundle is priced below the book alone so the subscription is effectively forced; 'Not one review in 175 describes choosing to subscribe to this app because of something the app does.' The book itself is liked (BOOK_PRAISE 14 vs BOOK_CRITIC 8: 'Love the book, don't fall for the scam') — a liked physical product cannot rescue the app that bills for it. §8.3: separate lines, subscription default off, full total before charging, recurring terms in the confirmation email. Related: [[C285]] (a paid add-on is never bought on a single tap), [[C210]] (bill App Store users through the App Store), [[C111]] (show the price up front), [[C283]] (never sell by manipulation).

**Reports:** [82](<../App Store Reports/82. Lasting Change - Habit Builder - Daily Habits & Mental Wellness (REPORT).md>)

<a id="c302"></a>
### C302 — A premium currency must have a slow, honest earned path — a currency free players cannot earn turns free-core goodwill into 'pay-to-win' and rewards lying

**Moderate** · 1 apps · 4 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 1 apps

*Why Moderate:* 1 app, exceptional magnitude (n=2026; n=3289; n=3445)

Report 85 (Habitica, 3,445 reviews over eleven years): the free core earns goodwill (PR_FREE 68, MON_NOT_REQUIRED 44: 'it doesn't hide functionality behind a paywall'; 'No annoying pop ups (which makes me actually want to spend money to support the devs)') and the gem economy spends it — MON_GEM_GATE 47 (1.36%, mean 3.34★): quests, hairstyles, backgrounds and pet food sit behind gems that free players can barely earn ('The quests and many customization items are stuck behind gem paywalls'); MON_P2W_PERCEIVED 19 at 1.84★ ('After subscribing you are allotted the ability to buy 24 gems for only $6 more dollars'); the complaint is growing — 4.2% of E5 reviews against at most 1.0% in any earlier era; the current free route is challenge prize draws, and 'you have to just lie and say you did it'; the request is not for free gems but for a slow, earned route (streak rewards, achievements, an expensive gold-for-gem exchange); §8.5 replace prize draws with a small earned trickle and measure subscription starts and honesty proxies, not gem balances. Stated purchasers are few (55, 1.60%) and buy as patronage — 'I upgraded just to help support the developers' (23.6% of payers) — so the subscription's value is trust, which the currency erodes. Related: [[C241]] (sell entitlements as non-consumables), [[C270]] (earned free capacity reads as generosity), [[C164]] (a random-rotation shop with paid re-rolls is a friction generator), [[C238]] (a rewarded path for those who cannot pay), [[C061]] (goodwill conversion).

**Reports:** [85](<../App Store Reports/85. Habitica - Gamified Taskmanager - Stay motivated and organized (REPORT).md>)

<a id="c304"></a>
### C304 — A discounted offer shown during or after a purchase must replace and refund the first purchase, visibly — never stack a timed second offer on a completed one

**Moderate** · 1 apps · 8 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 1 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Moderate:* 1 app, exceptional magnitude (n=182; n=2021; n=2026)

Report 88 (GetHabit / HabitBox, 490 reviews, mean 1.71★): the purchase flow charged people twice — BILL_DOUBLE_CHARGE 26 (5.31%), 13 of them describing the discounted lifetime offer that appears during or straight after a purchase; PAY_COUNTDOWN_OFFER 46 (9.39%), a half-price lifetime offer on a timer that 40 of the 46 who mention it accepted; BILL_WRONG_PLAN 15 (bought lifetime or yearly, billed weekly); the sequence is consistent — buy a plan, see a half-price offer with a countdown, accept it believing it replaces the first, and pay both: 'a pop-up showed that I get a 50%off for this deal if I subscribe within one hour. So I did' (vn 1★); 'Right after I clicked purchase, a pop up comes up claiming to be offering it to you for half off, so $19.99… It was simply a double charge' (us 1★); 'I also fell for the £19.99 offer… it is NOT telling me I have a lifetime membership but a WEEK membership' (gb); 24 of the 182 buyers (13.2%) report a double charge, and a support reply quoted in the corpus says 'we are unable to monitor every double-subscription case since there is a huge number of such mistakes'. §8.1: if a discounted plan is shown after a purchase it must replace and refund the first; remove timers from purchase screens; show the plan and renewal period on the confirmation screen and in settings. Related: [[C180]] (no exit discounts or countdown timers on the paywall), [[C285]] (a paid add-on is never bought on a single tap), [[C113]] (one stable disclosed price), [[C285]].

**Reports:** [88](<../App Store Reports/88. GetHabit - Easy Habit Tracker - Habits Tracker for a BetterMe (REPORT).md>)

<a id="c310"></a>
### C310 — A low request count for a feature the market leader already ships measures satisfaction with that implementation, not demand for the feature

**Moderate** · 1 apps · 2 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 1 apps

*Why Moderate:* 1 app, exceptional magnitude (n=56653)

Research: Quit Habit Decision.md. Of 56,653 reviews of the category's #1 app only 164 (0.29%) mention quitting — a count that reads as no demand until the reviews are read, at which point they are 'overwhelmingly complaints about the existing quit feature, not requests for one': 'the streak counter is sometimes wrong for Quit habits'; 'It is not possible to track if you want to quit drinking alcohol. You can only choose a max period of 1 month with a 2 drink minimum?'; "When habits are set to 'Quit' with 0 per day - nothing is readable because of the all dark colors"; 'I click the QUIT habit tab, I get the form error'; 'Bad for quitting habits'. The rule generalises to every request count in every report in this ledger: a request code is generated by absence, so a feature that already exists produces complaint codes instead, and the two must never be compared as if they measured the same thing. Its corollary is the opportunity statement: 'The leader ships quit-habits badly. Doing it properly is a differentiator inside your existing app - and costs you nothing in downloads, because the traffic is already coming for habit tracking.' Related: [[C019]], [[C309]], [[C142]] (users not finding features that already exist).

**Reports:** [Quit Habit Decision](<../Research Reports/Quit Habit Decision.md>)

`RQH-005`, `RQH-006`

</details>

<a id="part-6"></a>
## Part 6 — Features — free, paid, undecided, research

One block per capability, with the free/paid 2×2 computed from the cards: what each app did with
the feature, and how its users reacted. The verdict is read off the table — mostly `paid-resented`
means the evidence leans free, mostly `paid-converts` means it leans paid, and a split means the
conditions in the statement decide. Grouped by where the ledger currently files each feature; the
2×2 and the confidence are what should move a feature between groups, not the current grouping.

### free — 16 points



| apps | Confidence | Point |
|---|---|---|
| 12 | Certain | [C069](#c069) Check-off sound and haptic |
| 44 | Strong | [C172](#c172) Per-day / per-habit notes and journal text |
| 39 | Strong | [C009](#c009) Basic widgets, icons and colours are free |
| 37 | Strong | [C080](#c080) Colour themes / dark mode |
| 35 | Strong | [C020](#c020) Data export / backup / CSV |
| 35 | Strong | [C073](#c073) Manual reordering, renaming and editing of habits/tasks — free |
| 34 | Strong | [C010](#c010) Backfill missed days / edit start date |
| 24 | Strong | [C008](#c008) Daily check-in and reminders are free — never paywall the reminder |
| 13 | Strong | [C234](#c234) Statistics stay readable on the free tier — gating the progress view removes the motivation loop the category sells |
| 7 | Strong | [C074](#c074) Customisable, louder reminder sounds |
| 7 | Strong | [C252](#c252) Complete a habit from the notification — an actionable reminder is part of the one-tap loop |
| 5 | Strong | [C258](#c258) A 'nag until done' repeating reminder — the one reminder shape reviewers say no other app offers |
