<a id="c007"></a>
### C007 — Generous fixed habit cap (or unlimited) — never change it

**Contested** · 56 apps · 417 cards · positive in 40 apps · negative in 45 apps · tied to a purchase in 28 apps

*Why Contested:* 56 apps; free vs paid genuinely split — 26 apps' cards say build-free, 16 say build-paid

| | reaction positive | reaction negative |
|---|---|---|
| **app makes it free** | free-praised — 12 apps | free-expected-but-broken — 17 apps |
| **app makes it paid** | paid-converts — 5 apps | paid-resented — 7 apps |

**Verdict from the table:** mixed — conditions decide

A low or drifting free cap is the #1 monetization complaint; 'unlimited' also sells, so the level is a decision but the stability is not. Report 6: raising a 1-streak cap to 2 did not reduce complaints — the ask was unlimited — though the tone moved from 'scam' to 'love it, want more'. Report 7: a 4-habit cap held unchanged for 3½ years was still the top 2★ theme (0 of 27 complainers paid) while 11 users said 4 was plenty — stable is not enough if the level binds the 5–8-habit user. Report 11: 'First app that has more than 3 habits' was a reviewer's entire body — no cap was the acquisition wedge against the category, and whether it survived the paywall retrofit is unknown. Report 13: the free cap was cut from 5 to 3 in 2018 (the worst year, mean 2.85) and restored in 2020 without recovering the rating; 'hitting the cap while already engaged' is the one purchase trigger buyers name. Report 14: a 3-habit free cap drew its only 1★ free-tier complaint; the report's reading is that the cap must be generous enough to create the streak that creates the desire to pay. Report 16: a free tier of ONE habit drew 76 complaints at mean 2.22 ('a habit tracker that tracks one habit is not a habit tracker') and could not do trial work; 20 reviewers defended the earn-a-slot constraint at 3–6 habits (mean 4.60) — loved at 3–6, hated at 1. Report 20: 'unlimited habits, free' was the highest-mean theme in a 4,048-review corpus (54 explicit, mean 4.94) and the product's entire market position; capping it at 3 deleted the reason to exist — 63 reviews say exactly this, 99 complain about the cap, and 3 is below the threshold of usefulness (the report's defensible line is 7–10 free with paid depth elsewhere). Report 23 (a paid app, cap as design not paywall): raising the cap 6 → 12 → 24 cut complaints roughly in half each time and bought about three years; the request re-anchors on the new number and never falls below ~6%. Report 24 (counter-evidence): a coaching app's highest-rated property is that it refuses to let users add more habits — 'anyone shipping a habit tracker with unlimited habits is competing against the wrong thing'; the generous-cap rule is about paywalls, not about pacing. Report 25: a 3-habit free cap on a product titled 'Routines & Goals Planner' is the single largest fact in a 1,309-review corpus — 138 complaints (10.54%, mean 2.13) and 298 (22.77%) of all monetisation friction, 56% of every 1★; the cap prevents a purchase decision, not just usage ('how do you expect me to subscribe without trying anything??'), and reviewers name their own acceptable number — median 8–10; 19 defend the cap and 64 call the price fair, so the level is not the problem, the gate placement is. Cap complaints fall (17.4% → 6.7%) only because reviewers increasingly describe the whole app as locked. Report 26: a free cap of 3→5→6 habits plus a garden that stops growing at 17% — monetisation gating is 11.36% of reviews (57.8% of all 1★, 21.2% of substantive reviews) while price objection is only 0.76%; 57 defend the price and 45 call the free tier generous; the cap is the single most common reason for withholding the fifth star (47 of 535 4★: 'amazing app, but you can only add 5'); ADHD users who praise the simplicity say five slots cannot hold a morning routine. Report 27: unlimited habits on a free app is praised by name ('unlimited habit tracking without ads'; 'has no limitations'; 'i didn't need to pay to use a certain amount of habits') and 13 reviewers arrived after fleeing competitors' caps — a habit cap on the free tier 'directly attacks the stated reason users are here'. Report 28: a habit-count cap of ~8 (17, 2.07%) plus a priority-slot cap of 1 red / 2 orange (15, 1.83%) and paid moods (10); 'Had trouble finding a habit tracker that didn't need a subscription to add more than three habits' and 'free tier usage incredibly wide compared to other trackers' are stated reasons for choosing it; cap complaints fell 8.5% → 3.8% mainly because the ad load crowded them out. Report 29: 12 reviews (mean 4.92) praise the absence of a habit cap by naming competitors' caps — 'they all made me pay for more than 3 habits'; 'lets you have more than 6 habits'; 'up to 15 to 20 habits without getting charged' — the specific mechanism by which a free app wins comparison shoppers; 'do not cap habit count' is 'the single most protected property in the corpus'. Report 30: a 2-habit free cap (raised to 3 by Apr 2026) is the defining problem of a minimalist tracker — 15 reviews (9.04%, mean 2.00), 31.9% of substantive reviews, 8 of 19 one-stars and all three two-stars; 'if the app is about habits, allowing only 2 is too much'; 'it should be at least 5 free habit entry'; 'It would be smarter to create attractive features that persuade the user to pay rather than limiting tracking to a mere two'; the 2 → 3 raise changed nothing (same rate, same ratings) — an increment below the evaluability threshold does not help; the report's fix is at least 5 free and monetising depth instead of count. Report 31: a 3-habit cap (2 in 2016) drew 670 complaints (12.92%, mean 2.01) at 8–18% in every era, 13.5% in E1 and 14.0% in E4 — unchanged — while the price objection moved 4.1% → 13.0% with the subscription; the plurality objection since 2016 is evaluation ('With only 2 items makes it hard to get a feel'; 'I would like to start by tracking 5 habits, not 3'); a minority defend it ('if you've read The One Thing, three is already a lot!'); the report proposes testing 3 vs 5–6 habits vs a 14-day full trial; Spain shows the highest cap rate anywhere (28.6%). Report 33: a 3-habit cap (sometimes 2) draws 213 complaints (5.41%, mean 2.31) — 'isn't much of a test run'; 'if … 5 rather than 3 … I'd have … probably upgraded' — but is far milder than the take-backs; the report proposes testing 3 habits + unlimited check-ins vs 5 habits vs a 14-day full trial; Spain, the UK and Brazil show the highest cap rates (10.5–10.7%). Report 34: a 2-habit cap (2018–2025) is 39 complaints (5.25%, mean 2.44) and 15 of 37 1★ (40.5%), rising to 9.7% of E4; reviewers benchmark 5 as the norm ('Other apps usually have 5 free habits'; 'with three I'd have kept it for decency; with five I'd have … got hooked, and then bought'); the same cap is the most common purchase trigger for users whose two habits worked; the 2026 reports of a 4-habit tier are too few to read. Report 36: an unlimited free tier (praised: 'you can still get limitless habits w/ the free version — please keep it that way', 2023) capped at 2 then 1 in 2026; three reviewers volunteer three as the fair number ('Three would be reasonable for a paywall but only one??'; 'Ein Cap bei 3 Gewohnheiten hätte ich in Ordnung gefunden'); one mistook the cap for a bug; the cap upset US and non-US equally (5.56% each). Report 41: a 3-habit cap is 28 complaints (3.44%, mean 2.32) — 66.7% of 2★ and 31.0% of 1★, spiking to 6.4% in 2025 — while 5 describe it as a working trial and 4 of them paid; fans inside the complaint name 5–10 habits as the line ('at least 8 or 10'; '10ish'; '5/7'; '4/5'); the cap hurts 2.3× more outside high-spend markets. Report 42: a 3-habit cap where time, date, reminders and repetition are also paid is 55 complaints (26.70%, mean 1.96) — the largest theme — read as the product being broken ('Everything is paid! Writing a routine, only the title is free'; 'There is no reason to subscribe to the app to only have 3 habits'); four reviewers say the free tier proves there is no reason to subscribe; the number 3 has been cited every year 2022–2026. Report 43 (natural experiment): a 3-item cap held 2016–~2022 produced 66 complaints (10.34%, mean 2.36), 25 of 76 one-star reviews and 16 'bait and switch' accusations ('how can anyone set up a productive day with only 3 available habits?'; 'at least 8 - 10 habits for free'); loosening it removed the theme within two years and replaced it with free-tier praise at 4.63; the cap appeared at 5★ eight times from users who found three focusing; the report: do not re-tighten. Report 46 (the unchanged case): a 3-habit cap held from Jan 2019 to the listing in Sep 2026 is the largest negative (180, 8.26%, mean 2.43; 41.0% of one-stars; identical 8.27% vs 8.25% across market groups — 'a global constant of this product'); its count never fell (26 / 32 / 22 / 18 in 2022–25) while prompted volume halved its rate; the counter-offer is modest (29 name 4, 5, 6 or 7 — nobody unlimited) and the free tier cannot fill the product's own 4-row widget; 66 (mean 4.92) defend three on habit-science grounds; 'discovered after setup' is the indefensible version ('you've already spent 20 minutes or more setting it up', 16 votes). Report 47: the changed case — habit count unlimited 2019–2024 ('完全無料!!… タスクの登録数が無制限') then capped at 6 for free users from December 2024 (7 complaints, mean 2.29: 'Agora eu não posso mexer nos meus hábitos se não irei perder todos'); tracking multiple goals is praised by 17 (mean 4.76). Report 48 (the counter-case to a fixed cap): a cap that moved 10 → 7 → 3 produced the corpus's only growing grievance (211, 4.79%, mean 2.68) — 'No one has just one habit they need to track'; the three-tracker tier 'cannot show' a multi-goal product; the 2015–18 era with ~10 free trackers produced the highest ratings (4.62★), the most free-tier gratitude (7.82%) and a growing payer base; report's E1: raise the tier until the differentiator is demonstrable. Report 50 (the direct 5-vs-3 comparison): at 5 free habits reviewers defend the cap — 'Tienes 5 hábitos por elegir gratis lo que considero perfecto ya que te hace ser prioritario' ('perfect since it makes you prioritise'); '5 x free habits is a great option for new habit trackers'; 'I have 5 and it's all I need, when I get a job I will actually buy a subscription' — while at 3 nobody does: '3 hábitos gratis es una mierda'; 'la versión gratuita debería ser funcional' — 'Five habits was above the threshold at which a user can demonstrate a routine to themselves… Three is below it'; the 3★ band is five convinced users stalled by the cap (praise → cap → rating, none objecting to the price); 'Give me like 6 or 7 free habits and I'll be happy'; the report's S1: revert to 5, grandfather existing users, or disclose before install; experiment: A/B 3 vs 5 vs 7 on conversion, retention and rating. Report 52: the free quota (most often 5; 3, 4, 6, 8 and 10 also reported across cohorts) is the first wall and the persistent friction — PAY_CAP5 888 (4.30%, 2.96), 199 of them 5★ ('the quota is fine, the app is lovely'); a February 2020 install surge produced 51 quota complaints and 57 one-stars in one month. Report 53: a 3-habit free cap (PAY_CAP3 89, 5.11%, 3.04) splits reviewers — 35 at 4–5★ find three enough to try or live with, 33 at 1–2★ call it a trick; top theme in Canada (11.94%); the report's M3 asks for a retention test of 5 habits rather than assuming bigger is better. Report 54: a 3-habit cap — the most-discussed decision (44, 11.92%, 3.16; 11 more call the free tier useless at 1.91) — hit mid-setup ('I was having fun setting up my habits until I maxed out my 3 free habits … Deleted immediately'; 'sleep, wake, exercise, and all three are used up', TW); reviewers name their own number, modal 5–8 (5, 5–7, 7–8, 8, 9 as 3×3 across time-of-day sections, 10); 23 of 44 rated 1–3★; D1: raise to 5–8 as a measured experiment. Report 55: a five-habit free tier praised more often than resented (PAY_FREE_OK 96 at 4.86 vs PAY_CAP 87 at 3.98, 44 of them 5★) and contrasted favourably with 3-habit competitors ('some apps make the free version so debilitating you have no choice but to delete or buy. But this app has a great free version'); more than five habits is the leading reason among satisfied payers; M2: keep it, never shrink it. Report 56: unlimited habits named by 4, always against competitors — 'without limiting me to preset habits or a specific number without paying first' (AR); 3 left competitors specifically over caps. Report 58: unlimited free habits against rivals' caps — 'Finally a habit tracker app where you can add more than 5 habits for free!' (HR); 'all the other apps like tell me I have to pay to put more things on the checklist' (SA); 'when we normalised that a habit tracker app, doesn't allow us to track habits?' (UY); 14 praise the absence of a cap. Report 59 (Tappsk): a 2-habit / 2-recurring free cap is the most frequent objection in every era — MON_FREE_LIMIT 697 (4.59%, Very strong, 3.82★), the top 3★ theme (80 of 481), third in 4★ (247), and 'great app, but only two habits free' is the typical 4★ (praise + price objection share 601 reviews); 'two habits is too few to evaluate' ('неинтересно так пробовать'; '2 alışkanlıktan fazlasına premium istiyor', the most-voted Turkish review); the report's experiment is raising the cap to three (reviewers propose three or five) and stating the caps on the listing, predicting fewer 1–3★ with no loss of lifetime purchases because purchases are driven by discounts, not the cap (13 of 1,090 purchasers cite it); SA, TR, SE and ES over-index on the cap complaint. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): a 3-habit free cap is the most-named boundary — 4 of 45 (8.89%) and all four say 3, rated 5★ / 3★ / 2★ / 1★ ('Just a small suggestion to add… at least one more free task as we already have 3 but having 4 as free will give edge to the app', 5★; 'the free version only allows tracking 3 habits… so I ended up uninstalling' after a paragraph of praise; 'Only 3?????? … this app is useless') — 'not a complaint from people who dislike the app; it is a wall that people walk into on their way out'; the use cases described (water and steps, walking, three concurrent religious practices) need 4–6 habits, so the cap bites before the product proves itself; steady across 17 months; M1: raise the allowance from 3 to 5, or make the 4th habit a time-limited trial rather than a wall. Report 65 (Rabit): the free tier without a 3-habit cap was the positioning — PAY_FREE_OK 48 (9.64%, mean 4.88: 'you can log more than three habits for the free version'; 'te deja añadir más de 3 hábitos en su versión gratuita') — then a cap reported at 3, 4, 5 and 6 in different months of 2023 (PAY_FREE_LIMIT 34, 6.83%, mean 2.00; 26 of 99 reviews in Jan–Nov 2023, mean 1.85) — 'the limit was moved repeatedly rather than set once'; PAY_FREE_OK 15.3% → 2.2% as PAY_FREE_LIMIT 1.2% → 28.3% — 'the same axis, inverted'; two users in 2020 had pleaded in advance not to be capped at three. Report 69 (TheFor): the ledger's clearest case of an uncapped free tier as the moat — PAY_FREE_UNLIMITED 10 (12.50%, mean 4.80) naming the competitor behaviour avoided ('a maioria dos apps permitem de 3 a 5 itens de lista e so liberam mais no premium, esse tem quantidade de hábitos ilimitados no plano free'; 'I've been looking for this 😭'); free-offer praise 19 (23.75%, mean 4.89, none below 4★) rising 5.0% → 23.3% → 47.1% of reviews across 2023 / 2024 / 2025–26 as, reviewers say, the category capped at 3–5 — 'The moat is getting more valuable, not less'; zero cap complaints in 3.5 years; M1: publicly commit to unlimited free habits. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): here the habit cap is one and free — a design, not a monetization lever — and it is defended by the reviewers it limits (148 praise vs 44 asking for more). Report 71 (MyStreaks): a free streak cap reported at 3 active (Jan 2023, a 5★ user 'for over 2 years'), then 2 (Nov 2023, Feb 2024), then 1 (Nov 2024) — reported by one reviewer each, so the direction is reported, not established; the cap is the whole 1★ population (3 reviews, mean 2.00 vs 4.90 for the other 29): 'For an app all about self betterment i thought it wouldn't require me to pay to have MORE THAN 2 GOALS'; the only counter-offer: 'they could make the max like 5 or 10' (4★). Report 72 (Habit Hearts): the cleanest dated natural experiment on a cap in the ledger — reviewers name the free allowance as 3 (to 22 Dec 2024), then 1 (13 reviewers on six storefronts between 23 Dec 2024 and 3 Jan 2025, nobody before or after in 22 months), then 3 again; mean 4.848 → 4.293 → 4.725 and 1–2★ share 0.0% → 17.3% → 4.9%; version 1.0.8 (shipped 2024-12-18) covers 35 reviews at 3.80, the only release window below 4.0; the cap is 11 of 13 1★ and 5 of 7 2★ — 'This app is free but I literally can only make one habit before it corners me into paying'; 'Why download a habit tracker app for the purpose of tracking a single habit?'; 'Three is survivable; it is not comfortable' (8 complaints at 3; 'a limit of 6 habits would have been fine and would retain far more users'); §8.1 #1 'Set and hold the free habit cap at 3 or more. Never 1'; §8.7 'treat that number as a rating-sensitive setting, not a growth lever'. Report 75 (Habit Streak): a 3-habit free cap raised to 5 in Oct 2025 ('You asked, we listened') — cap objections stayed at 2 per era and turned from polite 3–4★ to hostile 1★ at the new number; 5 of 5 1★ reviews are about money and nothing else, four praising the product in the same sentence; a user reached a one-month streak on the free tier and called 3 'perfette per iniziare'. Report 76 (Way of Life): a 3-item free cap held for 16 years; MON_FREE_LIMIT 250 (3.22%, 3.53★, in every era 1.5–6.1%, peaking in E3) vs PR_FREE 249 (4.72★) — 'I actually think three habits is enough'; 'forced me to prioritize the three most important tasks by paywalling more than 3' (5★); cn: 'the free version's limit of three habits is actually better'; the cap is the #1 purchase trigger once the free tier has delivered value ('found myself wanting to add more and shelled out the $5'); 2★ reviews are 25% MON_FREE_LIMIT; 1★ 18.78%. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): a one-habit free cap — cap objections 4 of 71 (5.63%, mean 2.50★), all in the second half of the corpus (zero in the first 42 reviews, 4 in the last 29; the corpus cannot say whether the cap tightened or merely became visible); 'add one habit, then be interrupted repeatedly'; the report does not recommend raising the cap because converters are invisible, but notes the differentiator cannot be experienced at one habit ([[C296]]); E2 in §8.6: held-out cohort at cap=3. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): a 3-board free cap held for 770 days and converted on its own ('upgraded for more boards and to support the developer'); MON_FREE_GENEROUS 10 at 5.00★; the same cap read as a wall only after the widget left the free tier ([[C297]]). Report 83 (Roubit): an 8-routine free cap with a praised free tier (FREE_GENEROUS 14 vs FREE_LIMIT_ROUTINES 12); PAID_FOR_ROUTINES 3 ('the unlimited routines really make all the difference') — the cap converts a few and is tolerated by most; its value has been changed at least four times. Report 84 (HabitGrid): unlimited habits with no IAP — 'most of them only let you make around 4 habits before tealling you to pay. This one let me make as many as I wanted (10 so far)!'; two Russian reviewers searched 'a very long time' for a free app 'with unlimited habits and a clear chart'; U:paywall_contrast 16 (18.60%), all 5★, sets the app against the category's cap-then-pay default. Report 86 (Today): the clearest natural experiment on cap size in the series — the free tier went 1 → 3 (Mar 2016) → 5 (2017, n=1) → 1 (~2022): at one habit MON_FREE1 78 reviews at 1.97★ (71 in 2016 alone, the dominant theme of the first fortnight), raised to three within two weeks and noticed within a day ('because they actually listened to there customers I just paid full price for it!'), then zero one-habit complaints for four years (2017–2020); narrowing back to one in ~2022 re-imported the complaint in the same words ('you can only track ONE habit with the free version… If they had just advertised this as a paid app, it would have been fair', 2★); three-habit complaints (67) average 3.60★ — 'the same grievance, attached to a tier three times wider, arrives with a rating 1.63 stars higher'. Research: Feature Gating vs Quantity.md — the external floor for this number: a good free tracker should allow 'at least 5-10 habits on the free plan, ideally with no limit', and the caps actually shipped in this category sit below it — Habitify 3 (then locks you out), Productive 5 — which the cited HabitBox analysis reads as 'engineered to push you to Pro within a week' and as a wall someone hits 'once they try to build a routine'. The quoted user reaction is a lost buyer rather than a converted one: 'extend the habit limit for free users from 3 to 4…(or better make it unlimited) - my OCD is making me seriously consider switching apps because of this'. A paraphrased internal study found cap-complainers were less likely to ever pay.

<a id="c011"></a>
### C011 — Weekly / monthly / yearly reports

**Contested** · 34 apps · 90 cards · positive in 16 apps · negative in 27 apps · tied to a purchase in 7 apps

*Why Contested:* 34 apps; free vs paid genuinely split — 16 apps' cards say build-free, 14 say build-paid

| | reaction positive | reaction negative |
|---|---|---|
| **app makes it free** | free-praised — 6 apps | free-expected-but-broken — 0 apps |
| **app makes it paid** | paid-converts — 5 apps | paid-resented — 6 apps |

**Verdict from the table:** mixed — conditions decide

The #1 stated reason people pay; under-counted by keywords, dominant in the qualitative read. Report 25 (counter-evidence): paywalling all statistics — success %, graphs, per-habit calendar — averaged 1.40 and 'removes the motivation loop the category sells'; keep the basic progress view free, sell the deep report. Report 31: charts once unlocked are a named purchase trigger ('excited to see them … upgraded immediately'); stats 145 mentions, called weak by power users who want all-habit overviews, weekly totals and % of days. Report 33: statistics praised by 182 rated 4–5★ ('The statistics … is what sold me') and a named purchase trigger; 58 request an all-habit weekly grid, raw totals and multi-year history ('I want a GitHub type chart'); yearly and daily-ratio stats were removed in Habitify X. Report 34: statistics requests 14 (1.88%) — month %, all habits in one grid, counts rather than streaks; the free stats screen is 'a bit too simple'. Report 36: statistics / counts / year-in-review requested by 10, the newest rising request (4.6% of E5); one reviewer counts completions per month by hand. Report 41: statistics are Premium ('in free version… No statistics'), named as a purchase trigger ('love statistics now visible'), and 'better / deeper statistics' is still requested by 9. Report 42: statistics are the actual premium value proposition — three of six named purchase triggers ('Seeing the progress percentage of habits and which days they were done… because I found it in this app I bought the premium version'; 'The detailed stats in premium version are worth it') — while the same feature miscalculates for non-daily habits (a payer) and history is capped for free users. Report 43: percentages, grades, streaks and the green / red calendar praised by 55 (8.62%, mean 4.82) — 'Thank you for %'s and grades. This is how my brain works… I'm actually completing it so I can stay at a 90% grade' — free. Report 46: stats praised by 54 (mean 4.91 — 'I exercised 60% of the time, wrote 80% of the time'); richer statistics requested by 11 (4.55). Report 48: better reports / trends is the top open request (76, mean 4.07, still open Aug 2026) and comes almost entirely from people who like the app — the report's candidate next paid feature. Report 52: year statistics moved behind VIP in Dec 2025 and drew a one-month complaint window; the report's M3 test is a free basic year summary with a paid detailed report, a split one reviewer asked for verbatim. Report 53: extended statistics are a named purchase reason ('bought premium with extended statistics', ru) and the paid feature that broke. Report 54: long-range history requested by 28 (7.59%) and per-habit stats by 16; 48 unique (13.01%, 3.83) want 'proof that they have been consistent, over a period longer than a week, for a habit they can name' — the second-largest need after the paywall. Report 56: analytics / charts requested once in a fully free app. Report 57: weekly / monthly / yearly reports praised by 24 (the yearly report called unique); history of past reports requested by 11. Report 65 (Rabit): performance charts over time (REQ_GRAPH 2, 5.00) and a completion-% score beside the streak. Report 69 (TheFor): 'só sinto muita falta de análise de dados, gráficos dos hábitos, como no aplicativo concorrente Ripples' — the only named competitor, named for better charts. Report 75 (Habit Streak): more statistics requested (Apr 2025); an Insights screen with weekly / monthly / yearly views and a heatmap shipped in v1.57.1 six months later — no review mentions it. Report 76 (Way of Life): REQ_STATS 72 (0.93%, 4.19★), REQ_DATE_RANGE 22, REQ_CHART_CUSTOM 8, REQ_CALENDAR 29 (calendar view, 3.93★) — more statistics and other time ranges on top of free charts. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): REQ_MORE_STATS 1, REQ_MULTI_GRAPH 1 (compare several habits in one graph), PRAISE_STATS 5 (4.40★: 'good line graph view'). Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): PRAISE_ANALYTICS 9 (streaks, consistency, charts) at 5.00★; REQ_ANNUAL_VIEW 1 partially shipped in v2.7.0. Report 85 (Habitica): an eleven-year-old gamified tracker still lacks history and statistics — REQ_STATS 71 (2.06%), REQ_CALENDAR 33 ('if it had a calender for the habits and I could see how many days in a month I completed the task' carries 14 votes, more than any other request); §8.6 hypothesis: 'users who can see progress outside the avatar keep using the app past the point where the game content runs out'. Research: Feature Gating vs Quantity.md — detailed analytics is named as one of the four capabilities habit apps conventionally gate, and 'advanced analytics' heads the document's list of what to monetise once the core loop is free.

<a id="c063"></a>
### C063 — Free trial before purchase

**Contested** · 31 apps · 100 cards · positive in 6 apps · negative in 26 apps · tied to a purchase in 5 apps

*Why Contested:* 31 apps; free vs paid genuinely split — 4 apps' cards say build-free, 7 say build-paid

| | reaction positive | reaction negative |
|---|---|---|
| **app makes it free** | free-praised — 1 apps | free-expected-but-broken — 6 apps |
| **app makes it paid** | paid-converts — 0 apps | paid-resented — 6 apps |

**Verdict from the table:** evidence leans free (paid is mostly resented)

Weak but present complaint. Report 9: no trial in most storefronts drew 52 explicit requests, several saying they would have bought — and a trial offered in the US but not Saudi Arabia was compared in public. Report 23: a paid-up-front app with no trial — 15 (0.21%, mean 2.40) name the absence, it recurs as a stated regret in refund reviews, and accidental one-tap purchases drive Korea's 6.5% refund rate (7× global); counter-evidence: 'There's no trial because it doesn't need one'. Report 28: five reviewers wanted to pay and were stopped by the absence of a trial — 'I wouldn't have purchased until I was sure I liked the app, and it was impossible to like the app when it was a slew of ads'; 'Unlike Study Bunny, there is no $2.00 30-day trial… that's a full STOP sign'; the dominant purchase trigger is ad removal after sustained free use, which the 'unusable' churners never reach; the sibling app's reported $2 / 30-day trial is the proposed experiment. Report 30: 'I paid the anual subscription… It doesn't have a trial version and it wasn't what I was looking for' (1★); 'before buying something you should be able to try it' (1★); one 3★ could not tell whether the app was paid or free — introduce a trial or a reversible first purchase. Report 31: trial reaction is net-negative (56, mean 2.16) and the positive outcomes are first-year discount trials, not free trials ('an almost-free year is more than enough to know whether the €60 is worth it'). Report 33: for most of the corpus there was no trial ('Three habits, and three days, is simply too little'), and purchase intent 'would buy if…' appears in 44. Report 34: no trial (2022, 2024, 2026) vs a 3-day trial (2025) — 7 complaints (mean 3.00): 'I refuse to pay the min. $9 just to find out if I like it'; a 2018 reviewer proposes '21 days of all bells and whistles … Once you hook them on, charge them'. Report 36: TRIAL 7 (mean 2.43) — 'any sort of trial period — even just an hour — before you blow $15'; 'these issues aren't readily apparent from the free version when you only have two habits to look at'. Report 42: 'no trial' is the lowest-mean theme in the corpus (14, 6.80%, mean 1.29); reviewers name the length they wanted (1 day, 3 days, 7 days, a month) and four met the paywall before any use ('Literally two seconds after downloading'); the report distinguishes it from the cap complaint — a trial asks for temporary full product and is strictly cheaper to grant. Report 43 (counter-case): only 4 of 638 asked for a time-limited trial because a full-featured 3-habit free tier served as one ('The free version has all the features but limits the amount of habits… try it out and if it works for you, you can upgrade as I did') — vs 14 in report 42's 3-habit-plus-paid-basics corpus. Report 46: a 7-day trial is the top purchase trigger ('I paid for the full version after the trial because I could see how much it had helped in just a week'; 'Absolutely did not hesitate to purchase after the week trial'; 'used this app for 6 days and fully expected to delete it… I will be subscribing') — yet 32 (mean 1.88) say the 3-habit free tier is too small to evaluate ('I'd have to subscribe before even trying it'; 'try it for 30 days without limitation'). Report 47: 5-day and one-week trials reported; 'trial not disclosed' 2 (both 1★: '試用期間5日、最初から有償アプリと書け、時間を無駄にした'); a six-year user's app crashed the moment the trial payment went through. Report 49 (the natural experiment): 90 asked for a trial; one arrived 24 Jan 2026 card-gated, auto-charging, annual-only, with a forced loop — hard-paywall complaints went 17.24% → 34.96%, 'advertised as free' 2.13% → 6.50%, 11 new 'trial charged immediately' reviews, mean unchanged (2.77 → 2.78) — 'the reputational cost of a paywall plus the reputational cost of a billing surprise'; reviewers propose 'allow the first week to run freely. Get the user on a run, and they'll pay to continue'; the report: no card and a free first week, or no trial and an honest price — 'The half-measure is the worst of the three options.' Report 50: a 7-day trial ('Download, 7day free trial, then u gotta subscribe') with charges landing before it ended and no expiry reminder (see C029, C152). Report 54: no trial — 7 ask for one ('It's kind of expensive to buy the premium to see if I will like it'; 'use the app fully for 2–3 months before spending the twenty'). Report 57: no trial — 'you only get the urge to go paid after actually trying it free'; 'the Premium features don't land for me — a time-limited trial would be fine'. Report 59 (Tappsk): a trial that needs a card is itself a barrier ('полная версия в пробном периоде требует привязки карты', 1★) and the immediate-charge trial is the 1★ engine ([[C109]]). Report 64 (Critique AI): 'at least bring back the free trial' — the one review implying a trial was removed; 10 reviewers found a 3-day trial while 26 say there is none (possibly A/B-varied). Report 76 (Way of Life): three items is too few to evaluate for some (REQ_TRIAL 4, 1.75★); the subscription era added a free trial ('My trial ends Saturday', 2★). Report 76 (Way of Life): the free trial on the subscription (E6) — 'My trial ends Saturday' (2★). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): MON_NO_TRIAL 1 (4★: 'there should be somewhat of a free trial because you can't really explore the app'); zero reviewers mention using a trial; §8.6 E3: a 7-day trial arm vs the 1-habit cap arm. Report 86 (Today): the free tier is the trial and MON_TRIAL_REQ 33 (1.85%) — 'a real one' — was the most-requested monetisation change in 2016 and still asked in 2024. (Final consolidation: distinguish [[C109]] — this point is whether a trial should exist at all, which is a demand and conversion question; C109 is whether a shipped trial behaves as advertised, which is a billing-integrity question. The highest title-overlap pair in the final sweep, and deliberately not merged: an app can satisfy one and fail the other.)

<a id="c045"></a>
### C045 — Grouping / folders / categories / tags

**Contested** · 28 apps · 52 cards · positive in 7 apps · negative in 15 apps · tied to a purchase in 2 apps

*Why Contested:* 28 apps; free vs paid genuinely split — 6 apps' cards say build-free, 4 say build-paid

#2 feature request in report 1; the highest-mean request in report 3 (zero 1–2★, power users tracking 20–100 counters); named in report 8's only subscription-price statement. Report 20: categories/folders (58) and a compact row option (26) co-occur — both are what happens when a power user exceeds ~8 habits. Report 23: extra capacity is wanted for time-of-day pages (morning / work / evening / bedtime) and life-domain segmentation (health / work / relationships / creative). Report 25: groups and sub-groups are a praised paid feature (customisation 65, mean 4.49); group creation reported locked on free. Report 26: per-habit gardens or categories requested (18). Report 27: tags exist but existing tags cannot be selected and duplicates don't group — two storefronts, two months apart, same bug, both cost stars. Report 31: groups/categories (added Mar 2018) were paid and valued by buyers; forced daily/weekly grouping and order resets in v3.0 (22) drew complaints. Report 33: areas / folders (Dec 2019) are free and mixed (31). Report 41: lists / tags with per-list rings and widget filtering (2022). Report 46: folders / habit groups shipped Aug 2025 after 10 requests ('The new habit folder feature is — chef's kiss'). Report 48: tags / filters / a Today list are premium; requested by 26 (4.12). Report 50: journal notes filterable by activity or category. Report 53: 'so close to perfect… ability to group activities' (4★). Report 56: separate lists / habit groups requested once. Report 60 (Mindway): preset routine packs (self-care, hair care, exercise, chores, hydration) and a self-care guide are the praised entry point (P_CONTENT_PACKS 5, 4.80★: 'having a guide to which to refer'; 'rehberle çok yardım ettiler') and the inferred paid asset — but packs loaded by default are also a clean-up burden ('otherwise you would spend all day deleting tasks', a payer; 'It is overwhelming to set up tasks in the beginning'); E6: a bulk-remove-pack control and a first-run 'pick one of three ready-made days'; custom task creation is limited or gated and is the most-requested capability ('I wish there was a way to personalize or make my own'). Report 69 (TheFor): paid 'Routine' packs ($0.99–$2.99) and 'Routine AI' ($2.99) are listed, yet zero of 80 reviews mention buying one; the Explore surface is unfindable to one reviewer and empty to another — M4: make it findable and stocked, or remove it. I really feel motivated to tick things off, more than any other habit app'; 'It sets a craving, when I see the image, I want to accomplish the goal'; custom covers named as the one reason productivity improved most across 15 trackers; custom covers are a named purchase trigger ('I purchased the full thing just because to put my own photo covers'); PR_DESIGN holds at 15.25% even in the abandonment era — 'the app never stopped being beautiful. It stopped working'; §8.12 'copy: the full-screen personal photo per habit'; the costs: one page per habit does not scale ([[C254]]) and the image layer is blamed for slowness; a paid feature later taken away with users' existing covers ('you have to pay to use your own pictures and completely took everything i had on my profile off', 1★).

<a id="c102"></a>
### C102 — Inverse / 'good habit' mode for a counter

**Moderate** · 3 apps · 5 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 2 apps

*Why Moderate:* 3 apps

Recovery users want the number up; chore/ADHD users want it low — one counter, two mental models. Report 86 (Today): 'maximum N per period' as a habit type — five reviewers describe it; competitors Done and HabitBull are named as having it. <a id="c265"></a>
### C265 — Tracker types beyond yes/no — numeric target, rolling average and project milestones — as the reason people switch from binary habit apps

**Moderate** · 2 apps · 8 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 1 apps

*Why Moderate:* 2 apps

Report 48 (Strides): four tracker types — Habit (yes/no), Target (a number by a date), Average (rolling mean), Project (milestones, %) — are the defining feature and the differentiator: 485 reviews (11.02%, mean 4.82★) — 'I don't want to reduce everything to the binary yes/no' (2013) repeated in structure in 2024; a reviewer lists seven rivals before 'Strides is the only app that does both'; highest in GB (13.79%), AU (14.52%), IN (16.90%); bad-habit / 'less is better' inversion praised by 105; goal pacing (the projected-date and 'am I on pace' maths only Target and Project provide) praised by 56 at 4.97★ — 'This theme, not streaks or design, is why people switch to Strides'. The cost is a decade of setup confusion (118 reviews at 2–3% in every era, concentrated on choosing between the four types) and yes/no semantics that turn ambiguous for bad habits (12). Related: [[C108]] (goals / targets), [[C048]] (flexible units / partial progress), [[C019]] (quit-habit mode), [[C136]] (choose the mode at creation), [[C135]]. Report 76 (Way of Life): REQ_COUNT 129 and NEG_YESNO 36 ('In my life things aren't always yes or no', 4★) — the binary grid is the product's value and its ceiling; §8.4 counts as a separate journal type, never the default.

<a id="part-7"></a>
## Part 7 — Must-haves and must-never-break

**Must-have** is what the product needs regardless of the free/paid split. **Must-never-break** is
the reliability set — the things that generate 1★ reviews when they fail, which in this category is
where most of the rating damage comes from. Each statement carries the magnitude of what happened in
the apps where it broke.

### must-have — 43 points



| apps | Confidence | Point |
|---|---|---|
| 63 | Certain | [C036](#c036) A support channel that exists, is reachable outside the app, and answers |
| 53 | Certain | [C043](#c043) Flexible / custom frequency — N times per week, specific weekdays, counts — with non-scheduled days neutral in the statistics |
| 37 | Certain | [C075](#c075) Skippable, replayable onboarding tour and an in-app help screen — searchable FAQ and per-setting explanations for anything richer than the daily check-in |
| 33 | Certain | [C112](#c112) In-app cancellation |
| 29 | Certain | [C035](#c035) Account system from day one |
| 26 | Certain | [C171](#c171) Accessibility stack: VoiceOver, motion, sound and light sensitivity, text size |
| 25 | Certain | [C110](#c110) An obvious 'continue free' path on the paywall — the free/paid boundary must be legible |
| 24 | Certain | [C142](#c142) Surface existing features where users look |
| 22 | Certain | [C177](#c177) One clear SKU shelf — every plan distinctly named, stating its period, and delivering exactly what its label says |
| 21 | Certain | [C095](#c095) Neutral, non-judgemental tone on failure |
| 18 | Certain | [C216](#c216) A forgiving long-run measure — cumulative or decaying credit that a missed day does not zero — alongside streaks |
| 14 | Certain | [C255](#c255) An in-app language selector that respects the user's choice — shipping a localisation must never trap someone in a language |
| 14 | Certain | [C256](#c256) Skip, miss and not-yet-logged are visibly distinct states, and the stats explain which is which |
| 13 | Certain | [C123](#c123) Notifications are few and finely user-controllable — per-type settings, escalation opt-in, never spammy and never silently retuned |
| 11 | Certain | [C223](#c223) Undo / un-complete is a visible button — never a gesture-only path |
| 10 | Certain | [C148](#c148) The paid product must deliver what the ads and onboarding demonstrate |
| 10 | Certain | [C183](#c183) A pre-planned, structured day is the outcome ADHD and autistic users praise |
| 10 | Certain | [C221](#c221) A receipt with a working product link after every charge, and a renewal reminder before it |
| 9 | Certain | [C207](#c207) Let users hide surfaces they don't use — tabs, social, recommendations, streaks |
| 8 | Certain | [C217](#c217) An unexplained number reads as broken — explain the score, and any rule that moves it by itself, on-screen |
| 36 | Strong | [C012](#c012) Week / month / year grid views |
| 26 | Strong | [C143](#c143) Intra-day completion: tap N times to fill N/N |
| 10 | Strong | [C096](#c096) Privacy and discretion stack |
| 8 | Strong | [C237](#c237) The reward loop needs a content runway — finite gardens, themes or levels exhaust long-term users |
| 8 | Strong | [C254](#c254) An all-habits overview with one-tap check-off — never force one-habit-at-a-time navigation |
| 7 | Strong | [C215](#c215) Support reply time must be shorter than any cancellation deadline it serves |
| 7 | Strong | [C261](#c261) A colour palette users can extend — more defaults, a hex picker, softer sets — because colour is the reward surface |
| 6 | Strong | [C159](#c159) Launch-to-core-action path with no interstitials |
| 4 | Strong | [C120](#c120) Sequential routine timer with spoken next step and live finish-time estimate |
| 4 | Strong | [C201](#c201) A user-set partial-completion threshold — a 'good day' below 100% |
| 4 | Strong | [C235](#c235) A first-run failure escape hatch — skip setup / continue offline, with a visible error state |
| 32 | Contested | [C141](#c141) Native iPad layout |
| 23 | Contested | [C153](#c153) Automatic cloud backup on by default — never manual opt-in |
| 3 | Moderate | [C136](#c136) When an item can be tracked more than one way, make the user choose the mode at creation |
| 3 | Moderate | [C160](#c160) Honour what onboarding asks — a declared limitation must change the suggestions |
| 3 | Moderate | [C268](#c268) Journal / notes prompts are optional — a toggle to stop the post-completion journal prompt, and a text editor that never corrupts input |
| 2 | Moderate | [C308](#c308) Logging a lapse must not be the same action as destroying the count — a quit-tracker needs a way to record a slip, and non-judgemental wording around it |
| 1 | Moderate | [C121](#c121) Untimed / checklist mode as a per-routine toggle |
| 1 | Moderate | [C198](#c198) Edit one instance of a repeating block without changing the series; a slipped block pushes the ones after it |
| 1 | Moderate | [C233](#c233) Content the user paid for is saveable and replayable — a library, not a stream |
| 1 | Moderate | [C282](#c282) A generated plan belongs to the user — it persists, every assigned task can be deleted, declined and reordered, and it is built around the user's fixed commitments |
| 1 | Moderate | [C288](#c288) A user who declined notifications at first run must have an in-app way back — detect the denied state, explain it, and deep-link to iOS Settings |
| 1 | Moderate | [C289](#c289) An app with a personality voice needs one 'quiet mode' switch — encouragement lines, jokes and badges to plain neutral text — while the voice stays the default |

### must-never-break — 45 points



| apps | Confidence | Point |
|---|---|---|
| 60 | Certain | [C031](#c031) Crashes and launch failures are the largest complaint by volume — and one bad release can outweigh a year of goodwill in a week |
| 59 | Certain | [C065](#c065) Paying customers are the highest 1★ risk — every paid feature must work |
| 55 | Certain | [C034](#c034) Data must never be lost on update, reinstall or phone change |
| 45 | Certain | [C033](#c033) Restore purchase and entitlements must work immediately |
| 43 | Certain | [C029](#c029) Billing must be exactly right |
| 42 | Certain | [C039](#c039) Reminders fire reliably, once |
| 38 | Certain | [C175](#c175) Updates must not break function or wipe progress |
| 36 | Certain | [C038](#c038) Dates, streaks and statistics correct on every surface — month boundaries, week starts, DST and timezones |
| 36 | Certain | [C109](#c109) A free trial must be a real trial |
| 35 | Certain | [C040](#c040) Widgets must not go blank, stale or disagree with the app |
| 28 | Certain | [C113](#c113) One stable, disclosed price — no discount wheels |
| 24 | Certain | [C119](#c119) Redesigns must not regress layout — ship a density / text-size option or an opt-out |
| 16 | Certain | [C083](#c083) Performance must not degrade with habit count |
| 15 | Certain | [C152](#c152) A promised pre-charge trial reminder must actually arrive — in-app, with amount and date |
| 14 | Certain | [C077](#c077) Purchase and signup flow must not leak buyers |
| 12 | Certain | [C188](#c188) The app must open offline — never block launch on a network call |
| 10 | Certain | [C139](#c139) Cache entitlements locally — never block a paid surface on a live server check |
| 9 | Certain | [C156](#c156) Content and event releases need a crash gate across device generations |
| 8 | Certain | [C032](#c032) New Year peak-season robustness — year-end report and January onboarding |
| 8 | Certain | [C193](#c193) When a trial or subscription ends, the user lands on a usable free tier with read-only history — never a cliff |
| 7 | Strong | [C041](#c041) Editing a habit never wipes its history |
| 7 | Strong | [C072](#c072) Writes to shared system stores (calendar, health) must be exact and reversible |
| 7 | Strong | [C230](#c230) Sync merges an append-only, timestamped event log — never last-writer-wins state replacement |
| 5 | Strong | [C162](#c162) Automated suggestions from user text must be safety-filtered; notifications must be crisis-aware |
| 5 | Strong | [C228](#c228) Text fields must handle IME composition — Hangul and CJK input |
| 5 | Strong | [C249](#c249) Account deletion completes in one step, in-app and on the web, and is confirmed — never a spinner or a silent chatbot |
| 4 | Strong | [C090](#c090) Destructive actions on widgets, quick surfaces and running routines need confirmation or undo |
| 4 | Strong | [C219](#c219) A free cap must be concurrent, never lifetime — deleting a habit frees a slot |
| 30 | Contested | [C030](#c030) Sync must work — and prove it |
| 2 | Moderate | [C232](#c232) Payment retries are bounded — daily dunning against a declined card reads as fraud to the customer and their bank |
| 2 | Moderate | [C250](#c250) Marketing e-mail needs consent and a working one-tap unsubscribe — never e-mail dormant or deleted accounts |
| 2 | Moderate | [C266](#c266) A generated programme escalates on observed completion, never on a fixed calendar — and never past what a health limit the user declared allows |
| 2 | Moderate | [C272](#c272) Built-in timers survive backgrounding, a call and screen lock, and always alert at the end — store the start time, compute elapsed |
| 2 | Moderate | [C273](#c273) The reward mechanic must never silently stall — a plant, pet or garden that stops growing reads as the app taking the reward away |
| 2 | Moderate | [C295](#c295) Backup and sync must run on infrastructure reachable in every storefront the app is sold in — a blocked provider makes the app's data unsafe in that market |
| 1 | Moderate | [C122](#c122) Background battery and thermals |
| 1 | Moderate | [C149](#c149) Respect Reduce Motion — no rapid flashing animation |
| 1 | Moderate | [C151](#c151) Never cap or paywall a support conversation mid-crisis |
| 1 | Moderate | [C279](#c279) An AI analysis must consume its input — reject empty, silent or black input instead of returning a confident score |
| 1 | Moderate | [C280](#c280) An app-blocking focus mode must always unlock when its condition is met, never lock apps permanently, never override OS Screen Time, and never depend on a notification the OS can suppress |
| 1 | Moderate | [C284](#c284) Verify the rendered price string in every storefront currency — a decimal or tier error on the paywall suppresses conversion invisibly, because nobody who closes a paywall writes a review |
| 1 | Moderate | [C292](#c292) A preset or template must never write data on selection — choosing 'water' is not drinking 15 litres, and anything a preset writes can be rolled back |
| 1 | Moderate | [C301](#c301) The support form and account deletion must not live behind the surface most likely to break — a tab outage must never take the reporting and exit paths down with it |
| 1 | Moderate | [C303](#c303) Check-in latency must be independent of accumulated history — an app that slows with every completed day drives away exactly the users who proved it works and most likely paid |
| 1 | Moderate | [C306](#c306) Third-party ad code never sits on the launch path — the core surface renders first and any ad failure fails open |

<a id="c036"></a>
### C036 — A support channel that exists, is reachable outside the app, and answers

**Certain** · 63 apps · 226 cards · positive in 17 apps · negative in 54 apps · tied to a purchase in 2 apps

*Why Certain:* 63 apps, same direction (act on it, 97%), 27 reports label it high-priority

'No support channel' is ×34.7 over-represented among buyers and the second-worst-rated complaint. Report 5: the only support link was inside an app that would not launch; email went unanswered while public review replies were same-day. Report 10: AI and canned support replies; paying users 13× over-represented among support complaints. Report 11: 'there is no way in app to talk with developer or team' — with no support queue, billing bugs were filed as public 1★ fraud accusations instead. Report 12: five reviewers said the listed support email does not exist; refund and support failures were twice as prevalent in small storefronts, where users are charged and stranded. Report 18: support silence (32, mean 2.72★) landed hardest on payers — a week of silence on a lifetime account with purchase screenshots; the Japanese in-app feedback form rejected every valid e-mail and its text was invisible in dark mode, so Japanese users could only file bugs through the App Store; KakaoTalk was the only Korean channel and closed at weekends; a Canadian found the in-app support link resolved to an ad. Report 20: support went from answering reviews and fixing bugs same-day in 2019–2020 to a dead 'Contact Us' e-mail with an autoresponder and a dormant Instagram account (0.05% → 13.0% of reviews by era); among 148 support-silence reviews the mean was 1.33 versus 3.63 for the 30 who were restored or fixed — the same defect produced either rating depending only on whether anyone answered, worth ~+2.3 stars per recoverable incident. Report 23: support praised (49, 0.67%) with fixes bringing edited upgrades, but genuine silences recur and one reviewer says support implied they don't own an Apple Watch for testing. Report 24: 947 (2.18%, mean 1.528) automated-only support; the refund path works when reached — several 1★ → 4★ edits after a refund — so the failure is reaching it. Report 25: a solo developer answering within a day ('feature requests implemented in less than 24hrs'; 'I can't believe one developer made this') is a purchase trigger — 'After testing the app and interacting with the developer… I've decided to pay without any hesitation' — but support praise thinned 3.0% → 1.6% → 0.9% and one 1★ says the developer 'preferred to argue about what I could see on my end'. Report 26: support unreachable 13 (mean 2.77), support praised 10 (all 5★); support's own advice to reinstall destroyed a paying user's progress and purchase; a premium subscriber's crash went unanswered for months. Report 27: not one review in four years mentions contacting support or a developer reply; the website link in Settings leads to an inactive domain, so the support path is broken — and a solo-developer app with no support channel absorbs an OS-transition break entirely through its public rating. Report 28: 'There is no Support button in the app. Nor on developer's website'; 'no matter how many emails you send, they don't reply'; yet the four who reached the developer got excellent service — a 1★ converted to 5★ after a verification reset 'within an hour… on a Sunday, on a 3 day holiday weekend'; support quality is not the problem, discoverability is — an in-app 'Contact support' and 'Restore purchases' entry point is the cheapest rating intervention available. Report 29: support effectively unreachable — 'I contacted the dev twice but got no response'; a support link that 'takes you to a super-sketch website, circumventing Apple's privacy settings'; with no account and no backup the review page is the only support channel, which is why bugs arrive as public 1★. Report 31: 460 reviews (8.87%, mean 1.32) say support never replied or the contact path was broken (dead typeform links, a Mail-app-only link), rising 0.6% (E1) → 20.3% (E4) → 20.8% (E5); in E1 support was praised (11 of 18 support-praise reviews) — staff a single working contact path with a published response time and resolve by receipt, not by argument. Report 33: support is two-sided — praised 103 (mean 4.73; 'Hana … sent me a video'; 'within one minute') vs support failure 131 (1.70; 5 weeks without reply then the review deleted); English-only replies frustrate Japanese and Chinese users; AI-only support is an emerging negative (8 reviews, 7 in 2025–26: 'Their support is AI'; the chatbot 'stops answering'). Report 34: a single 'Support doesn't respond to emails' in an app whose main asset is a named, responsive solo developer. Report 36: both support-failure records are payers ('contacted the developer twice … I waited too long for a reply and I have now paid. Service matters'; 'a small company and cannot solve problems in mainland China'). Report 41: the only support channel is a mailto: link that dead-ends users without the Mail app ('forcing me to add a mail account'; a trial user 'likely will cancel'), in an app where support closes sales and is the only data-recovery path; support praise collapsed to 1.7% in 2025 as volume tripled, then recovered. Report 42: a paying customer with data loss had no route to a human — 'it says mail isn't connected, but there's no section in the app to connect it' — and replies are canned ('they just reply the same thing to everyone', a 10-vote review). Report 43: support is bimodal because the intake is broken — praised by 24 (mean 4.67; a 2★ raised to 5★ after the exact fix shipped; 'requested a small new feature… added a few days later') vs 7 with no response (mean 1.29, the lowest theme) and 4 reporting the in-app feedback form itself fails ('Feedback email can not send'; 'They have a report bug feature, but that also doesn't work'); 'no response' rose 0.57% → 2.60% by era while praise stayed flat. Report 46: 7 unanswered (mean 1.57; 'sent 3 different email… Not a single reply'), four of them 2024–26 and two paying customers with unresolved data loss or an unrecognised subscription; support praise 53 (4.94) is falling 4.30% → 1.82% as volume grew. Report 47: no findable support route — unresponsive 7 (mean 2.57): '問い合わせ先もわからない'; 'サポートサイトにも窓口がない'; a feedback form that crashes; account-deletion messages unanswered — while 12 reviews (mean 4.42) acknowledge a fix: the gap is the channel, not responsiveness. Report 48: support is reachable only inside the app, so users whose app will not open have no route — 14 reviews (1.08% of 2022–26 and growing) are 1★ reviews written as support tickets, nine from payers; the report's fix #3: publish a support e-mail on the website and the listing; separately 29 got no response (1.55). Report 49: 'contact support' is not a button (3), App Support resolves to a 404, multi-day silence — 21 unreachable (1.43), 10 of them payers; when support does answer it is outstanding (9 at 4.89 — a refund plus a free year) — 'The capability exists; the routing and the staffing do not.' Report 50: in-app support chat praised by 8 (5.00) and developer responsiveness by 11 (4.91) — 17 unique; one negative ('sometimes customer service give is not very caring'); support re-sent a lost discount offer and closed the sale — 'an asset to protect… not a cost centre to optimise'. Report 52: support silence rises with each crash wave (SUP_BAD 184, 2.33; payers ×4.53 at 1.92) across e-mail, WeChat, Weibo and Xiaohongshu; a support address that bounces; fast fixes are among the strongest praise (SUP_GOOD 148 at 4.93: a purchase crash fixed the next day, a request shipped within days). Report 53: support went from praised to silent — SUP_GOOD 31 (4.71) all Nov 2017 → Mar 2022 (a proactive follow-up, an icon idea shipped in days, VoiceOver added on request) and SUP_BAD 64 (1.58), 41 in 2023–26; the in-app contact needed a configured Mail account and later 'the support email it opens does not send'; payers with silent support average 1.17; F4: a contact that works without Mail, an auto-acknowledgement and a known-issues note. Report 54: support unresponsive 6 (1.50), rising to 4.2% of 2023–26; 'Your support pages and email are down' (GR, Aug 2026); 'there's no app support to write any of this to… which I feel like should be a thing if you have to pay for an app'. Report 55: support silence from Jan 2016 to Apr 2026 (SUP_BAD 83, 1.45, 66 at 1★; payer lift 6.21) — a developer site returning errors, a contact form that won't send, ticket numbers with no reply, canned answers; 'will update my review based upon their response'. Report 56: four in-review support questions (data recovery, widget transparency in Korean, language reset, back-dating) left unanswered, each answerable in one sentence. Report 57: Korean users write support tickets in the review box — 50 direct questions to the developer (49 Korean, 8.10% vs 0.57%), mostly 5★ about existing features; support praised 2019–24 for fast KakaoTalk replies ('got a reply the moment 9am hit') then silent ('they just read it and never replied. What a waste of money'); 'the support link goes to some Asian industrial company'; the in-app bug-report form crashes on Submit; F6: a support link and FAQ where users are already asking. Report 59 (Tappsk): reviewers praise Telegram and condemn e-mail — 'пишу на почту уже 2 раза, ответа нет' (e-mailed twice, no reply); 'На почту пишешь не отвечают, в тг пишешь бот' (e-mail unanswered; on Telegram you get a bot); SUP_NONE 64 (6.09× among purchasers), SUP_CONTACT 31, both more frequent in the latest eras; fix: route billing and sync tickets to the channel that answers and acknowledge bug reports with a status. Report 60 (Mindway): seven reviewers (3.24%, mean 1.43) used a 1★ public review as a help desk — 'the absence of a visible support path', six of the seven about money; the one who tried the proper route ('asked this question of the developer and awaiting the reply') rated 3★ where the other six went straight to 1★ — 'the one payer who found a support route rated the app two stars higher than the ones who didn't'; F3: put an in-app support route in front of the review prompt, and answer it — seven support tickets became permanent public 1★ reviews. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): no reviewer — including three paying customers with a broken app — reports contacting the developer; the reviews are the support channel by default. Report 64 (Critique AI): three 1★ reviews are unanswered, resolvable tickets — a parent's three emails on a login issue got one 'please clarify' then silence ('My son was so excited to use this app, but now it's just taking up space'); billing; a frozen paid app — F5: 'low rate, 100% conversion to 1★'. Report 65 (Rabit): SUP_SILENT 5 — every one 1★ and every one a payer ('Mandei dois e-mails solicitando o estorno da compra, mas até o momento não deram retorno'; 'ninguém responde… Um descaso total!') — each a problem one reply would have converted; F3: 'the cheapest rating repair available'. Report 67 (Habio): U_SUPPORT_FAIL 425 (20.72%, mean 1.04) — no reply 213, slow 78, templated 59, evasive 46; 'Funny how when it's public your response is timely'; retention questions in reply to cancellation requests; 37.7% of reviewers whose money left their account report a support failure. Report 68 (Ultiself): SUP_NONE 352 (7.80%; 20.8% of the Dec 2024 → Mar 2025 era); replies that seem automated ('the bot responds with nonsense'); in 2026 fast named replies with refunds lifted PR_SUPPORT to 5.0% of reviews — refunds reported in 1★ reviews stayed 1★. Report 69 (TheFor): the developer answers but cannot be found — 'Unable to contact developer on their website'; 'Let me know if I can email the suggestions'; a 1★ 'Phishing spam scam' demanding cancellation in public — 'a support-surface problem, not a support-quality problem'; F7: an email link in settings and a Manage-subscription row deep-linking to Apple. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): 5 reviewers used the public review as a support ticket (mean 3.00) though the developer answers email fast — E4: an in-app 'suggest a feature' route. Report 76 (Way of Life): support silence arrives from 2016 and peaks in the subscription era (SUP_NONE 20 at mean 2.05★, 9 of them in E6) alongside restore failures; the website contact section did not work ('secção de Contact no website não funciona', pt 1★); 'received no response at all' (1★); §8.3 a working in-app contact form and an auto-reply with restore steps; reviewers excuse a solo developer ('I think they are just one person, so be patient') until money is involved. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): zero customer-support-failure mentions in 71 reviews; the schema has no developer-reply field. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the single support-silence report is the worst case — a lifetime buyer whose restore failed: 'Developer doesn't respond. Waste of time' (1★); §8.1.1 a visible support path from the entitlement-failure screen. Report 82 (Lasting Change): the App Store listing prints a support address at a domain that does not exist — hello@lastingchange.app returns NXDOMAIN with no MX record, while the same page links the working domain thelastingchange.com; a reviewer hit it ('I tried to email hello@ and was told this was invalid'); email is the only cancellation route, so a dead address is a structural failure; the one satisfied payer used the working help@ address and was confirmed within a quarter of an hour; SUP_UNFINDABLE 5, SUP_CANNED 8 ('Your feedback has been taken into consideration…'), SUP_RESPONSE_FACADE 4. Report 83 (Roubit): the in-app support form sits inside the Settings tab that blanked in two bug waves, so the corpus became the support desk (SUPPORT_QUESTION 43, 8.60%; 31 of 33 rating/text contradictions are high-star bug reports); support_negative 15 (3.00%, 2.53★): unanswered email ('I emailed the person in charge twice with no reply'), unread KakaoTalk, a promised same-day fix then three days of silence, 'it's starting to feel like the app is being neglected'; where support worked it raised ratings ('The support helped me fix the ad issue by using the Restore Subscription button' → 5★; 'sorted within 24 hours'). Report 86 (Today): SUP_ASK 54 (3.03%) ask the developer a question in a review — 'a signal that the in-app support path is not obvious'; the embedded support address is misspelled (toda@neybox.com) and the corrected one got no reply; §8.11 'the cheapest fix in this report'. Report 88 (GetHabit): SUPPORT_UNRESPONSIVE 59 (12.04%, 1.22★) — emails unanswered, 'Failed to send email', no contact details; 61 of 227 money-taken reviewers (26.9%) report a support failure; SUPPORT_QUESTION 13 used the review to ask how to cancel; 'seeing as the creator isn't responding to these reviews, I don't hold much hope'. Report 89 (Check Calendar): SUPPORT_UNRESPONSIVE 2 ('no way to contact support'; 'Lodged a support ticket- no answer') and SUPPORT_QUESTION 5 — three paid users asking in a review how to restore their purchase on another device; §8.3 'give support a reachable path'. Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): no developer response appears on either captured listing and no reviewer reports contacting support or getting a reply; SUPPORT_QUESTION 15 (2.44%), 14 of them Russian, ask in the review how to set the goal, how to set the start date, whether progress transfers to a new phone and how to fix the crash — the review page is the only support channel the app appears to have.

<a id="c031"></a>
### C031 — Crashes and launch failures are the largest complaint by volume — and one bad release can outweigh a year of goodwill in a week

**Certain** · 60 apps · 209 cards · positive in 8 apps · negative in 55 apps

*Why Certain:* 60 apps, same direction (act on it, 97%), 41 reports label it high-priority

Largest complaint by volume; a two-day launch crash produced more 1★ than years of minor bugs. Report 23: crashes 46 (0.63%, mean 2.80, 34.8% 1★) on three dated bugs — iPhone X freeze-on-close 2017–18, an iOS 14-era freeze, a stuck splash screen 2023–26 — plus Watch-app crashes on each watchOS generation. Report 24: crash / freeze / won't load 944 (2.17%, mean 2.367) — the recurring shape is freezing on the 'first mountain' / Journeys screen on day one. Report 25: a post-onboarding freeze — the main screen stops responding to touch — is the fastest-rising negative theme (51, 3.90%, mean 1.63; 1.3% → 2.9% → 5.8%; 27 of 34 E3 reports in May–Jul 2026; Colombia 18%, Germany 7.8%, GB 0%); iPhone 11 and iOS 26.x named, reinstalling does not fix it, one reviewer says it survived two updates; every one of these users got zero value. Report 26: crash/launch failure fell 3.37% (2021–22) → 0.13% (2024) after a visible engineering turnaround, then a 2026 cluster (n=4, three Russian, two paying — a premium subscriber crashing on the onboarding screen after reinstall) flagged for telemetry. Report 27: a September–November 2025 update-and-iOS-26 launch crash ('Ever since I updated to iOS 26 the app immediately crashes when I try to open') accounts for almost every bad rating the app ever received — all 4 1★, the only 2★ and 4 of 6 3★ fall in a five-week window (window mean 4.162 vs 4.822 elsewhere); fixed by Feb 2026 (mean 4.829, zero 1★); a solo-developer app with no support channel pays for an OS-transition break entirely in public rating. Report 28: launch failure / crash 15 (1.83%, mean 2.40) concentrated in 2022 (orange-screen failure), then a 2026 uptick ('freezing every time I open the app, I think it needs an update to keep up with ios') consistent with OS drift on a build last updated Nov 2025. Report 29: one 2026 launch failure ('Lässt sich nichtmal öffnen'); overall bug reporting fell by two-thirds (22.3% → 6.5%). Report 30: two launch-week crashes (Jul 2025, 'It just doesn't open… on iOS 18.5 and on the iOS 26 beta') and none in the following 13 months. Report 31: the app would not open in 1,052 reviews (20.29%, mean 1.30) in five waves — launch season 2016, intro freeze Oct–Dec 2021, v1.19.0 crash on launch 22 Dec 2021 → ~8 Jan 2022 (918 in the window), a post-update white-screen hang May–Jun 2022, freezes after subscribing 2022–23; devices from iPhone 6 to 12 Pro Max, so not an old-device issue; 1★ in E3 is 66.4% launch failures; the fix did not recur at scale. Report 33: an 11 Sep 2025 'Liquid glass' update crashed on launch on iOS 18 and was fixed in ~1–3 days with no lasting rating shift; in Oct–Nov 2019 Brazilian users could not open the app after purchase. Report 34: the 10–11 Apr 2024 update crashed on launch and was fixed a day later (E4 reliability 6.7% → E5 2.6%); in Feb 2026 a reviewer needed 20–30 launches to load. Report 42: a launch-blocking regression 4 Dec 2024 – 11 Jan 2025 — 7 'won't open' reviews (mean 1.71), 5 Russian inside 40 days, one a payer three months into an annual subscription ('Give my money back, crooks'). Report 43: crash / won't open is the largest single defect (20, 3.13%, mean 2.15; 18 of 20 US) with a persistent won't-open cluster Dec 2021 → Feb 2023 recurring Dec 2025 → Apr 2026; 'after purchasing, the app crashed every single time I opened it'; 'Crashes if you have less than 500MB free'. Report 47: crashes arrive as dated incidents — 19 crash reviews in January 2021 (10 of them attaching a photo, 9–24 Jan), a white screen when typing a custom habit name Oct 2020 → Jan 2024 (13, all JP, mean 1.54), 4 in January 2026 — 64 crash / cannot-open (10.87%, mean 2.84), 13 of 51 crash reviews still 5★. Report 48: two crash crises — iOS 8 / iPhone 6 (late 2014, crash on adding a tracker and on the back button, 20 reviews Sep–Dec 2014) and the v3.0 release (81 crash-on-launch reviews in 2015) — then a 2020 iOS 13 / 14 freeze (25 reviews) that vanished; the crash union fell from 37.3% of E2 to 2.9% of E5 — 'fixed, and stayed fixed… defended, not revisited'; crash / won't open is 23.3% of all 1★. Report 49: a launch-crash cluster (Oct 2024, 37.5% of the window), a 22 May 2025 update that stopped the app opening for users 20–39 days into a 66-day programme (37.8% of the fortnight), a June 2026 crash-on-task-completion wave (32.1% of the month); crash on launch fell 10.2% → 0.0% by E4 while unspecified bugs rose to 7.9% in the new game layer. Report 50: reliability flat and thin (21, 10.24%, no defect above 4 reviews in 31 months) — 'a well-built app and it has stayed well-built… the rating risk… cannot be engineered away'; 4 of 20 one-stars never used the product (crash, would not initialise, login failed). Report 52: crashes arrive in release waves — 175 of 412 crash reviews (42.5%) in six of 110 months (Jul 2018, Oct 2019, May 2023, Sep 2024, Apr 2025, Sep 2025), roughly every 12–18 months, three of them destroying data; a launch crash on iOS 14.x for 20+ days despite a stated iOS 14 floor. Report 53: crash waves at launch (Nov 2017, fixed within days), on iOS 11.3 and iOS 13, an app that quit on open for several days (Mar 2022), and the 2024–26 statistics-view crash (BUG_CRASH 133, 7.63%, 2.82). Report 55: four crash waves each tied to an update and concentrated in one storefront — Jul 2017 (all 12 UK), Jan 2018 purchase and registration (US), Nov 2018 iOS 12 (23 of 24 Brazil), Oct 2020 – Feb 2021 (26 of 30 UK) — BUG_CRASH 197 (9.73%, 2.04, 107 at 1★); the written-vs-public gap tracks incident exposure (gb 1.07★, br 1.18★ vs ca 0.30★, au 0.14★). Report 59 (Tappsk): four dated regression clusters in three years — 2021-10-22→25 an iOS-15-era update left iPhone 6/6+/7 on iOS 12–14 unable to open the app (33 crash reports in four days); 2023-06→10 completing a recurring task closed the app (trigger isolated by a reviewer to the 'show completed tasks' setting, build 2.5.397 named, 'no progress on this bug in three months'); 2023-08→12 the calendar opened on the same month of 2022; 2023-10 freezes after one action — the regression era carries the highest crash rate after launch (2.6%) and U_REGRESSION 296 'produced most of the product's 1–3★ reviews outside billing'; a launch-crash cluster in 2026-05; a locale-specific crash when setting a habit reminder appears almost only in Turkey (BUG_HABITS 19.99×, BUG_REMINDER 11.80×, BUG_CRASH 8.43×; 1–2★ 15.7% vs 5.9% global) with two Korean reports — test reminder flows under each locale. Report 60 (Mindway): only 2 of 216 (0.93%) report a crash, both within five days in 2024-10 and never again — consistent with one bad build; 'the product is barely reported as broken', which is what makes the monetization findings unambiguous. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): a 1–2 June 2026 build with broken hit-testing — taps did not register (six reviewers; one found that a swipe still worked) — produced 8 reviews in 39 hours across six storefronts (17.78% of the app's entire written history, 40% of all its 1★, −0.32 on the mean), caught a premium buyer and a $10 buyer one week after purchase, and blocked first-run habit creation ('I couldn't get past the start creating a habit step, the button won't press'); fixed within days (16 reviews from 3 Jun average 3.875, zero tap reports) but 'the regression is closed; the reviews it produced are not'. Report 64 (Critique AI): the one repeated defect is a freeze during AI plan generation (May 2025 and Apr 2026, independently), then on every launch for one reviewer; crashes on every AI review and on the coach tab 'after the update' ('I expect better from an app which costs like 30 dollars'). Report 65 (Rabit): stability union 73 (14.66%, mean 2.04) in release-tied waves — a first-run block (Jul 2021, 46.2% of its fortnight), a crash-on-launch wave (Apr–Nov 2022, eight of 13 from payers: 'Paguei o premium a toa, pq já tem mais de 7 dias que não consigo usar o app'); an unexplained crying-woman sound on every launch ('c'est effrayant') kept as an asset-integrity issue. Report 68 (Ultiself): on 2023-01-04, 13 reviews in one day, 12 saying the app would not load ('App won't even open'; 'the app support link on the App Store also doesn't work'); BUG_LAUNCH 10.7% of that era. Report 75 (Habit Streak): a crash on launch four weeks after release from a user who had 'really loved the simple, easy design' — the only blocking defect; no later crash report; defects 1 → 3 → 1 by era, none since 2026-01-08. Report 76 (Way of Life): BUG_CRASH 39 (0.50%, mean 2.08★) in two waves — 11 on cn in one week of 2015-01 immediately after buying premium, 10 in 2016-05 after an update; BUG_LAUNCH 4; 10.50% of 1★. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): DEF_CRASH_LAUNCH 2 (1.50★) — one a lifetime buyer, one 'the new update, where the app can't even open without crashing' that opened the 70-day one-star window; the last defect report is 2025-08-26 and the 37 reviews since contain none. Report 82 (Lasting Change): zero crash or freeze reports in 175 reviews — the reliability complaint is login and account state; §8.9 do not prioritise stability work. Report 83 (Roubit): U:cant_use_app 88 (17.60%, 3.23★) — blank tabs 40, launch/load 26, login/sign-up 16 (Google and Facebook login, lost items), crash 11, update loop 7; 46 of 62 one- and two-star reviews describe a defect or being blocked; an earlier launch cluster March–April 2023 ('it breaks every like 3-4 days'). Report 84 (HabitGrid): one launch failure 12 days after release ('worked pretty well for the first 7 days and then just stopped opening', the only 3★), never repeated; zero crash or freeze vocabulary since; §8.8 no stability overhaul. Report 85 (Habitica): BUG_CRASH 415 (12.05%, 2015 → 2026) in dated waves after updates; 'The latest 2 versions of the app have ceased to work at all for me. They crash on startup' (1★); crash share 16.2% of reviews in 2015–16 → 2.1% from 2024. Report 86 (Today): BUG_CRASH 126 (7.06%, 2.71★), BUG_LAUNCH 58 (3.25%, 2.26★ — the lowest defect mean); the launch crash under an Editors' Choice feature pinned 228 reviews (12.77% of the whole corpus) at 3.25★ to the listing; a black-screen build shipped and was never fixed for 1,030 days. Report 88 (GetHabit): DEF_BUG_UI 28 (5.71%) — layout broken on iPhone SE, stuck set-up, black or blank screens; one crash report in 490; a lifetime buyer's app 'has just an freeze screen' by 2022. Report 89 (Check Calendar): zero crash or freeze reports in 253 reviews over five years; one 'wouldn't open' after two years of tracking (DEF_WONT_OPEN, whose reinstall then lost data and purchase); §8.9 no stability overhaul. Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): the sharpest single-release regression in the series — BUG_CRASH 65 (10.59%), 64 of them in the seven days after 1.2.0, 92.8% of that week's reviews, taking the era mean to 2.41★ against 4.62–4.70★ in every other era; devices named include iPhone 13, 14 and 14 Pro Max on iOS 26.5.2 and iPhone 17 Pro, and reinstalling did not help; the fix (1.2.1, six days later) ended it completely — 30 later reviews, no crash report, 4.70★ ([[C306]]). (Consolidation after report 90: title widened from 'Crashes / launch failures' to carry the single-release burst pattern — how fast one release can produce a year's worth of one-star reviews, and how completely a fast fix ends it; see [[C306]] and [[C156]].)
