<a id="c059"></a>
### C059 — Be visibly responsive; fixes bring reviewers back

**Certain** · 62 apps · 198 cards · positive in 48 apps · negative in 27 apps · tied to a purchase in 5 apps

*Why Certain:* 62 apps, same direction (act on it, 92%), 30 reports label it high-priority

Users who see their bug fixed return to raise their rating. Report 18: the developer shipped what users asked for — widget, Watch, dark mode, bundles, timer, routine modes — roughly 18–36 months after the request, often breaking something else in the same release; six reviewers raised their rating after a developer reply, and one returning churned subscriber wrote '神✨'. Report 20: users restored in Feb 2021 came back and raised their ratings (23 five-star reviews carry the revocation theme as amended reviews); a 20 Oct 2020 launch failure fixed next day drew praise for the speed. Report 23: 12 edited reviews, several visible upgrades after a developer fix; sync-migration recoveries within weeks; reviewers upgraded on learning a backup path existed. Report 24: a 2018–19 billing crisis was fixed in one month and the mean snapped back from 2.884 to 4.206 for four years; refunds that land turn 1★ into 4★ edits. Report 25: a Turkish localisation request made eight times in Jan–Jun 2026 was answered on 27 Jul 2026 ('Türkçe dil desteği sonundaaa! 🌟') — the clearest shipped-fix-visible-in-reviews event in the corpus. Report 26: a visible 2024 engineering turnaround — crashes 3.37% → 0.13%, the 'music can't be turned off' bug 2.88% → 0.00%, mean 4.339 → 4.675 — with the substantive-only mean rising too; a reviewer thanked the team for adding a calendar; Russian localisation criticised in 2023 was praised by 2025. Report 27: requested features ship on a 6–18 month lag — per-weekday flexibility (Jul 2025 → Mar 2026), reordering (Sept 2024 → Aug 2025), goal end date and archiving (Dec 2025 → on the listing by Sep 2026); the crash was fixed within about four months and the mean recovered to 4.829. Report 28: a 1★ upgraded to 5★ after one support e-mail ('The devs pay attention. 5 stars now'); bugs collapsed from 11.3% (2023) to 0.7% (2025) after a genuine stabilisation. Report 29: the calendar bug fell ~8× between 2025H2 and 2026H1 and the mean rose 4.39 → 4.66; habit editing missing in 2024 was added by May 2025 — but 'a fix ships, and the reviews it caused remain on the store page forever'. Report 30 (counter-evidence): the developer's response to the cap complaint — one more free habit — did not change the rate or the ratings. Report 31: the original solo developer shipped a wished-for feature two days later, replied to a crash e-mail and fixed it 'ASAP', restored a purchase 'within minutes' — support praise 18 (mean 4.78), 11 in E1; after the sale, public developer replies began only in 2024 with split outcomes (restored within days vs a promised refund never issued, 'they sneakily changed their developer response') and support-unresponsive stayed at 20.8% in E5. Report 33: fast fixes after a review earn thanks and rating rises ('thank you for responding right after my review'; a 1★ raised to 4★ after a fix); a public roadmap and feature voting; the Jan 2018 purchase wave fixed in two weeks and the Sep 2025 launch crash in 1–3 days; 'An update improved it' 112 (mean 4.78). Report 34: 52 developer-praise reviews (mean 4.96), 31 naming 'Kevin'; replies turned ratings up ('Updated to 4 stars - thank you devs for the response!'); weekly habits and a reviewer's suggestion built on request; an in-app 'in progress' roadmap list ('this informing and communicative attitude was a huge plus'); the share fell 13.2% (E1) → 5.2% (E5). Report 41: eleven requested capabilities shipped inside the corpus with requesters returning to confirm (notes, Watch, % widget — review edited twice, Shortcuts in the same month, CSV export, vacation mode, heat maps, mood, custom day start 'It was not available at that time, but it is now', Czech / Italian / Traditional Chinese); a support reply 'within hours. Twice' closed a lifetime sale. Report 42: reviewers notice fixes — 'Thanks for the update, it helped remove the lag. I'll bring my subscription back'; 'how much the app has improved in that time! Progress details, results info, charts' — vs 'they just reply the same thing to everyone'. Report 43: at least four verified cases of shipping what reviewers asked — Apple Watch (12 requests, none after it shipped), drag-to-reorder (7 asks, shipped Nov 2025), the timer music fix that turned a 2★ into 5★, and a feature 'added a few days later' (Jan 2026); three of the top four feature gaps have since closed. Report 46: each shipped request stops and a praise theme starts — widgets (Sep 2020), Watch (Mar 2021), journal / calendar (Dec 2023), folders (Aug 2025), no-account use (2024), Turkish and Chinese UI; personal support praised by 53 ('reach out to Joan and received a response in less than 30 minutes'; 'Joan helped me add my previous habit data from a different app'), eight ratings raised after contact. Report 47: 12 reviews (mean 4.42), 10 since 2024, acknowledge a fix — photo multi-select within a week of the request ('まさか本当に意見を取り入れてくださるとは'), late-night gap, Sunday week start, hiding non-scheduled days; stagnant-development complaints 3 ('1年以上更新がないのも残念', 2023). Report 48: 103 praise shipped updates and the public feature-voting board (4.80); 55 confirm a specific fix (4.78); Australia has the highest dev-listens rate anywhere (6.45%); several reviewers raise their rating in place after contact. Report 49: an official Discord with an active developer (17, 4.65) and visible responsiveness (19, 4.74) both rise across eras; an Indonesian reviewer abandoned over rigidity, wrote in, returned months later to find customisation built — 'THIS APP HAS BEEN IMPROVED A LOT'; 8 more noticed. Report 50: 'the developer implemented what I asked and more - he pretty much filled all the gaps I identified'; 'crowdsourcing feature ideas from the community(!!!)'; 'reorder habits without scheduling (*this was updated very soon, thank you)'; requests moved from 'does it exist' (widgets, Watch, to-dos) to 'does it go deep enough' within ~18 months. Report 53: VoiceOver unlabeled buttons reported Dec 2021 and a fix confirmed Mar 2022; an icon suggestion implemented within days. Report 54: 'I know from Reddit that you aren't spending much time on this app anymore, but please fix this small necessary thing! I would pay for the premium version again in a heartbeat!' (4★). Report 55: a reviewer raised their rating when version 1.4.11 fixed the crash, after 'nearly nine months of complaints'. Report 56: 'It didn't have options for reminders & shuffling the order of your habits, but it does now! -Even more happy with it' — visible shipping raised a verdict; 13 of 67 thank the developer by name. Report 57: seven of the ten largest early complaints were fixed (streaks, backup, Watch, custom widget restored after complaints, widget tap, keyboard, past-date, accidental purchase) — 'Recent update is a godsend. They fixed an issue with the widgets and this app is back to being one of my top 3 apps'. Report 59 (Tappsk): PR_DEV 1,244 (8.20%, 4.96★, rising to 10.0% of the latest era) — reviewers thank the developer by name, praise fast Telegram replies ('Поддержка решила вопрос очень быстро'; 'j'ai réussi à joindre le support par Télégram qui a été d'une grande aide'; 'поддержка подарила мне подписку навсегда другой аккаунт'), and a fixed bug earns a 'P.S. Все исправлено, спасибо'; the report says keep the developer's visible presence. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): zero customer-support mentions in 45 reviews — nobody reports contacting the developer, including the three whose app broke after paying; failed purchasers asked for a fix, not a refund. Report 65 (Rabit): a first-run block (12 of 26 reviews in 16–31 Jul 2021, mean 1.42) was fixed within days and reviewers came back — 'CORRIGIRAM O BUG — OBRIGADAAAA! Amei!' (DEV_FIX 3, mean 5.00) — 'the corpus's proof that fast fixes are visibly rewarded'; the Apr–Nov 2022 crash wave (13 of 67, eight payers) was not visibly fixed and one reviewer could not open the app for seven months. Report 67 (Habio): MKT_REVIEW_MISLEAD 74 (3.61%) cite other reviews, mostly as a warning to would-be buyers — 'the first several top-rated reviews were all previous users warning others not to pay'. Report 68 (Ultiself): named agents answering within hours ('Nick responded within hours. He canceled my subscription, issued a refund…') converted complainants — but partly via gifts and review requests (see C054). Report 69 (TheFor): a widget requested by 20% of 2023 reviews shipped by Jan 2024 and requests fell to zero; 'I reported a bug and the developers responded quickly and resolved the bug soon after. A+ response'; 'the developer reacts quickly to feedback' — 'this developer reads reviews and acts on them'. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): 'It's also the first app I've seen that replies to every review one by one' — U_DEV_BOND 364 (15.90%, 4.92), release notes written as essays read as content (PR_RELNOTES 28); the bond is what purchases run on, and it is fading (PR_DEV 18.5% → 5.2% of eras); unanswered support mail in 5. Report 71 (MyStreaks): the rename followed a one-line 4★ complaint within 3½ months, while five of six feature requests (widget, cadence edit, retired history, Discover integrity, a larger free cap) stayed open across 25 releases. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): support praise 50 (20.00%, 4.96) — 'a rate this analyst has not seen in any other app in this series'; requests ship ('Atienden tus recomendaciones con actualizaciones (en mi caso poder reordenar los hábitos)'; 'a big thank you for adding a feature I requested—I really feel seen and appreciated!'); a 'Notification bug' review arrives as 5★ because 'they were incredibly kind and patient'. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): 'The undeletable tab was the drawback that had me hesitating on buying. I sent a request through feedback… an update made them deletable, so I bought it immediately!' — 'a specific defect, fixed, converts a hesitant user at full price'; one bought purely to thank the developer. Report 75 (Habit Streak): three reviewers addressed the developer directly with no visible reply — a 2★ who calls the app 'perfekt' asks 'klärt mich bitte auf'; 'The 2★ one would very likely convert to a higher rating on a one-sentence answer'. Report 76 (Way of Life): fast fixes turn regression reviewers around — PR_SUPPORT 68 (4.79★) and REV_UPDATED 74 include reviewers who returned to raise their stars ('Has been fixed - good response', 5★); through 2016 'developer emailed me back in less than 5 minutes', 'solved within a day'; gb over-indexes on support praise 2.75×. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): PRAISE_DEV 3 (5.00★: 'Developer is also very responsive and takes feedbacks very positively'; 'dev actually listens to feedback'; 'the dev updates fairly frequently') all inside the first 90 days and none in the 61 reviews since — 'an early-community signal that is cheap to lose and expensive to rebuild'; three requests visibly shipped (Chinese localisation, more gamification, a widget within 33 days of a day-one request). Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): PRAISE_DEV 14 (8.14%, 4.93★: 'Der Entwickler antwortet schnell'; 'developer provided very fast support'; 'Appreciate the updates. Keeps improving'); three E1 request codes shipped and two reviewers came back to acknowledge it — the request pipeline visibly works; SUP_NO_RESPONSE 1 from a lifetime buyer whose purchase broke. Report 82 (Lasting Change): the counter-example in the series — where a request or fix is visibly acknowledged, reviewers edit upward elsewhere; here all five edited reviews stayed negative or became more so, and the four reviewers who received a public developer reply all edited their review to be more hostile. Report 83 (Roubit): a developer reply promising a widget-order fix for October 2024; support that worked raised two ratings; but 2026 brought unanswered email, unread KakaoTalk, a promised same-day fix followed by silence and 'it's starting to feel like the app is being neglected' (NEGLECT_PERCEIVED 7). Report 84 (HabitGrid): DEV_RESPONSIVE 4 — 'send him a bug report, expect to hear back in <24 hours'; 'I suggested adding a watch app; I talked to the developer, he replied quickly and said he would try'; no review reports being ignored; the request → release record is visible: frequency requests 5 before 'Smarter habit goals', 0 of 27 after; categories praised 21 days after shipping. Report 85 (Habitica): REV_UPDATED 35 edited after a fix or relapse ('When that issue is fixed, 5 stars'); PR_UPDATE 170; PR_DEV 11 in Russia; the developer-relationship counter-signal is SUP_NOT_LISTENING 4.7% of E4 and the moderator dispute. Report 86 (Today): responsiveness was visibly the conversion engine early — 'They reply very quickly and kindly' (2016); 'not only did I get a reply, the problem was fixed within days' (cn 2017); FIX_CONFIRM 33 (4.76★), 21 of them before 2019; PR_DEV 39 (4.59★), 30 pre-2019 — 'and it stopped': SUP_NORESP 25 (2.20★), 'haven't heard back from anyone in 6 months +' (2023), a three-week wait for a one-line 'import is currently not possible' (jp); RATING_LEVERAGE 16 withhold a star until something ships. Report 88 (GetHabit): no developer reply to a review is quoted except one seen months later; the two reviewers refunded within 24 hours revised their tone upward — the only responsiveness signal in 490 reviews. Report 89 (Check Calendar): DEV_IMPROVEMENT_NOTICED 3 — 'I sent feedback to the developer to ask for one change: to be able to adjust the period displayed in the graph. And today I looked at the update, and it's done!' (5★); PRAISE_DEV_THANKS 19 (7.51%, 4.58★: 'Thank you to the developer for opting for simplicity!'); widget and notification requests (5 each) stop the moment both appear in the listing — no request for either after 2025-08-23.

<a id="c062"></a>
### C062 — Weight English-speaking rich markets; volume ≠ revenue

**Certain** · 60 apps · 203 cards · positive in 15 apps · negative in 23 apps · tied to a purchase in 3 apps

*Why Certain:* 60 apps, same direction (unresolved, 66%), 23 reports label it high-priority

Purchase-signal density is 8.5× higher in the US than China; BR/MX/ES/FR volume is localisation-blocked. Report 16 (contested): the price backlash was STRONGER in high-spend markets — a value-comparison effect ('not worth it at any price', measured against Streaks, Notion, Procreate) — while the rest of the world's complaint was language. Report 20: revocation and delivery grievances were concentrated in the high-spend storefronts (us, gb, de, ca, au, fr: revocation 19.3% vs 8.1% in ru/ua; widget 7×) — the damage landed on the revenue-generating cohort; Russia's higher mean reflected when its users arrived and what they bought, not a better product. Report 23 (counter-evidence): in a paid-up-front app the high-spend and high-volume storefront groups are statistically indistinguishable (4.22 vs 4.22) and only marginally better than the rest of the world (4.12) — what varies by country is which complaint dominates, not how much. Report 24 (counter-evidence): the rich English-language storefronts were the worst — US/UK/CA/AU/NZ/IE (62.87% of the corpus) all above the corpus billing rate and all collapsing to 2.1–2.6 in 2024–26, while Latin America and the Gulf held 4.12–4.59; what varies by country is the funnel, not the product. Report 25 (third corpus in a row): high-spend and high-volume storefront groups are indistinguishable (3.74 vs 3.73) and only marginally above the tail (3.62); monetisation friction is identical (22.5% vs 23.0%) — the paywall objection is global, not a low-income-market phenomenon; what differs is the mix (rich markets praise the price and buy lifetime; the rest hit the launch blocker and billing). Report 26 (the reverse pattern): the high-spend markets (us, gb, de, fr, ca, au = 40.84%) rate lowest (4.489 vs 4.626) and complain most about the paywall (15.3% vs 8.7%; cap 6.2% vs 2.2%) — the free-tier design is costing most where the money is; Russia (19.18%, mean 4.697, 85.3% 5★) and Brazil (4.663) are the happiest markets. Report 27: high-spend markets (92, mean 4.641) and the rest (46, 4.652) are indistinguishable; free-praise appears in 12 of 23 storefronts with no income split — the anti-paywall stance is category-wide. Report 28: the high-spend group (us, cn, jp, gb, de, fr, kr, ca, au, tw = 67.1%) rates lower (3.956 vs 4.181) with ad complaints 5.5pp higher and paywall friction 2.5× higher; GB complains about ads more than the US yet rates higher ('I love this, please fix the ads'); the US carries 71% of payers and the most precise criticism. Report 29 (fourth corpus): high-spend markets rate 0.27 lower and report bugs 3.5× more while praising zero cost at the same rate (48.0% vs 44.0%) — the appeal of free is uniform across income bands; India (mean 4.895, zero bug reports) is not comparable as satisfaction because its reviews are shorter and post-fix, but its dark-mode rate is the strongest country-level feature signal. Report 30 (fifth corpus): the high-spend group (US, GB, FR, DE, JP, KR — 58 reviews) is 67% templated and yields 8 substantive reviews at mean 3.50 vs a 4.79 headline; volume and signal are inversely related — the long tail (36 reviews, 69% substantive) carries the real signal: 47.2% monetisation complaints at mean 3.19. Report 31: high-spend storefronts (78.0%) and the rest of world are almost identical on sentiment (2.34 vs 2.42) but high-spend reports the money story (1.9× cap, 1.4× friction, 1.9× support-unresponsive) and the rest of world the crash wave and language (3.3× localisation); the tail of 71 small storefronts rates better (2.58) than the 9 core ones (2.30) — the more reviewers engaged with paying, the worse the rating. Report 33: high-spend storefronts rate lower (3.60 vs 3.93; ≈3.70 without China) and differ in what money buys — 1.6× payers, 3× Premium not granted, 2.3× billing integrity — with price objection identical (5.2%); the 81-storefront tail rates higher and pays less (3.89 vs 3.71). Report 34: the US (265) is the comparison-shopping market — competitors named 2×, payers 9.06% vs 5.65%, price praise 2× — with less wall friction but 9 of the 14 explicit churn reviews; non-US users hit the cap (6.07% vs 3.77%) and the English-only UI more. Report 36: US 252 (4.095) is the outcome market (outcomes 15.08% vs 6.94%) and reports confusion 3.4× more (onboarding 4.76% vs 1.39%); non-US reviews are feature-request-shaped (unmet 25.69% vs 11.90%) and ask for sync 4× more (9.72% vs 2.38%); the monetisation problem is identical across both. Report 41: high-spend markets self-report paying 2.4× more (9.59% vs 4.00%) and hit the cap 2.3× less; subscription objections are 9 of 10 inside high-spend markets; the UK is the best market (zero cap complaints, 12.5% payers), Canada the most price-sensitive yet most-converting (17.6% objections, 13.7% payers). Report 42: a $39.99–$59.99 app almost absent from high-spend markets (63 of 206; Germany, Australia, China zero) and rated worst there once bursts are removed (2.587); its review base moved to Brazil and Russia, and 20 long-tail storefronts show 46.9% cap complaints with one payer — 'an uncontrolled A/B test of paywall-first onboarding with no trial' (mean 2.906). Report 43: a 64% US corpus where the high-spend group (79.15%) is indistinguishable from the rest (4.006 vs 4.045) and every language request comes from outside it; non-US reviewers self-report paying more (10.04% vs 6.11%, weak) and criticise the dated design more (4.37% vs 1.47%). Report 46: the least US-concentrated corpus (33.43%); the payer rate is twice as high in high-spend markets (5.61% vs 2.85%) and highest in the US (6.04%) while the cap objection is identical everywhere; every regional-price complaint is outside the group; Germany loves the product and disputes the model most (price 2.4×, anti-subscription 3.8×), Russia calls the price fair on an apparently lower tier, China wants a buyout and fears the app will vanish (跑路), India negotiates for 4–7 free habits, Turkey is the clearest regional-price market. Report 47: Japan 369 (62.65%, mean 3.54 — where the full arc plays out) and Korea 92 (15.62%, 4.33 — a requesting market: crash 14%, widget and back-dating over-indexed, praise 4.33) are the only eligible storefronts; the high-spend group is 86.93% of the corpus; Korean reviews fell from 32 (2020) to 1 (2025) — the report's E5 is a Korea re-engagement around the widget and back-dating. Report 48: high-spend markets (US, JP, GB, DE, CA, AU, FR, KR, CN; 77.81%) hold 82.6% of identified payers, complain about price and the model more and about the cap less; the UK is the most paid-engaged storefront (6.51% payers vs 3.91%); Japan (18) and Korea (24) are nearly absent — a distribution gap, not a sentiment one; Brazil is the highest-rated and least analytical storefront. Report 49: US 47.00% at 2.97 (behaviour change +4.58pp); UK 2.43 is 'transaction-damaged' (payers 13.92%, misleading checkout +7.48pp); Germany rigidity-focused (cannot edit +9.70pp, no trial +8.08pp); Australia AI-critical (10.34%); the paywall grievance varies only 14.7–19.8% across five markets — universal; the praise is American. Report 50: monetisation friction 9.0% in the US vs 17.0% elsewhere and 10.8% in the (effectively English-language) high-spend group vs 20.5%; every 3-habit-cap report is non-US (TR, AU, MX ×3) — 'US-only dashboards would not have surfaced finding 1 at all'; Japan returned zero written reviews. Report 54: a developed-market proxy group (70.73%, mean 4.103) vs rest of world (3.685): price resistance 2.7% vs 8.3%, restore failures 0.8% vs 4.6%, outcome language 16.9% vs 4.6%. Report 58: all four 'please stay free' pleas and 3 of 4 budget self-identifications are outside high-spend storefronts (PH 3) while free praise is flat — test any monetisation in high-spend storefronts first because they have not publicly asked for the model to be preserved. Report 59 (Tappsk): the English-speaking group (us, gb, ca, au, in: 725 reviews) and Latin America (br + mx: 639) describe outcomes at about twice the global rate (20.3% / 21.3% vs 9.6%) with billing at 1.0% / 0.8% vs 3.7% Russian-speaking; Brazil is the growth market of the late corpus (32.1% of its reviews in the latest era, lowest 1–2★ share above 500 reviews); continental Europe carries the highest price objection (10.6%) and SA + TR 13.6%; no market uniquely asks for a desktop. Report 60 (Mindway): the US (101 of 216) is simultaneously the biggest market, the only paying market in evidence (11 of 13 payers) and the angriest (3.56★; 26 of the 38 1★; 10 of 11 billing failures) — 'Americans complain about value; everyone else complains about access'; a definitional high-spend group (178 reviews) rates 0.62 lower, complains about money half again as often and holds every confirmed payer, while the rest-of-world 4.11 mean is 'users who never got far enough in to be disappointed expensively'. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): on 11 high-spend reviews (3.455) vs 26 high-volume (2.846), high-spend reviewers ask for capability (sync, statistics, granularity, legibility) and none objects to the price, while high-volume and long-tail reviewers raise access (the cap, paying at all) — 'consistent with the corpus but not established by it'; India is the most product-engaged storefront (both widget-outcome reviews, the streak-integrity request, the purchase trigger and the brand risk) and the one the report says to research. Report 64 (Critique AI): the visible real user base is overwhelmingly American — all but two price defenders and 9 of 11 focus-mode mentions are US. Report 65 (Rabit): the inversion — the high-spend tier supplies 61 written reviews (12.25%) at 3.33 while the high-volume tier supplies 433 (86.95%) at 3.74; Brazil holds 77.2% of public ratings at rank 3, the US ranks 39th. Report 68 (Ultiself): the US (724, 3.73; 3.39 outside E5; public 4.33) is 24.9% billing complaint against 48.1% in Ukraine and 56.8% in Belarus. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): a single-market app — Japan 2,259 of 2,290 reviews and 53,106 public ratings — with localised Chinese and English listings rated 4.88–4.96 on under 100 ratings each. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): high-spend markets are more critical (cap complaints 12.1% vs 6.4%, mean 4.589 vs 4.642) and hold the developer relationship (support praise 27.0% vs 11.0%); the UK (cap 26.67%, price 20.00%) and Canada (3.64, public 4.32) are the worst cap markets; France (4.94) and Germany (4.93) the happiest. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): Japan is the home market — 68.21% of reviews and a public base 25× the next storefront — and its risk concentration (grievance 31.07% vs 8.33%); the non-Japanese trial grievances show the disclosure problem 'travels across language and storefront'. Report 75 (Habit Streak): money complaints are slightly more common in the high-spend group (31.0%) than the rest (25.0%) and the two most hostile cap complaints are French (France: 4 of 5 1★, the largest public base, the widest gap) — 'price sensitivity is an emerging-markets problem is not supported here'; the one affordability statement is from Somalia via the ST storefront (n=1). Report 76 (Way of Life): the six storefronts with the most public ratings (us, ru, ca, de, gb, jp — an install-base proxy) run 6.1% price objection vs 7.5% global and 16.9% in East Asia; the US (40.12% of reviews) sets the global profile; cn's second-largest volume in 2014–15 vanished after 2018 (≤12 reviews/yr). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the high-spend group (US, CN, GB, DE, KR, FR, CA) supplies 34 of 71 at 4.62★ with 17.6% money-negative vs 4.03★ / 21.6% elsewhere — direction consistent with higher price tolerance in high-spend markets, not separable from noise; Japan, Australia and Taiwan produced no review at all; Germany (home market, 17 reviews, 4.76★) holds all three named-behaviour-change reviews, the only stated subscriber and the only entitlement failure. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): high-spend (fixed list, 82 reviews) 4.62★ vs rest of world 4.58★ — noise; money-negative slightly higher in the high-volume group (India, Spain) on 6–8 reviews; the five price objectors are all European; 'this corpus does not support' the claim that price sensitivity concentrates in low-income markets; the one-star mass sits in the US (6 of 11) and the single-review long tail has zero 1★ at 4.50★ — the opposite of the usual small-corpus pattern. Report 82 (Lasting Change): 90.9% of the corpus originates in 16 high-spend storefronts; the Anglophone UK+AU+CA block is the most negative (1.20★, 94% 1★) and escalates to trading standards, FTC, FCC and BBB; no price differentiation by market — amounts cluster by billing period. Report 83 (Roubit): the defined high-spend list (US-dominated) is more positive and less broken (defects 28.2% vs 38.0%) but excludes Korea and Japan, the two largest storefronts; outside Korea reliability is the bigger issue (cant_use_app 22.8%, 3.904★). Report 84 (HabitGrid): the defined high-spend group (25 reviews) mentions the free model and paywall contrast far more than everyone else (64.0% vs 37.7%; 32.0% vs 13.1%) — the 'no cap, no subscription' argument is a high-spend-market argument; the high-volume group is Russia's profile (gratitude, short reviews, frequency requests). Report 85 (Habitica): payment and gem-gating signals concentrate in English-speaking storefronts (paid signal 2.4% US vs 0.8% non-English eligible) while non-English storefronts carry the language complaint (15.7% vs 0.3% US); defect shares 15.4% (kr) to 53.2% (cn); Germany the lowest-rated eligible storefront (3.31★, 1–2★ 34.3%). Report 86 (Today): the high-spend (us, jp, cn, gb, de) and high-volume (us, cn, gb, ca, de) groups differ only in Japan vs Canada and profile almost identically at 3.96★ — 'there is no market where this app is quietly working well'; the US is the most negative eligible market (3.81★) and China the most positive (4.27★); Japan reports the most defects and rates generously; Germany diagnoses performance; Canada objects to a regional price. Report 88 (GetHabit): the paywall and ad complaints are a large-market pattern (high-spend paywall 52.4% vs 34.7%, ad mismatch 24.7% vs 10.2% — the cleaning-checklist ad ran in the US) while billing harm is uniform (unwanted charges ~19% everywhere) and web checkout more common in small storefronts (6.5% vs 2.7%); German reviews average 1.00★ ('Abzocke'), Spanish 1.18★; non-English reviews rose to 22.7% in the web-checkout era — 'the web-checkout complaints came from more countries'. Report 89 (Check Calendar): high-spend storefronts (11 present, US 61 of 99) buy less (8.1% explicit buyers vs 14.9% outside — Japan 18.3% and Brazil are outside the list) and object to price at the same rate (13.1% vs 13.0%); Japan is the largest buyer market and the one where the developer replies in writing. Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): the high-spend list holds 83 of 614 reviews and 56 of them are the US storefront written mostly in Russian — the group is a language cohort, not a market; it carries the crash (19.3% vs 9.2%) and almost none of the feature requests.

<a id="c005"></a>
### C005 — Know which competitors buyers compare against

**Certain** · 59 apps · 135 cards · positive in 36 apps · negative in 24 apps · tied to a purchase in 11 apps

*Why Certain:* 59 apps, same direction (act on it, 72%), 38 reports label it high-priority

Buyers shop around before paying; competitor names and price anchors appear in reviews. Report 19: departing payers named Fabulous and Triimo — the latter because 'customer service aren't trying to rob you'; trust is a feature people comparison-shop on. Report 20: 145 reviews (3.58%) named an alternative — Streaks 26 times, and one churning customer wrote the complete gap analysis: 'it adds things to apple health and has custom icons and you can set multiple reminders. apple watch support and an updated ios14 widget.' Report 23: Momentum 14 (4.64, 'switched from'), Strides 13 (both directions — some leave over the cap), Productive 6 ('Streaks is simpler / not a subscription'), Habitify 5 (year calendar view), Habitica 3 (reward economy), Apple Reminders 9 (mean 3.67, 'does this free'); the frame is Reminders below and subscription rivals above. Report 24: competitors are named rarely (102, 0.23%) and almost always as a switching destination in anger — Finch 19 (mean 1.579) for business-model trust ('Finch is much less greedy'), Noom and Duolingo as comparisons of mechanic (click-through lessons; streak freezes), Notion 13, Stoic 11, Way of Life 6, Habitica 4. Report 25: 37 (2.83%, mean 4.16) arrive after abandoning a named competitor — Streaks 6 (outgrew it), Habitify 4 (cluttered, no widget completion), Habitica 3 (became work), Strides 3 (dull colours, weak sound), Done 2 (buggy), HabitKit/Ripples 2 (better heat-map widget), Me+, Tiimo (calendar import) — 'I have tried them all and this is the one'; among gated users the frame is Apple Reminders and paper. Report 26: reviewers compare against 'too busy', 'too technical', 'aggressively productive' trackers and choose calm; Chinese users compare to the discontinued 种子习惯. Report 27: 13 (9.42%, mean 4.85) arrived from other trackers ('I have tried like 20+ apps including notion, atoms'; 'replaced Streaks'; 'I've tried dozens upon dozens of apps and this is literally unmatched'), and 13 name the competitive paywall — a net receiver of category churn whose position is defined by rivals' monetisation, not its own features. Report 28: 13 (1.58%, mean 4.15) arrive from other trackers — 'a more affordable and functional alternative to another well known self care pet' (Finch), 'Not overloaded with features and tabs (like Finch)', 'didn't need a subscription to add more than three habits'; the losing comparison is a full teardown against Finch where multi-device sync wins and no trial plus ad load lose. Report 29: 52 (14.21%, mean 4.83) tried or rejected other trackers — 65% of them name price or habit caps; one 2★ uses 'Check Me' instead because it has a widget and is waiting to switch. Report 30: a user left for a competitor whose widget is free. Report 31: competitor mentions flipped direction after 2020 — E1 arrivals (89, 9.5% of E1) from Productive ('$5/month??? Have they lost their minds???'), Streaks, Habitify, Habit-Bull / Way of Life, Strides; E2–E5 departures to Streaks, Habit, Way of Life, DayStamp, Onrise, Habitify, Grit, Finch, Daylio, Structured. Report 33: 217 competitor mentions (5.51%, mean 4.31, 152 5★) and Habitify is mostly the destination — arrivals from Productive, Way of Life, HabitBull, Strides, Momentum, Done, Notion, Streaks; departures to Streaks (one-time price, iCloud sync, better Health, 'a tenth of the price'), TickTick, Loop (free), Fabulous, Atoms. Report 34: 98 competitor mentions (13.19%, mean 4.85, only one 1★) — arrivals from Streaks, Ladder, HabitKit, ADHD-specific apps and paper; departures only to an app with more free habits or one with iPad and Mac apps; the US names rivals twice as often (19.62% vs 9.62%). Report 36: rivals named — Streaks (one-time £5.99, where payers say they will go), Atoms, Me+, Onrise, Dayrise (cheaper in India), Habitica, Things, Notion, Habit Grid, Apple Reminders; the app wins on feel and loses on price model. Report 41: 160 comparison-victory reviews (19.63%, mean 4.94, zero 1–2★) — arrivals after WabiTime, Focus, Structured, Habitify, Habitica, Done, Strides, Grit, Loop; Streaks named in 21 as the benchmark being displaced ('I loved Streaks, but hated its UI'; 'Streaks has a limit of 12'). Report 43: 50 comparison winners (7.84%, mean 4.88 — 'I have checked 22 habit tracker apps'; 'I tested 5… It won for its simplicity… also the cheapest') and 22 naming alternatives — Streaks, Strides, Apple Reminders ×4, the phone calendar ×2, MyFitnessPal, paper; the only 'I left for' destinations are Apple Reminders and the built-in calendar; no reviewer in 638 leaves for a named paid competitor. Report 46: 198 competitive-displacement reviews (9.09%, mean 4.92) — 'nearly every habit tracker… all the way back to Chains.cc'; 'so much better than Streaks!!!! It's not even close'; 'habitica but without the stupid game mechanics'; named rivals Streaks, Productive, Fabulous, Done, Habitica, HabitShare, Finch, Momentum, Way of Life, mem:o, TickTick, (Not Boring) Habits, Awesome Habits, Habitty, Onrise, 习惯口袋; departures only to spreadsheets, Reminders, cheaper lifetime trackers ('Awesome Habits is $22.99 for a LIFETIME license'; 'Habit Pocket… buyout is only ¥45') or bundles ('Done app gave me SIX different apps… $25 for the year') — no design competitor, only price competitors. Report 47: 'best of the many I tried' 33 (5.60%, mean 4.88), strongest in Korea (13% of KR reviews — '진심 다 써봤는데 이게 제일 좋음'); competitors rarely named — Dots ('そちらの方が操作性が良い', better to operate), RecStyle as the CSV-export model, Duolingo as the widget benchmark; departures to 'その辺のシンプルな野良アプリ' ('any random simple app'). Report 48: 453 'best of many' (10.29%, mean 4.89) and 105 competitor-named (3.16) describe one trade — wins on tracking flexibility, loses on price model; rivals Streaks, Habitify, Productive, Way of Life, Done, HabitBull, Habit, Loop, TickTick; 'reviewers concede Strides is more powerful and leave anyway' — 'no evidence of a capability gap that is losing users… repeated evidence of a packaging gap that is'. Report 49: rivals named — Me+, Finch, Atoms (the model for customisation), Habitica ('a stylized version of Habitica but with cards'), Habit Legends ('no subscriptions… MUCH MUCH more flexible with editing tasks'), Level-Up ('At least it's free'), Opal, Notion templates; the threat named most is ChatGPT — 36 say the plan can be generated free; 'None of those [loop, art, community, removing the daily decision] is reproducible with a prompt. The checklist is.' Report 50: 37 reviews (18.05%, 4.89) rank it first after trying others — the largest theme — 'I reckon I've tried almost every habit tracking app on the App Store, and this is the one I've settled on'; 'trying different habit trackers since 2018 and HelloHabit is the only one that stuck'; the one counter-teardown says 'Reminders, Things, etc, all do a much better job'. Report 54: displacement 35 (9.49%, 4.83) — 'I literally downloaded 30 different habit/productivity/tracker apps… this is the only one that came remotely close' — halved in 2023–26 (11.3% → 5.0%). Report 55: switchers from Strides, Way of Life, Productive, coach.me, Streaks, Todoist, Habit List and paper (USER_SWITCH 194, 4.68) accept its dated looks for its function ('I'll take function over form any day'). Report 56: 15 of 67 (22.39%, all 5★) describe a search that ended here, rising 17.6% → 31.8% — 'i've uninstalled like 5 habit trackers this year lol… the one i actually kept'; the two named criteria are free and widgets ('I have not found others that have both'). Report 57: 69 (8.86%, 4.884) settled here after trying the category ('I'm a habit-tracker nomad, tried over ten and settled here') — collapsing from 10.36% of 2019–21 reviews to 4.23% of 2024–26. Report 58: 35 of 91 (38.46%, all 5★) rank it against rivals they tried ('I have spent the last 3 years trying out all the different habit tracking apps'); the only rival named is Finch ('really great when I was younger, but now it was just overwhelming'); comparative language fell 37.8% → 15.2% between halves as early category shoppers gave way to later arrivals — composition, not erosion. Report 59 (Tappsk): switchers to the app (COMP_SWITCHED_FROM 110, 4.87★) outnumber leavers to another app (CHURN_SWITCHED 43) — they come from Notes and Reminders ('Гораздо удобней стандартных заметок и напоминаний'), paper, Todoist, Trello and Notion (after those services left Russia) and Things ('Desinstalei o Things por causa desse app'); leavers name TickTick and Things, for the missing Mac support and task time; COMP_MENTION 211 (1.39%). Report 60 (Mindway): the competitors reviewers name are not habit apps but Apple Reminders, Notes, Calendar and a paper planner (6, 2.78%) — the free tools already on the phone ([[C277]]). Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 'From what i have tested this one is the one i liked the most' (won a comparison shop); a 4★ considering alternatives over statistics and within-day counting; no competitor named except the implied 'original' Streaks. Report 64 (Critique AI): ALT_TOOL 13 (3.10%, mean 1.92) — ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini for the AI half; Apple Notes, Google Sheets, Google Calendar for the tracker; Clearspace for focus mode; Duolingo as the freemium model to copy — 'Nobody names a competing self-improvement app'. Report 65 (Rabit): COMP_BEST 31 (6.22%, mean 4.68) tried others first ('Baixei uma dúzia de Habit Trackers e esse, sem dúvidas, é o melhor'; 'He probado varias y siempre regreso a esta') and still 5.5% of the latest era — 'people who still rate it best while telling you it is broken'. Report 69 (TheFor): 'I've tried almost 10 apps'; 'it's better than so many of the other more expensive paid apps'; the only named competitor is Ripples, for charts. Report 71 (MyStreaks): habit tracking is a commodity and reviewers say so — 'there are so many alternatives'; 'if I find a better one I'll definitely switch'; no competitor is named. Report 75 (Habit Streak): competitors named — atoms, Duolingo (as the streak model), 'apps that charge up to $70 a year'; category fatigue in a 1★: 'Deçu comme tout les apps de routines'. Report 76 (Way of Life): COMP_MENTION 113 (1.46%, 4.29★); PR_BETTER_THAN 428 (5.51%) — the grid of three states and good/bad habits is what users say other trackers lack; leavers name data loss, price or the subscription, returners name simplicity. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): COMP_TRIED_MANY 4 and COMP_BEST 3, all 5.00★, all praising the no-streak concept — the comparison set is 'the streak focus that is everywhere else'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): U:competitive_win 27 (15.70%) — 'spent the past 2 hours comparing which habit tracking app I want to invest into'; the only rival named in 172 reviews is 'Blossom' ('For anyone poor, I recommend Blossom', 3★) and 'other alternatives by chinese developers' (1★). Report 83 (Roubit): COMP_NAMED_APP 8 — Todo Mate (cheaper, Apple Watch), me+, Study Bunny, Finch, Duolingo (as nag and as widget model), Animal Crossing (as a price anchor), iPhone's built-in apps ('no better than iPhone's built-in apps', a regretful payer). Report 84 (HabitGrid): HabitKit named as the paid comparison ('a monthly sub for an app like habitkit, which offers no benefit over this app'); a near-identical name that is paid ('HabitGrid - Goal tracker' by another developer) exists on the store; Apple Reminders is the tool replaced. Report 85 (Habitica): 'this is essentially a planner pretending to be a game' (3★); CMP_OTHER_APPS present; compared as a game against 'tripple AAA' titles on price. Report 86 (Today): CMP_NAMED 48 — Way of Life, Momentum, Coach.me, Streaks, Done, Productive, HabitBull, Habity, Strides, Due, Shanbay, Todoist, Notion, and Apple's Reminders/Calendar/Health/Activity as both the thing replaced and the fallback; the corpus's most-voted review (38 up / 82): 'blew Momentum, Strides, and Way of Life out of the water… Momentum is too minimalistic… Strides has a bubbly interface I can't stand'; PR_BEST 204 (11.43%, 4.78★); the UK writes the most detailed comparisons ('over 15 different habit trackers in the last three years').

<a id="c094"></a>
### C094 — Ask for reviews well — tone converts; cadence and ignoring the OS opt-out backfire

**Certain** · 53 apps · 160 cards · positive in 18 apps · negative in 29 apps

*Why Certain:* 53 apps, same direction (act on it, 92%), 14 reports label it high-priority

A charming review request produced dozens of reviews; frequent prompts that ignore the iOS opt-out, especially to payers, read as 'scammy'. Cross-promoting the developer's other apps inside the product draws the same complaint (report 2). Cross-promoting the developer's other apps inside the product draws the same complaint (report 2). Report 14: at least three reviews existed only because the app demanded one ('Happy now??'; a body reading 'Review'), polluting the ratings data. Report 20: a review prompt whose decline button read 'let the developers be sad' — 26 reviewers say it is why they wrote (inflating 2019's 5★ count) and two docked stars for the manipulation. Report 23: review-prompt nagging 25 (0.34%, mean 2.72, 40% 1★). Report 24: an in-app review prompt on day 1–3 makes the 5★ band (57.89%, median 105 characters) a first-impression measure — 'they asked me to review it now which I find kind of ridiculous'; the highest-voted reviews are all pre-2024 5★s. Report 25: an onboarding review prompt — 'Why won't it progress without me writing a review?'; 'in the middle of the onboarding questions the app interrupts me to ask me to rate' — pushed ≤25-character reviews from 7.2% to 33.4% of the corpus (150 of 196 5★ in 2026) and median body length from 156 to 53 characters; the all-records mean falls 0.27 while the substantive mean falls 0.73, and 1★ share (16.1% → 26.6%) is the only trustworthy trend line; 43 reviews (mean 4.21) are from people who say they have not used the app yet. A prompt at first launch buys a store rating and costs your own telemetry. Report 26: the app rewards a review with a cosmetic unlock and 13 reviewers say so ('I'm just doing this to get the backgrounds 😋 I haven't even used the app at all'; '(I'm NOT a bot btw)'); ≤25-character reviews rose from 16.5% to 35.0% of the corpus, 83–91% of them 5★; true inflation is unmeasurable and there is App Store policy exposure. Report 27: exactly one reviewer discloses a prompt ('Saw the message and had to rate'), no reward-for-review, and only 12 of 138 reviews are ≤25 characters — the substantive mean (4.594) equals the headline (4.645); a corpus of people who wrote something. Report 28: a rating prompt on open and on check-off shipped in 2026 (5 of 7 complaints are 2026) and already produced a 1★ 'until the rate me notification spam gets fixed'; 134 contentless 5★ records (median 38 chars) suggest the 2026 rating recovery is partly solicited; 'prompting into an ad-frustrated session is actively harvesting negative ratings'. Report 29: a rating prompt fired on the first check-off ('Used the app for 2 minutes then a reminder popped up for me to rate the app. -1 star'; 'so here I am, on day 1') — 39 contentless reviews, all 5★, median 27 characters; the 4.552 mean is partly a prompt-timing artefact that also starves the developer of diagnostic feedback; delay it to day 7 or ~10 completions. Report 30: 83 templated 5★ reviews and a near-absence of 2–3★ (7 of 166) consistent with a prompt routing satisfied users to the store; the public 4.4★ is a decaying artefact. Report 31: no review-prompt inflation — 20 prompt complaints (0.39%) and short reviews ≤7.7% of every era; about 1–2% of 5★ are complaints rated 5 'so people see it'. Report 33: in-app rating prompts 'three in 10 seconds' (Nov 2017 – Jan 2018) made review-nag complaints 3.8% of 2017 before falling to ≤1% every later year; 82 of 88 rating-contradicts-text reviews are 5★ reporting a bug or block; 820 short reviews (20.8%) inflate the positive side. Report 34: a rating prompt during setup ('you want me to rate it before I even finish setting it up'; 'App asks for 5 stars review'); the report recommends prompting after setup and after a 7-day streak. Report 41: 'it asks for a review every day which is needlessly annoying even if you've rated the app' (1★, Aug 2026); 111 of 815 (13.6%) contentless praise at a 69-character median — the signature of prompted reviews. Report 42: a rating prompt inside onboarding — 'Asking for a rating the first time I log in? How could I possibly know. But, since I'm being asked I must give it a one star' — the clearest causal chain to a 1★ in the corpus (2, both 1★). Report 43: the review prompt fires 'every time I open this app', 'every 2 minutes', and to people who already paid ('Paid $3, still kept asking for review. Annoying!') — 4 reviews, mean 2.75, plus a prompt whose Submit stays greyed out; 'a rating-acquisition mechanism actively lowering the rating'. Report 46: the largest self-inflicted problem in a 2,178-review corpus — an in-app rating prompt with no 'don't ask again' (50 complaints, mean 3.22, 10 one-stars; 'App asks me to review 4 times in 10 minutes. I haven't even setup 2 habits yet. Only option is Not now… Think twice before adding dark patterns'; 'you keep asking me for a review? → I'm punishing you'), asked during setup, of subscribers, and across platforms, 'fixed' in June 2023 yet live in August 2026; it capped 11 of 143 three-star ratings; the report's #1 fix: never in the first week, never twice per version, never after a rating or dismissal, never for subscribers. Report 47: rating prompt nag 3 (2023–26, mean 2.33) — a paying user asks it to stop 'せめて課金してる人に対してくらいは' ('at least for people who pay'). Report 48: review-prompt nag 9 (2.22); a prompt existed 2013–15 and ~2021; the prompt-driven share of 379 five-star low-information reviews is unknowable. Report 49: 1★ used as leverage — 'I am enjoying the app and will change the review once they fix it'. Report 50: the review prompt fires during onboarding alongside 'a page of positive reviews less than two minutes after I opened the app' — two 1★ reviews about nothing else ('I don't even star using this app and you ask me for a review'; 'participant reactivity bias plus peer pressure… Absolutely disgusting'); 27 of 142 five-stars ≤ 60 characters — fix F3: move it behind a streak milestone, which also stops inflating the corpus. Report 52: from 2020 a review prompt on the Nth launch ('第500次打开', '第3000次打开') — 40 mentions at 4.50; complaints when it fires before use and when it still insists after the user paid ¥8 to remove ads. Report 53: one jp reviewer nagged to review every time they open the app to log. Report 55: 'You have asked me 4 time within 1 minute to rate your app'; a lock screen and rating dialog that trapped a user (META_PROMPT 9, 2.44); R8: throttle the prompt. Report 58: no review prompt and a 3.30% contentless-praise rate — if a prompt is ever added, gate it behind a real usage milestone so the corpus keeps its value as a discovery instrument. Report 59 (Tappsk): a guilt-trip dismiss button — 'пусть разработчики грустят' (let the developers be sad) — is named in 2.04% of reviews (REV_SOLICITED 309, mean 4.77★, 1.6–2.5% of every era from 2020-01, coinciding with a 10× volume jump); most reviewers quote it fondly ('adorei a estratégia para deixarmos a avaliação'), but 12 of 309 are 1–2★ about the prompt itself ('это манипуляция эмоциями' — emotional manipulation; 'Хватит меня каждую секунду просить оставить отзыв'; 'Saudumme Formulierung') and it feeds distrust of the other reviews (REV_DISTRUST 32: 'начитались купленных отзывов'); the report's experiment: keep the prompt, change the dismiss wording, suppress it after a purchase, a crash or a support ticket. Report 60 (Mindway): a rating prompt fired on first session plus a paid acquisition push produced a 4-month burst — 98 of 216 (45.37%) in 2025-03/04, mean 4.12, 63 at 5★, from 32 storefronts, 52.76% of them content-free — that raised the mean 0.62 stars while adding almost no product evidence; when the push stopped, volume fell from 59 a month to 2 and the mean fell to 3.21, below launch level: 'the burst bought a rating, not a reputation, and it decayed the moment it stopped'; the modal 5★ is nine characters ('Love it') and only 37 of 128 5★ (28.91%) state a reason connected to using the product. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): three of 17 five-star reviews (17.6% of the band) do not endorse the product — 'App doesn't work', a pricing question, a critical entitlement bug — so the public 5★ count overstates satisfaction by roughly that much; seven low-information 5★ ('Good', '👍🏻', 'Excelente') are evenly spread. Report 64 (Critique AI): 11 contradicting reviews, ten at 5★, three explicitly using the star as a message about price ('im only doing 5 star just for you to take the payment subscription away'; 'I only gave 5 stars so you can see this'; 'i'm rating this 5 stars because i support your content bro but just please, please lower that price') — 39.8% of the 5★ band is not a product endorsement. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): an in-app 'rate this app' menu item and milestone-day reviews — the corpus agrees with the public rating (4.73 vs 4.78 on 53,106) and over-represents people for whom it worked. Report 71 (MyStreaks): no 3★ and no 2★ review exists (81.2% 5★), two US 5★ posted 38 seconds apart, an author handle 'Streaking User', a campaign-register review ending '#streakingforthewin' — consistent with in-app prompting after success moments and a founder community asking members to review; removing the 7 flagged reviews changes no headline band. Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): a 3★ whose entire content is that the app asked for a rating again the day after they rated — 'the review-prompt logic is directly manufacturing mediocre ratings'; §8.1 #5 never re-prompt a user who has rated. Report 76 (Way of Life): 20 days carry 20+ reviews (520, 6.70%, 86.15% 5★) after updates and in-app rating prompts, no campaign marks; the prompt draws resentment when mistimed — 'Quit bugging me with review me review me crap' (1★); 'app solicited a review 3 days in, after I paid for the premium version' (4★); §8.7 suppress the prompt for 30 days after a purchase or a crash-free launch following a failure; REV_SOLICITED 18 (4.06★). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): no burst or solicitation pattern detectable (largest day 2 reviews), though at n=71 'a detectable pattern is not the same as none existing'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): solicitation confirmed by the corpus — two reviewers describe the in-app prompt and both rated 1★ specifically because of it: 'I always leave one star reviews for apps that harass me with 'enjoying the app? Please leave a review' popups. It's gross. Change that behavior and I'll update this to 5 stars'; 'I keep getting the review prompt after every check in. Lowering to 1 stars until fixed' — 18.2% of the app's worst ratings from a growth mechanic; the 83.14% 5★ share is 'what a satisfied user gives when asked at a good moment'; §8.1.4 cap it once per user, never after a check-in, never after a user has already rated. Report 82 (Lasting Change): the star-only rating stream (673 raters, 3.838★) sits two stars above the written reviews in every major market and includes at least one 5★ that is a fraud warning — where and when stars are being asked for is the open question ([[C300]]). Report 83 (Roubit): an in-app 'review-writing mission' and invite-code reviews produced seven 5★ reviews with little product content (1.40%). Report 84 (HabitGrid): an in-app review prompt in every version since 1.0.1 (2025-07-03; 1.0.6 'Love the app? Now it's easier to leave a review') — 83 of 86 reviews postdate it, yet neither prompt release is followed by a rise in review rate; the rise follows localisation: 'the prompt alone does not explain the volume'. Report 85 (Habitica): a 1★ given in protest at a rating prompt (CONTRA_RATING); reviewers use the 5★ field as a contact form for bug reports (44 of 46 contradictions). Report 86 (Today): reviews used as a support desk (SUP_ASK 54) and a bug tracker (40 complaint-only 5★); RATING_LEVERAGE 16 withhold stars until a feature ships ('I'll be sure to change my rating to 5 stars when the updates come out!'). Report 88 (GetHabit): rating requests gating content produced five-star reviews from people who had not used the app ('Excited to try this in the new year!'; 5 five-star, 2 four-star and 4 three-star not-yet-used) and a buyer who gave 5★ so the warning would be seen ('the reviews tend to show to 5 star reviews first so that's why I gave it 5 stars. don't download this app'). Report 89 (Check Calendar): REVIEW_PROMPT_EXCESS 1 — 'a review request every day, very excessive' (br, 1★, 2026-09); the rating–text contradictions (7 five-star reviews with negative text) are 'consistent with' a prompt that captures the star before the complaint is written. Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): no review in 614 mentions a rating prompt, a reward, a survey or a referral code, and the only bursts are crash reports — 'nothing here looks like coordinated positive reviewing. The corpus's weakness is short text, not manipulation' — against 45.77% of reviews under 60 characters and a public mean only 0.515★ above the corpus.

<a id="c042"></a>
### C042 — Aim at ADHD / neurodivergent users, students, medication & chronic-illness trackers

**Certain** · 52 apps · 148 cards · positive in 42 apps · negative in 10 apps · tied to a purchase in 3 apps

*Why Certain:* 52 apps, same direction (act on it, 82%), 28 reports label it high-priority

Highest-fit, highest-satisfaction audiences (ADHD 7% of US at 4.79; students 4.87). Report 10: 7.36% of 70,041 reviewers self-identify as ADHD/autistic/ND; Australia's base is 11.4%. Report 18: ADHD/ASD/depression/burnout reviewers were the highest-rated audience (36 at 4.53★; 5.95% of US reviews) and the developer put 'ADHD' in the Korean store title — but the same population is most damaged by streak mechanics and excluded by a 9-to-5 onboarding; the positioning ran ahead of the product. Report 23: self-identified ADHD/autism/executive-dysfunction users are a growing, high-satisfaction segment (73, 1.00%, mean 4.45; 0.66% → 0.70% → 1.90% across eras) the app never marketed to; 28 arrived on a therapist/coach/doctor recommendation (mean 4.50); several of them are the strongest capacity complaints because task decomposition is what executive-function support requires, and one calls the help-page wording ableist. Report 24: ADHD/autism/executive-dysfunction users are 933 (2.15%) and grew 30× across eras to 6.01% of 2024–26 reviews — but they are the angriest segment (mean 2.747, 54.2% 1–2★) because the interface overstimulates and the cancel flow exploits executive function; depression/anxiety/PTSD/grief context is 1,256 (2.89%, mean 3.938); clinicians review it and recommend it (24 + 9). Report 25: ADHD/autism/OCD self-identified users are the highest-satisfaction segment (41, 3.13%, mean 4.44, 32 5★; plus 24 at mean 4.67 describing executive difficulty without a diagnosis; three arrive via a clinician including a psychologist recommending it to clients) — and they supply the sharpest paywall anger ('just another app trying to profit off of your disability'); ADHD vocabulary is 4.8× more common in high-spend markets, a diagnosis-prevalence difference not a needs difference. Report 26: ADHD/neurodivergent users (81, 2.11%, mean 3.84 — the lowest of any positively-framed segment) succeed because of simplicity and are hit hardest by the 5-habit cap; mental-health users (32, mean 4.66) are the highest-affect reviews; teens and students (25, ages 10–21, mean 4.16) cannot pay. Report 28: ADHD/autism users (15, mean 4.33) say the reward loop 'works so well for my brain' — and produce the harshest ad verdicts ('whenever I click to complete a habit, it shows me an advert'; 'Bad for ADHD — Has Potential'): interruption cost is not evenly distributed; kids and students are 40 (4.87%), several aged 8–10. Report 31: ADHD / autism / OCD users 33 (mean 4.09 — 'every other app overcomplicates… this app is BEAUTIFUL and simple'), medication and body-care tracking 36 (3.42), mental-health context 38; coaches, clinicians and therapists recommend it — they are the most loyal and the most hurt by regressions (monthly frequency, streak display, medication streaks). Report 33: ADHD, neurodivergent and health users praise the structure ('as an adult with ADHD'; 'I'm neurodivergent and I really hate routine'; medication) and object most clearly to guilt copy and unclosable banners ('I have adhd … huge banner … you CAN NOT CLOSE'). Report 34: ADHD users (5) prefer the simple general tracker — 'apps designed specifically for ADHD … too detailed … This app is simple with just the right amount of detail'; 'MUST. FILL. BOXES.' Report 43: ADHD (18, mean 4.61) and other accessibility accounts (12, 4.75; autism, depression, chronic illness, head injury, ASD, anxiety) are the fastest-growing theme (0.00% → 4.22% → 7.79% by era) and almost entirely US (24 of 25) — 'severe ADHD… complete tasks that would otherwise take hours on end — cooking, cleaning, and even applying makeup'; 'motivated me to shower for the first time in a week'; 'when I don't have the brain power to think it just tells me what to do next'; the mechanics are the multi-step timer and the widget; the listing's 'ADHD-friendly interface' claim is earned without targeting. Report 46: neurodivergent and chronically ill users (30, mean 4.83, 23 US, growing 0.54% → 1.70%) name the forgiving skip ('one off day doesn't kill your streak'; 'neutral data instead of a personal failing'), the widget ('if I don't see something I forget it exists') and minimal input ('a simple yes/no input, which is perfect for me and my ADHD because I've quickly become burnt out by decision fatigue on other apps'; 'Literally 3 click options'). Report 47: study / learning users 9 (mean 4.78; 'ピアノ練習100日目'), neuro / focus 2; fitness / diet 24 (4.08; a high-schooler's diet log with 14 votes). Report 48: ADHD is the lowest-rated segment (13, mean 3.77) in a corpus where every other segment averages 4.6+; students 24, mental health 23 (4.78), health / medical 24. Report 50: ADHD users 7 (3.41%, 4.29; 5 US at 4.80 — 'ADHD life saver ❤️'; 'the best app to help me with my crazy ADHD'; 'ADD/ADHD/OCD me Loves You!!!'); the one 1★ is an ADHD user whose household tasks no longer fit in 3 free habits; mental health 4 (5.00 — depression, bipolar 1, memory loss, low mood). Report 52: medication and chronic-illness logging named in reminder praise (an IVF medication schedule; a chronic-illness patient agitated by ads); the ADHD subtitle has only 6 supporting reviews (0.03%) in a 20,634-review Chinese corpus. Report 53: medication, stroke, bariatric care, alcohol recovery and brain-injury users ('I haven't missed a dose since I started using this app') — a small set of older, disabled or recovering users most exposed to confusing billing. Report 54: 7 self-identified ADHD, autistic or anxious reviewers all at 4–5★ discovered the fit themselves though the subtitle names ADHD; 'with my adhd, once it's closed i never use it' (widget). Report 56: one ADHD reviewer — 'tried countless apps that claim to help neurodivergent people… They end up being made for quick cash grabs or having a wildly confusing interface… With Dots, you get exactly what you download' — the report advises earning the audience by staying simple, not claiming it (n=1). Report 57: two US ADHD reviewers disagree — one left over the ad at first setup, one calls colour coding and views 'amazingly functional for my ADHD'; a medication user asked for multiple stamps per day in 2019. Report 58: 8 of 91 self-identify as ADHD or neurodivergent, unprompted, across 6 storefronts, all 5★, 5 tying it to simplicity ('ADHD HEAVEN… Not overwhelming or complicated… my brain is happy'; 'Setting up is simple. No extras') while the listing does not target ADHD — 'produced by users, not by marketing'; one wants more celebration for dopamine. Report 59 (Tappsk): 'As an ADHD person'; 'keeps me together with my bad ADHD'; 'Я очень забывчивая, и это приложение буквально спасает меня' (very forgetful; this app literally saves me) — OUT_MEMORY 326 (2.15%), USE_HEALTH distinctive in the US (6.89×) and UK (8.76×), OUT_MEMORY in France (3.34×) and Sweden (5.01×); these users are the most exposed to the missing task time; students (USE_STUDY 90 — 'made a student's life five times easier') and managers (USE_WORK 163 — 'the flow of tasks is endless') are the other named contexts. Report 60 (Mindway): an app named for ADHD — 4 of 216 (1.85%) mention it, 3 praise the fit at 5.00 with zero ADHD-related complaints, across US, TR and CH: 'This app helps me a lot since I was suffering from ADHD from my childhood. It helps me organize my day'; 'As someone with ADHD. This helps me stay on task instead of getting distracted'; 'Parfait pour un TDAH'; and 'I don't think I have ADHD but it really helps' — the positioning reaching beyond its target rather than narrowing the market; D4: commit to the ADHD positioning and say so in the listing — the only differentiated claim the corpus supports and one Reminders / Notes / Calendar cannot match. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): an Arabic reviewer became consistent with morning adhkār, dhikr and daily Qur'an reading ('even if just a page') and advises others to include remembrance of God in their habit — a religious-practice use case the 'Atomic Goals & Accountability' positioning does not address, already running 3+ habits, i.e. over the free cap. Report 65 (Rabit): subtitled 'ADHD Help' but only 2 of 498 reviewers name ADHD or autism — one ADHD user: 'Esse App é tudo que eu sempre quis', one autistic user uncomfortable with the icon; medication adherence and depression use cases rely on reminders that stopped firing; §9.4: re-examine the positioning before spending further on it. Report 67 (Habio): the ADHD audience the ads target is the most harmed segment (97, mean 1.25) and finds the product 'way too overwhelming' for ADHD; §8.9: a short path to the first tracked habit, skippable pop-ups, the quiz after first value. Report 69 (TheFor): one ADHD reviewer ('Finding this app though CHANGED the game') on an app whose listing never mentions ADHD — 'do not build an ADHD strategy on a single review'. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): 5 name ADHD, ADD or hypersensitivity as why the visual approach works where others failed — 'Ich (ADHS) habe schon so viel ausprobiert… Nichts hat funktioniert. Diese App macht mich froh.'; mental health / anxiety 7 ('a space where you want to be yourself and grow without pressure or shame'). Report 74 (Habit Check Calendar): health uses 9 (medication 5, diet 4, ADHD / rehab 2), all Japanese. Report 76 (Way of Life): USE_ADHD 23 (4.91★), USE_MENTAL 27 ('someone who lives with a mood disorder'; 'I used this to get me out of a rough depression'), USE_ADDICTION 46 (4.96★), USE_COACH 20 (4.95★) — all above the corpus mean. Report 83 (Roubit): ADHD 4, autism 1 ('I am autistic and find it very hard to manage routines', 5★), depression 2, anxiety 2 — USE_MENTAL_HEALTH 16 at 4.75★; 3 of 27 payers name a condition. Report 85 (Habitica): USE_ADHD 71 (2.06%, 4.41★) is the fastest-growing audience — 6.0% of E5 vs ≤1.3% in E1–E3; the instant reward of XP and gold is the mechanism they name ('The first app that helps me with my ADD'; 'I have ADHD and find it hard to do tasks, but this app has been a game changer'); the same audience names the failure modes: pop-ups that derail the task, punishments that feel arbitrary or absent ('ADHD, autism, and executive dysfunction, not helpful', 2★), too much stimulus ('Demasiados impulsos texto y provoca que te distraigas', 2★), and the loss of a guild that worked as a support group; USE_MENTAL 51; professionals recommend it (SEG_PRO 16: a psychotherapist, a life coach, an autism/ADHD support worker). Report 88 (GetHabit): 'I have ADHD and need help organizing my life' — two ADHD reviewers among the handful who reached the product. Report 89 (Check Calendar): USE_HEALTH 14 (5.53%, 4.57★) — medication, insulin, supplements, diet — 7 of 14 Japanese; the developer's site says the app began as a way to remember medication; 'with the app I don't forget my pills' (mx); and the trial wall lands on exactly these uses — 'I installed it so I wouldn't forget my supplements, but it was usable for only 7 days' (jp, 3★); §8.2 locked records 'matter more for a medication tracker than for a to-do list'.

<a id="c093"></a>
### C093 — No upsell nagging without a 'never ask again' option

**Certain** · 36 apps · 108 cards · positive in 7 apps · negative in 30 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Certain:* 36 apps, same direction (act on it, 90%), 10 reports label it high-priority

Full-screen interstitials, permanent banners and upsells before first value draw complaints even from 5★ users; a subscription launch with nagging cost ~3 points of 1–2★. Report 9: upsell-pressure complaints quintupled (2.16% → 4.84% → 10.23%) as the funnel was tuned harder, becoming the fastest-growing 1★ source. Report 14: the cleanest before/after in the set — rating-and-upsell pop-ups on every launch drew six star-docking reviews in nine weeks ('I docked one star for this'; 'Deleted'), and removing them produced unsolicited 5★ praise ('They removed the pop ups. Nice!!') and a named edge over a rival still 'begging for an upgrade within the first minute'. Report 18: a persistent bottom promo bar and a Dynamic Island discount countdown in 2025–26 were experienced as worse than the 2022 interstitial ads ('Absolutely the worst choice'); upgrade-nag was among the lowest-rated themes (40, mean 2.40★). Report 20: a 'limited time offer' countdown that reset to 60 hours on expiry ran for over four years (Jan 2021 → Mar 2025) beside a full-screen launch interstitial with a low-contrast dismiss — 225 reviews (5.56%, mean 1.80); 'Dark patterns make bad UX!'; 'first the consumer must see the value of the product. And what do you have? Every 2 seconds a subscribe banner.' Report 23: 4 reviews object to ads for the developer's other apps inside a paid app. Report 24: sister-app upsells (308, mean 1.932), referral/share prompts (131) and pop-ups/unskippable steps (182, mean 2.082) inside a paid subscription. Report 25: navigation-blocking upsell sheets — '10 popups in 20 seconds which kills the use'; 'not even my first second on the app 4 ads asking for payment'; a 5-second forced delay on the premium prompt; 'a habit app that starts right away with dark patterns' — 35 reviews (2.67%, mean 1.80); cap the prompt to one dismissible surface per session; a French reviewer notes explosive pop-ups are actively harmful for ADHD users in an app marketed to them. Report 28: forced interstitials on every action ('Ad while you write a habit. Ad while you review habits. Ad while you breathe.') and a rating prompt on open and check-off. Report 31: upsell nag 676 (13.04%, mean 1.72) rising 1.9% (E1) → 22.6% (E4) through a full-screen offer on every launch (2021), a permanent 'Just for you' list cell (2023) and two pop-ups per launch (2024, mean 1.47) — 'the only habit I'm developing is closing the upsell pop up'; a share of E4 purchases were made 'to get rid of the incessant pestering', and when relief did not arrive they produced the angriest reviews; E1 buyers valued 'that they don't prompt you to update every 3 clicks'; cap offers at one dismissible surface per week. Report 34: upgrade nagging 4 (mean 2.00) — 'constantly being nagged to upgrade to premium. I only track one thing'. Report 36: a full-page subscribe screen on every launch — POPUP 24 (mean 2.67), rising to 15.0% of 2026 H2, the only negative theme regularly in 5★ (4 of 24): 'i said no already, please respect that'; 'Can't use the app on my iPhone 13 mini because of a freaking pop up' (5★ titled 'Unusable'); the report calls a once-a-week cap the cheapest change available. Report 42: upsell interstitials 'annoying and difficult to click out of' (3, mean 1.67). Report 43 (counter-case): the in-app upsell is never complained about; the nag is the review prompt. Report 46: the upsell twin of the rating prompt — 'everytiime I try to add a new habit or move between screens the upgrade to premium screen appears and has to be x multiple times' (4, mean 1.50); a paywall on first open for some ('Take a subscription straight away or look at the start screen. That's all'). Report 47: upsell nag 4 (mean 1.25, Jul–Nov 2025) — 'タスクを完了するたびに毎回有料版の導入を進めるページに移るのがうっとうしいから消した' (a paid-version page after every completed task; deleted); the 2024 lesson did not carry over to 2025's upsell screens. Report 48: a full-screen / post-log upgrade prompt introduced around July 2024 drew 6 nag reviews in three months from long-term free users who say it reduced their willingness to pay ('I might even consider paying money for the app. But I darn sure will not… as long as the nag screen is still in place'); one records it being softened and raised their rating — 'the only monetization mechanic in the corpus that users say actively reduced their intent to pay'. Report 53: a 'new year, new me' premium pop-up with a countdown that 'never ends, it just starts over', shown every app open from 2023 (PAY_NAG 42, mean 1.93, 39 of 42 from 2023) — reviewers call the app's own offers 'ads'; M1: once a week at most, never to payers, no resetting countdown. Report 54: upgrade nag including after paying (5, 2.80); 'The paywall is so obtrusive' (GB). Report 55: a full-screen premium pop-up on every launch from July 2020 (PAY_NAG 44, 2.02; still reported Dec 2024) — 'Just ask once and don't make it pop up every time I launch the free app and it gets 5'; M5: one upsell, frequency-capped. See [[C274]]. Report 59 (Tappsk): MON_UPSELL 97 (0.64%, 3.33★) — 'Каждый день по 30 раз пихают мне всплывающее окошко «Купите нашу полную версию»' (thirty times a day the buy-our-full-version pop-up); Germany reports it at 2.36×, purchasers at 2.44×. Report 60 (Mindway): 'every 5 seconds it keeps brining up these Hey pay me now Pop Ups… let me do my activities and move on with my life' (1★); 'It keeps saying do you want a free trial for something'; 'it won't allow me make a plan without showing free trial vip' — an upsell that fires inside the task the user came to do; F5: stop firing the upsell inside an in-progress task — 'a description of a broken interaction, not of a pricing disagreement'. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): 'Get one star for annoying me with pop-ups' (PL, 1★) — one review, a full star, 'a setting, not a build'; M5: cut in-session upsell pop-ups or cap their frequency. Report 67 (Habio): NEG_POPUP 19 ('I just wish it was voluntary'); a 2026 dashboard described as 'a mini Time Square Billboard showcase' of upsells. Report 69 (TheFor): 'Even better - there's no constant barrage of prompts asking you to upgrade!' — the restraint earns 5★. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): 'if you don't pay at least $10, most of your screen is taken up by a huge ad encouraging you to upgrade the app, and nearly every feature you click brings you back to this ad'; 'I just wish we didn't get an ad to buy premium every time we enter the app' (5★) — in an ad-free app 'the paywall is being experienced as the advertising'; §8.1 #2 take the full-screen upgrade prompt off every app entry. Report 76 (Way of Life): MON_UPSELL 13 (mean 2.85★). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): MON_PROMPT_NAG 1 (1★, title 'annoying'): 'can only add 1 habit then after that this subscription keeps popping up 😑'; §8.4.4 fix the prompt frequency — 'invisible in aggregate metrics until it shows up as churn'.

<a id="c134"></a>
### C134 — Lead the store listing with what users actually love

**Certain** · 35 apps · 79 cards · positive in 30 apps · negative in 5 apps · tied to a purchase in 3 apps

*Why Certain:* 35 apps, same direction (act on it, 83%), 16 reports label it high-priority

Report 6's most-loved feature (the free widget) was one bullet at the bottom of the description and its differentiators (no daily check-in, user-defined day boundary) were not marketed at all — yet they are why people switched. Report 23: lead with the streak mechanism and HealthKit automation, not 'to-do list' — the 'just a checklist' 1★ block is an expectation failure; award/editorial traffic (17 reviews naming the Apple Design Award, mean 2.53, the worst channel) arrives expecting 'best app'. Report 24: reviews invoking Apple or Editor's Choice average 1.085 (95.7% 1★) — 'Apple should not feature this'. Report 25: reviewers say the app feels first-party ('went back to check if the app was made by apple') and 37 switched from named competitors — the listing can lead with configurability and Apple-platform depth; measurable outcomes are claimed (45 kg lost in 8 months). Report 26: reviewers convert on the aesthetic within minutes — the listing's visuals and music are doing the selling; the German listing typo 'Gewohnheitstrinker' shows the listing is read closely. Report 27: the origin story in the listing produces 10 all-5★ developer-gratitude reviews; 'From one developer to another — nice piece of work'. Report 28: 'It's a game, not a tracker' (10, mean 2.40 — 'not at all what I was expecting'; 'the only thing I'm tracking is the amount of adds') is a listing and first-run expectation-setting problem costing 2★ reviews with no defect present. Report 31: lead with simplicity, colourful friendly design, build + quit in one list, 'N times per week' and musical sounds — 458 simplicity and 250 design praise reviews prove the brief. Report 41: an app that wins 19.63% of reviews on comparison is under-discovered ('It deserves a way higher ranking and visibility in the search results'; 'I didn't find it the first time'); the listing does not lead with the one-time option, the non-binary ring, full Apple-ecosystem coverage or no ads / no account; outcome stories (10.4% of 2026) are an unused asset. Report 47: why people give 5★ — simplicity 31.8% of the band, the filling grid 18.4%, behaviour change 13.7% ('三日坊主' no longer), design 12.6%, best-of-many 10.5%. Report 48: five-star reviews are simplicity 23.7%, flexible tracker types 13.7%, best of many 13.6%, behaviour change 8.4%; US reviewers talk about outcomes and accountability more than anyone else. Report 50: a Reddit user was acquired by a screenshot of the monthly report ('so pretty'); Instagram-ad and Reddit acquisitions are all 5★. Report 56: the listing leads with the category's language ('simplicity, clarity, and daily consistency') while users say 'actually free, no strings, nothing extra' — E5: rewrite it in the corpus's words; the US over-indexes on outcomes (25.0% vs 9.3%). Report 58: acquisition is founder-dependent and the listing does not claim the ADHD audience that found it; test copy leading with simplicity (the US already leads with simplicity, 50.0% vs 33.8%). Report 60 (Mindway): the marketable asset is concrete habit outcomes in reviewers' own words — 'makes me drink more water'; 'We will drink 4 glasses of water each day'; 'even got me to stretch'; 'This actually helps me with my chores, even though I'm seven'; 'It made me calm'; 'THIS APP MAKES ME FEEL SO MUCH BETTER' — 43 (19.91%) at 4.79★, 'Mindway's value proposition translates' across ten languages, while the listing and the paywall sell task slots. Report 64 (Critique AI): R4 — lead with what works: reported physical outcomes are the highest-rated theme (12, mean 4.92: 'It helped me lost 50 pound'; 'i'm in shape now because of this app') and social / confidence outcomes 4.75 ('you go from not talking to anyone to talking to everyone'), against 2.17 for the AI layer the name sells. Report 65 (Rabit): design is the durable asset — 106 (21.29%, mean 4.57): DES_CUTE 79 ('fofo/fofinho', hand-drawn icons) and DES_SIMPLE 58, 19.4% → 13.0% → 10.2% of eras, praised even inside 1★ and 2★ reviews; 'one of the few apps where UX was taken seriously. 5 stars for that alone' (uk). Report 67 (Habio): what survives among non-seeded reviews is the calm, soft visual design (PR_DESIGN 39, in every era, often from complainants: 'I love the look and feel of the app, it's calming') and the reflection journal — keep them (§8.11). Report 68 (Ultiself): outside E5 47.3% praise something specific — ease of use (255), design (148), tracking (119), library with sources (90: 'large library of habits plus corresponding sources'), routines (78), reminders (68), insights (63); §8.9 keep them. Report 69 (TheFor): the three reasons behind almost every 5★ — it looks good, it has nothing extra, it beat the apps tried before; the listing leads with transformation instead. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): design praise 152 (60.80%, 4.75), flat across eras — 'the design is not a differentiator to be protected alongside features — it is the feature'; the listing omits the 50+ widgets; E5: lead the listing with the aesthetic and icon library. Report 76 (Way of Life): the listing cites Tim Ferriss / Kevin Rose and reviewers cite the same source for a decade — earned press in the listing compounds; §8.8 keep the three-state grid, the charts, the 3-habit free tier and one-person development in front. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the title and description already lead with the concept ('The first habit tracker without streaks') — the only thing with no detractors — and it is the paywall that does not; §8.4.1. Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): what the listing sells (smoking, alcohol, gambling, nail-biting) is narrower than what reviewers use it for — self-harm 13, drugs 8, phone addiction, face picking, swearing, a habit that caused stuttering — and the most-praised quality, a non-triggering minimal counter, is not what the description leads with.
