<a id="c111"></a>
### C111 — No long quiz before the price; show the price up front

**Certain** · 12 apps · 40 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 12 apps

*Why Certain:* 12 apps, same direction (act on it, 82%), 8 reports label it high-priority

A 10–20 minute quiz followed by a paywall turns a price objection into anger (mean 1.98, 71.9% 1–2★); 'lower the yearly price a bit and show it at the very beginning'. Report 24: a large share of buyers take the questionnaire in a web browser and enter payment details before ever opening the app; onboarding-too-long runs at mean 1.600. Report 42: ~15–30 unskippable setup screens before the price, with a rating prompt inside them (3 reviews, all 1★, never used the app). Report 49 (the strongest case): a 10–20 minute questionnaire plus a pledge before a hard paywall — onboarding-before-price 156 (12.66%, mean 1.15, the lowest of any theme above 20; 140 of 156 at 1★); many do not object to paying, only to the sequence ('they ask for tons of personal stuff before displaying the price wall instead of after'; '30分かけて設定したのに…初めに言って欲しい'), identical in 15+ languages; the never-used cohort (331) grew to 33.1% of the latest era; all 40 'scam' accusations are about this payment experience; the report's fix #1: 'A price shown on the first screen converts a one-star review into a non-download.' Report 60 (Mindway): the sequence ad → onboarding questionnaire → price is what the two ad-sourced reviewers (both 1★) and the scam accusers describe — 'Put the price next to your product in the App Store. Its the only correct way to go about selling a product above board'. Report 64 (Critique AI): PAY_QUIZWALL 23 (5.49%, mean 1.35) — a long survey, a physique photo and an account, then the price: 'why the need to do a survey if it isn't free? couldn't it be mentioned before the survey?'; rose from 3.2% to 8.7% in the latest quarter; M1: disclose the price before the quiz — 'Zero engineering cost, zero revenue cost'. Report 67 (Habio): the quiz doubles as the sales funnel — NEG_ONBOARD_LONG 29 ('so we don't waste our time filling up a bunch of useless data in the first place'), paid on the web before installing. Report 82 (Lasting Change): a quiz funnel that never mentions a payment plan (ACQ_QUIZ_FUNNEL 2: 'No where during the process does it mention payment plan'), descending-price urgency (ACQ_PRESSURE 4: 'they continually advertise and offer at lower and lower prices until you bite'; 'fake questions, artificial delays, pseudo customization, pseudo last time offers'), and a listing whose 'SUBSCRIPTION PRICING & TERMS' heading contains no price, period, trial length or SKU ('App does not show there is a payment plan anywhere in description'). Report 83 (Roubit): PRICE_OPAQUE 8 (1.60%) — 'services that don't show the price clearly aren't very trustworthy' (jp 3★); an elementary-schooler asking whether it keeps charging; §8.5 show price and renewal terms before the trial. Report 88 (GetHabit): a purchase screen after the name field with no price shown before install — 'immediately when opening it and putting in a user name it asked you to pay $39.99'; the trial's cost ($0.49) and the weekly renewal were the surprise.

<a id="c140"></a>
### C140 — Market the generic-tracker use case

**Certain** · 12 apps · 15 cards · positive in 9 apps · negative in 0 apps

*Why Certain:* 12 apps, same direction (act on it, 60%), 8 reports label it high-priority

Report 7: users track medication, migraines, supplements for a pet, art-project days — any yes/no daily thing — at mean 4.91, while the listing only says 'build habits'. Report 60 (Mindway): outcomes named are hydration, workouts, tidying, stretching, getting out of bed and chores — a routine planner is used as a generic self-care tracker. Report 62 (Streaks, yusuf kildan): use cases described — fitness / sport progress, hydration and step counts (unserved by a binary daily check), religious practice, daily task focus; no review describes breaking a bad habit despite the accountability subtitle. Report 76 (Way of Life): 'journals' rather than habits — items can be anything, good or bad; USE_WORK 16, USE_STUDY 18, USE_FAMILY 13 alongside fitness and health; PR_CUSTOM 206 (2.65%). Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): 'boards' with custom units track study hours, gym, medication, music production, driving-theory tests, coding lessons and work days — the generic-tracker use case, praised as 'a task with a completely open schedule'. Report 84 (HabitGrid): USE_NON_HABIT — a Russian reviewer uses it to remember watering plants; one moved from Apple Reminders 'to keep track how many times I actually completed them'. Report 85 (Habitica): Habits (+/− counters with no schedule), Dailies and To-Dos plus custom real-life rewards — 'a planner pretending to be a game'; PR_CUSTOM 66; PR_ORGANIZE 95. Report 86 (Today): 'just a yes/no - did you hit the gym today?' — reviewers draw the line against to-do lists and workout trackers; PR_OUTCOME 106 (4.84★, the highest mean): 60lbs, 50 meat-free days, quitting soda, five languages, 200 days of fitness, quitting smoking, six years of habit-formation. Report 89 (Check Calendar): USE_OTHER_PURPOSE 4 — work attendance (2), homestay bookings, piano practice ('I bought this app to track my piano practice'); a yes/no calendar generalises beyond habits. Research: Quit Habit Decision.md — quit terms are a keyword surface one listing can annex: Days Since ranks #3 overall in the category on ranking strength and #1 in 10 rich markets purely on quit terms, so shipping a proper quit mode lets a single listing compete for 'quit habit', 'break bad habits' and 'sobriety tracker' alongside the habit keywords.

### C145 — Every promotional or onboarding modal must be dismissible on the smallest screen

**Certain** · 12 apps · 23 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 12 apps

*Why Certain:* 12 apps, same direction (act on it, 95%), 6 reports label it high-priority

Report 8's full-screen 'add a widget' prompt had an unreachable close button on small iPhones and blocked the app for 20 months. Report 24: pop-ups and unskippable steps (182, mean 2.082) and unskippable completion celebrations; make animations skippable. Report 31: a 'Self-care Christmas' banner hid the bottom habit; a permanent 'Just for you' list cell slowed scrolling and tapping — never let a promotional element occupy a habit row or slow the list. Report 33: a full-screen offer on every open and a banner covering the third habit that cannot be closed (2023–26; upsell 1.7% of E5). Report 55: see [[C274]] — a pop-up whose X started a purchase. Report 64 (Critique AI): a paywall that reads as uncloseable — PAY_SOFTLOCK 39 (9.31%, mean 1.72) across 20 storefronts and 17 months ('no cancel button, no ignore button, no X button. NOTHING!'; 'I cannot press the don't pay now button even if I press it 20 times'; returns after relaunch) — reconciled by one German reviewer: the X 'is invisible, tiny and impossible to find'; two trapped users rated 4★ while asking for help; the rate fell 16.9% → 6.8% after launch but 7 reports remain in the latest quarter; F1: large, visible, reachable on first paint, verified on small screens and after force-relaunch. Report 64 (Critique AI): 'Doesnt work on smaller phones' and 'I can't scroll in the app, which means I can't choose the correct options' — defects that exclude rather than annoy (R7). Report 65 (Rabit): the onboarding questionnaire's advance button rendered below the visible screen (2023–2024) — 'a layout bug, not a logic bug, and trivially fixable' (F6); an ad close button under the status bar on iPhone 13.

<a id="c189"></a>
### C189 — Public review replies answer the specific complaint — never canned, never argue price, never press a reviewer to change the rating

**Certain** · 10 apps · 24 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 9 apps

*Why Certain:* 10 apps, same direction (act on it, 100%), 5 reports label it high-priority

Report 13: copy-paste replies restating Apple's cancellation instructions under reviews had a mean of 1.40 with zero 5★, and multiple reviewers edited their rating downward afterwards ('If you're just going to copy-paste an answer again, don't leave one at all'). Report 25: 'the developer preferred to argue about what I could see on my end' — an argumentative support reply ended a trial. Report 31: a support reply 'full of emojis' offered a free trial instead of honouring a purchase; a public developer response was edited after the fact. [Merged from C260: Report 46: 6 reviews (0.28%, mean 1.33, all 2021 or later, five in 2024–26) say a public developer reply was rude or defensive — 'snarky remarks about working for free and making an overpriced app isn't the way to do it'; 'developer takes any criticism with such a nasty attitude'; 'After reading developer's response I am degrading rating to 1 star from 2… 5/5 rating for app but 0/5 for your behaviour' (13298363427) — and 2 say the developer pressed them to change their review ('the developer keeps contacting me to pressure me into changing my review', 11709301622). Every one of these reviews went from 'too expensive' to 'and the developer is hostile', a reputational cost no pricing change recovers, while 53 reviews (mean 4.94) praise the same developer's private support. The report's zero-cost fix: thank, state the free tier and lifetime option factually, never argue value, never ask for a rating change.] Report 60 (Mindway): five explicit warn-offs ('Don't waste your money'; 'Don't ever download this app'; 'Don't download if you need for a routine'), all 1★, remain visible on the listing at the point of decision — an upgrade barrier the report counts alongside billing trust damage. Report 67 (Habio): a templated public developer reply under reviews is mentioned by 19 reviewers; §8.6: no identical public replies. Report 71 (MyStreaks): a public developer reply defending the cap as good for users drew 'Comment from creator that it encourages people to keep it simple? 🙄' in a 1★; §8.1 #4: retire that defence — 'asymmetric downside, and it is free to stop'. Report 82 (Lasting Change): public developer replies on reviews are read as PR — SUP_RESPONSE_FACADE 4: 'The responses on each of these reviews from the company is a facade, and for public appeal only… I have no doubt you will paste it below to seem as though you care'; 'Addendum to developer response: they're full of it… they've ignored my emails'; four reviewers who received a reply edited their review, all hostile, none more positive; the one documented remediation (a disclaimer added beneath the terms consent after an email exchange) came with a denial that it was ever missing, contradicted by the reviewer's screenshots. Report 89 (Check Calendar): seven public replies — a design rationale, two apologies for the pricing mechanism, a correction that Premium is 'a one-time payment, not a monthly fee', two feature acknowledgements and one confirmation of a shipped request; the apologies were specific and polite and still became evidence against the developer because the listing did not change ([[C298]]) — a reply that promises a fix is only as good as the fix's ship date.

<a id="c130"></a>
### C130 — Use the lead-user market as the beta cohort

**Certain** · 8 apps · 16 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 2 apps

*Why Certain:* 8 apps, same direction (act on it, 67%), 5 reports label it high-priority

Report 5's home market (Korea) carries the deepest engineering feedback and most detailed feature specs — and uses the review page as a support desk. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the developer's home market (Germany) is the largest and strongest storefront — 17 of 71 at 4.76★, 9 written in German and 8 in English. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): Germany (17 reviews, 4.82★, zero 1★) supplies both pre-committed-star requests, both negative-board requests and the only price-rise review — the densest, most articulate storefront; the developer is Ukrainian and Ukraine holds 55 public ratings. Report 83 (Roubit): Korea (home market, 246 reviews, 4.37★) is where the buyers, would-be buyers, price objections, platform requests and widget bugs concentrate (PAID 6.9%, WOULD_PAY 4.5%, IPAD_WATCH 6.1%, BUG_WIDGET 4.9%); other markets report reliability (Japan blank-diary 32.1%, US launch failure 11.5%). Report 84 (HabitGrid): the developer's home region (Romania/Hungary) supplied 6 of the first 13 reviews and then went silent — a launch cohort, not a market. Report 85 (Habitica): the US (42.99%) carries the pay-to-win objection (15 of 19), the professional recommenders (13 of 16), trading requests (11 of 12) and the guild-closure grievance (19 of 32). Report 86 (Today): China (353, 19.78%) values simplicity above beauty, pays more (12.18%), suffers restore failures most (8 of 18), and was the first market to get — and to criticise — a localisation. Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): Russia is both the volume (66.29%) and the specification — 27 of the corpus's 28 tree-growth requests, 68 of 86 widget requests, 14 of 15 support questions and every perceived-paywall review come from the RU storefront, and the most-voted review in the corpus (109 votes) is a Russian feature request that later reviews cite back ('I'll voice everyone's request: PLEASE ADD TREE GROWTH').

<a id="c132"></a>
### C132 — Do not sell in a storefront where the app cannot function

**Certain** · 8 apps · 34 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 7 apps

*Why Certain:* 8 apps, same direction (act on it, 75%), 4 reports label it high-priority

Seven years of 'will not open' from mainland China, with users charged for an app that shows 'no network'. Report 9: in Russia 46% of reviews say the app loads for minutes or only works over a VPN, while 32% of Russian reviewers had paid. Report 33: a mandatory account backend unreachable from mainland China made the app unusable there for eight years — 173 reviews (4.39%; 57.8% of China; 79 of its 101 1★), 18 payers who could not use or restore what they bought (328 RMB lifetime, refunds refused), and an App Store 'Today' feature in Dec 2018 that sent 68 Chinese users into a registration failure ('can't register — and you recommended it on the home page?'); China was lost on reachability, not fit — reviewers praised the design and localisation and asked to pay ('I'd pay 188 RMB lifetime if you fixed the server'). Report 47: registration and login fail from mainland China — 6 of 8 login failures are Chinese ('好像需要vpn'), consistent with a blocked backend; China 32 reviews at mean 4.28 otherwise. Report 76 (Way of Life): Dropbox-only backup was unusable on the Chinese storefront (17 of 18 complaints, 2014–16) — the app was sold where its data-safety feature could not function. Report 85 (Habitica): the service is unreachable from mainland China without a VPN for the whole eleven years (NEG_CHINA_NET 16, 14 of them on the cn storefront, 15× lift) — cn is the second-largest storefront (201 reviews) and its defect share (53.2%) the highest of the eleven eligible.

<a id="c225"></a>
### C225 — A one-off free promotion (App of the Week, partner promo) acquires durable users

**Certain** · 8 apps · 16 cards · positive in 4 apps · negative in 3 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Certain:* 8 apps, same direction (act on it, 80%), 2 reports label it high-priority

Report 23: a Starbucks 'Pick of the Week' promo in 2015–16 drew 13 reviews at mean 4.62, and one of those users was still active in July 2025 — ten-year retention from a free promo on a paid-up-front app. Report 34 (counter-case): a ~29 Jun 2023 free-lifetime giveaway brought 27 short 5★ reviews in three days and a wave of non-English users asking for a language the app did not have; no durable-retention evidence. Report 41: two early users were given the full version free at the 2020 launch and rated 5★. Report 50: two 5★ reviewers ask for a referral / discount programme ('rewards for recommending the app to friends… in the form of discounts') while 37 evangelise it — S3: build one. Report 76 (Way of Life): a podcast mention (Tim Ferriss / Kevin Rose, 2014–2016) shows up in reviews for a decade and converts the same day — an earned-media wave (E4 'the podcast wave', 26 of 51 MKT_PRESS) behaves like a promotion. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): a third-party giveaway (AppAdvice lifetime promo) drew a 1★ when the code could not be redeemed — a promotion is only an acquisition if the redemption works. Report 85 (Habitica): the counter-case — an App Store feature on 2018-02-26 landed on a day the servers could not register new users: 22 reviews that day, 67 in the month at 2.91★ ('Downloaded the app this morning because of the App Store recommendation', 1★); a promotion the service cannot serve converts into a 1★ wave. Report 86 (Today): launched 8 March 2016 as an Apple Editors' Choice (MKT_EDITORS 6) — and crashed immediately for a large fraction of users while gating the free tier at one habit: 209 reviews that month at 3.11★, 54 on a single day, 228 reviews (12.77% of the ten-year corpus) permanently attached to the listing at 3.25★; 'When I saw this was an editors choice app I checked it out… all I get is the screen that says today. And then everything crashes' (1★).

<a id="c092"></a>
### C092 — Regional pricing

**Strong** · 27 apps · 73 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 21 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

*Why Strong:* 27 apps, directions mixed (open 31, act 30, paid 3)

IN, TR, UA, BR, MX, SA reviewers name price as the only blocker; India likes the product and has not yet been asked a price it can accept. Report 23: price objection concentrates in au (5.7%), de (3.8%), ca (3.6%) against us 1.3%; China's number is ¥25–30. Report 25: price-display confusion is a Mexico-specific repeated issue — three reviewers cannot tell pesos from dollars, others name MXN 500, 40, 300, 599 and 299.99 — a pricing-display problem that is cheap to fix; Argentina's hostility (mean 2.95) warrants a look at its pricing display and trial mechanics. Report 33: regional price objections from Vietnam, Turkey (270 TL), Korea ('I'll buy if it's discounted') and Japan (¥19,000 lifetime, 'unfair to base your pricing on [exchange rates] alone'; 「前に比べて値段が爆上がり」) — regionalise lifetime pricing. Report 36: regional pricing complaints from Turkey and a cheaper local rival in India (₹499/yr vs Dayrise). Report 41: purchasing-power-adjusted lifetime tiers proposed for the 63 sub-50 storefronts, where cap complaints are 2.1× the high-volume markets. Report 46: regional price complaints 8 (all non-US — Turkey ₺179 / ₺30 a month, Saudi 109 SAR, Vietnam, Latin America, Israel cannot buy online, Kazakhstan) while Russia calls its price fair; the report's E2 is regional lifetime pricing. Report 48: China's lifetime objection is cost-of-living framed (a lifetime plan near a quarter of a second-hand iPhone); price sensitivity clusters in CA / AU / DE / CN. Report 49: Canada itemises CA$79.99 plus 14.99% Quebec tax; Türkiye objects to dollar-pegged pricing. Report 54: price objections 3.1× more frequent outside developed storefronts; D2: storefront-tiered pricing for CN/TW/PH/TR/BR/CO. Report 57: price objection 8.05% outside Korea vs 0.99% inside, Japan 26.92% — three reviewers on three continents independently propose a cheaper tier of ad removal + groups + backup (~¥2,000), one a monthly plan. Report 59 (Tappsk): the same lifetime unlock is named at 449 ₽ and 2,500 ₽ and at $14 / €4–10 within a year; regional prices could not be established from the corpus. Report 64 (Critique AI): M6 — price for the actual audience: an age- or region-tiered price as an experiment on a teen-heavy creator audience; volume markets ask for free rather than cheaper (20.0% vs 14.3%). Report 76 (Way of Life): China carries 82 of 306 price objections (26.8%); MON_PRICE is 15.5% of cn reviews (3.94×) and several name the price at which they would buy — '价格太贵了，要是12块我就买了' (at 12 yuan I would buy it, 5★); '30块也是最贵的' (at 30 yuan also the most expensive); East Asia group price objection 16.9% vs 7.5% global; the US sits at 4.8%. Report 86 (Today): a regional price visibly above the US price (CA$7 vs $4.99 at launch) produced Canada's 13.92% MON_FREE1 rate — the highest among eligible markets; US reviewers argue price in public ('just a cup of coffee?… come on people, app devs gotta make a living' vs 'In a market where most apps are $2.99 or less…').

<a id="c025"></a>
### C025 — Scholarship / hardship / discount program

**Strong** · 22 apps · 62 cards · positive in 9 apps · negative in 15 apps · tied to a purchase in 5 apps

*Why Strong:* 22 apps, directions mixed (open 25, act 21, paid 3)

The cleanest 5★ generator in report 1 (91 of 101 mentions 5★); also works around broken payment rails; never switch it off. Report 10: a 'Guardian' pay-it-forward sponsorship programme is one of the only monetisation themes with a positive mean (4.76 across 708 mentions); its one complaint is that there is no visible way to apply. Report 31: ~110 teen and low-income reviewers (2.12%, mean 2.31) in the 2022–23 TikTok cohort ('your target market at this point is us teenagers'; ages 14, 12, 11; a mental-health user who can't work) — lead with a student / low-income price in those markets. Report 34: a 50% annual offer converted ('I paid £9.99 for a whole year - bargain!'), affordability complaints come from students, Vietnam and ADHD users; the report proposes a student / regional price and New-Year sales. Report 36: AFFORD 5 (mean 2.20) — two on disability, a student, and 'there is no way I can afford it without being part of the demographic which can drop 60$ on a reminder app'. Report 41: a high-school student asks for a student deal; a Turkish 5★ says the one-time fee is too much 'at least in my country'; the report proposes purchasing-power-adjusted lifetime tiers in the long-tail storefronts. Report 42: 'I was ready to pay, but it has to be reasonable… I'm sure if you lower the price, revenue will grow' (RU); price objections at $39.99–$59.99 in high-income markets vs '500₽ a year, that's nothing'. Report 46: students and minors ask for a discount ('the only money i get is chore money and i have to wash the windows for it', 5★; a Cambridge scholarship student; 'please offer discount for students'; 'Is there a discount code for lifetime?'); the report's E5 is a student / youth discount; a discount honoured after it expired won a 5★. Report 49: 30 cannot afford it, 12 of them self-identified minors, in a 9+ app marketed on anime social media; an under-18 / student free programme exists but only 3 reviewers know of it — the report's experiment: surface it. Report 52: students without money are a named barrier ('forty-plus yuan, any conscience?', Grade 7; '¥30 when I was a student, ¥80 now'). Report 54: in CN the one-time ¥98 price competes against a ¥3/month anchor (a pricing-architecture problem). Report 57: 'how about a two-week trial then a discount — I'd just pay under ₩20,000'; a Mexican reviewer 'please put a discount on it'. Report 58: budget-constrained adopters ('as a broke student'; 'Good for broke but productive people'; 'I'm a young lady trying to save up') will not convert to a subscription. Report 72 (Habit Hearts): an informal hardship programme — 11 reviewers say the developer gave them premium free after they asked (six cite hardship, student status or being between jobs: 'I reached out to them about not being able to pay right now due to being in between jobs and they offered a free premium!'), all 11 are 5★, 10 of 11 US; grant union 15 (6.00%), all 5★; but it is invisible — others ask for a discount in public, and a 2★ ('I'm to tight for money') and a 1★ price objection are exactly its population; Russia (payment impossible) produced 1 grant and 4 unhappy reviews; §8.1 #4 / E3: surface the route inside the paywall in every shipped language — 'the cheapest available experiment in this whole report'; the cohort shifts the corpus mean 4.612 → 4.587 and must be disclosed as a selection effect. Report 76 (Way of Life): stated willingness to pay differs by market — 12 yuan (cn), 200 roubles (ru), £50 lifetime (gb) — and price objection is 15.5% of cn vs 4.8% of us. Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): 'looking forward to buying it the moment I can afford it' (mx 5★) — an affordability barrier from a user sold on the concept and the one-time model. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): 'a monthly subscription which isn't cheap for a student like me' (cz 3★); 'budget conscious buyers' asked for two free widgets (in 4★). Report 82 (Lasting Change): 'The only drawback is the price, especially for retirees or disabled people. It is just too steep' (4★) — the one accessibility-framed price objection. Report 86 (Today): the most self-aware affordability review in the series — 'Why 4 stars — mainly because I'm poor… I hesitated for one day and 22 hours over whether to uninstall… under 10 yuan I could accept. Isn't the point of making an app to let more people use it?' (cn 4★; MON_AFFORD 3); Canada's CA$7 launch price vs US$4.99 drew the highest cap-complaint rate among eligible markets ('$7 in the app world is premium').

<a id="c097"></a>
### C097 — A tip / donate option

**Strong** · 14 apps · 39 cards · positive in 11 apps · negative in 4 apps · tied to a purchase in 10 apps

*Why Strong:* 14 apps, directions mixed (act 18, open 10, paid 7)

People asking to give money with no mechanism to do so. Report 8: in a completely free app, 7 users asked unprompted for a tip jar (all 5★) and 13 more volunteered to pay — mostly one-time, not subscription. Report 27: exactly two reviewers volunteer money unprompted — 'Keep the free app, consider adding a tip jar for users who are thankful'; 'it would be nice to donate to the dev since it's a free app' — both 5★, both framing payment as gratitude, both pairing it with staying free; with 10 developer-gratitude reviews (all 5★) a tip jar is the only monetisation the corpus positively endorses, and Canada is where the evidence says to start. Report 29: 'love to be able to contribute to use it' — a contribution offered in a free app, alongside a lifetime-purchase offer tied to a widget. Report 56: one unprompted donation request in 67 reviews of a fully free app; E1: an unobtrusive tip jar in Settings — no gating, no prompt, no nag — and watch for any negative review mentioning it. Report 58: a voluntary in-app tip is the only payment surface, received warmly ('there are no ads! But you can leave a tip, which is very nice ✨'), zero objections — unlikely to scale alone. Report 59 (Tappsk): MON_DONATE_WISH 18 — reviewers buy the lifetime unlock explicitly to support or thank the developer. Report 69 (TheFor): intent to buy framed as supporting the developer — 'I'm sure to support you, and I believe it's worth every Thai bath'. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): a patronage model — 'completely free; in-app purchase is only for people who want to support us' — with 39 framing payment as support and explicit asks for a repeatable small tip ('Please add a way to donate ¥100 at a time, as often as I like'; named thresholds ¥100–300, ¥500), a 'watch an ad' button as non-monetary support, and two buying the developer's book instead; a donation link named in 23 reviews was intermittent (not accepted in 2020); §8.7: a repeatable ¥100–300 tip or one-time pack beside the monthly plan. Report 71 (MyStreaks): a listed tip ladder — Friend $0.99, Ally $1.99, Advocate $2.99, Endorser $4.99 — beside Premium; no reviewer mentions any of it. Report 76 (Way of Life): a tip jar from 2018-11 — MON_TIP 15 (4.60★): 'jumped at the chance to tip the developers' (au 5★); 'supporting the developer' is a named purchase trigger in a corpus that thanks the developer by name (PR_DEV 268). Report 84 (HabitGrid): §8.4 — if revenue is needed, test an optional one-time purchase or tip for unshipped capabilities rather than gating the free core. Report 85 (Habitica): donations were an option 2015–2018 (MON_DONATE 2) and five reviewers ask for a donate button instead of add-ons — for an open-source, free-core product, patronage is the stated purchase motive.

<a id="c267"></a>
### C267 — No AI-generated art, copy or content in a paid product — reviewers accept an AI coach and reject AI decoration

**Strong** · 7 apps · 14 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 4 apps

*Why Strong:* 7 apps, directions mixed (act 4, open 2, paid 1)

Report 49 (Life Reset): AI-generated task icons, achievement art, motivational copy and book summaries are criticised by 53 reviews (4.30%, mean 1.85) — the only product criticism rising in every era (0% → 4.4% → 4.0% → 5.5%), spreading from images to the writing ('replete with the odd linguistic signatures characteristic of an LLM'), typos and code, and double the global rate in Australia (10.34%). The objection is craft tied to price: 'I cannot see myself paying full price for something that is completely built by AI… Only then can I say this is something I'd actually tell my friends about'; 'for an app promoting ideas of doing the work and not being lazy, using AI instead of just paying an artist… seems like a very cheap move'; 'Just pay humans to do work'. AI planning is welcomed (6, mean 4.50) — 'The distinction is decoration versus function.' The report: commission at least the hero assets; fixing typos removes the most visible AI tell. Report 47 (DotHabit) is the complementary case: an AI coach replying to check-ins is praised unprompted ([[C263]]). Related: [[C056]], [[C185]]. Report 52: AI-generated note titles (Feb–Apr 2026) that could not be switched off — every review mentioning them negative. Report 64 (Critique AI): TRUST_AISLOP 4 (0.95%, mean 1.50) accuse the app itself of being AI-generated, one from inside after paying; the community page read as 'probably fake'. Report 68 (Ultiself): objections to AI-made design and text appear only in 2026 (NEG_AI_CONTENT 8) — the same era the app adds AI-assisted plans. Report 82 (Lasting Change): the German edition of the paid 'personalised' book reads as machine-translated — 'Die Übersetzung aus dem Englischen hat eine KI besorgt' — and 'all they customize is the name on the cover'. Report 83 (Roubit): AI-written letters are accepted and loved ('Even if it's ai, they've always been really well done'); AI_CONTENT_DISLIKE 1 ('very cliche answers that don't resonate with me'); Dr. Eddy hallucinated an author's work. Report 85 (Habitica): NEG_ART 35 — the 16-bit art divides; NEG_CHILDISH 3; NEG_RPG_UNWANTED 3.

<a id="c278"></a>
### C278 — Do not name the app after an established competitor — a name collision makes the product 'the fake one' before it is tried, and the cost cannot be measured from reviews

**Strong** · 6 apps · 12 cards · positive in 1 apps · negative in 2 apps

*Why Strong:* 6 apps, same direction (act on it, 100%)

Report 62 (Streaks – Daily Habit Tracker by yusuf kildan, 45 reviews): 'If you are planning to get such app based on online review them do not download this app. This is fake and similar name app to the original one. The og has orange colour logo' (IN, 1★) — the collision is real and corroborated in this repository: folder 23 is Streaks by Crunchy Bagel Pty Ltd (app ID 963034692, 7,270 reviews vs this app's 45), so a user searching 'Streaks' meets both and the smaller app is 'losing on brand identity before the product is even tried'; the icon-colour claim could not be verified; how much the collision costs in installs is a research question the corpus cannot answer. Related: [[C184]] (a neutral name is already tested), [[C134]] (lead the listing with what users love), [[C114]] (ads must match the app). Report 77 (Streak-Free / Momentumly): the product reaches users under many names — Store title 'Habit Tracker: Streak-Free', bundle and reviewer usage 'Momentumly', a subscriber calling it 'Streak Free', and the paid tier under five names while the listing sells under three — a search and support liability. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): the app was renamed Checker → Ripples mid-life (v2.0.0) and the US storefront then went further to 'Visual Habit Tracker: Ripples' while 42 storefronts keep another title; six reviews use the old name and one attributes data loss to the rename. Report 84 (HabitGrid): a near-identical paid app ('HabitGrid - Goal tracker', 2023) shares the name; a reviewer distinguishes this one as the free one — a name collision that so far works in the free app's favour. Report 88 (GetHabit): renamed from HabitBox to GetHabit at an unknown date in 2021 after the launch wave; seven reviews name the old app; a billing descriptor under a third name ('PersonalityPath') — three names on one product. Research: Quit Habit Decision.md — the same reasoning applied to your own catalogue: a generic quit app shipped beside your habit app 'would compete with your own app for the same keywords… and read as a repackage'; a second listing has to be a different product with different content 'so it wouldn't look like spam'.

**Reports:** [62](<../App Store Reports/62. Streaks – Daily Habit Tracker - Atomic Goals & Accountability (REPORT).md>), [77](<../App Store Reports/77. <a id="c286"></a>
### C286 — Never advertise or sell in a language the app does not ship — a localised ad, quiz or checkout for an English-only app is a refund request waiting to happen

**Strong** · 6 apps · 15 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 6 apps

*Why Strong:* 6 apps, same direction (act on it, 91%)

Report 67 (Habio): MKT_LANG_BAIT 86 (4.19%, mean 1.07), every one dated 2024-03-28 or later — the ad and web quiz ran in French, Spanish, German, Arabic or Japanese and the paid app turned out English-only (lookup API declares EN; listing titles localised as 'Habio: Tagesplaner. Checkliste', 'Habio: Habitude et Objectif'): 'L'ensemble des publicités ansi que les questionnaires avant l'achat sont en français, et l'application n'est dispo qu'en anglais'; France 30 of 91 reviews (32.97%), Germany 12 of 85, Chile 10 of 25; 34.9% of these reviewers ask for or are refused a refund ('nunca me contestaron para decirme si podía cambiar a español o no'); the language request itself predates the ads (6 in the free era) — 'The ads made it worse; they did not create it'; §8.5: localise, or state 'English only' in every non-English ad, quiz and checkout. Related: [[C027]] (localise early), [[C148]] (deliver what the ads show), [[C218]]. Report 68 (Ultiself): 'Реклама була українською мовою' (the ad was in Ukrainian) while Ukrainian (261 reviews) and Kazakh (47) are not among the 12 declared languages although ua and kz are the second- and third-largest storefronts; interfaces in Russian or Spanish with videos and notifications in English (NEG_LANG 32); §8.5: do not advertise in a language the content is not in; declare and localise Ukrainian and Kazakh if targeted. Report 82 (Lasting Change): an English-only app and English-only T&Cs sold into at least six language markets — 17 non-English reviews (es 8, de 4, fr 2, pl, nl, it) and six of them report being charged without understanding they had agreed to anything ('yo no he autorizado ningún cobro'; 'Abofalle'); 'a disclosure problem before it is a localisation problem'; the German book translation 'hat eine KI besorgt'. Report 83 (Roubit): the listing claimed English in 2022 while the app was Korean-only — 'in developer the language said it was on korean and english but inside the app you can only use korean' (4★). Report 85 (Habitica): sold on the Korean and Turkish storefronts for a decade with no Korean or Turkish UI — kr NEG_LANG 76.9%, tr 40.0% and the corpus's most-voted reviews. Report 88 (GetHabit): sold in 63 storefronts with five UI languages — LANG_NOT_AVAILABLE 6 ('bought the app and it's all in German', pt); two ask for Spanish.

<a id="c285"></a>
### C285 — A paid add-on is never bought on a single tap — its own price on the button, its own confirmation (never the trial's stored authorisation), 'no thanks' by default and worded neutrally, repeat taps ignored, and a clear way to turn it off

**Strong** · 5 apps · 20 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 5 apps

*Why Strong:* 5 apps, same direction (act on it, 78%)

Report 67 (Habio, 2,051 reviews): a $29.99 'workbook' / 'Get my PDF' button shown straight after the paid-trial payment and charged against the card just authorised with no second confirmation — MON_WORKBOOK 189 (9.22%, mean 1.01, 2023-10-15 → 2025-05-04, 41 in 2024-04 alone): 'The consent to charge text is in such a low contrast colour with the background, and such a tiny type size that it hurts my eyes to even read it!'; 'la vérification est demandé donc ils ne la redemande pas ensuite'; 'cliqué en un espacio para informarme más acerca de un pdf y directamente me cobraron 29€!' (es — 39.62% of the Spanish storefront); MON_DOUBLECHARGE 157 (7.65%) often two workbooks ('adhd_workbook' + 'habits_workbook') from a button that seemed not to respond; support answered 'we do not offer refunds for in-app purchases', which in EU storefronts collides with the 14-day withdrawal right; ADHD reviewers: 'They use lack of focus among the targeted ADHD group and trick You into in app purchase without confirming payment!'; §8.2: price on the button, separate confirmation not the trial's stored authorisation, default 'No thanks', idempotent repeat taps, refund an unopened PDF on request. Related: [[C211]] (no second separately-cancelled add-on subscription), [[C274]] (a dismiss control never starts a purchase), [[C213]]. Report 68 (Ultiself): a small intro plan ($6–10) followed on the next screen by add-on charges — the number 57 appears in 60 reviews, 58 describing an unrequested extra charge ('along with the $9.92 charge, another $57 has been taken'; 'Кликнул на кнопку списало еще 57$ кликнул на другую кнопку еще 28$'; 'AUTOMATIQUEMENT vous venez d'acheter 3 PROGRAMMES SUPPLÉMENTAIRES, sans confirmation bancaire'); a decline button worded to shame — 'no I do not wish to improve my health'; 'Los botones estaban puestos de manera engañosa y confusa'; MON_ADDON lift 10.14× among purchasers; §8.2: no charge without an explicit second confirmation and a neutral 'No thanks'. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): 「しかも誤課金しやすい画面。970円も誤課金した。」 ('the screen makes mis-purchases easy. I mistakenly paid ¥970'); 'I couldn't work out how to turn the useless feature off' then charged ¥960; 'a sudden demand for money' — 'close to fraud'; §8.4: explicit confirmation on the add-on and a clear way to turn a pack off. (Consolidation after report 70: title widened from 'Never charge a one-off add-on on a single tap against the authorisation just given for a trial — …' to cover the report 68 and 70 shapes; the report 67 finding stays in the statement.) Report 82 (Lasting Change): BILL_CHECKOUT_TRICK 5 — a post-pay upsell page where a standalone £74.69 lifetime price 'made it appear as though this amount was simply the difference between the original price and the higher total… no explicit confirmation step showing the full amount being charged… I only realised after receiving two separate receipt emails'; 'I accidentally pressed one wrong button and got immediately charged a further £80'; 'Chose the cheapest option and they charged me for a lifetime app which was not even an option'; 'automatically tried to charge me for speeding service, something I never selected'; all three lifetime-purchase mentions in the corpus are complaints about being charged for one unintentionally. Report 88 (GetHabit): PAY_PREMIUM_INCOMPLETE 38 (7.76%), 30 of them buyers — having paid, PDFs, checklists and challenges cost more ('the first thing I chose, they want $9.99 to unlock the PDFs'; 'Not worth 3 different life time membership fees I had to pay'; a 'Full-Time-Pass' 10,99€ on top; 'an additional $16 per month to access further content'); the listing still sells 'Access to all printable items' separately; §8.7 include printables in any lifetime or yearly plan.

**Reports:** [67](<../App Store Reports/67. Habio - Daily Habit Tracker - Routine planner & To do list (REPORT).md>), [68](<../App Store Reports/68. <a id="c294"></a>
### C294 — When the pricing model changes, the historical review corpus keeps advertising the old one — state the current model on the listing and paywall, and honour every old receipt automatically

**Strong** · 5 apps · 15 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 3 apps

*Why Strong:* 5 apps, same direction (act on it, 73%)

Report 76 (Way of Life, 7,764 reviews over 16 years): premium was a $4.99 one-time unlock from 2010 and became a subscription in 2023; in the subscription era (E6, 906 reviews) MON_SUBSCRIPTION is 40 reviews at mean 2.70★ (4.42% of the era, 15 of the corpus's 181 1★) and splits three ways — lifetime buyers told to subscribe again ('Ich hab mir die App 2015 oder so als voll Version gekauft', 1★; '之前永久内购没了？重新订阅？', 1★), new users who arrived expecting the one-time price because 'reviews said it was a one time payment' (3★), and prices differing week to week ('last week the price was $29, this week is $99', 4★); some veterans were grandfathered ('grandfathered into the new system', 5★), so the path existed but was not reliable; restore failures rose 0.91% → 1.55% and support silence peaked (SUP_NONE 9 of 20 in E6). A decade of 5★ reviews praising 'a one time charge' keeps recruiting users who then feel misled; §8.1 restore premium for any old receipt on any device without a subscription prompt, and show one stable price per region stating monthly / annual / lifetime. Related: [[C186]] (never revoke what earlier buyers paid for), [[C218]] (listing copy stays true), [[C113]] (one stable disclosed price), [[C003]] (lead with lifetime). Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): year-one reviews sold the app as 'no subscriptions… one time payment of $10'; when the model changed the description still said nothing about money at all and the only 'used to be great' review (1★) lists 'the lack of a subscription' among what it lost — 'a market that was sold a specific promise — one payment, no subscription — encountering a different one, with no listing text to mediate the change'. Report 86 (Today): 'I paid for this app and reviewed it years ago (when it was under a different pricing model)… for the $300 you're asking for now' (5★) — a decade of one-time-price reviews now sits beside a $299.99 SKU. Report 89 (Check Calendar): reviewers keep quoting 600円 through 2026-03 and $3.99 while the listing shows ¥780 / $4.99 — 'Prices quoted by reviewers are what they saw at the time, in their currency'; a 2026-05 reviewer records the change ('it used to be 600 yen, now 800'). Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): the opposite constraint — with no archived listing history (the Wayback Machine was not queried, §9.E) the corpus is the only record of the app's past pricing and ad behaviour, and it disagrees with itself: one 2023 review already says 'only ads' while ad complaints as a pattern start in June 2024 and two 2026 reviewers describe ads as newly added. When the reviews are the only history, 'when did this change' cannot be answered at all.

**Reports:** [76](<../App Store Reports/76. Way of Life - Habit Tracker - Build a better, stronger you (REPORT).md>), [79](<../App Store Reports/79. Habit Tracker - Ripples - Routines, streaks, reminders (REPORT).md>), [86](<../App Store Reports/86. Today Habit tracker - For to-dos, routines & goals (REPORT).md>), [89](<../App Store Reports/89. Check Calendar - Habit Tracker - Check your habit calendar! (REPORT).md>), [90](<../App Store Reports/90. Quit Bad Habits & Addiction - Sobriety Counter & Tracker (REPORT).md>)

<a id="c274"></a>
### C274 — A close or dismiss control must never start a purchase — no fake X, no dismissal that lands on the payment sheet

**Strong** · 4 apps · 11 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 4 apps

*Why Strong:* 4 apps, same direction (act on it, 100%)

Report 55 (Habit-Bull): a full-screen premium pop-up shown on every launch from 5 July 2020 had a close control that started a purchase — 'I clicked on the x at the top, but instead of giving me the data screen, it acted like I'd tried to make a purchase' (us, 4★); 'The pop up has a fake X in the top corner to close the message, which if you press, causes your account to agree to the premium subscription' (gb, 1★); 'after mistakenly upgrading' (2024). PAY_FORCED 20 (0.99%, mean 1.25, 18 at 1★, all 10 Jul 2020 → 3 Jan 2021) plus PAY_NAG 44 (2.02); in July 2020 35 of 68 reviews (51.5%) carried one or both, the month's mean was 2.09 with 39 one-stars and 11 reviews on 12 July alone; the German-speaking storefronts took it hardest (PAY_NAG 10.7%). The report's F2: make close controls unambiguous so no dismissal can start a purchase — 'the cheapest change with the clearest rating effect in the data'. Related: [[C093]] (no upsell nagging), [[C145]] (every modal dismissible), [[C180]] (no exit discounts or countdowns), [[C269]] (hijacking ad mechanics). Report 57: 'I tapped to see what Premium was, pressed OK to close the sheet, and it bought it' — 6 accidental purchases (2019–2023), all refund requests. Report 67 (Habio): NEG_DARKUX 163 (7.95%, mean 1.01), used by reviewers who work in UX — 'As a UX designer I should have seen the dark patterns from the start'; '환불을 어렵게 만드는 전형적인 다크 패턴'.

<a id="c275"></a>
### C275 — Never gate the core create action behind an ad — an interstitial at setup is the churn engine, and an ad that fails to load must never block creation

**Strong** · 4 apps · 17 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 4 apps

*Why Strong:* 4 apps, same direction (act on it, 88%)

Report 57 (DayStamp): a free tier that requires watching a full-screen interstitial to create a habit (from Jan 2021; 5 seconds in 2021, 29–30 seconds from Sep 2023) is the single most destructive mechanic — ads 47 of 779 (6.03%, mean 2.234, half of them 1★), 26 naming the creation gate (2.154), and 20 of the 25 reviewers who state they deleted the app (80%) name ads, against zero stated deletions for crashes or data loss: 'A full screen ad after just creating one habit? Wow, immediately uninstalled'; 'The developer is losing a lot of app sales because the full screen ads are so horrible that you will stop using the app before finding out if you like the functionality'; an ADHD user 'as soon as I made a single activity scheduled it gave me an add. Literally distracted me before I could get familiarized with the app'. From 2024 the gate started failing — 8 reviewers (7 since 2024, latest 24 Aug 2026) could not create a habit at all because no ad loaded ('Can't add a task - no ads to show'; 'seven ads to add three goals… I got angry trying to build good habits and deleted it') — 'a monetization mechanic that can hard-block the product's core action is a reliability bug, not a pricing decision'. Six reviewers who tolerate ads all gave 5★ and all describe them as short and confined to creation ('survivable at 5 seconds and not at 30'); ads run 9.20% of non-Korean reviews vs 2.48% Korean and 15.15% of US reviews, where 8 of 10 uninstalls blame ads. Options the report supports: back to ~5 seconds, move to a session boundary, or gate after the nth habit rather than the 3rd–4th. Related: [[C269]] (hijacking ad mechanics), [[C246]] (no ads), [[C240]] (never on the completion moment), [[C147]] (use before pay). Report 83 (Roubit): an ad that fails to load blocks the recovery action it gates — a month of unloadable past-day ads ended in an uninstall; 'even after watching them I can't get into Roubit at all' (1★, a user of several years). Report 88 (GetHabit): ADS_IN_APP 21 (4.29%, all before 2021-04-07) — 'Impossible to use because of enormous number of long video ads' — inside an app that also charged $7.99 a week. Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): the ad load did not merely block an action — it crashed the app on launch for a week (BUG_CRASH_AD_LOAD 14), so the free tier's ad path took down the counter itself; ADS_TOO_MANY 18 describe a long unskippable ad after every action ('a long ad after every action; deleting'; 'the ads are long and can't be skipped'; 'to close it you have to exit completely').

**Reports:** [57](<../App Store Reports/57. Habit Tracker - DayStamp - Daily Routine, Streak & Widget (REPORT).md>), [83](<../App Store Reports/83. Roubit  - Fun Routine Planner - Bunny Diary & Tasks (REPORT).md>), [88](<../App Store Reports/88. GetHabit - Easy Habit Tracker - Habits Tracker for a BetterMe (REPORT).md>), [90](<../App Store Reports/90. Quit Bad Habits & Addiction - Sobriety Counter & Tracker (REPORT).md>)

<a id="c061"></a>
### C061 — Goodwill conversion — a generous free tier and 'support the devs'

**Contested** · 45 apps · 116 cards · positive in 41 apps · negative in 3 apps · tied to a purchase in 33 apps

*Why Contested:* 45 apps; free vs paid genuinely split — 13 apps' cards say build-free, 16 say build-paid

Small, pure-margin, mean 4.69. Report 5: the dominant purchase path was years of free use followed by upgrading to scale it or to say thanks. Report 20: a large share of pre-2021 purchases were donations — 'I'll definitely choose the highest one because this developer deserves the best'; 'I bought the paid function not because I needed it, but as a thank you.' Report 26: 'bought premium right away just to support the developers'; 45 call the free tier generous (mean 4.49). Report 28: 'I've spent money on this app SOLELY to support the developer because I can't thank him enough'; 'the actual habit tracking is FREE' praised by 13. Report 31: 'supporting a small team' was an E1 purchase trigger ('there is a small team behind so I was happy to pay'; 'happy to support the designers'). Report 33: supporting a small team was a purchase trigger ('I can see this team cares'); 48 call the free tier sufficient (mean 4.85); Vietnamese reviewers take pride in a Vietnamese-built app. Report 34: supporting a solo developer is a named purchase motive ('I paid the app to support solo developer'); 13 of 51 payers praise the developer. Report 36: patronage 5 of 34 payers (14.7%) — 'l'idée de payer 15€ par an pour féliciter, soutenir et remercier le travail d'une équipe indépendante'; proof-first 6 of 34 (17.6%) — 'Have been having it for free until today and decided to purchase'. Report 41: 'Just bought the premium to support the developer i don't even need the features tbh'; decisions made in 20 minutes to a few days on a 3-habit free tier. Report 43: 'I purchased the premium version because I want to support the excellent privacy and pricing policies!'; 'you wouldn't do your job for free. Don't expect programmers to work for free either'; 'I wanna donate the developer'. Report 46: 'I paid the subscription fee because it's a great app with a developer who obviously cares' (ADHD); 'I bought it to support the developer' — 13 (mean 4.92), 12 of them before July 2023; three free users state their condition ('If it helps me build three habits, I'll come back and pay!'). Report 47: gratitude that the app is free 25 (4.24%, mean 4.68 — 'この手のアプリはタスク増やすと課金が必要だけど…'); willing to pay 14 (mean 4.57), 9 before 2022, mostly to remove banners — the 'I'd pay to remove ads' user of 2019–23 became either a subscriber or a leaver after 2024 (ad-removal requests 2.6% → 0%). Report 48: 'free is enough' 248 (5.63%, 4.82) — the load-bearing praise of the freemium era; 38 payers describe months or years of free use before paying 'to support the developers'; pay-to-support-dev 7–9 at 5.00 — 'sustained free use first, then payment as endorsement'. Report 50: free tier praised by 12 (4.92) and price-positive 16 (4.81) — 14 five-stars volunteer the fair price unprompted; 'Has everything that u need and even more for free'; the documented purchase path runs through sustained free use first (a month; six months; 'Once [the habits are] internalised I'll be delighted to pay for more options'). Report 52: supporting an indie developer is a named purchase trigger (DEV_TRUST ∩ paid 52 at 4.98; bought 'so the app can keep running'). Report 54: 4 bought to support the developer, all 5★ — 'make a high quality product, offer it for free without junky ads, and without high pressure sales tactics. Let the app speak for itself'. Report 56: a fully free app with no commercial surface — 0 of 67 mention paying — and exactly one unprompted request to donate ('Eager next for notification and donation options'), backed by 13 (19.40%) who thank the developer; the only monetisation path the corpus supports is voluntary (D3). Report 57: 'you made a good app, so I bought Premium'; 'the purchase option is one-time rather than subscription, so I intend to pay soon as a gesture of thanks'. Report 58: willingness to pay is patronage-shaped, not access-shaped — 'I wish and hope and pray it will continue to be free and to those who can, please support the developers! <3' (PH); 'The framing that works is support the creator, not unlock the feature'. Report 59 (Tappsk): PR_FREE 493 (3.25%, 4.91★ — 'no limit on the to-do list in the free version'), PR_NO_ADS 127, and buying 'чтобы поддержать разработчиков' (to support the developers) / 'чтобы отблагодарить разработчиков' (to thank the developers) as stated purchase triggers; the report says keep a free tier genuinely usable for tasks. Report 65 (Rabit): 'Rabit's free tier was not a cost — it was the acquisition engine and the review engine' (48 reviews at 4.88); 'no ridiculous paywalls. everything you need is free'. Report 67 (Habio): the non-seeded 5★ reviews are mostly free-era — 'Let's you have as many habits you want for free'; 'This app doesn't ask for payments which I really love'. Report 68 (Ultiself): the free tracker is what earns the praise — 'Free Version is Great' and 'Best habit tracker I've come across' (19 votes each, the most-voted reviews); 'I find the basic non-paid version to be plenty' (PR_FREE 26); only 2 of 408 purchasers mention liking the free version as the path to paying. Report 69 (TheFor): purchases are goodwill, not value exchange — the only stated purchase reason is the design ('clean simple UI loved it thats why purchased the pro plan'), intent is price- or support-led ('the price isn't too much even for my country, so I'll get it'; 'I'm sure to support you… worth every Thai bath'), and no review in 80 describes a single Pro feature — 'fragile in a specific way — it depends on the free tier staying good and the developer staying visible'. Report 70 (Habit / 継続する技術): the only paid item is an optional message pack named 「無駄機能」 ('useless feature') — 44 reviews name it; 54 bought (mean 4.76), support-the-developer lift 15.22×, developer-bond among 35.19% of buyers; 90 more say they will ('after 30 days', 'when I have money'); 'I felt guilty about using it for free'; 'This app doesn't smell of money at all'. Report 76 (Way of Life): PR_FREE 249 (4.72★) 'free version is enough' and the cap converts only after the free tier has delivered value — 'found myself wanting to add more and shelled out the $5'; 'bought the upgrade to have more than three lines to track'; MON_INTENT 93 (4.65★). Report 84 (HabitGrid, 86 reviews, 4.93★, no IAP at all): the free model is the reason 45.35% of reviewers give (U:free_model_any 39: MODEL_FREE 30, NO_ADS 12, NO_PAYWALL 7, VS_PAID 7, UNLIMITED 3), stable at 44–47% in every era through a language-mix change from 23% to 77% non-English — 'the one reason that does not depend on who is writing'; reviewers thank the developer for keeping it free ('the dev has generously made it free'; 'a big thank-you for keeping it free and without ads'); the free model is usually one item in a list of reasons alongside simplicity, the grid, widgets and fast replies. Report 85 (Habitica): the subscription sells as patronage — MON_SUPPORT_DEV 13 of 55 purchasers (23.6%: 'I upgraded just to help support the developers'; 'I don't mind contributing $5 a month to keep the app and website going'), long-term users 21.8% of payers vs 3.86% of all; 'No annoying pop ups (which makes me actually want to spend money to support the devs)'; MON_ALT_SUPPORT 5 want 'a donate button not add ons'. Report 86 (Today): MON_SUPPORT_DEV 8 ('I bought the full version to support an app I use often'); China frames the price as buying the developer a meal ('what's 30 yuan — think of it as buying the developer dinner'); PR_WORTH 73 at 4.84★; 'because they actually listened to there customers I just paid full price for it!' Report 90 (Quit Bad Habits & Addiction): with every feature free, one of the three would-pay statements is pure patronage — 'I see the ad-free subscription as a plus; thinking of using it to support you' (kz) — and the two actual buyers bought ad removal and stayed satisfied: 'paid at once — you can't start a tracker like this by watching smelly ads'.

<a id="c239"></a>
### C239 — A personal origin story in the listing builds trust — and turns any later gate into a betrayal

**Contested** · 8 apps · 21 cards · positive in 7 apps · negative in 2 apps · tied to a purchase in 3 apps

*Why Contested:* 8 apps; free vs paid genuinely split — 2 apps' cards say build-free, 2 say build-paid

Report 27: a solo developer's story in the listing produced 10 reviews (7.25%, every one 5★) thanking her by name — 'Thanks Emily'; 'It's clear that someone made this with joy, not for money'; 'built/maintained by an individual female developer — THANK YOU'; 'you are a hero'. The origin story does measurable acquisition work, and it is a constraint: a trust-based relationship is what makes a paywall feel like a betrayal rather than a transaction. Report 25: 'I can't believe one developer made this' and 'after interacting with the developer I decided to pay without any hesitation'. Report 59 (Tappsk): the developer's own vc.ru article brought the first users (MKT_PRESS 13) and a Russian creator is itself praised ('это еще и русский создатель а не зарубежный'). Report 71 (MyStreaks): 'Thank you to Jeff & Jami and their team for the great book & app!' — founder presence is praised in 4 reviews, all 5★. Report 76 (Way of Life): a named solo developer is part of the product — PR_DEV 268 (3.45%, mean 4.96★) rising from 2.1% of E1 to 6.7% of E6, thanked for 'steady updates' over a decade; ru 1.99×, kz 4.06×, ua 2.68×; §8.8 keep 'one-person, responsive development'. Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): U:developer_equity 36 (20.93%, 4.94★) — a solo, named, Reddit/YouTube-facing developer with a public roadmap was a purchase motive (MON_SUPPORT_DEV 3: 'because I like your approach'; 'to support the developer'); the equity eroded 26.4% → 12.2% as the audience changed, and the one paying customer who reports being ignored writes 'Developer doesn't respond. Waste of time' in a 1★. Report 84 (HabitGrid): U:dev_relationship 25 (29.07%), every one 5★ — 'we need more developers like this'; 'the poor guy works on it alone ❤️'; the gratitude is for keeping the app free and localising it (17 of 37 Russian reviews thank the developer, none of them report a reply). Report 85 (Habitica): 'an open-source app run by a small team that's made better by the work of volunteers' — the listing's framing is why purchasers pay (support, 23.6%) and why the 2023 dispute with volunteer moderators cut so deep (STAFF_CONTROVERSY 19 at 1.74★). Report 86 (Today): the sister app (Pillow) being 'updated, working well' while Today sat unreleased for 1,030 days is what reviewers cite when concluding the developer moved on — a studio's other products are read as evidence of intent.

### C187 — No paid acquisition into an auto-converting trial in frictionless-payment markets

**Moderate** · 3 apps · 8 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 2 apps

*Why Moderate:* 3 apps

Report 13: a Douyin campaign drove Chinese installs into a 7-day trial that opened a ¥208/yr subscription with password-free payment and no authentication step; China became 73% one-star and 51% of all involuntary-charge reviews. Report 67 (Habio): paid Instagram / Facebook acquisition into a web quiz and a $1 auto-converting trial across 81 storefronts; volume tripled in the web-funnel era (572 reviews, mean 1.17, scam language 51.4%). Report 68 (Ultiself): ad → web questionnaire → paid plan by card, Apple Pay or PayPal across 106 storefronts; billing complaints 63.0% of reviews in the Dec 2024 → Mar 2025 era as Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan became major sources.

<a id="c211"></a>
### C211 — No second, separately-cancelled add-on subscription

**Moderate** · 3 apps · 15 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 3 apps

*Why Moderate:* 3 apps

Report 19: an e-book/PDF plan at $17–$45/month was enrolled on top of the programme subscription with its own cancellation path; 11 of 105 (10.48%) across five storefronts described it, and two reviewers on two continents reported the same asymmetry — the main plan cancels, the add-on does not. Collapse add-ons into the main plan or delete them. Report 24: 324 reviews (0.75%, mean 1.398) describe being enrolled in a multi-app bundle (Clarify, Shape, Sphere…) during onboarding through near-identical full-screen offers whose decline is a small corner 'skip'; the $39.99 + $29.99 same-day pair is the signature in hundreds of 2024–26 reviews, each subscription must be cancelled separately, and 338 report a charge with no consent at all (mean 1.047, the lowest in the corpus). Bundle complaints went 0.30% → 0.06% → 0.17% → 2.62% across eras. Report 88 (GetHabit): content packs sold on top of a paid plan — PDFs $9.99, a 'Full-Time-Pass', 'an additional $16 per month' — drove PAY_PREMIUM_INCOMPLETE 38, 30 of them from buyers; 'I'm out $60 and there are 16 challenges... total'.

<a id="c247"></a>
### C247 — Never make a sibling-app bundle the only way to buy this app's own premium

**Moderate** · 3 apps · 9 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 2 apps

*Why Moderate:* 3 apps

Report 31: from mid-2021 the Growth Bundle (Tally, Do, Grateful, Moody, Last, Time Block, Reflectly) was the only upgrade path — 36 reviews (0.69%, mean 2.03): 'There is no way to only upgrade this app to premium'; 'the renewal jumps up to 10x the price in a year's time'; buyers of a $19.99 'lifetime' were routed into a 'gift' bundle upsell, and dismissing it dropped them back to Basic. A bundle can be offered alongside, never instead of, a single-app purchase. Report 36: 'I only want to buy this one' / 'Me gustaría que vendieran el premium de solo esta app' — SUITE- 9; one buyer bought Habits alone as 'the only app in the pack truly worth it'; the report: sell Habits standalone, prominently. Report 82 (Lasting Change): a six-app developer whose charges arrive under a sibling app's name — 'I was charged by Effecto'; 'you'll get charged by medical score or Effecto App'; a Lasting Change review titled 'Walking Yoga a scam' — a reconciliation failure and an attribution problem: some reviews on this listing may describe a sibling product's checkout.

(co) — 'the highest-leverage finding in the report that costs nothing to fix': the product is not mispriced, it is mis-expected, and every such reviewer 'was acquired at full marketing cost and converted into a permanent 1★'; the only major theme with no downward movement across 17 months (6.5% / 8.8% / 5.6% / 7.8%); M2, and with price-before-quiz (M1) it addresses 53 reviews (12.65%) at mean 1.28. **Moderate** · 3 apps · 10 cards · positive in 2 apps · negative in 3 apps

Related: [[C112]] (in-app cancellation), [[C215]] (support faster than the deadline), [[C036]], [[C180]] (no 'wait, don't go' offers on the paywall). ### C298 — A public roadmap converts — and becomes a promise users hold you to

**Moderate** · 2 apps · 10 cards · positive in 2 apps · negative in 2 apps · tied to a purchase in 1 apps

Report 79 (Ripples / Checker): PRAISE_ROADMAP 17 (9.88%, mean 4.94★) — reviewers repeatedly cite a public roadmap as a reason for confidence and for buying: 'following a roadmap full of nice upgrades'; 'what I personally miss (notes and custom units) is already planned by the developer! So I'll probably buy the full version soon'; one bought and then said they were waiting on the roadmap ('чекатиму на здійснення усього задуманого по роудмепу'); three purchase intents were conditional on named roadmap items (reminders + sync; notes + custom units; Russian) and all three later shipped. The counterweight is a 3★ whose entire text is 'Please complete roadmap', and a solo developer's pipeline that ships incremental asks (notes, reminders, compact widgets, start-of-day, multi-board view — mostly within 12–18 months, one reviewer editing the review up: 'so happy to have compact boards now!') but leaves the structural ones (Watch, iPad, import) open. Report 89 (Check Calendar): the inverse case — a public promise that was not kept. <a id="c242"></a>
### C242 — Never monetise by routing the user's device or bandwidth for third parties — and never gate first launch behind any such opt-in

**Moderate** · 1 apps · 13 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 1 apps

*Why Moderate:* 1 app, exceptional magnitude (mean 1.0★; mean 5.0★; n=100)

Report 29: a free tracker whose whole reputation was 'actually free' (46.99% of reviews) added a launch-screen prompt in May 2026 asking users to enable 'web indexing' — letting third parties use the phone's IP to download web data — in exchange for an ad-free experience. Every reviewer who described it gave 1★ ('This app now interrupts use unless you agree to run a malware proxy downloader'; 'Didn't get past the opening screen… No thanks'; 'You PAID for this free app'); two of three quit before using the product; a reviewer had already asked 'Am I trading off data privacy for this?'; the listing's privacy label ('analytics and diagnostics') does not obviously cover it. It turned the 1★ band from bugs into privacy in one half-year. If any consent-based monetisation is used, ask after first value, in plain language, reversible, never as a gate. (Consolidation after report 90: see [[C306]] for the other half of the rule — what third-party monetisation code may do to the user is one question, where it is allowed to run is another.)

**Reports:** [29](<../App Store Reports/29. Habit Tracker - Daily Goals - Motivation & Accountability (REPORT).md>)

<a id="c309"></a>
### C309 — Quit tracking belongs inside the habit app as a habit type — never as a second, generic 'quit anything' app

**Moderate** · 1 apps · 7 cards · positive in 0 apps · negative in 0 apps

*Why Moderate:* 1 app, exceptional magnitude (lift x10; n=10621; n=186328)

Research: Quit Habit Decision.md (evidence base: 56,653 reviews of the category's #1 app, 10,621 reviews of the leading quit tracker, App Store ratings counts). The generic quit market is one incumbent and a graveyard — Days Since 19,073 US ratings, Quitzilla 1,473, Quit Bad Habits & Addiction 1,061, Days Without 6, ZeroBadHabits 0 — so a generic quit app's ceiling is roughly 19k US ratings. The money is in verticals, which beat every generic quit app by 3-10x: I Am Sober 186,328, Smoke Free 57,263, Reframe: Drink Less 44,339, Sober Time 41,632, Nomo 16,398, QuitNow! 13,572; someone quitting smoking searches 'quit smoking', not 'quit tracker', and wants lung-recovery milestones, craving support and a community that a generic counter does not provide. A generic quit app therefore loses on both sides: 'too vague for the vertical searcher, and redundant for the habit-tracker user.' The audiences barely migrate — only 2.4% of Days Since reviewers ask for good-habit building — which removes the cannibalisation risk and the cross-sell case at once: 'Two apps, two ASO efforts, two support queues, for two groups that don't migrate.' Three costs are named for the second listing: it competes with your own app for the same keywords, caps out around 19k ratings, and reads as a repackage. The upside of keeping it in one listing is a keyword surface: Days Since ranks #3 overall in the category on ranking strength and #1 in 10 rich markets purely on quit terms, so a proper quit mode lets one listing compete for 'quit habit', 'break bad habits' and 'sobriety tracker' alongside the habit keywords 'without splitting your ASO across two listings'. If a second app is ever built it must be vertical and genuinely different — the named opening is phone/social-media quitting, 2.0% of Days Since reviews and the third-biggest quit reason with no large dedicated app owning it — and the bar is content, not skin: 'That is a different product with different content, not a reskin, so it wouldn't look like spam.' Related: [[C019]] (the quit-habit mode itself), [[C060]] (cross-selling an app family), [[C278]] (a name that collides with a competitor), [[C140]] (marketing the generic-tracker use case).

**Reports:** [Quit Habit Decision](<../Research Reports/Quit Habit Decision.md>)

</details>

## Part 9 — High-impact rare findings: the complete nuance register

Every card that attached to **no** canonical point — 1,035 of 7,590. A card lands here when nothing
in the ledger fitted it and widening an existing point to swallow it would have destroyed the detail.
That makes this section the opposite of a leftovers pile: it is where the one-app tactics, the
market-specific blockers and the single findings with extreme magnitude survive intact.

Ordered by magnitude strength — cards whose numbers hit the exceptional thresholds (mean ≤ 1.7★ or
≥ 4.8★, lift ≥ ×4, 50+ reviews) first. Each is reproduced with everything the card carries.

#### `R17-002` · [17](<../App Store Reports/17. Daily Routine - Organise your time into blocks (REPORT).md>) Daily Routine - Organise your time into blocks · *data-caveat*

Method: n=38 so one review = 2.63% and 'high-priority' is 3 reviews — counts are the honest unit; but reviews are unusually substantial (median body 236 chars, ~4× other small corpora) so the corpus supports mechanism findings better than rates; no country reaches 50 (US 18), global only; 18 of 30 crawled storefronts (incl. GB, AU, FR, IT, JP, KR) returned zero reviews; selection bias runs to both poles — nostalgic returners and blocked non-buyers — the quiet paying middle is under-represented; 12 pure-praise (all 5★) vs 26 with criticism (mean 2.27), almost no middle; judgement calls: a 1★ containing its own pasted prior 5★ counted once; the sabotage allegation coded as grievance not defect; a 5★ reading 'support ipad icloud' coded as a request; store 3.4★ vs written 3.13 are close because written reviews are nearly the whole rating population

**Where:** How to read this; ⚠️ Three warnings; §1.1 Files used; §1.2 Schema; §1.3 Coverage and reconciliation; §1.4 Processing method; §1.5 Limitations and judgement calls; §9.1 counting rules · **App does:** n/a · **Reaction:** none · **Magnitude:** 38/38 read; 0 duplicates; 12 storefronts reconcile; 5★14 / 4★6 / 3★1 / 2★5 / 1★12; vote_count non-zero on 12; is_edited false on all (understated); 3 non-English (2 ES, 1 DE) · **Direction:** none · **Report confidence:** method · **Generalisable:** yes · **Review IDs:** `9244113250`, `9289248731`, `9957602682`, `13120304447`

#### `R31-002` · [31](<../App Store Reports/31. Do Habits - Get It Done - Daily Routine & Goal Planner (REPORT).md>) Do Habits - Get It Done - Daily Routine & Goal Planner · *data-caveat*

Method: 5,186/5,186 read in full in date order in 26 batches (~200 each), bodies over 1,500 chars wrapped not truncated; taxonomy built inductively from reading notes before any pattern; 82-theme multilingual regex classifier + 4 unions; precision validated by reading every match of high-impact themes, recall by reading broad-pattern untagged candidates for 8 themes; corrections before use — adhd 36→33 (verb 'add'), monthly_yearly_request replaced by a hand-read list of 58 (from 96), entitlement_failure −97 false positives +136 recall → 468, promo_charged_full −33 +16 → 69 (49 'actually charged'), launch_fail +151 wave phrasings −8 → 1,052, streak_removed +24 → 52, cancel_difficulty +22 → 66, support_unresponsive +13 → 460, support_positive hand-read 18, payer dropped conditional phrasings → 625; ambiguous surfaces split into mention/problem; aggregates with and without the 22 Dec 2021 – 15 Jan 2022 wave; one 25-day event dominates (1,135 reviews, 21.89%, mean 1.44, 35.0% of all 1★ — excluding it mean 2.61 and 1★ 41.2%); four products over ten years so eras compare different products; no version field (reviewers name 1.3.1 … 3.0.1); payer evidence self-selected (625, 12.05%, 304 with a delivery problem); short-review inflation is not a factor here (≤25-char never above 7.7% of any era, prompt complaints 20, median body 160); theme rates under-count outside English; price claims not reconcilable (60+ price points, 15 currencies, anchors to CA$499.99); 35 cap complaints are 5★ and 104 simplicity praises are 1★ so positive themes also reported as the 4–5★ subset; storefront ≠ language; unverifiable claims flagged (€1,600 bi-weekly charges; charges 'not through Apple'); no download/revenue data; no external source; 4,707 (90.8%) carry ≥1 theme, 479 short affective reviews (mean 3.1, median 75 chars)

**Where:** How to read this; Seven warnings; §1.1 Files used; §1.2 Schema; §1.3 Coverage and reconciliation; §1.4 Processing method; §1.5 Known limitations; §11.1 counting rules; §11.3 manual corrections; §11.4 validation · **App does:** n/a · **Reaction:** none · **Magnitude:** 5,186/5,186; 80 storefronts; 4 duplicate groups (11 records) kept; is_edited 20 (several dated update logs); 716 with votes (top 8202074659 at 120) · **Direction:** none · **Report confidence:** method · **Generalisable:** yes · **Review IDs:** `8202074659`, `2463611317`, `13602037395`, `12554960249`, `8756283245`, `11443832766`, `10323742685`

Method: all 1,743 reviews read individually in original language (English, Chinese Simplified and Traditional, Japanese, Korean, Russian, Ukrainian, Kazakh, Turkish, German, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Dutch, Swedish, Czech, Polish, Arabic) in chronological order, 14 chunks of 125; hand-assigned from an 85-code, 12-family inductive taxonomy (Temp/53-cls, Temp/53-review-classification.py), 3,074 assignments (1.76 per review, median 1); validated 0 unknown IDs, 0 unassigned, 0 duplicate keys, 0 intra-review duplicates, 0 undefined codes, 0 of 85 declared-but-unused; reconciliation exact against 76 by_country files, manifest (1,743; 5:762 · 4:306 · 3:219 · 2:115 · 1:341; mean 3.5927) and _state.json (144 storefronts polled, 76 with reviews, all complete); no deduplication — no title+body pair repeats; a near-identical kr pair (5580879385 1★ / 5580890253 5★, 26 Feb 2020, Family Sharing refund request) kept, the 5★ copy a contradiction; every global % divides by 1,743; signal bands <0.1% ignore · 0.1–0.5% weak · 0.5–1% emerging · 1–3% meaningful · 3–5% very strong · >5% high-priority; text sub-cuts only inside hand-coded themes ('8 am' within REM_CONTROL, dollar figures within PAY_*); every PAY_PROMO, PAY_REGRESS, PAY_CHARGE, STAT_CRASH, BUG_LAUNCH, SUP_BAD, META_CONTRA, HK_WRITE, OUT_MED, OUT_ADHD and PRIV review re-read; no automated classifier; 13 fields, author/app_id/app_name/country_name unused; is_edited 90 (5.16%), 17 say in text they were updated (META_EDIT); vote_count>0 on 360 (20.65%), max 274 (6487531368), never weights; body median 97 characters, mean 165.1

**Where:** §How to read this; §1.1–1.5 · **App does:** n/a · **Reaction:** n/a · **Magnitude:** 1,743 (100%) · **Direction:** none · **Report confidence:** method statement · **Generalisable:** app-specific · **Review IDs:** `5580879385`, `5580890253`, `6487531368`

The written corpus is far more negative than the public rating: written reviews are 6.64% of public ratings (1,743 of 26,245) and their mean (3.59) sits 1.01★ below the public average (4.6); in every eligible storefront the gap is 0.75–1.12★ — treat the corpus as the complaint and request channel of a well-rated app, not a satisfaction survey

Method: 43,469/43,469 read in full in 260 batches, country-then-date order, coverage verified programmatically (0 missing, 0 extra); 57-theme multilingual regex classifier with five disclosed corrections before use (religious objection 901→195 because 'cult' matched 'difficult'; ADHD 1,569→933 because 'add' matched the verb; coaching 6,433→6,095 because 'kind' matched 'kind of'; repetitive content 285→103 because 'repeat' matched 'charged repeatedly'; religion-censorship rebuilt 2→14); residual false-positive tail in scam language (10 of 3,468 about art plagiarism); 1,435 of 3,468 scam-language reviews carry no other billing theme but are one-line billing complaints (mean 1.107); two composites — bill_core (9 dispute themes) and bill_any (adds refund, support failure, price, bundle); corpus is bimodal (57.89% 5★, 23.96% 1★, 7.58% middle) and back-weighted (2024–26 = 24.47% at mean 2.662 vs 2020–21 = 40.16% at 4.244); theme rates under-count in zh/ja/ko/th/ru/he/ar — China mainland only 15.3% Latin-script so its billing rate 0.24% is an artefact (its rating 3.431, 28.6% 1★ is real); 'scam' is a word not a legal finding; no version field; review-selection bias runs both ways — in-app review prompt on day 1–3 inflates early praise, billing disputes arrive at renewal months later; not every reviewer is a payer (11,200, 25.77% discuss the transaction); storefront ≠ nationality ≠ language; prices are testimony in mixed currencies; no download/revenue/retention/refund-outcome data
